title: Bridging Loans for Uninhabitable Property: What Lenders Want to See
excerpt: Standard mortgages won't touch a property with no kitchen or working services, but bridging loans are built for exactly this. Here's how they work and what lenders actually want to see.
metaTitle: Bridging Loans for Uninhabitable Property: What Lenders Want to See
metaDescription: Struggling to mortgage an uninhabitable property? Bridging loans fund purchases and refurbishments where standard lenders won't. See rates, LTVs and how it works.
keywords: bridging loan for uninhabitable property, short-term property finance uk, bridging loans uk rates, developer finance refurbishment, auction property bridging loan, habitable vs uninhabitable mortgage, fast property finance uk
author: Mark Higgins
content:
A bridging loan for an uninhabitable property is short-term property finance secured against a house or flat that lacks a working kitchen, bathroom, heating or safe electrics, and which standard mortgage lenders will refuse to touch until it's brought up to a habitable standard. Bridging loan uninhabitable property uk solutions bridge that exact gap, funding the purchase and often the works, with the loan repaid once the property is mortgageable or sold on.

We see this situation more often than most people realise. A run-down terrace, a fire-damaged flat, a farmhouse with no functioning bathroom, an ex-council house stripped back by the previous owner. On paper these are ordinary residential properties. To a high street lender, they represent uninsurable risk until the work is done. Bridging loans exist to fill that gap. If you'd like an introduction first, our guide to what bridging finance actually is covers the basics.

Most first-time buyers of these properties find the situation far more common than expected. Estate agents up and down the country have properties sitting unsold for months simply because standard lenders won't mortgage them in their current state. The seller wants a quick sale, the buyer has spotted a genuine opportunity, but the deal stalls because a normal lender walks away at valuation stage. Short-term property finance offers the only realistic way to complete these transactions within a sensible timeframe. If you want to know what these deals cost, our breakdown of current bridging loan rates in the UK is worth reading before you apply.

Uninhabitable doesn't always mean derelict either. We've arranged bridging loans on properties that look perfectly liveable from the kerb but fail on a technicality. Missing a bathroom because the previous owner ripped it out, no working central heating system, or a kitchen removed entirely during a botched renovation. Valuers and mortgage underwriters work to strict definitions, and even one missing element can be enough to trigger a decline.

What this means in practice

In practice, you can buy or refinance a property that no bank will mortgage, using a lender who assesses the bricks, the location and your exit plan rather than whether the boiler currently works.

Most residential mortgage lenders require a property to be wind and watertight, with a working kitchen and bathroom, before they'll lend against it. Anything less falls outside their criteria automatically, regardless of how good the deal looks. This catches out many buyers, particularly at auction, where the property is often uninhabitable by design because that's why it's cheap.

Bridging lenders take a different view. They're used to lending against properties in poor condition, part-converted buildings, or properties with structural issues, because their underwriting centres on the value of the asset and the credibility of your exit, not the current state of the kitchen. Many of our clients are surprised how straightforward this is once they're talking to the right lender rather than a high street bank. Not sure where to start? You can get a bridging loan quote before you commit to an offer.

A broker earns their fee here. Not every bridging lender has the same appetite for uninhabitable stock. Some will quietly decline anything with a missing kitchen or roof damage while others actively specialise in exactly that type of asset. Knowing which lender to approach first, rather than working through a long list of rejections, saves weeks on a deal where the auction clock is ticking. Our roundup of the best bridging loan lenders in the UK is a useful starting point.

How it works

A bridging loan works by securing lending against the property's current value or sometimes its expected value once works are complete, releasing funds quickly, and being repaid in full through a clear exit such as sale or refinance onto a standard mortgage.

Lenders typically advance against the purchase price or open market value in its current state, usually up to 65-75% loan to value for uninhabitable stock, sometimes lower if the condition is severe. Some lenders also release a second tranche of funds to cover renovation costs, drawn down in stages as work progresses and is inspected.

Terms usually run from 3 to 18 months. Interest is normally retained or added to the loan rather than paid monthly, which matters if the property isn't generating income yet. Completion can be fast, often 10 to 21 working days from full application, though we've seen deals move quicker when the legal work is straightforward and the borrower has everything ready upfront.

Costs are worth understanding before you commit. Bridging rates for uninhabitable property typically sit between 0.65% and 1.1% per month, depending on the lender, the loan to value and the strength of the exit. On top of the rate, expect a lender arrangement fee of around 1.5% to 2%, a valuation fee that varies with property value, and legal costs for both your solicitor and the lender's solicitor. Some lenders also charge an exit fee, though many of the more competitive products in this space have moved away from that.

Budget for contingency as well. Uninhabitable properties frequently reveal more problems once work starts. Hidden damp, old wiring needing a full rewire rather than a patch, or roof timbers requiring replacement rather than repair. Sensible borrowers build in a 10% to 15% contingency on top of quoted renovation costs, and good brokers will push you to do the same before the loan is agreed rather than after the money has run out.

Typical scenarios

Two situations come up repeatedly in our work: residential buyers rescuing an unmortgageable property, and developers using bridging loans as the funding bridge into a full refurbishment or conversion project.

A residential example: a buyer looking at bridging loans in Norwich found a three-bed terrace at auction for £145,000, £60,000 below market value once refurbished, but with no kitchen, exposed wiring and a collapsed section of roof. A standard mortgage lender declined outright. We arranged a bridging loan of £101,500 (70% LTV against the purchase price) over a 9-month term, with funds released in 14 working days to meet the auction completion deadline. The buyer refurbished the property, remortgaged onto a standard buy-to-let product once habitable, and exited the bridge in month 7.

The Norwich case illustrates how the numbers work in practice. The buyer spent a further £38,000 on the refurbishment, funded partly from savings and partly through a staged drawdown built into the bridging facility. Once the works were signed off, an independent valuer confirmed a completed value of £215,000, comfortably supporting a standard buy-to-let remortgage at 75% LTV and repaying the bridge in full with room to spare.

A developer example: a small developer arranging bridging loans in Birmingham took on a semi-derelict pair of cottages needing full conversion into three flats. We secured £310,000 against a £480,000 gross development value (65% LTV), with staged drawdowns for the build costs, over a 12-month term. The exit was a sale of two units and a refinance of the third onto a rental mortgage, completing 11 months in. Developers commonly use this kind of finance structure where planning has already been granted and the numbers stack up on paper but no conventional lender will fund the works.

The staged drawdown structure mattered as much as the headline loan amount on the Birmingham deal. Rather than releasing the full £310,000 upfront, the lender advanced funds in four tranches, each triggered by a site inspection confirming work had reached an agreed stage. This protects the lender, but it also protects the developer, keeping interest costs down on money that hasn't actually been spent yet. Anyone new to bridging loans should expect this kind of structure on anything beyond a simple purchase and light refurbishment. We've also arranged similar deals for clients seeking bridging loans in London and bridging loans in Reading.

What lenders look for

Lenders want a clear valuation of the property as it stands, a realistic exit strategy, and evidence you can service or repay the loan without relying on hope. Everything else in the underwriting flows from those three elements.

Loan to value for uninhabitable property typically sits between 60% and 75% of current value, occasionally with an uplift if works funding is included and the GDV supports it. Lenders send a surveyor who specifically values the property in its current, uninhabitable condition, not what it might be worth done up, unless you're on a development-style facility with staged releases.

On the exit, lenders want to see either a credible sale strategy backed by comparable evidence, or a refinance exit supported by an Agreement in Principle from a mortgage lender confirming they'll lend once works are complete. Applications get declined most often, in our experience, because the exit is vague, the schedule of works lacks costed detail, or the borrower hasn't proven they can fund the project through to completion without relying entirely on the bridging facility itself.

Beyond the property itself, lenders look closely at your track record. First-time buyers of uninhabitable stock aren't automatically ruled out, but a lender will feel more comfortable if you can show some experience of project management, whether that's a previous renovation, a background in construction, or a well thought through schedule of works with realistic costings and named contractors. Where experience is limited, some lenders will ask for a project manager or experienced contractor to be named on the file as reassurance.

Getting your legal and financial position ready

Have your solicitor lined up early. Bridging lenders move quickly, and the biggest cause of delay on these deals is rarely the lender. Legal work that hasn't kept pace causes the problem. A solicitor used to bridging transactions, rather than standard residential conveyancing, can make the difference between hitting an auction completion date and losing your deposit.

If you're weighing up a bridging loan against an uninhabitable property, speak to a broker before you make an offer, not after. Getting an idea of likely loan to value, rate and timescale before you commit means you go into the purchase with realistic numbers, rather than discovering at survey stage that the lender's valuation doesn't match your expectations.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can you get a bridging loan on a property with no kitchen or bathroom?
Yes. Bridging lenders specialise in exactly this type of asset and will lend against the property's current condition, unlike standard mortgage lenders who require a working kitchen and bathroom before they'll consider an application.

What loan to value can I expect on an uninhabitable property?
Most lenders offer between 60% and 75% of current value, with the exact figure depending on the severity of the condition, the strength of your exit strategy and whether renovation funding is included.

How quickly can a bridging loan complete?
Completion typically takes 10 to 21 working days from a full application, though this can move faster where legal work is straightforward and all documentation is ready upfront, which matters for auction deadlines.

What does a bridging loan for an uninhabitable property cost?
Rates typically sit between 0.65% and 1.1% per month, plus a lender arrangement fee of around 1.5% to 2%, valuation fees and legal costs for both sides.

Do I need renovation experience to qualify?
No, but lenders feel more comfortable if you can show some project management experience or a well costed schedule of works with named contractors, especially for first-time renovators.

What counts as a valid exit strategy?
Lenders want either a credible sale backed by comparable evidence, or a refinance exit supported by an Agreement in Principle from a mortgage lender confirming they'll lend once the works are complete.

Can I fund the renovation as well as the purchase?
Many lenders release a second tranche of funds specifically for renovation costs, drawn down in stages as work progresses and is inspected, in addition to the initial purchase advance.

For a full breakdown of rates, criteria and lender options tailored to unmortgageable property, explore our funding solutions hub, or get a bridging loan quote to get things moving.

title: Bridging Loan Timeline: From Application to Completion
excerpt: The UK bridging loan process typically takes 2 to 4 weeks from application to funds, though experienced brokers can push this to under 10 days when a deal is genuinely urgent.
metaTitle: Bridging Loan Timeline: From Application to Completion
metaDescription: Bridging Loan Timeline: From Application to Completion. Expert advice from Boxx Finance, a whole-of-market UK bridging finance broker.
keywords: how long does a bridging loan take, bridging loan timeline, bridging loan application process, fast bridging loan completion, bridging loan solicitors process, short-term property finance timeline, developer finance timeline
author: Tara Jameson

mainEntity.name: How long does a bridging loan take to complete in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: A UK bridging loan typically takes 2 to 4 weeks to complete from initial application to funds being released, though well-prepared cases with a clean title and responsive solicitors can complete in 7 to 10 working days. Complex cases involving planning, unregistered land or multiple securities can take 4 to 6 weeks.

mainEntity.name: What causes delays in the bridging loan process?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most delays in the bridging loan process come from slow legal work rather than the lender, particularly title issues, missing planning documents, or solicitors who are slow to respond to standard enquiries. Valuation scheduling and a weak or unevidenced exit strategy are the other common causes.

mainEntity.name: Can you get a bridging loan in under two weeks?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, a bridging loan can complete in under two weeks when the borrower has documents ready on day one, the property has a clean title, and the lender can use a desktop valuation rather than a full physical inspection. Auction purchases with hard completion deadlines are often pushed through this fast.

mainEntity.name: Do you need a solicitor for a bridging loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, both the borrower and the lender instruct solicitors for a bridging loan, and this dual legal process is usually the longest single stage in the timeline. Using a solicitor experienced in bridging transactions, rather than general conveyancing, meaningfully speeds up completion.

mainEntity.name: What is the fastest way to speed up a bridging loan application?

acceptedAnswer.text: The fastest way to speed up a bridging loan application is to have ID, proof of income, the exit strategy evidence and property details ready before applying, and to instruct a solicitor experienced in bridging transactions on day one. Choosing a lender who accepts desktop valuations for lower LTV cases also helps.

mainEntity.name: Is a bridging loan more expensive if it completes faster?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, a faster completion does not usually cost more, because bridging loan pricing is driven by loan-to-value, security type and exit strength rather than speed of completion. Fees can rise if a lender has to expedite a valuation or use additional legal resource, but this is the exception rather than the rule.

content:
The bridging loan process timeline in the UK usually runs 2 to 4 weeks from application to completion, though a well-prepared case can complete in as little as 5 to 10 working days. Businesses and property buyers use bridging loans when speed matters more than the interest rate, such as auction purchases, chain breaks or funding a refurbishment before a mortgage lender will touch the property. Timing depends almost entirely on how quickly legal work and valuations move, not on the lender's appetite.

At Boxx Finance we arrange bridging loans every week. Preparation before the application goes in determines how fast a deal completes. Lenders themselves rarely cause delays. Solicitors, valuers and slow-moving clients do. If you want to talk through your own timeline, you can get a bridging loan quote before you commit to anything.

Short-term property finance is not one product with one fixed timeline. A regulated bridging loan on a main residence follows a different path to an unregulated commercial bridge on an investment property. The paperwork, the checks, and even the level of consumer protection involved vary between the two, and this affects how quickly a case can move. Our guide on what bridging finance actually covers explains these distinctions in more detail.

We've seen straightforward deals complete inside a week when everything lines up, and we've also seen simple-looking cases drag on for six weeks because a leasehold management pack took forever to arrive. Knowing where the risk points sit before you start makes a real difference to how the timeline actually plays out.

What this means in practice

In practice, the bridging loan timeline consists of three separate processes running in parallel: underwriting, valuation, and legal work. When these run smoothly together, a straightforward residential bridge can complete within two weeks. When any one of them stalls, the whole deal stalls with it.

For a homeowner breaking a chain, this might mean instructing a solicitor the same day they get a decision in principle, rather than waiting for full loan documents. For a developer exiting a refurbishment scheme, it means having the exit strategy, whether a sale or a remortgage, evidenced from day one rather than promised verbally.

Most delays we see are avoidable. A client who has their proof of income, property details, exit plan and ID ready on day one will almost always beat a client who is still gathering documents a week into the process, regardless of which lender is used.

We often tell clients to think of the process in terms of what they control and what they don't. You cannot force a valuer to attend a property sooner than their diary allows, and you cannot make a local authority return a search faster. But you can have your bank statements, three months of proof of income, ID documents and a clear one-page summary of your exit strategy ready before you even speak to a lender.

This preparation work typically takes a client half a day. It can save two weeks further down the line. Brokers who push clients to get this right early are usually the ones who deliver the fastest completions, simply because there is less back and forth once the case is with underwriting.

How it works

The bridging loan process moves through five broad stages: initial enquiry, decision in principle, valuation, legal work, and completion. Each stage has its own typical timescale, and understanding these helps set realistic expectations.

An initial enquiry with full financials can usually generate a decision in principle within 24 to 48 hours. From there, the lender instructs a valuation, which for a straightforward residential property in London or the South East typically takes 3 to 5 working days to book and complete. Rural or unusual properties, and anything needing a commercial valuer, can take longer. This applies equally to clients arranging bridging loans in London or further afield.

Legal work runs alongside this. The lender's solicitors and the borrower's solicitors exchange enquiries, and this is where most bridging loans genuinely lose time. Title issues, missing planning documents, or a slow response on standard enquiries can add a week or more. Once legals are cleared and the valuation is back, funds can typically be released within 24 to 48 hours.

Lenders offering specialist property finance increasingly use automated valuation models (AVMs) or desktop valuations for lower-risk, lower-LTV cases, which can shave several days off the process. This isn't universal, but it's becoming more common across the bridging market.

Breaking the timeline down into rough working days, most bridging cases follow this pattern. Day 1 to 2 covers the initial enquiry and decision in principle. Day 2 to 3 is when formal terms are issued and the client signs to proceed. Day 3 to 7 covers valuation instruction and completion, running alongside solicitors exchanging initial enquiries.

Day 7 to 12 is usually where legal enquiries are raised, answered and, where needed, chased. Day 12 to 14 covers final underwriting sign-off, satisfaction of any conditions, and release of funds. Complex cases with multiple securities, company structures, or unusual titles naturally push beyond this, sometimes into the 20 to 28 working day range.

Broker choice matters. Lenders who deal directly with experienced bridging brokers tend to move faster, simply because the broker has already checked the case fits the lender's criteria and pre-empted likely questions. Going direct to a lender without that filtering sometimes means more rounds of queries once underwriting gets involved, because nobody has stress-tested the application beforehand. If you'd rather compare options side by side, you can compare bridging loan rates with a broker who already knows the lenders' criteria.

Typical scenarios

Real deals show the timeline better than any general description. Here are two we've arranged recently, one residential and one for a developer.

A homeowner in Reading needed £220,000 to complete on a new purchase before their existing property sold, avoiding a broken chain. The loan was £220,000 against a £480,000 property (45.8% LTV) over a 6-month term, exiting on the sale of their current home which was already under offer. With ID, proof of the sale contract and a straightforward title, funds were released in 9 working days. This kind of case is common for anyone arranging bridging loans in Reading or elsewhere in the South East where property chains move quickly but not always in sync.

A developer in Birmingham needed £340,000 to complete a light refurbishment on a semi-derelict property before refinancing onto a term buy-to-let mortgage once works were finished. The loan was £340,000 against a £560,000 post-works valuation (60.7% LTV based on GDV), over a 9-month term. Because the exit relied on a refinance, the lender wanted a mortgage agreement in principle from the exit lender before releasing funds, which added roughly a week. Total time from enquiry to completion was 18 working days, well within what a bridging loan process timeline UK borrower should expect for a slightly more complex developer finance case, similar to other bridging loans in Birmingham we've arranged.

A third example worth mentioning is an auction purchase we handled for a client in Essex. Auction bridging is its own category, because completion is usually fixed at 28 days from the fall of the hammer, with no room for negotiation. The client needed £175,000 against a £310,000 property, a 56.4% LTV, with the exit being a straightforward sale to a buy-to-let landlord once light works were completed.

Because auction timelines are fixed, we had the valuation booked before the auction even took place, using the legal pack published in advance. This meant that once the client won the lot, the valuation was already scheduled and legal work could start immediately. Funds were released on day 21, giving a comfortable buffer before the 28-day deadline. This kind of pre-planning is standard practice for anyone using short-term property finance to buy at auction, and it's often the difference between hitting the deadline and losing the deposit. We've seen the same discipline pay off for clients arranging bridging loans in Norwich, where legal packs can vary widely in quality.

What lenders look for

Lenders assess three things above everything else: the security, the exit, and the speed at which the borrower can move. Loan-to-value typically ranges from 65% to 75% on residential property and 50% to 65% on commercial or semi-commercial assets, though some specialist lenders will stretch higher with additional security.

Timescales from enquiry to funds usually sit between 7 and 28 working days. Sub-10-day completions are achievable but require a clean title, a cooperative solicitor, and a valuer who can attend quickly. Acceptable security ranges from residential and commercial property to land with planning potential, though unregistered land or properties with unusual leasehold structures slow things down considerably.

On the exit, lenders want more than a stated intention to sell or remortgage. They want evidence: an estate agent's marketing appraisal, a mortgage agreement in principle, or a signed sale contract. In our experience, the most common reason applications get declined or delayed is a weak or unevidenced exit strategy, not affordability at all.

A borrower who says they plan to sell within six months but has no marketing appraisal, no agent instructed and no evidence of local demand will face far more scrutiny than one who can show a live listing and recent comparable sales. Lenders aren't trying to be difficult here. They simply need to know the loan will be repaid on time, because short-term property finance is designed to be short term by nature.

Costs and regulation

Interest rates on bridging loans typically range from around 0.55% to 1.25% per month depending on LTV, loan size and the strength of the exit. Arrangement fees usually sit between 1% and 2% of the loan amount, with valuation and legal fees payable separately. Most borrowers prioritise speed and certainty over costs, but they should still be factored into the exit calculation from day one. For a fuller breakdown of pricing, see our guide to current bridging loan rates.

Bridging loans are regulated differently depending on the security. Loans secured against a borrower's main residence fall under FCA regulation, which adds certain protections and, in some cases, slightly more paperwork. Loans secured against investment or commercial property are typically unregulated, which usually means a faster and more flexible process, though with fewer statutory protections attached. Knowing which category a deal falls into from the outset helps everyone plan the timeline more realistically, and it's exactly the kind of detail a good broker will flag before an application ever goes in. It's also worth comparing lenders directly, and our roundup of the best bridging loan lenders in the UK is a good starting point.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does a bridging loan take to complete?
Most bridging loans complete within 2 to 4 weeks, though well-prepared cases with a cooperative solicitor and a quick valuation can complete in 5 to 10 working days.

What causes the biggest delays in the bridging loan process?
Legal work is the most common source of delay. Title issues, missing planning documents, and slow responses to solicitor enquiries can add a week or more to the timeline.

Can a bridging loan complete in under 10 days?
Yes, but only with a clean title, a cooperative solicitor, and a valuer able to attend quickly. Full documentation ready on day one also makes a significant difference.

Do lenders use automated valuations to speed things up?
Increasingly, yes. Automated valuation models (AVMs) and desktop valuations are used for lower-risk, lower-LTV cases and can shave several days off the process.

What documents should I prepare before applying for a bridging loan?
Have your bank statements, three months of proof of income, ID documents, property details, and a clear one-page summary of your exit strategy ready before speaking to a lender.

Are bridging loans regulated?
Loans secured against a main residence fall under FCA regulation, offering additional protections. Loans secured against investment or commercial property are typically unregulated, allowing a faster process.

How quickly can I get an auction bridging loan?
Auction purchases usually require completion within 28 days of the hammer falling. With the valuation and legal pack prepared in advance, funds can often be released within 21 days.

If you're weighing up your options, you can arrange bridging loan process timeline uk today with one of our brokers, or explore our full range of funding solutions to see which route suits your situation best.

title: No Kitchen, No Mortgage? How to Finance a Property Anyway
excerpt: No kitchen doesn't mean no mortgage, but it usually means no mortgage. Bridging loans fund unmortgageable properties fast, letting you buy, refurbish, then refinance or sell.
metaTitle: No Kitchen, No Mortgage? How to Finance a Property Anyway
metaDescription: Struggling to mortgage a property with no kitchen? Bridging loans fund unmortgageable UK property fast. See rates, eligibility and how the deal actually works.
keywords: bridging loans for unmortgageable property, property without a kitchen finance, bridging loan no kitchen bathroom, short-term property finance UK, developer finance refurbishment, auction property finance no kitchen, habitable condition mortgage requirements
author: Mark Higgins
content:
Finance for a property without a kitchen in the UK usually means a bridging loan for unmortgageable property, because high street mortgage lenders require a home to be habitable before they'll touch it, and no kitchen almost always fails that test. Bridging lenders don't care about habitability in the same way. They lend against the property's value and your exit plan, releasing funds in days rather than the weeks a standard mortgage application would take. If you'd like to talk through your situation, you can get a bridging loan quote before you go any further.

This situation comes up more often than people expect. Probate properties, ex-rental stock stripped by a departing tenant, part-way-through refurbishments where the seller ran out of money, even new-build flats missing final fit-out. In every one of these cases the property is perfectly sound structurally, but a mortgage underwriter will decline it on paper the moment they see the words no kitchen or no bathroom in the valuation report. Our guide to how short-term property finance works covers the basics if you're new to this type of lending.

We deal with this at Boxx far more regularly than outsiders realise. A typical week might bring in an auction buyer who's just discovered the vendor ripped out the kitchen units before completion, a landlord whose tenant trashed the property on the way out, or someone who's inherited a house that's been sitting half-renovated since a relative went into care. The story changes, but the funding problem is always the same. We see this pattern with clients arranging bridging loans in London and with landlords sourcing bridging loans in Birmingham alike.

Standard mortgage lenders work from a valuation report, and that valuer has a checklist. A working kitchen and bathroom are almost always on it, along with things like a functioning heating system and no visible damp or structural movement. Miss one of those boxes and the case gets referred, downvalued, or declined outright, regardless of how good the location is or how much equity sits in the deal.

Short-term property finance sidesteps that entirely because the lending decision is based on the property's current value, the loan to value ratio, and how you intend to repay the loan at the end of the term. Most bridging lenders will happily lend on a property in any state of repair, including one that's been stripped back to bare walls, provided the numbers stack up and there's a credible exit.

High street lenders answer to regulators and their own risk committees, and they treat a property without basic facilities as a red flag regardless of context. Bridging lenders operate under a different model entirely, often funded by private capital or specialist funding lines, which gives them far more flexibility to make a commercial judgement call on a property by property basis.

How Bridging Lenders View a Kitchen-Less Property

A bridging lender's surveyor will still visit the property, but they're valuing it in its current condition rather than marking it against a habitability checklist. They'll usually give you two figures, the value as it stands today and the estimated value once works are completed. That gap between the two numbers often matters more to the lender than the missing kitchen itself.

Loan to value on these deals typically sits between 65% and 75% of the current, as-is value, though some lenders will stretch further if the end value and exit are particularly strong. On a property valued at £180,000 in its current state, that might mean a bridging loan of somewhere between £117,000 and £135,000, released within two to four weeks depending on how quickly legal work moves.

Rates on this type of bridging loan generally run from around 0.55% to 0.95% per month at the time of writing, though pricing depends heavily on the loan to value, the strength of your exit, and your own credit and experience. Our breakdown of current bridging loan pricing goes into more detail on how these rates are set. Arrangement fees typically sit around 1.5% to 2% of the loan, and most lenders also charge exit fees, valuation fees, and legal costs, so it's worth getting a full breakdown before you commit.

Lenders want to see a sensible plan for finishing the kitchen and any other outstanding works, along with a clear route to repaying the loan. That might mean refinancing onto a standard mortgage once the kitchen is fitted and the property becomes habitable, or it might mean selling the property on once the works are done.

Regional Considerations for Bridging Finance

Local market conditions can affect both valuations and exit strategy, so it's worth thinking about where the property sits. Landlords arranging bridging loans in Norwich often see different demand patterns to those looking at bridging loans in Reading, and a good broker will factor local comparables into the exit plan from the outset.

A lender reads a case file by looking at the purchase price or current value, the cost of works still needed, the projected end value once the kitchen and any other snags are sorted, and your track record if you've done similar projects before. A first-time buyer taking on a stripped-back probate property will usually face more scrutiny than an experienced landlord doing the same thing, simply because the lender has less to go on.

Deposit or equity requirements also tend to surprise people. Even at 70% loan to value, you'll need to fund the remaining 30% yourself, plus the cost of the kitchen fit-out and any other works, plus fees. On that £180,000 example, a £126,000 loan at 70% still leaves you finding around £54,000 in cash or existing equity, before you've spent a penny on the kitchen itself.

Getting the Property Mortgage-Ready

Once the bridging loan completes, the priority becomes finishing the works fast enough to refinance before the bridge term runs out. Most bridging loans run for six to twelve months, and lenders expect you to have a realistic timeline for getting the kitchen fitted, the bathroom sorted if needed, and the property back to a standard a mortgage valuer will accept.

A basic kitchen fit-out in the UK typically costs anywhere from £3,000 for a straightforward budget job to £15,000 or more for something higher spec, depending on the size of the room and whether you're moving plumbing or electrics around. Builders and kitchen fitters can usually turn a standard installation around in one to two weeks once units are ordered, though lead times on cabinetry can add a few weeks to the overall project.

Get quotes lined up before you draw down the bridging loan, because lenders like to see that you've thought this through rather than working it out as you go. Some bridging lenders will even release funds in stages, holding back a portion for the works and releasing it once an inspection confirms progress, which can help keep costs under control.

Staging the Works and Managing the Timeline

A sensible order of operations looks something like this. Get two or three kitchen fitter quotes before applying for the bridge, agree a realistic works timeline with a bit of contingency built in, draw down the loan, get the kitchen fitted alongside any other snagging the valuer flagged, then instruct a mortgage broker to start the refinance application the moment the property is genuinely liveable.

Don't overlook the smaller items that can trip up a revaluation even after the kitchen goes in. Missing extractor fans, incomplete tiling, no flooring in the kitchen area, or a boiler that hasn't been serviced can all cause a valuer to flag the property again. Walk the property with a checklist before the second valuation, ideally the same checklist a standard mortgage valuer would use.

Once the kitchen is in and the property is genuinely habitable, a fresh mortgage valuation should come back clean, assuming everything else about the property checks out. This is the point where you'd normally look to refinance onto a standard residential or buy to let mortgage, using the new mortgage to repay the bridging loan in full.

Timing this well matters because people often start refinance conversations too late. Talk to a broker two or three months before your bridging term ends, not two or three weeks, since mortgage applications still take time even when the property is in good order. Leaving it too late is one of the most common reasons bridging exits go wrong.

Build in a buffer for delays that have nothing to do with the kitchen itself. Tradesmen fall behind schedule, materials get held up, and mortgage valuers get booked out weeks in advance in busy periods. A three month cushion at the end of the bridge term gives you room to absorb these hiccups without the whole plan unravelling.

Why Broker Support Makes a Real Difference

Not every bridging lender takes the same view on unfinished or stripped-back properties, and pricing can vary considerably between lenders who all technically say yes to the deal. Some lenders are genuinely comfortable with a bare-bones property and price accordingly, while others will quote a rate that reflects nervousness rather than genuine risk. Knowing which lenders actually enjoy this type of deal saves both time and money, and our review of the best bridging loan lenders in the UK is a useful starting point.

At Boxx Finance we spend a lot of time matching the specifics of a case to the right lender rather than sending every enquiry to the same handful of names. A probate property with no kitchen and a strong exit through sale is a very different proposition to a landlord refurbishment with a refinance exit, even though both look similar on paper. The lender who's right for one often isn't right for the other.

We also help clients think through the exit properly before the loan even completes, because a bridging loan without a solid exit plan is where problems start. That might mean speaking to a mortgage broker colleague about likely refinance terms once works are done, or stress-testing a sale price against recent local comparables so there's no nasty surprise later.

We also manage the paperwork side, which tends to move faster when a broker is pushing it along. Solicitors, valuers, and lenders all have their own timescales, and a case can drift if nobody is chasing it. Having someone keep the process moving often shaves days or weeks off completion, which matters when you're working against a fixed bridge term.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can you get a mortgage on a property with no kitchen?
Standard high street mortgages are very difficult to secure on a property without a kitchen, because valuers mark it as uninhabitable. A bridging loan is the usual route, allowing you to buy or refinance the property now and switch to a standard mortgage once the kitchen is fitted.

How much deposit do I need for a bridging loan on an unmortgageable property?
Most bridging lenders offer between 65% and 75% loan to value on the current, as-is value of the property, so you'll typically need to fund the remaining 25% to 35% yourself, plus the cost of any works and fees.

How quickly can a bridging loan complete on a property without a kitchen?
Bridging loans can often complete within two to four weeks, depending on how quickly legal work and valuations move, which is considerably faster than a standard mortgage application would allow.

What does it cost to fit a basic kitchen before refinancing?
A straightforward budget kitchen fit-out typically costs from around £3,000, while a higher spec installation can run to £15,000 or more, depending on size and whether plumbing or electrics need moving.

How long do I have to repay a bridging loan?
Most bridging loans run for six to twelve months, giving you time to complete the kitchen fit-out and any other works before refinancing onto a standard mortgage or selling the property.

What happens if the bridging loan term ends before I've refinanced?
This is why it's important to start the refinance conversation two or three months before the term ends. Leaving it too late, with no buffer for delays, is one of the most common reasons bridging exits run into trouble.

Will every bridging lender accept a property with no kitchen?
No, lenders vary considerably in their appetite for stripped-back or unfinished properties, and pricing can differ significantly between them. A broker who knows which lenders genuinely favour this type of deal can save you time and money.

If you're dealing with a property that's missing a kitchen, stripped back mid-renovation, or otherwise sitting outside what a standard mortgage lender will touch, it's worth having a conversation before you assume the deal can't be funded. These cases come up regularly, and we've found there's almost always a workable route through, provided the numbers make sense and the exit is realistic. Explore our funding solutions hub to see the full range of options, or get a bridging loan quote to get started.

title: Bridging Finance vs Remortgage: Which Is Right for You?
excerpt: Deciding between a bridging loan and a remortgage comes down to speed, purpose and exit strategy. This guide breaks down when each option makes sense for UK property buyers and developers.
metaTitle: Bridging Finance vs Remortgage: Which Is Right for You?
metaDescription: Bridging Finance vs Remortgage: Which Is Right for You?. Expert advice from Boxx Finance, a whole-of-market UK bridging finance broker.
keywords: bridging loan vs remortgage, short-term property finance, remortgage vs bridging loan, developer finance UK, fast property finance, bridging loan rates UK, specialist property finance
author: Tara Jameson
content:
A bridging loan is short-term property finance used when speed matters more than rate, typically arranged in 7 to 21 days to fund a purchase, chain break or refurbishment before a longer-term exit is in place. A remortgage replaces an existing mortgage with a new one, usually taking 4 to 8 weeks, and suits borrowers who want a cheaper long-term rate on a property they intend to keep. Choosing between a bridging loan vs remortgage uk decision depends almost entirely on your timescale and what happens after completion.

We get asked this question most weeks, usually by someone who has found a property they need to move on quickly, or a landlord who wants to release equity without waiting two months for a standard remortgage to complete. The straightforward answer is that these two products rarely compete for the same job. Once you understand what each one is actually built for, the choice tends to make itself. For a broader introduction to how this type of lending works, our guide on understanding how bridging loans work is a useful starting point.

These products sit at different points in a property journey. A remortgage is usually the destination, the product you settle into once everything else is sorted. A bridging loan is usually the vehicle that gets you there when the normal route is too slow or the property does not yet qualify for standard lending. Confusing the two, or trying to force one to do the other's job, is where most delays and unnecessary costs come from.

What this means in practice

In practice, the decision usually hinges on one question: do you need the money before your current lender or process can deliver it? If yes, a bridging loan fills that gap. If you have weeks to spare and simply want a better rate or to release equity for the long term, a remortgage is almost always cheaper.

Bridging loans are priced for speed and flexibility, not for holding long term. Monthly rates typically sit between 0.55% and 1.25%, which annualises to a cost most homeowners would find uncomfortable over several years. Remortgage rates, by contrast, are priced for the long haul, sitting far closer to standard mortgage rates because the lender expects to hold the debt for years, not months. If you want a closer look at how pricing varies across the market, our breakdown of current bridging loan rates in the UK covers this in more detail.

To put that in real terms, a £250,000 bridging loan at 0.75% a month costs roughly £1,875 in interest per month, or around £22,500 a year if left running. A remortgage on the same balance at a typical five-year fixed rate might cost £900 to £1,100 a month depending on the product and term. Run side by side over a full year, the gap is stark, which is exactly why nobody should be using short-term property finance as a substitute for a mortgage they could otherwise get.

The other practical difference is underwriting depth. A remortgage goes through full affordability checks, income verification and often a fresh valuation, all of which take time. A bridging loan is secured primarily against the property and the exit route, which is exactly why it can complete so much faster. Boxx Finance arranges both regularly, and the starting point with every enquiry is always the deadline, not the rate. If your situation is time-sensitive, you can get a bridging loan quote with our team before deciding which route fits.

You should also weigh the cost of delay. If a remortgage would take eight weeks but the purchase needs to complete in three, the bridging loan is not really competing with the remortgage on price at all. It is competing with the cost of losing the property, the deposit, or the chain entirely. Framed that way, a bridging loan often looks like the cheaper option even at a higher headline rate.

How it works

A bridging loan works by lending against the value of a property, usually up to 75% loan-to-value on a straightforward residential security, with interest either rolled up, retained or serviced monthly, and the full balance repaid at the end of the term through a defined exit.

The exit is the single most important part of the structure. Lenders want to see exactly how the loan will be repaid, whether that is a sale, a remortgage onto a standard product, or funds from another source such as inheritance or a business transaction. Without a credible exit, most bridging lenders will not proceed, regardless of how strong the security looks.

Rolled up interest means the monthly cost is added to the loan balance and paid in one lump sum at the end, which suits borrowers with no spare income during the term, such as someone mid-refurbishment. Serviced interest means paying the monthly cost as you go, which keeps the final redemption figure lower but requires proof you can afford the payments alongside any other commitments. Retained interest sits in between, with the lender deducting an agreed number of months' interest from the loan advance upfront.

A remortgage works differently. The new lender assesses your income, credit history and the property value, then replaces your existing mortgage balance with a new facility, sometimes releasing additional equity on top. There is no separate exit to plan because the remortgage is the end point itself, not a stepping stone to something else.

A typical remortgage timeline runs something like this: application and initial checks in week one, valuation instructed in week two, offer issued around week four to five, and legal completion by week six to eight. Solicitors, conveyancers and the Land Registry all add their own time into that process, which is why even a straightforward remortgage rarely completes inside a month.

Where the two genuinely overlap is when a remortgage becomes the exit strategy for a bridging loan. This is one of the most common structures we arrange: bridge now to secure the property or complete the refurbishment, remortgage later once the property qualifies for standard lending.

This combined approach is particularly common with unmortgageable properties, those without a working kitchen or bathroom, missing a certificate, or affected by short lease issues. A mainstream mortgage lender will simply decline these outright. A bridging loan gets the purchase and works funded, and once the property is habitable and compliant, the remortgage clears the bridge and moves the borrower onto a normal long-term rate.

Typical scenarios

Real numbers make this clearer than theory ever does. Here are two scenarios we see regularly, one residential and one developer-led.

A homeowner in Reading found a property at auction but her existing house sale had fallen through the week before completion. She needed £310,000 against a purchase valued at £420,000 (74% LTV) over a 6-month term, exiting via the eventual sale of her current home. Funds were released in 9 working days, well within the 28-day auction deadline. A standard remortgage or mortgage application simply could not have moved fast enough, and this is a pattern we see constantly with bridging loans in Reading and other fast-moving property markets.

In that case, the monthly cost sat around 0.85%, meaning roughly £2,635 a month in rolled up interest. Over the six month term that added up to just under £15,800, a cost she accepted without hesitation given the alternative was losing a £15,000 deposit on the auction property and starting her search again from scratch. We see similar patterns with bridging loans in London and bridging loans in Norwich, where auction purchases and chain breaks are common triggers for short-term property finance.

A developer in Birmingham bought a semi-derelict terrace requiring full refurbishment before it would meet mortgage lending criteria. He borrowed £145,000 against a purchase price of £190,000 plus works (58% LTV against the projected end value), over a 9-month term, exiting by refinancing onto a buy-to-let mortgage once the property was let. Completion took 14 working days from initial enquiry. This kind of developer finance case is exactly where bridging loans and remortgages work in sequence rather than in competition, and it is a structure Boxx Finance sees regularly among clients pursuing bridging loans in Birmingham for refurbishment projects.

By month seven the works were finished and the property was let to a tenant on an assured shorthold tenancy. The buy-to-let remortgage completed in month eight at 74% LTV against the new, higher valuation, clearing the bridge in full and releasing a small amount of surplus equity back to the developer. Without the bridging stage, none of this would have been possible, since no mainstream lender would touch the property in its original condition.

What lenders look for

Bridging lenders look primarily at the security value, the credibility of the exit, and the speed at which legal work can complete, rather than focusing heavily on income or credit score in the way a mortgage lender would.

Typical LTV ranges sit between 65% and 75% on residential property, dropping to 50-65% on unmortgageable or heavily unmodernised stock, and lower again for land or commercial security. Timescales from enquiry to funds released usually run 7 to 21 working days where the legal title is clean and the solicitor is responsive, though we have completed cases in under a week when everyone moves promptly. Acceptable security includes residential and commercial property, land with or without planning, and in some cases multiple properties cross-charged together. If you want to understand how different lenders approach these criteria, our comparison of leading bridging loan lenders in the UK is worth reading alongside this article.

Evidence of exit is scrutinised closely. For a sale exit, lenders want to see the property on the market or a credible marketing plan agreed with an estate agent. For a refinance exit, they want an agreement in principle from the onward lender or at minimum a clear statement of how the property will meet lending criteria by the end of the term.

Beyond the exit, most bridging lenders will also want a recent valuation from a surveyor on their panel, proof of ownership or a memorandum of sale for the purchase, and a solicitor instructed and ready to move. Having these in place before you approach a lender can shave several days off the whole process. A broker adds significant value by chasing these documents in parallel rather than one after another.

For remortgages, lenders focus more heavily on the standard package: three to six months of bank statements, proof of income through payslips or accounts, a credit check, and an updated valuation of the property. Landlords remortgaging a buy-to-let will also be asked for the tenancy agreement and, increasingly, evidence that the rental income comfortably covers the mortgage payment at a stressed interest rate, usually somewhere between 125% and 145% of the monthly payment depending on the lender and tax status of the borrower.

In our experience, the most common reason bridging applications are declined is the exit, not the property. Applicants often assume that having enough equity or a saleable asset is sufficient, but lenders want a specific, provable route to repayment, not just confidence that one will appear. Getting this right from the outset, with a proper exit strategy mapped out before the application goes in, is usually the difference between a smooth completion and weeks of back and forth. This is where speaking to a broker who arranges both bridging loans and remortgage finance regularly makes the biggest practical difference, since the right structure often uses both products at different stages rather than picking one over the other.

Key takeaways

Speed and exit strategy are the deciding factors: a bridging loan makes sense when the deadline is tight and the exit is clear, while a remortgage suits borrowers who have time on their side and want the lowest long-term rate. Many of the strongest outcomes come from combining both, using a bridge to secure or improve a property and a remortgage to settle onto a permanent rate once it qualifies. Whatever your timescale, getting the structure right from the outset saves money and stress later.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a bridging loan more expensive than a remortgage?
Yes, on a like-for-like monthly basis a bridging loan carries a higher rate than a remortgage, because it is priced for speed and short-term use rather than long-term borrowing. However, when a remortgage cannot complete in time to secure a purchase, the effective cost of not using a bridging loan can be far higher.

Can I remortgage straight after taking out a bridging loan?
Yes, this is one of the most common structures we arrange. The bridging loan covers the immediate purchase or works, and the remortgage repays the bridge once the property meets standard mortgage lending criteria, often once refurbishment is complete or a tenancy is in place.

How quickly can a bridging loan complete compared to a remortgage?
A bridging loan typically completes in 7 to 21 working days, whereas a remortgage usually takes 4 to 8 weeks from application to legal completion, depending on the lender, valuation and conveyancing process.

What happens if my exit strategy falls through on a bridging loan?
Lenders will usually want to discuss alternative exit routes, such as extending the term, switching to a different remortgage product, or in some cases selling the property. This is why a credible, well-evidenced exit is scrutinised so closely before the loan is even approved.

Do I need a deposit for a bridging loan in the same way as a remortgage?
Not in the traditional sense. Bridging loans are assessed primarily on loan-to-value against the security property, typically up to 75%, rather than a separate deposit requirement, though the remaining equity functions in a similar way.

Can landlords use a bridging loan before remortgaging a buy-to-let property?
Yes, this is common where a property needs refurbishment before it qualifies for a standard buy-to-let mortgage. The bridging loan funds the purchase and works, and the buy-to-let remortgage then repays the bridge once the property is let and meets lending criteria.

Which option is cheaper if I only need funds for a few months?
For a genuinely short-term need, a bridging loan is usually more practical despite the higher headline rate, since a remortgage involves setup costs, valuation fees and a longer timeline that may not suit a short holding period. Speak to a broker to get a bridging loan quote tailored to your timescale.

Whichever route suits your circumstances, exploring the full range of funding solutions available alongside bridging loans and remortgages can help ensure the structure fits both your timescale and your long-term plans.
