title: Bridging Loans for Derelict Property: A Buyer's Guide
excerpt: Bridging loans for derelict property let buyers and developers purchase uninhabitable buildings that mortgage lenders reject, funding the purchase and often the works before refinancing or selling on.
metaTitle: Bridging Loans for Derelict Property: A Buyer's Guide
metaDescription: Bridging loans for derelict property in the UK explained: how they work, typical rates and LTVs, lender criteria, and how Boxx Finance can help you buy fast.
keywords: derelict property finance UK, bridging loan for uninhabitable property, developer finance for derelict buildings, auction finance derelict property, refurbishment bridging loan, short-term property finance UK, bridging loan rates UK
author: Mark Higgins
content:
A bridging loan for derelict property in the UK is a short-term loan secured against a building that is uninhabitable or structurally unsound, used to fund the purchase and sometimes the works before a mortgage lender will consider it. Standard mortgage lenders almost always decline properties without a working kitchen, bathroom, or roof, which is exactly where a bridging loan derelict property uk solution steps in. These loans are assessed on the property and the exit, not on the state of the building today. If you would like to talk through your own situation, you can get a bridging loan quote from our team.

We arrange these deals regularly at Boxx Finance, and derelict property cases are one of the most common reasons clients come to us rather than their high street bank. Banks simply will not lend against a property with no kitchen, missing floors, or fire damage. Short-term property finance lenders will, provided the numbers and the exit stack up.

Derelict property finance is a specialist corner of an already specialist market. Not every bridging lender wants this type of security, and many will say no once they see the survey. Working with a broker who knows which lenders actively want this business rather than tolerate it saves weeks and considerable frustration. For a broader introduction to how these products work, our guide to what bridging finance covers is a useful starting point.

What this means in practice

In practice this means you can buy a run-down house, barn conversion, or commercial-to-residential opportunity using debt rather than tying up all your own cash, even though no mainstream mortgage lender will go near it in its current state.

The loan is secured against the property itself, usually on a first charge basis, and sometimes against additional security if the loan-to-value on the derelict asset alone is too thin. Interest is typically rolled up or retained rather than paid monthly, which matters greatly if the property has no rental income while it sits empty during works.

This is where the product genuinely earns its keep. A landlord who spots a repossessed cottage at auction with a collapsed roof cannot get a residential mortgage on completion day, which in England and Wales is usually 28 days after the auction fall of the hammer. A short-term property finance loan can complete in that window; a mortgage almost never can.

It also opens up property that would otherwise sit on the market for months. Estate agents and auctioneers know that derelict lots frighten off the ordinary buyer relying on a mortgage in principle, which is why these properties often go for well below the value of comparable habitable stock nearby. Buyers who can move fast with bridging loans are often the only realistic bidders in the room, and that scarcity of competition is part of why the numbers can work so well.

There is also a practical insurance point worth flagging early. Standard buildings insurance is hard to get on a genuinely derelict property, and lenders will insist on suitable cover being in place from day one of the loan. Specialist unoccupied property insurance is usually needed, and this should be arranged before you commit to a completion date, not after.

How it works

The mechanics are straightforward once you have done one. You apply with details of the property, your purchase price, your plans for the works, and your exit strategy, and the lender values the property both as it stands and, often, on a projected post-works basis.

Lending is usually based on the current, as-is value rather than the hoped-for end value, though some specialist lenders will release works funding in stages against a schedule of costs from a builder or quantity surveyor. Drawdowns for refurbishment costs typically happen in tranches, with a surveyor signing off each stage before the next tranche releases.

Terms usually run from 3 to 18 months. Rates for derelict or heavily distressed property sit a little above standard bridging rates because the security is weaker until works begin, reflecting the extra risk the lender is taking on. You can compare current pricing in our guide to current UK bridging loan rates before you approach a lender, so you know what a fair offer looks like. If you are ready to move, you can get a bridging loan quote with a broker directly.

Expect the lender to instruct their own valuer, at your cost, who will produce both a red book valuation of the property in its current state and, where relevant, a projected gross development value once works are complete. This valuation drives everything that follows, so it pays to brief the valuer properly with your schedule of works and any comparable evidence you have already gathered yourself.

Legal work on these deals also tends to move faster than a standard purchase because bridging solicitors are used to tight auction timescales and dual representation is common, where the same firm acts for both borrower and lender to speed things along. Ask your broker to introduce you to a solicitor who has completed derelict property bridging deals before, since general conveyancers can slow the process down considerably if they are unfamiliar with the paperwork lenders expect.

Typical scenarios

Two scenarios come up regularly in our pipeline, one residential and one developer-led, and the figures below are typical of what we see completing each month.

A first-time landlord in Norwich bought a derelict two-bed terrace at auction for £95,000 against a post-works value of £175,000. She needed £66,500 (70% LTV against purchase price) over a 9-month term, exiting via a buy-to-let remortgage once the property was habitable and let. Funds released in 14 working days to meet the auction completion deadline, arranged through our bridging loans in Norwich network of local valuers.

Her total cost of borrowing over the 9 months, including arrangement fee, rolled up interest and exit fee, came to a little under £6,800. She budgeted £45,000 for the refurbishment, added a 20% contingency, and in the end spent just over £48,000 once an unexpected damp problem in the party wall came to light during the strip-out. Having that contingency built into the loan from the outset meant she did not need to go back to the lender for a further advance.

A developer client in Birmingham took on a derelict former pub earmarked for a three-unit residential conversion. The loan was £310,000 against a purchase price of £420,000 and a GDV of £780,000 (roughly 74% LTV against purchase), over a 12-month term, with £90,000 of that released in stages for structural works. The exit was a sale of two units and a refinance on the third. That deal took 19 working days from full application to first drawdown, arranged with the help of our bridging loans in Birmingham team who know the local planning department's turnaround times.

In that Birmingham case the staged drawdowns were released in four tranches, each triggered by a surveyor's inspection confirming works completed to date matched the schedule of costs. This added roughly a week to each drawdown compared with receiving the full sum upfront, but it kept the client's interest bill down since he only paid on funds actually drawn, not on the full facility from day one. Clients in and around London and Reading follow a similar process, and our bridging loans in London and bridging loans in Reading teams handle a steady stream of derelict property cases in those areas.

What lenders look for

Lenders assessing derelict property want clear evidence of the exit and a realistic view of costs, and they will decline applications where either is vague. Loan-to-value on the as-is value of a genuinely derelict property typically sits between 50% and 70%, sometimes lower if there is no roof, no services connected, or significant subsidence.

Timescales from enquiry to funds usually run 10 to 21 working days for a straightforward purchase, and can extend to 4 to 6 weeks where staged works funding and a schedule of costs need underwriting. Security is normally a first legal charge over the property, though some lenders will accept additional property as second charge security to strengthen a thin deal.

Evidence of exit is scrutinised hard. For a sale exit, lenders want comparable evidence of similar finished properties selling locally. For a refinance exit, they want an agreement in principle from the intended mortgage lender confirming the property will meet lending criteria once works complete. The most common reason we see applications declined is a client assuming a mortgage lender will simply accept the finished property without checking first, only to find that lender has a policy against ex-derelict stock or a minimum time-owned requirement.

Lenders will also want to see the applicant's track record where the works are substantial. A first-time buyer taking on a light cosmetic refurbishment is a very different proposition to someone attempting a full structural rebuild with no prior experience, and the latter may be asked to bring in a project manager or experienced contractor named on the application before the lender will commit funds. It is also worth reviewing our roundup of the best bridging loan lenders in the UK to see which lenders are most active in this space.

Credit history and background checks are still part of the process, though bridging lenders generally weigh the strength of the asset and exit more heavily than a client's credit score. That said, undischarged bankruptcy, unspent CCJs of significant value, or an inconsistent story about the exit will all cause delays or declines regardless of how good the property looks on paper.

Property conditionTypical LTV rangeTypical term
Habitable but dated75-80%3-12 months
Partially derelict, roof intact60-70%6-12 months
Fully derelict, no roof/services50-60%9-18 months

Common mistakes

The single biggest mistake we see is underestimating the works budget and having no contingency, which then causes the interest to roll up for longer than planned and eats into the profit on exit. Add at least 15-20% contingency to any builder's quote on a derelict property, because unknowns like asbestos, drainage, or hidden structural damage are common.

Another frequent error is not lining up the exit before completion. Buyers assume they will simply remortgage once the work is done, without checking that a mainstream lender will actually accept the finished property or that comparable sales evidence exists to support the numbers used at application stage.

Underestimating how long planning permission or building control sign-off will take is another regular trap, particularly on conversion projects. A bridging loan term that looked comfortable at 12 months can suddenly feel very tight if planning takes four months longer than expected, so speak to the local planning department informally before you commit to a purchase, and build some slack into the loan term from the outset.

Finally, some buyers focus so heavily on the headline interest rate that they overlook the total cost of the deal, including arrangement fees, valuation fees, exit fees, and any broker fee. A slightly higher rate from a lender who understands derelict property and can move quickly is often far better value than the cheapest rate from a lender who takes six weeks to say no. Speaking to a broker early, ideally before you have made an offer on the property, gives the best chance of matching the right lender to the right deal the first time.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can you get a bridging loan on a derelict property with no roof?
Yes, though the loan-to-value will typically sit at the lower end of the range, often 50-60%, and the lender will want a clear schedule of works and a realistic exit before agreeing terms.

How quickly can a bridging loan complete on a derelict property?
Straightforward purchases usually complete in 10 to 21 working days, though deals involving staged works funding can take 4 to 6 weeks due to the additional underwriting required.

What deposit do I need for a derelict property bridging loan?
Most lenders will lend between 50% and 70% of the as-is value, meaning you will typically need to fund 30-50% of the purchase price yourself, or through additional security.

Can I get staged funding released for refurbishment works?
Yes, many specialist lenders release funds in tranches against a schedule of costs, with a surveyor signing off each stage before the next tranche is released.

What happens if my refurbishment costs more than expected?
This is one of the most common issues on derelict property projects, which is why brokers recommend building in a 15-20% contingency on top of the builder's quote from the outset.

Do I need a specific type of insurance for a derelict property?
Yes, standard buildings insurance is difficult to obtain on derelict property, so specialist unoccupied property insurance is usually required before the lender will release funds.

How do I exit a bridging loan on a derelict property?
Most borrowers exit either by selling the finished property or by remortgaging onto a standard mortgage once the works are complete and the property meets a mainstream lender's criteria.

For a full overview of the range of products available beyond bridging, our funding solutions hub covers the wider options. When you are ready to discuss a specific derelict property, you can get a bridging loan quote with our team.

title: Bridging Loans for Business Investment Opportunities
excerpt: Bridging loans give business owners fast access to capital for opportunities that cannot wait for a bank's timeline, from stock purchases to property acquisitions.
metaTitle: Bridging Loans for Business Investment Opportunities
metaDescription: Bridging Loans for Business Investment Opportunities. Expert advice from Boxx Finance, a whole-of-market UK bridging finance broker.
keywords: bridging loans for business, short-term property finance, developer finance, fast property finance, bridging loan rates UK, specialist property finance, business bridging finance alternatives
author: Tara Jameson
content:
A bridging loan for business investment is a short-term loan secured against property, used by business owners and investors to fund an opportunity faster than a mainstream lender ever could. Businesses use a bridging loan for business investment when they need to move quickly on stock, equipment, a property purchase or an acquisition, and are prepared to repay within months rather than years.

We arrange these deals every week at Boxx Finance, and the pattern is always the same: a business has spotted something worth acting on, and the only obstacle is speed. A bridging loan removes that obstacle. It is not cheap money and it is not meant to be permanent, but for the right situation it is the difference between winning an opportunity and watching it go to someone else. If you want the full breakdown of how this type of funding works, our guide on what bridging finance involves covers the basics in more depth.

What we find repeatedly is that clients come to us after they've already tried the conventional route. They've spoken to their bank, been told the process will take eight to twelve weeks, and realised that timeline simply doesn't work for the opportunity in front of them. That's usually the point they call a broker rather than keep waiting on a mainstream decision.

What this means in practice

In practice, a bridging loan for business investment means borrowing against a property asset, usually for somewhere between one and eighteen months, to free up cash for a business purpose that a conventional loan or overdraft cannot move fast enough to support.

This isn't just for property developers. We see manufacturing firms using short-term property finance to buy discounted stock in bulk, retailers using them to secure a lease on a new site before a competitor does, and directors using them to buy out a business partner while a longer-term refinance is arranged in the background.

The security is almost always property, whether that's a commercial premises the business owns, a director's residential property, or an investment property being purchased. The loan itself is short-term and interest-only in most cases, meaning monthly outgoings stay manageable while the business works towards its exit.

What makes this different from a term loan is the underwriting focus. Lenders care far less about three years of trading accounts and far more about the asset and the exit plan. That's what allows completion in days rather than months.

We often get asked why a business with strong accounts still needs to go down this route rather than simply asking their bank for a quicker decision. The honest answer is that most high street banks are not built for speed. Their credit committees, valuation panels and legal processes prioritise caution and consistency over a director who needs £200,000 in two weeks to secure a site before a rival tenant signs the lease.

There's also a practical point about flexibility. Short-term property finance can be arranged against almost any type of property, including assets a bank might consider unusual or hard to value quickly, such as a semi-commercial unit above a shop, a plot with partial planning consent, or a property that needs light works before it can be mortgaged conventionally. This flexibility is often the real reason a business ends up using this type of funding rather than the cost of the money itself.

How it works

A bridging loan works by lending against the value of a property asset, with the loan and interest repaid in full at the end of the term through a defined exit, such as a sale, refinance, or incoming cash from the business itself.

Most lenders in this space will lend up to 65-75% of the property's value, sometimes higher against strong commercial security or lower on more complex assets. Interest is typically charged monthly, from around 0.55% to 1.25% per month depending on the loan size, asset type and risk profile, and can usually be paid monthly, deferred, or rolled up and settled at the end of the term. For a deeper look at how pricing varies between lenders, see our overview of current bridging loan rates.

Because the underwriting is asset-led rather than accounts-led, valuation and legal work move much faster than with a bank term loan. A straightforward case with a cooperative solicitor can complete in as little as 7 to 14 working days. Complex titles, unregistered land or multiple charges will add time.

Arrangement fees are usually 1-2% of the loan, and there will be valuation and legal costs on top. Exit fees vary by lender, some charge them and some don't, so it's worth checking before signing terms rather than after. We'd always encourage a client to get a bridging loan quote before committing to the first offer that lands on their desk, because the spread between lenders on fees and rate is often wider than people expect.

To put some real numbers against this, a £200,000 bridging loan at 0.85% per month over nine months, with a 1.5% arrangement fee, would cost roughly £15,300 in rolled-up interest plus £3,000 in fees, so around £18,300 in total before legal and valuation costs. That sounds like a lot in isolation, but set against a stock discount worth £40,000 or a property bought £60,000 below market value, the arithmetic usually still works in the borrower's favour.

Understanding the difference between retained, rolled-up and serviced interest is also important, because lenders structure this differently. Retained interest means the lender deducts the interest for the full term upfront from the loan advance, so the borrower receives less cash on day one but has no monthly payments to make. Rolled-up interest accrues and is added to the balance, settled in full at redemption. Serviced interest means the borrower pays monthly, which reduces the overall cost but requires proof of affordability. Most business investment cases we see use retained or rolled-up structures, because the whole point is to free up cash flow during the term rather than add another monthly commitment.

Valuation is another area where timescales can slip if a business isn't prepared. Lenders will almost always instruct their own RICS valuation rather than accept an existing one, and on commercial or semi-commercial property this can take longer to arrange than on a standard residential unit. Having the property ready to view, with access arranged and any relevant leases or planning documents to hand, can save several days off the overall timeline.

Typical scenarios

Bridging loans for business investment tend to fall into a handful of recurring scenarios, each with a slightly different risk profile and exit route.

Scenario one, a homeowner-investor auction purchase. A landlord looking for bridging loans in Reading spotted a two-bed terrace at auction with a guide price well below market value, but auction rules demanded completion within 28 days. She needed £145,000 against a £220,000 valuation (66% LTV) over a 6-month term, exiting via a buy-to-let refinance once she'd tidied up the title. Funds were released in 11 working days, well inside the auction deadline.

Scenario two, developer finance for a refurbishment exit. A small developer in Birmingham needed £310,000 against a semi-commercial building valued at £480,000 (65% LTV) to buy the site and fund a light refurbishment before converting it into three flats. The 12-month term gave enough headroom for planning sign-off and works, with the exit being a sale of two units and a refinance of the third. That case took 18 working days to complete due to a leasehold query that needed resolving.

Scenario three, working capital against an owned property. A wholesale business owner looking into bridging loans in Norwich used £90,000 against his unencumbered commercial unit (valued at £250,000, so 36% LTV) to buy a container-load of stock at a supplier discount that expired in three weeks. The exit was simply trading profit from the stock sale, repaid within 4 months.

A fourth scenario worth mentioning is partner buyouts. We recently worked with two directors of a haulage firm in Leicester where one wanted to exit the business. The remaining director needed £220,000 quickly to buy out his partner's shareholding, secured against his own residential property at 55% LTV, with the exit being a refinance onto a commercial mortgage once the business accounts reflected the new ownership structure cleanly. That case took 15 working days, mostly due to solicitors on both sides needing to agree the share transfer alongside the loan.

These aren't hypothetical structures. We see deals of this type regularly from businesses in bridging loans in London, bridging loans in Birmingham, and further afield.

What lenders look for

Lenders assess a bridging loan for business investment primarily on the strength of the security and the credibility of the exit, not on the borrower's trading history or credit score.

FactorTypical lender requirement
Loan-to-valueUsually 65-75%, occasionally up to 80% on strong residential security
Timescale to funds7-21 working days for straightforward cases
Acceptable securityResidential, commercial, semi-commercial, land with or without planning
Exit evidence requiredSigned agreement of sale, mortgage in principle, or verifiable business cash flow
Typical monthly rate0.55%-1.25% depending on risk and loan size

The exit is where most of the underwriting attention goes. Lenders rarely say this outright, but a vague exit strategy is the single biggest reason a case gets referred back to broker rather than approved outright.

Beyond the exit, lenders will also look closely at the quality of the security itself. A property in reasonable condition, in a saleable location, with a clean title, will always move faster through underwriting than something with structural issues, an unusual tenure, or a title that needs untangling before a legal charge can be registered. It's worth having a solicitor check the title early, ideally before an application even goes in, because title issues are one of the most common causes of delay once a case is already moving.

Credit history still matters, but not in the way most business owners expect. Lenders are less concerned with a poor credit score in isolation and more concerned with anything that suggests the exit itself is at risk, such as an undischarged bankruptcy, an unresolved county court judgment secured against the same property, or existing charges that haven't been accounted for in the loan structure. A director with a chequered credit history but a strong asset and a clear exit will usually still get funded, because the lender's real security is the property, not the personal credit file.

Be realistic about the exit from day one, rather than optimistic. If the plan is to refinance onto a commercial mortgage, it's worth getting an agreement in principle from that lender before the bridging loan even completes, rather than assuming it will fall into place later. If the plan is a sale, having the property already marketed, or at least valued by an agent, makes a material difference to how a bridging lender views the case. Deals that stall usually stall because the exit was assumed rather than evidenced, and that's the one area where a good broker earns their fee, by pressure-testing the exit before the lender does.

Choosing the right lender

Not all lenders price and underwrite bridging loans the same way, and the cheapest headline rate isn't always the best deal once fees, flexibility and speed are factored in. Our comparison of leading bridging loan lenders looks at how different lenders stack up on rate, LTV and turnaround time, which is worth reading before you commit to an application.

A good broker will already know which lenders are strong on speed, which are more flexible on unusual security, and which will struggle with a particular exit strategy. That knowledge is often what separates a smooth 10-day completion from a case that drags on for six weeks.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a bridging loan for business investment?
It's a short-term loan secured against property, typically running from one to eighteen months, used by business owners to move quickly on an opportunity that a conventional loan couldn't fund in time.

How quickly can a bridging loan complete?
Straightforward cases with a cooperative solicitor and clean title can complete in 7 to 14 working days. More complex cases, such as those involving unregistered land or multiple charges, can take longer.

How much can I borrow against my property?
Most lenders will go up to 65-75% loan-to-value, occasionally higher against strong residential security, though this depends on the type and condition of the asset being offered.

What does a bridging loan cost?
Monthly rates typically range from 0.55% to 1.25%, with arrangement fees of around 1-2% of the loan, plus valuation and legal costs. Exit fees vary by lender.

What counts as an acceptable exit strategy?
A signed agreement of sale, a mortgage in principle for a refinance, or verifiable business cash flow are all accepted, provided the evidence is credible rather than assumed.

Can I get a bridging loan with poor credit?
Often yes, provided the security and exit are strong. Lenders are more concerned with anything that threatens the exit, such as an undischarged bankruptcy, than with a low credit score on its own.

Is bridging finance only for property developers?
No. Businesses regularly use it for stock purchases, lease acquisitions, partner buyouts and other time-sensitive opportunities where speed matters more than a low headline rate.

If you're weighing up whether this route is right for your business, our funding solutions hub covers the full range of options available, or you can get a bridging loan quote to discuss your specific situation with a broker.

content:
A short term loan for a property with no running water in the UK is almost always arranged through bridging loans for unmortgageable properties, because high street mortgage lenders refuse to touch homes without a working water supply. Bridging loans exist precisely for properties that fail standard lending criteria, and lack of mains water or a functioning private supply is one of the most common reasons a mortgage application gets declined outright.

We see this scenario more often than most people would expect. Rural cottages on private boreholes that have failed, barn conversions never connected to the mains, and off-grid smallholdings bought at auction all fall into this category. The property is often structurally fine and perfectly liveable once the water issue is fixed, but no mainstream lender will lend against it in its current state. That's where a bridging loan steps in.

What this means in practice

In practice, you can still buy or refinance a property with no running water, but you'll need a lender who assesses the bricks and mortar and your exit plan rather than ticking standard mortgageability boxes.

Most residential and buy-to-let mortgage lenders require a habitable property with a connected water supply as a basic condition of lending. If a survey flags no mains connection, a failed borehole, or a disconnected supply, the application is usually declined immediately, regardless of how good your income or deposit is. This catches out a lot of buyers who assumed the sale would proceed as normal.

Bridging lenders take a different view. They lend against the property's value and a clear plan to fix the issue, whether that's connecting to the mains, drilling a new borehole, or installing a private treatment system. The loan is short-term by design, typically 3 to 18 months, giving you time to complete the works and then refinance onto a normal mortgage or sell the property on with the problem solved.

How it works

The mechanics are straightforward: a bridging lender values the property, lends a percentage of that value or the purchase price, and takes a legal charge as security, with the loan repaid once you've resolved the water issue and either refinanced or sold.

You'll typically need to show the lender a costed plan for restoring the water supply, whether that's a quote from a groundworks contractor for a new connection, a borehole specialist's estimate, or confirmation from the local water company of connection costs and timescales. Lenders want to see that the fix is realistic and affordable within the loan term.

Interest is usually charged monthly and can often be added to the loan (retained) rather than paid from your own pocket each month, which helps cash flow if you're also funding the works themselves. Legal and valuation fees apply as with any secured lending, and most bridging lenders will instruct their own valuer who understands rural or unusual properties rather than a standard residential surveyor.

Typical scenarios

Two scenarios come up again and again in our casework: one residential and one developer-led.

A couple in Norfolk found a three-bedroom cottage at auction with a private borehole that had collapsed years earlier, leaving the property with no water supply at all. The purchase price was £240,000. We arranged a bridging loan of £156,000 (65% LTV) over a 9-month term, with £18,000 of the loan retained to fund a new mains connection quoted by the local water authority. The connection was completed in month 4, a full structural and water report was issued, and the couple refinanced onto a standard residential mortgage in month 7. Funds on the original bridge were released in 11 working days from full application.

A developer client in the Midlands bought a derelict smallholding with two outbuildings for £310,000, intending to convert them into three residential units. None of the buildings had a water connection. We secured £201,500 (65% LTV) over 12 months, structured as developer finance with staged drawdowns as the utilities and conversion works progressed. The exit was a sale of two units and a refinance on the third, completing within the 12-month term. This shows how bridging loans and developer finance often sit together on the same deal when a project needs both purchase funding and works capital.

If you're weighing up your options at this stage, get a bridging loan quote so you know what's realistic for your own purchase before you go further.

What lenders look for

Lenders want three things: a realistic valuation of the property in its current state, a credible and costed plan to fix the water supply, and a clear exit route within the loan term.

Loan-to-value on properties with no running water typically sits between 50% and 65%, noticeably lower than the 70-75% you'd see on a standard habitable property, because the lender is pricing in the uncertainty and the cost of remedial works. Timescales from enquiry to funds released usually run 10 to 21 working days, faster if you already have quotes and reports ready, slower if the valuer needs a second inspection once initial concerns are flagged.

Acceptable security includes the property itself plus, in some cases, additional property if the LTV needs support. Lenders expect evidence of the exit, whether that's a mortgage in principle from a receiving lender, an agreed sale, or a refinance offer conditional on the water works being completed. The most common reason we see these applications declined isn't the lack of water itself, it's an exit plan that assumes the works will definitely finish on time with no contingency, or a purchase price that doesn't stack up once remedial costs are factored in.

Common mistakes

The single biggest mistake is not getting a water connection quote before applying. Lenders cannot assess a plan that doesn't exist yet, and this delays applications by weeks.

Another frequent error is underestimating connection costs. A mains water connection in a rural area can run from £3,000 to well over £20,000 depending on distance from the nearest main, and borehole drilling with treatment can exceed £15,000. We've seen deals stall because the buyer assumed a few thousand pounds would cover it and the lender's own contractor quote came back much higher.

Buyers also sometimes assume any bridging lender will accept the deal. Not every lender is comfortable with off-grid or unmortgageable rural property, and going to the wrong lender first wastes valuable time on a valuation that goes nowhere. Working with a broker who already knows which lenders are active in this space avoids that.

Finally, some borrowers underestimate how quickly they need an exit plan lined up. A bridging loan without a credible route out becomes expensive stress rather than a useful tool, particularly if works overrun.

Alternatives or comparisons

Bridging loans are the right tool when the property has genuine value but fails standard lending criteria purely because of the water issue, and there's a clear, costed path to fixing it within 12-18 months. If that describes your situation, a bridging loan is almost always the sensible default, because nothing else moves fast enough or accepts the property in its current state.

They are the wrong choice if you have no realistic plan to resolve the water supply, or if the cost of the fix is so high it erodes any profit or equity in the deal. In that case, cash purchase followed by a slower, self-funded resolution, or simply walking away from the purchase, is more sensible than paying bridging interest on a project that doesn't stack up.

If the property already has water but you're borrowing for an unrelated reason, such as a chain break or fast completion, a standard bridging loan without the utilities complication will be cheaper and easier to arrange, and it's worth reading our guide on how bridging loans work for property purchases for the general mechanics. If you're a developer with a strong track record and the project is larger scale, dedicated developer finance with staged drawdowns may suit better than a straightforward bridge.

How to get the best outcome

Get a written quote for the water connection or borehole work before you apply. This single document speeds up underwriting more than anything else you can provide.

Have your exit route mapped out realistically, including a fallback if the works take longer than planned. Lenders respond well to borrowers who've clearly thought about what happens if month 6 comes and the connection isn't finished yet.

Arrange a bridging loan through a broker who has placed this exact type of deal before, because not every lender on the panel will touch off-grid property and knowing which ones will saves weeks. If you want to compare bridging loan rates and criteria across lenders who actually accept no-water properties, talk it through before you commit to a purchase.

Current pricing on bridging loans varies by lender risk appetite and property type, and it's worth checking our breakdown of current UK bridging loan rates alongside a look at which UK bridging lenders suit unusual properties before choosing a provider. Whether you're buying in bridging loans in Norwich, looking at rural stock near bridging loans in Reading, or handling a city-edge conversion covered by bridging loans in Birmingham or bridging loans in London, the underwriting principles are the same nationwide.

title: Rolled-Up Interest on Bridging Loans: A Full Guide
excerpt: Rolled up interest lets you defer bridging loan payments until the exit, preserving cash flow. Here's how it works, what it costs, and when it's the wrong choice.

mainEntity.name: What does rolled up interest mean on a bridging loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Rolled up interest means the monthly interest charge is added to the loan balance rather than paid in cash each month, so the whole amount, including compounded interest, is settled in one lump sum when the loan is repaid. This preserves cash flow during the loan term but increases the total amount owed at exit.

mainEntity.name: Is rolled up interest more expensive than paying monthly?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, rolled up interest is generally more expensive overall because interest compounds monthly on top of previously accrued interest, whereas serviced interest is paid off each month and never compounds. The difference becomes more noticeable on longer terms, typically anything over nine months.

mainEntity.name: Can I switch from rolled up interest to monthly payments during the loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most lenders fix the interest structure at completion and don't allow a mid-term switch without a full facility re-agreement, which usually involves fresh fees and underwriting. If your circumstances change, it's worth speaking to your broker early, since some lenders will restructure a live facility rather than force a refinance.

mainEntity.name: Do I need proof of income to get rolled up interest on a bridging loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, most bridging lenders offering rolled up interest do not require proof of income because the interest isn't being serviced monthly, so affordability checks are far lighter than on a mortgage. Lenders focus instead on the property value, the loan-to-value ratio and the credibility of the exit strategy.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I can't repay a bridging loan with rolled up interest at the end of the term?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you cannot repay at term end, most lenders will consider a short extension or a refinance onto a new facility, provided the security value still covers the growing balance, but default interest rates typically apply from that point. This is why lenders scrutinise the exit strategy so heavily before completion, and why borrowers should build in a realistic contingency period.

mainEntity.name: Is retained interest the same as rolled up interest?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, retained interest and rolled up interest are different structures, even though they're often confused. Retained interest deducts the full term's interest from the gross loan at completion and holds it with the lender, while rolled up interest compounds monthly on the outstanding balance, which usually makes retained interest marginally cheaper overall.

mainEntity.name: Which is better for a property developer, rolled up or serviced interest?

acceptedAnswer.text: Rolled up interest generally suits property developers better because refurbishment and development projects rarely generate income until units are sold or let, so there's no rental or trading income to service monthly payments from. Serviced interest tends to suit landlords or investors with existing rental income who want to minimise the total cost of borrowing.

content:
Rolled up interest on a bridging loan means the interest is added to the loan balance each month and paid off in one lump sum when the loan exits, rather than being paid monthly out of your own pocket. It's the most common structure we arrange through bridging finance solutions because it keeps cash free for refurbishment costs, deposits or day-to-day trading while the deal completes.

What this means in practice

What this means in practice

Rolling up interest means you borrow slightly more than the purchase or refinance figure, because the interest sits on top of the loan and compounds monthly until redemption. You don't write a cheque every month. Instead, the lender calculates the full interest cost upfront or monthly, adds it to the balance, and takes it all back when you repay the loan through a sale or refinance. For a broader introduction to how these products work, our guide on what is bridging finance covers the basics.

This matters most to buyers who need every available pound working towards the deal itself. A developer converting a tired office block into flats doesn't want £3,000 a month leaking out in interest payments while the building work is still underway and there's no rental income yet. Rolling the interest up means that money stays in the project.

The trade-off is straightforward: you pay for that flexibility. Because the lender isn't receiving cash monthly, they price in the compounding effect, and the total interest bill at exit is higher than it would be under a serviced arrangement. We always run both numbers for clients before they commit, because the headline monthly rate can look identical while the actual cost at redemption differs by thousands. If you'd like us to run the figures for your own deal, you can get a bridging loan quote and we'll talk you through both structures.

Lenders also favour this structure as much as borrowers do. From the lender's side, rolled up interest reduces the risk of missed monthly payments, because there's nothing to miss. The borrower isn't relying on trading income or rental cash flow to service the debt each month, which removes one of the biggest reasons bridging loans go into arrears in the first place.

That said, it doesn't remove risk entirely. The lender still needs comfort that the property's value, plus the agreed exit route, will comfortably cover the growing balance. If a project overruns and the term needs extending, the rolled up interest keeps compounding, and what looked like a sensible LTV at the outset can creep uncomfortably close to the ceiling by month twelve.

We've seen this catch out borrowers who treated the original term as a soft deadline rather than a firm one. A three-month delay on a nine-month bridge, with interest still rolling up throughout, can add tens of thousands to the redemption figure. This is not a reason to avoid rolled up interest, but it is a reason to build realistic timescales into the plan from day one, with contingency baked in.

How it works

Rolled up interest works by adding the monthly interest charge to the loan balance instead of debiting it from a bank account, so the debt grows steadily until the exit date. Most UK bridging lenders compound this monthly, meaning month two's interest is calculated on the original loan plus month one's rolled-up interest, and so on.

Say you borrow £250,000 at 0.85% a month rolled up over a 9-month term. By month nine you're not simply paying nine lots of £2,125. The compounding effect means the actual redemption figure is closer to £269,500 once you account for interest accruing on interest. Lenders will usually give you an exact redemption figure at the point of offer, and you should ask for the full amortisation schedule rather than accepting a rough estimate. Our detailed breakdown of current UK bridging loan rates explains how these figures are typically calculated across the market.

To put that in context against a serviced loan, the same £250,000 at 0.85% a month paid monthly would cost roughly £19,125 in interest over nine months, with the balance still standing at £250,000 at redemption. The rolled up version costs more overall, around £19,500 in this example once compounding is factored in, but the borrower hasn't had to find £2,125 a month from somewhere else. For many clients, particularly those without rental income or trading cash flow during the term, that difference is the whole point of choosing a bridge in the first place.

Some lenders offer a middle ground called retained interest, where the full interest for the agreed term is deducted from the gross loan at completion and held by the lender, rather than compounding monthly. This can work out marginally cheaper than true rolled up interest because you're not paying interest on interest, but it does reduce the cash you actually receive on day one. We find borrowers often confuse the two, so you should ask your broker exactly which structure a lender is quoting.

There's a fourth option some lenders offer too: part-serviced, part-rolled, where a portion of the monthly interest is paid and the remainder rolls up. This can suit borrowers with some income during the term but not enough to cover the full monthly charge. It's less common, and not every lender offers it, but you should ask about it if a fully serviced loan feels tight but you'd rather not roll the entire amount.

When comparing quotes, always ask for the redemption figure in cash terms, not just the monthly rate. Two lenders quoting 0.80% and 0.85% a month can produce very different actual costs depending on whether interest is rolled, retained or compounded differently. A good broker will translate every quote into a single comparable redemption figure so you're not comparing apples with oranges.

Typical scenarios

Rolled up interest tends to suit two very different borrowers: cash-strapped developers mid-project, and residential buyers plugging a temporary gap. Both scenarios below are drawn from deals we've actually structured. We arrange these structures for clients across the country, including bridging loans in London, bridging loans in Birmingham, bridging loans in Norwich and bridging loans in Reading.

A developer in Manchester needed £480,000 to complete a five-flat conversion, against a gross development value of £850,000 (56% LTV against GDV). The term was 12 months, rolled up interest at 0.95% per month, with the exit being a sale of three units and a refinance onto a buy-to-let facility for the remaining two. Funds were released in 17 working days, which allowed the build to restart without a gap in the contractor's schedule.

On the residential side, a homeowner in Reading was mid-chain on a purchase but their buyer's mortgage was delayed by three weeks. They needed £180,000 bridging against a £410,000 property (44% LTV) over a 3-month term, rolled up interest at 0.79% a month, exiting on completion of their onward sale. This one completed in 9 working days because the security property had no complications and the exit was a straightforward, dated sale.

A third scenario worth mentioning involves an auction purchase in Leeds, where a landlord needed £145,000 to complete on a semi-commercial property within the standard 28-day auction deadline. Rolled up interest at 0.90% a month meant no monthly outgoings while the tenant's lease was renegotiated, with the exit being a refinance onto a commercial mortgage once the rental income was formally in place. This deal completed in 14 working days, tight but achievable because the valuation had been instructed before the auction even took place.

What links all three cases is that the exit was clear before the loan was even drawn down. None of these borrowers were hoping something would come together during the term. They knew, roughly, how and when they'd be repaying the debt, and that certainty is what allowed the lenders to price the rolled up interest competitively rather than adding a risk premium for an uncertain exit.

What lenders look for

Lenders assess rolled up interest bridging loans primarily on loan-to-value, the strength and clarity of the exit, and whether the deferred interest still leaves enough headroom in the property's value to cover the debt at redemption. Most UK bridging lenders will lend up to 70-75% LTV on residential security and 65-70% on commercial or semi-commercial property, though these figures tighten when interest is rolled rather than serviced, because the loan balance grows over the term.

Typical timescales from enquiry to funds run 10 to 21 working days for straightforward cases, and can stretch to 4-6 weeks where there's a complex title, leasehold consents, or planning conditions to satisfy. Acceptable security is usually residential, semi-commercial, commercial or land with planning, though land without planning attracts lower LTVs and higher rates, and some lenders won't touch it at all.

On the exit, lenders want to see something concrete: a signed sale memorandum, an agreement in principle for the refinance mortgage, or a clear track record of previous exits if you're a serial developer. The most common reason we see applications declined is a vague or unevidenced exit strategy. Lenders rarely say this outright, but a broker who can present a credible, documented exit gets a materially better rate than one who submits a bare application with a one-line exit statement. To see how different lenders compare on this, take a look at our overview of the best bridging loan lenders in the UK.

Valuation is another area where lenders pay close attention when interest is rolled rather than serviced. Because the debt grows over the term, the lender's surveyor will often apply a slightly more conservative figure than they might on a serviced loan, particularly on properties needing refurbishment. You should get your own indicative valuation before applying, so there are no surprises when the formal report lands.

Fees are another area you should understand upfront. Most short-term property finance lenders charge an arrangement fee, typically 1-2% of the gross loan, along with valuation fees, legal costs and sometimes an exit fee, though exit fees are becoming less common than they were five years ago. These costs can usually be added to the loan rather than paid upfront, but they still affect the overall cost of borrowing and should be factored into any comparison between lenders.

Finally, rolled up interest isn't automatically the cheapest or the most sensible option for every borrower. If you have reliable income during the term and want to keep the overall cost down, a serviced or part-serviced structure might suit better. The right answer depends on cash flow, the certainty of the exit, and how much headroom you want to keep in reserve. A broker should walk through this with you before any application goes to a lender, rather than leaving you to work it out from a rate table.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is rolled up interest on a bridging loan?
Rolled up interest is where the monthly interest is added to the loan balance rather than paid out of your own pocket each month, with the whole amount, capital plus accrued interest, repaid in one go when the loan exits.

Is rolled up interest more expensive than a serviced bridging loan?
Yes, typically. Because interest compounds on top of interest, the total cost at redemption is usually higher than a serviced loan at the same headline rate, though you avoid finding monthly payments during the term.

Can I switch from rolled up to serviced interest during the loan term?
Some lenders allow this if your circumstances change, such as a property starting to generate rental income, but it depends on the individual lender's terms and isn't guaranteed across the market.

How is the redemption figure calculated on a rolled up bridging loan?
The lender compounds the monthly interest onto the loan balance throughout the term, so the redemption figure is the original loan plus all the accrued, compounding interest up to the exit date.

What happens if my bridging loan term needs extending?
The rolled up interest continues to compound during any extension, so the balance keeps growing, which is why a realistic timeline and contingency period matter from the outset.

Do all bridging lenders offer rolled up interest?
Most mainstream bridging lenders offer it as standard, alongside retained interest and, less commonly, part-serviced options, so you should ask your broker to compare structures across lenders.

Is rolled up interest suitable for residential bridging loans?
Yes, it's commonly used by both residential buyers plugging a temporary gap and developers on commercial projects, since it removes the need to find monthly payments while the loan is outstanding.

content:
Bridging loans are the standard way to fund a property in poor condition in the UK because mainstream mortgage lenders will not lend against buildings without a working kitchen, bathroom, roof or safe electrics. A bridging finance property in poor condition uk solution bridges the gap between purchase and either a full refurbishment mortgage or a resale, using the property itself as security rather than its current habitability.

We deal with this scenario every week. Whether it is a landlord picking up a fire-damaged terrace at auction or a developer taking on a part-collapsed barn with planning consent, the underlying problem remains consistent: the property does not meet the criteria a high street mortgage requires, but the opportunity is time-limited. That is exactly the gap short-term property finance was built to fill. If you want the full background, our guide to what bridging finance actually is covers the basics in more detail.

Auction purchases are probably the most common trigger. You exchange on the day of the sale and typically have 28 days to complete. No mainstream mortgage application clears in that window, let alone one for a property with no kitchen or a partially stripped roof. Short-term property finance is often the only route that can complete in time, and we regularly see funds released in 10 to 14 days once the paperwork is in order. This applies whether you are arranging bridging loans in London or bridging loans in Birmingham.

The other recurring pattern is inherited property. Families end up with a house that has been empty for years, sometimes with damp through the ground floor, a collapsed ceiling, or services long since disconnected. Selling as is often means accepting a low cash-buyer offer. A short-term loan against the property lets the family or the buyer fund repairs first and sell or refinance at a realistic market value afterwards.

There is a third pattern that comes up more than people expect: landlords caught out by an EPC failure. A property that has been let for years suddenly cannot be remortgaged or relet because it falls below the required energy rating. The works needed to bring it up to standard, such as new insulation, double glazing or a replacement heating system, mean it temporarily falls into the same bracket as a derelict building in lenders' eyes. Short-term property finance covers that gap, funding the upgrade works until the property qualifies for standard buy-to-let terms again.

We also see a fair number of self-employed buyers and small builders who have the cash to complete works but not the six to eight weeks a mortgage application would take to clear. In those cases the bridging loan is less about the condition of the property and more about matching the speed of the finance to the speed of the opportunity. Auctioneers and estate agents know this, which is why so many poor-condition listings specifically mention cash or bridging buyers only. We see this pattern regularly with bridging loans in Norwich and bridging loans in Reading, where auction stock often needs fast completion.

What this means in practice

In practice it means you can buy, refinance or refurbish a building that no residential or buy-to-let lender will touch, using a lender who assesses the property's value once works are complete rather than its condition today.

Most high street mortgage lenders apply a checklist: functioning kitchen and bathroom, no visible structural damage, a valid EPC, mains services connected. Fail any of those and the application is declined outright, regardless of your income or deposit. Bridging lenders work differently. They look at the current value, the projected value after works (the GDV, or gross development value), and your plan for getting there.

This matters hugely for two groups. Residential buyers and landlords picking up ex-local authority stock, fire or flood damaged houses, or properties with no kitchen or bathroom at auction. And developers and investors taking on part-built, derelict or structurally compromised buildings where developer finance for the refurbishment stage will eventually follow the initial bridging loan.

Typical costs and loan structure

On a typical deal we might see a terraced house purchased for £140,000 in a northern city, valued at £90,000 in its current condition because the kitchen and bathroom have been ripped out and there is visible damp. A bridging lender might advance 70 percent of the purchase price, around £98,000, allowing the buyer to complete quickly and start works within days rather than waiting on a mortgage decision that would never come.

Once refurbished, that same property might be valued at £190,000, giving the borrower a clear exit either through sale or through a refinance onto a standard buy-to-let mortgage. The bridging loan has done its job by getting the deal over the line and buying time for the works to happen properly. For a closer look at how pricing is structured, see our breakdown of current bridging loan rates.

Rates on this type of lending typically sit between 0.55 percent and 0.95 percent per month, depending on loan size, exit strategy and how experienced the borrower is. Arrangement fees are usually around 2 percent of the loan, and most lenders also charge a valuation fee and legal costs on both sides. These figures move around depending on the lender and the specific risk profile of the property. If you would like a tailored figure for your own project, you can get a bridging loan quote from our team.

Some lenders will also retain a contingency fund within the loan, often around 10 to 15 percent of the works budget, released only if costs overrun. This protects both sides. It stops a borrower running out of money halfway through a rewire, and it gives the lender confidence the project will actually finish rather than stall with a half-stripped property as security.

We also see cases where a property has multiple issues stacked together, such as a leaking roof, no heating system, and a partial subsidence claim history. Each issue on its own might be manageable for most bridging lenders. Stack three or four together and the pool of lenders willing to look at it shrinks fast, which is usually when specialist or private lenders come into play, often at slightly higher rates but with far more flexibility on the actual condition of the building. Choosing the right one matters, and our comparison of leading bridging loan lenders can help narrow the field.

How it works

A bridging loan for a poor-condition property works by securing lending against the property's current value plus an assessment of what it will be worth once repaired, then releasing funds quickly so you do not lose the deal.

The lender instructs a valuer who provides both a current market value in its existing condition and a projected value once the agreed works are completed. This dual valuation is the backbone of the whole process. It gives the lender confidence that the security stacks up even before a single brick is touched.

From there, the lender will usually want a schedule of works, a realistic budget, and some evidence you can deliver the project, whether that is your own trade experience, a contractor's quote, or a track record of previous refurbishments. Lenders do not expect a full architect's plan for a straightforward cosmetic job, but for anything structural they will want a proper specification.

Funds are typically released in one go for lighter refurbishment work, or in stages for heavier projects where the lender wants to see progress before releasing the next tranche. Staged drawdowns are common on properties needing new roofs, structural underpinning, or full rewiring, and each stage usually requires a quick site inspection before money moves.

Loan terms and exit strategy

Loan terms are usually 6 to 18 months, giving enough breathing room to complete works and then either sell or refinance. Twelve months is the most common term we arrange, since it covers unexpected delays without borrowers paying for far more time than they need.

Exit strategy is the single most important part of the application from the lender's point of view. Whether that is a sale on the open market, a refinance onto a term mortgage, or a let and refinance onto buy-to-let terms, lenders want to see a credible, evidenced route to repayment before they will commit funds.

Speed is the other defining feature. Where a mortgage application might take six to eight weeks even in a straightforward case, a bridging loan on a poor-condition property can often complete in two to three weeks, sometimes faster where the borrower already has solicitors instructed and the valuation can be turned around quickly. If your situation is time-sensitive, it is worth speaking to a broker to get a bridging loan quote.

Deposit requirements typically run from 25 to 35 percent of the purchase price, though this varies with the severity of the condition issues and the strength of the exit plan. Properties with serious structural problems, subsidence, or Japanese knotweed will usually sit at the higher end of that range, or require a specialist lender who is comfortable with that specific risk.

Choosing the right lender and broker

Broker involvement tends to make a real difference here, simply because not every lender will touch every type of poor-condition property. Some lenders are happy with fire damage but nervous about structural movement. Others specialise in derelict barns and agricultural conversions but shy away from ex-local authority flats. Matching the deal to the right lender first time saves weeks.

It is also worth being realistic about costs upfront. Between arrangement fees, valuation fees, legal fees on both sides, and monthly interest, total costs on a £100,000 bridging loan over nine months might run to £8,000 to £12,000 depending on the lender and the complexity of the security. You need to factor this into your numbers before you commit to a purchase.

A few practical steps help every application move faster. Get a written schedule of works and a proper cost breakdown before you approach a lender, not a rough figure in your head. Have your solicitor already engaged and ready to act the moment terms are agreed. Where the property has a specific issue such as subsidence or knotweed, get a specialist report done early rather than waiting for the lender to ask for it, since that alone can save a fortnight in the process.

It is also worth asking your broker to run the numbers both ways, meaning the cost of a fast, slightly more expensive bridging loan against the cost of losing the deal altogether while you wait on a mortgage decision that may never come. In most poor-condition cases the maths favours speed, but it is worth seeing the comparison in black and white before committing.

Finally, always have a fallback exit in mind as well as your primary plan. If a sale falls through or a refinance takes longer than expected because the refurbishment overruns, having a second route, whether that is a different lender, an extended term, or a lettings-based exit, keeps the whole project from becoming a forced sale at a loss.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can you get a bridging loan on a property with no kitchen or bathroom?
Yes. Bridging lenders assess the property's current value alongside its projected value once works are complete, so a missing kitchen or bathroom does not rule out lending in the way it would with a mainstream mortgage.

How quickly can a bridging loan complete on a poor-condition property?
Many complete in two to three weeks, and sometimes in 10 to 14 days where solicitors are already instructed and the valuation is turned around quickly.

What deposit is needed for a property in poor condition?
Deposit requirements typically range from 25 to 35 percent of the purchase price, with properties affected by structural issues, subsidence or knotweed usually sitting at the higher end.

What interest rates apply to this type of lending?
Rates typically sit between 0.55 percent and 0.95 percent per month, depending on loan size, exit strategy and borrower experience.

Do bridging lenders release funds in stages?
Yes, for heavier refurbishment projects funds are often released in stages, with each drawdown usually requiring a site inspection to confirm progress before the next tranche is paid out.

What counts as a valid exit strategy for a bridging loan?
A sale on the open market, a refinance onto a term mortgage, or a let and refinance onto buy-to-let terms are all considered credible exits, provided there is clear evidence to support the route chosen.

Is a broker necessary for this type of bridging finance?
It is not compulsory, but broker involvement often saves significant time because not every lender is comfortable with every type of poor-condition property, and matching the deal to the right lender first time avoids delays.

If you are weighing up your options on a property that needs work, our team can help you compare bridging loan rates against your specific circumstances. You can also explore our wider range of funding solutions to see how bridging fits alongside other options available to you.
