content:
A bridging loan for working capital is a short-term loan secured against property that gives a business fast access to cash, typically within days rather than weeks, to cover cash flow gaps, urgent tax bills, stock purchases or supplier payments. Businesses use it when speed matters more than the interest rate, and when a clear exit route exists to repay the loan.

We arrange this type of funding regularly at Boxx Finance. Established SMEs with property on the balance sheet need short injections of cash to keep trading smoothly. Property developers and investors need working capital to keep a project moving while a sale or refinance completes. Both use the same mechanism, just for different reasons. We regularly arrange bridging loans in London and bridging loans in Birmingham for exactly this kind of client.

What drives every case we deal with is timing. The business rarely comes to us months in advance with a leisurely plan. Often a director calls explaining that a payment has not landed when expected, or that an opportunity has come up that will not wait for a bank's standard six week decision process. Short-term property finance exists precisely for that gap between a problem appearing and a solution being needed. If you want a broader introduction first, our guide on how bridging finance works covers the basics in more depth.

This is not cheap money, and no broker worth their fee should pretend otherwise. It is a tool for a specific job. Used well, it protects a business, keeps suppliers onside, and buys time to sort out a longer term funding structure. Used badly, without a clear repayment route, it simply adds another layer of cost and pressure. Our job is to make sure it falls into the first category, not the second. If you are weighing up whether this is the right route for your business, you can get a bridging loan quote and talk it through with our team.

What this means in practice

In practice, a bridging loan for working capital means unlocking equity tied up in property, usually commercial premises, a residential investment, or even the director's own home, and turning it into usable cash within a matter of days.

This is not a replacement for a business overdraft or invoice finance facility. It is a short-term, interest-bearing loan, usually running from one month up to eighteen months, with the loan secured by a legal charge against the property. Interest is often added to the loan rather than paid monthly, which helps cash flow during the term but increases the total cost.

The money itself can be used for almost anything the business needs. We have seen it used to settle a VAT bill before HMRC applied penalties, to pay a supplier who was threatening to stop deliveries, and to bridge the gap between paying staff wages and an invoice being settled by a slow-paying client. The common thread is urgency and a defined repayment date.

We have also seen it used more strategically. One client used a bridging loan to take advantage of an early payment discount from a key supplier, saving more on the discount than the loan cost over the term. Another used it to buy stock ahead of a known price rise, effectively locking in margin before costs went up. These uses focus on taking advantage of trading opportunities rather than crisis management.

This product sits alongside, rather than instead of, your normal funding lines. Most businesses that use a bridging loan for working capital still have their day to day overdraft, invoice finance or asset finance running in the background. The bridge simply plugs a specific, time-limited gap that those facilities were not designed to cover.

How it works

The mechanics are straightforward: you offer a property as security, the lender values it, agrees a loan-to-value, and releases funds once legal work is complete, usually secured by a first or second charge.

Lenders will want to know your exit strategy from day one. That might be refinancing onto a commercial mortgage, selling an asset, receiving an expected payment, or trading your way to repayment through improved cash flow. Without a credible exit, most lenders will decline outright, no matter how strong the security is.

Rates for business-purpose bridging loans in the UK currently run from around 0.55% to 1.25% per month depending on the lender, loan-to-value and strength of exit. Arrangement fees typically sit between 1% and 2% of the loan, with valuation and legal costs on top. It is worth comparing options properly rather than accepting the first offer, and reviewing current UK bridging loan rates before committing gives useful context on what a fair deal looks like.

To put those figures into context, a £100,000 bridging loan at 0.75% per month over six months would cost roughly £4,500 in interest if rolled up, plus a 1.5% arrangement fee of £1,500, before legal and valuation costs. That is a meaningful sum, which is exactly why the exit route matters so much. Borrowing at this cost only makes sense if it solves a problem worth more than the fee.

Because these are regulated and unregulated products depending on the security and purpose, the process can move quickly. Many lenders can turn a straightforward case around in seven to fourteen working days from application to funds landing, sometimes faster if the legal title is clean and there is no chain of ownership complications.

A few practical steps speed the process up considerably. Having up to date proof of ownership, a recent valuation or at least an idea of current market value, and your solicitor's details ready to go at the point of enquiry can shave several days off the timeline. We always ask clients for these details upfront, precisely because the legal stage is usually where delays creep in, not the underwriting.

Most lenders in this space will only deal through a broker or will prioritise broker-introduced cases, simply because a broker has already packaged the deal, checked the exit makes sense, and pre-empted the obvious questions. That tends to translate into faster decisions and fewer surprises further down the line. We see this pattern consistently whether we are arranging bridging loans in Norwich or bridging loans in Reading.

Typical scenarios

A manufacturing business in the Midlands needed £150,000 to cover a large raw materials order after a key customer delayed payment on a £400,000 invoice. They held an unencumbered commercial unit worth £350,000. The lender agreed 43% LTV over a six-month term, with the exit being repayment once the customer's invoice cleared. Funds were released in nine working days.

A property developer in Norwich was mid-way through a refurbishment when a cost overrun left them short of cash to complete the final fit-out. They needed £90,000 against a part-completed property valued at £260,000 once finished (roughly 35% LTV on completed value), over a nine-month term, exiting via sale of the finished units. The deal completed in eleven working days, allowing work to restart within two weeks. This is a common pattern we see with developer finance and working capital bridging loan solutions, where the loan bridges a genuine funding gap mid-project rather than funding the whole scheme.

A landlord with a small portfolio needed £60,000 quickly to cover an unexpected corporation tax bill while waiting for a buy-to-let refinance to complete. Security was a second charge on a residential investment property worth £310,000, giving roughly 45% combined LTV across both charges, over a three-month term. Funds cleared in eight working days, and the loan was repaid in full once the refinance completed.

A wholesale business in Leeds was facing a seasonal stock crunch and needed £220,000 to buy inventory ahead of their busiest quarter. They had already used most of their existing trade finance facility. Against a commercial investment property worth £480,000, the lender agreed 46% LTV over a five-month term, with the exit being seasonal trading income supported by forward orders already on the books. That case took thirteen working days from enquiry to completion, slightly longer because a title query needed clearing with the Land Registry.

Across all four examples, the pattern holds. Loan-to-values sit comfortably below maximum lending limits, terms are short and specific, and every single exit is something concrete rather than a hope. That combination is what makes these deals gettable in a realistic timeframe.

What lenders look for

Lenders assess the property security and the credibility of the exit primarily, not the day-to-day trading performance of the business, which is what makes this product accessible even to businesses with imperfect accounts.

Typical loan-to-value ranges sit between 50% and 70% on residential security, and 50% to 65% on commercial property, though some specialist lenders will stretch higher for very strong exits. Realistic timescales from initial enquiry to funds in the account run from seven to twenty-one working days, depending on how quickly valuations and legal work move. Security is usually a first or second legal charge on residential, commercial or mixed-use property, and lenders increasingly accept property outside the business owner's personal name, provided the ownership structure is clean.

Evidence of exit is the single biggest factor in getting an application approved. Lenders want to see a signed refinance offer, a sale agreed at a specific price, a contract confirming an incoming payment, or a credible trading forecast showing repayment capacity. The most common reason we see applications declined is a vague or unevidenced exit, such as an assumption that trading will simply pick up, without anything concrete behind it.

Lenders will also look closely at the quality and marketability of the security property. A specialist unit in a remote location with limited buyer demand will always be viewed more cautiously than a standard commercial premises in a strong local market, even if the numbers on paper look identical. Valuers are instructed to consider a realistic resale timeframe under pressure, not just an open market value, which is why some properties attract lower LTVs than owners expect.

Director credit history still plays a role, even though it is secondary to the security. A string of recent county court judgments or an active insolvency history can make lenders nervous, not because the loan depends on personal income, but because it signals wider risk around how the business is being run. Most lenders will run a light touch credit check rather than a full affordability assessment of the type you would see with a mortgage. For a sense of which lenders are most active in this space, our review of leading UK bridging loan lenders is a useful starting point.

Speed of instruction on both sides matters more than people expect. We often see deals stall not because a lender is slow, but because a client takes several days to return signed documents or instruct a solicitor. Given that the whole point of this product is speed, treating the early stages with urgency on your end is just as important as choosing the right lender.

Finally, a bridging loan for working capital is a bridge in the true sense of the word. It is designed to get a business from one stable position to another, not to become a permanent fixture. Any broker or lender suggesting otherwise, or proposing repeated rollovers as a long-term strategy, is not looking after your interests. Used correctly, for the right reason, over the right term, it remains one of the most useful tools available to a UK business that owns property and needs cash quickly.

Costs and fees to budget for

Beyond the headline interest rate, you should budget for the full picture of costs before committing to short-term property finance. Arrangement fees, valuation fees, legal costs on both sides, and sometimes an exit fee can add up to a meaningful sum on top of the monthly interest. Asking a lender or broker for a full breakdown of costs upfront, rather than just the headline rate, avoids unwelcome surprises at completion.

You should also check whether interest is rolled up or serviced monthly, since this changes both the cash flow impact during the term and the total cost of borrowing. Rolled-up interest tends to suit businesses with tight monthly cash flow, while serviced interest can work out cheaper overall if the business can comfortably afford the monthly payments.

Frequently Asked Questions

How quickly can I get a bridging loan for working capital?
Most straightforward cases complete in seven to fourteen working days from application to funds landing, though this depends on how quickly valuations and legal work move and whether the title is clean.

What can a bridging loan for working capital be used for?
It can be used for almost any short-term business need, including settling tax bills, paying suppliers, buying stock, covering payroll gaps, or taking advantage of early payment discounts, provided there is a clear exit route.

How much does short-term property finance cost?
Rates for business-purpose bridging loans currently run from around 0.55% to 1.25% per month, with arrangement fees typically between 1% and 2% of the loan, plus valuation and legal costs.

Do I need a good credit history to qualify?
Director credit history plays a secondary role to the property security. Lenders generally run a light touch credit check rather than a full affordability assessment, though a poor history can make them more cautious.

What loan-to-value can I expect?
Typical loan-to-value ranges sit between 50% and 70% on residential security and 50% to 65% on commercial property, though some specialist lenders will stretch higher for very strong exits.

What do lenders need to see for the exit strategy?
Lenders want evidence such as a signed refinance offer, an agreed sale price, a contract confirming an incoming payment, or a credible trading forecast showing repayment capacity.

Can I use a bridging loan for working capital alongside my existing finance facilities?
Yes, most businesses that use this type of loan still run their normal overdraft, invoice finance or asset finance in the background. The bridge simply covers a specific, time-limited gap those facilities were not designed for.

If you own property and need funds quickly, it is worth exploring the full range of business funding solutions available before committing to a particular route. Alternatively, you can get a bridging loan quote directly from our team today.

mainEntity.name: How fast can auction finance actually complete?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most auction bridging loans complete in 7 to 14 working days once terms are agreed, which comfortably fits inside the standard 28-day auction deadline. Speed depends on how quickly a valuation can be instructed, how clean the legal pack is, and whether provisional terms were arranged before the sale rather than after.

mainEntity.name: What loan-to-value can I get on an auction bridging loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most lenders offer between 65% and 75% loan-to-value of the property's current market value for auction bridging loans. Higher percentages are occasionally available against stronger security or with additional collateral, but 70% is a realistic planning figure for most straightforward purchases.

acceptedAnswer.text: Missing the 28-day auction deadline usually means losing your deposit, typically 10% of the purchase price, and the auctioneer can resell the property and pursue you for any shortfall. This is exactly why arranging provisional finance terms before you bid, not after exchange, is so important.

content:
Auction finance uk is the practical solution for buyers who exchange contracts at a property auction and then have as little as 28 days to complete. Traditional mortgages cannot move that fast, so buyers turn to bridging loans for auction property instead, drawing down funds within days rather than the weeks or months a standard mortgage application takes.

Anyone who has bid at a UK auction house knows the rules do not bend. Once the hammer falls, you are contractually bound to complete, usually within 28 calendar days, sometimes 20 for online sales. Miss that deadline and you lose your deposit, usually 10% of the purchase price, and the auctioneer can resell the lot and chase you for the shortfall. Bridging loans exist because mainstream lending was never designed to move at this speed.

What this means in practice

You use a bridging loan to complete on time, then refinance onto a mortgage or sell the property once the immediate pressure is off. This separates the speed of completion from the speed of your long-term finance.

This matters because auction properties are often the ones mainstream lenders dislike most at first glance: no working kitchen, no bathroom, a short lease, or planning uncertainty. A bridging lender looks past the current state of the property and lends against what it is worth now and, where relevant, what it will be worth once works are done. That is why so many of our clients buying at auction come to us having already been told no by their high street bank.

We also see experienced landlords who understand exactly what they are buying and simply want the fastest route to completion, because speed itself is part of the deal they negotiated on price. For them, a bridging loan is a deliberate strategy, not a rescue product.

How it works

The mechanics are straightforward once you understand the timeline. You register for the auction, view the legal pack in advance, and ideally get provisional lending terms agreed before you bid, not after.

Once you win the lot, you exchange immediately and pay your deposit. From that point the clock starts. A bridging lender will need a valuation, sometimes a desktop valuation if the case allows it, proof of your exit strategy, and confirmation of the loan-to-value they are comfortable with, typically 65% to 75% of the property's current market value for a straightforward case.

Legal work runs in parallel with underwriting rather than after it, which is the single biggest reason bridging completions are so much faster than mortgage completions. Many specialist bridging lenders use the same solicitor panel for both sides of the transaction to shave days off the process. Interest is usually charged monthly and can often be retained within the loan, so you are not finding cash for interest payments during the term itself.

Typical scenarios

Numbers make this real, so here are two anonymised examples we have arranged.

A landlord in Norwich bought a three-bed terrace at auction for £142,000 with no working bathroom and an expired gas certificate. He needed £99,000, 70% LTV, over a 9 month term, exiting via a buy-to-let refinance once the works were complete and the property was let. Funds were released in 11 working days from exchange, well inside the 28 day deadline, and he refinanced onto a standard buy-to-let mortgage at month 6.

A developer client bought a former shop with residential upstairs at a Birmingham auction for £310,000, planning to convert it into three flats. He borrowed £217,000 at 70% LTV against the purchase, with a further drawdown for refurbishment costs agreed on day one as part of a wider developer finance package. His exit was a sale of two of the three units on completion of works, with the third retained and refinanced. Completion happened in 14 working days.

What lenders look for

Lenders want three things above all else: a credible exit, adequate security, and a borrower who can evidence both quickly. Get these right and a bridging loan can complete in 7 to 14 working days. Get them wrong and you will miss the auction deadline.

Loan-to-value for auction purchases typically sits between 65% and 75% of open market value, occasionally higher against very strong security or with additional collateral. Lenders want a recent valuation, ideally instructed the moment you have provisional terms rather than after exchange, because valuation delays are the most common cause of missed completions we see. They will also want to see the legal pack reviewed by your solicitor before you bid, because unusual lease terms, restrictive covenants or missing title information can stall a case even when the finance itself is ready to go.

Evidence of exit matters just as much as the property. If your exit is a sale, lenders want to see realistic comparable evidence for the resale price, not optimistic guesswork. If your exit is a refinance onto a mortgage, they want to know you would plausibly qualify for that mortgage once works are done, including rental coverage calculations for buy-to-let. The most common reason we see auction bridging applications declined at the eleventh hour is an exit that was never properly tested against the numbers, only assumed.

Common mistakes

The single biggest mistake is bidding before finance is arranged. Provisional terms should be in place before you register a paddle, not after the hammer falls, because a lender declining the case after exchange leaves you personally on the hook for the deposit and any shortfall on resale.

The second mistake is underestimating refurbishment costs. Auction properties are frequently sold precisely because they need work, and lenders will factor realistic costs into their assessment. Borrowers who lowball the schedule of works often find themselves short of cash mid-project, which then jeopardises the exit.

Buyers also regularly skip a proper legal pack review, assuming their solicitor will catch anything important once instructed. By then it can be too late to renegotiate or walk away, since the exchange has already happened. A rushed search or missing planning history costs far less to deal with before you bid than after.

Alternatives or comparisons

A bridging loan is the right tool when speed is the constraint, not when the property itself is fundamentally unmortgageable or your numbers do not stack up. If a standard mortgage lender would happily fund the purchase and you have more than 28 days available, a mortgage will almost always be cheaper and a bridging loan would be the wrong choice.

Development finance is the better option than a straightforward bridging loan when the project involves substantial structural work, a change of use, or new build units, because those facilities are built around staged drawdowns against build costs rather than a single advance. If your credit history and income would support a mainstream buy-to-let mortgage and there is no genuine time pressure, applying for that directly and skipping the bridge altogether will save you money in fees and interest.

Auction finance earns its cost where the 28-day deadline itself is the constraint. No other mainstream product reliably completes that fast, which is why it remains the default choice for serious auction buyers.

How to get the best outcome

Get an agreement in principle before you bid, not after, and choose a lender or broker who understands auction timelines rather than a generalist who has never dealt with a 28-day completion. It genuinely makes a difference to how quickly your case moves through underwriting.

Instruct your solicitor to review the legal pack the moment it is available, ideally days before the sale, and flag anything unusual immediately. Have your deposit funds ready and confirmed, and be realistic with your refurbishment budget rather than optimistic. If you want to compare structures before you commit, take time to compare bridging loan rates across a handful of specialist lenders rather than accepting the first quote you see, since pricing and speed both vary more than most buyers expect.

Boxx Finance arranges auction bridging loans across England and Wales, and we see the same pattern repeatedly: buyers who plan finance before the sale complete comfortably, and buyers who leave it until after exchange spend the next three weeks stressed. We would rather have the conversation early.

Summary

Auction finance uk exists to solve one specific problem: the 28-day completion deadline that mainstream mortgages cannot meet. Used properly, a bridging loan lets you buy with confidence at auction and refinance or sell once the pressure is off, and Boxx Finance can help structure that from agreement in principle through to completion. For a broader look at short-term lending options beyond auction purchases, our UK commercial funding solutions hub covers the full range of products available to property buyers and developers. If you are weighing up whether a bridge is right for your purchase, our guide to how bridging loans work in general is a useful starting point, and our breakdown of current UK bridging loan rates will help you budget accurately before you bid.

We arrange auction bridging loans for buyers and developers across the country, including bridging loans in London, bridging loans in Birmingham, bridging loans in Norwich and bridging loans in Reading. If your next auction date is already booked in, now is the time to arrange a bridging loan quote rather than waiting until after the sale.

Frequently Asked Questions

How fast can auction finance actually complete?

Most auction bridging loans complete in 7 to 14 working days once terms are agreed, which comfortably fits inside the standard 28-day auction deadline. Speed depends on how quickly a valuation can be instructed, how clean the legal pack is, and whether provisional terms were arranged before the sale rather than after.

What loan-to-value can I get on an auction bridging loan?

Most lenders offer between 65% and 75% loan-to-value of the property's current market value for auction bridging loans. Higher percentages are occasionally available against stronger security or with additional collateral, but 70% is a realistic planning figure for most straightforward purchases.

What happens if my bridging loan does not complete in time for the auction deadline?

Missing the 28-day auction deadline usually means losing your deposit, typically 10% of the purchase price, and the auctioneer can resell the property and pursue you for any shortfall. This is exactly why arranging provisional finance terms before you bid, not after exchange, is so important.

Can I get auction finance on a property that needs major refurbishment?

Yes, bridging lenders regularly fund auction properties needing significant refurbishment because they lend against current value and, where relevant, projected value once works are complete. This is often structured as developer finance with staged drawdowns for larger refurbishment or conversion projects.

Is a bridging loan more expensive than a normal mortgage for buying at auction?

Bridging loans generally cost more per month than a standard mortgage, reflecting the speed and flexibility they offer, but they are usually held for a short term of 6 to 12 months. The overall cost is best compared against the alternative of losing your deposit by missing the auction completion deadline.

Do I need to arrange finance before I bid at auction?

Arranging provisional lending terms before you bid is strongly recommended because bidding without agreed finance risks losing your deposit if a lender later declines the case. Reputable brokers can usually provide an agreement in principle within a day or two, which gives you confidence to bid.

content:
A bridging loan second charge ltd company is a short-term loan secured against a company-owned property that already has a mortgage or loan against it, sitting behind that existing charge in priority. Businesses use a bridging loan second charge ltd company arrangement when they need to raise capital quickly without disturbing, redeeming or refinancing the first charge lender. It is one of the fastest ways for a limited company to unlock equity tied up in property. If you want to understand the basics first, our guide to what bridging finance actually involves is a good starting point.

We arrange these regularly for company directors who own commercial units, HMOs, or development sites through a limited company and need funds released within weeks rather than months, whether they need bridging loans in London or elsewhere in the UK. The structure is straightforward in principle, but the underwriting requires more attention than a first charge bridging loan, and mistakes at application stage create most delays.

What surprises many directors is how often the need arises from good fortune rather than a crisis. A company might have agreed an excellent price on a second property or spotted a short window to buy back stock at a discount, and simply wants to avoid touching a first charge sitting on a competitive rate. A second charge bridge lets that equity be tapped without triggering early repayment charges or a full remortgage process on the existing facility.

What this means in practice

In practice, a second charge bridging loan means two separate lenders hold security over the same property, with the first charge lender ranking ahead for repayment if the property is ever sold or repossessed. The second charge lender takes on more risk because they are repaid only after the first lender is settled in full.

For a limited company, this typically means the business already has a commercial mortgage, a development loan, or a first charge bridging loan on an asset, and now needs additional funds without unwinding that arrangement. Common reasons include releasing equity for a deposit on another purchase, funding a refurbishment, covering a VAT bill on a property transaction, or bridging a cash flow gap while a sale completes.

The first charge lender almost always needs to give formal consent before a second charge can be registered. This is called a deed of priority or consent to second charge, and it is frequently the single biggest hold-up in these transactions. Lenders vary hugely in how quickly they respond to this request, and some high street banks take three to four weeks just to issue consent.

Not every first charge lender charges for this consent, but many do. Fees for issuing a deed of priority typically range from £100 to £500, sometimes more if the lender insists on instructing their own solicitor to review the paperwork. These are small sums in the context of the overall loan, but they catch directors out if nobody has budgeted for them upfront. If you'd rather talk it through with a specialist, you can get a bridging loan quote.

How it works

A second charge bridging loan works by the lender taking a legal charge registered at HM Land Registry behind the existing first charge, secured against the equity remaining in the property after the first loan is accounted for.

The lender calculates available equity by taking the property's current open market value, subtracting the outstanding balance on the first charge, and lending a percentage of what remains. Most second charge bridging lenders will go up to 65-70% combined loan to value across both charges, though this varies by lender appetite and asset type. For a broader view of pricing across the market, see our breakdown of current bridging loan rates.

For a limited company borrower, lenders examine the company structure, checking the directors' personal guarantees, the company's trading history if it is trading, and the assets and liabilities of any group structure. Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) set up purely to hold property are common in this space and lenders are generally comfortable with them provided the exit is credible.

Interest is almost always charged on a monthly basis and can be retained, rolled up, or serviced, depending on the lender and the company's cash position. Retained interest is popular with second charge bridges because it removes the need for monthly payments, which matters when the company is already servicing the first charge. Rates on second charge bridging loans for limited companies typically sit between 0.85% and 1.25% per month, reflecting the increased risk position compared to a first charge.

Arrangement fees usually run between 1.5% and 2.5% of the gross loan, plus valuation fees and legal costs on both sides. On an £85,000 loan, for example, a 2% arrangement fee equates to £1,700, plus a valuation fee that might run from £350 to £750 depending on the property type and location.

Once the valuation, legal work and first charge consent are all in place, funds can be released. This is where fast property finance solutions for limited companies genuinely earn their keep, because a well-prepared case with cooperative solicitors on both sides can complete in two to three weeks even with the added complexity of a second charge.

Typical scenarios

Real examples make this easier to picture, and we see variations of the same two scenarios most weeks.

A residential investor scenario: a landlord operating through a limited company owned a buy-to-let property in Reading worth £410,000 with an existing buy-to-let mortgage of £220,000 (54% LTV on the first charge). The company needed £85,000 to complete a cash purchase at auction of a second property before the standard 28-day auction deadline. We arranged a second charge bridging loan for £85,000, taking the combined LTV to 74%, over a 9-month term, with the exit being a remortgage of the newly purchased property. The first charge lender issued consent in nine working days and funds were released 17 working days after initial enquiry. We handle similar cases for bridging loans in Reading on a regular basis.

The monthly cost on that facility, at a rate of 0.95% per month retained, worked out at roughly £808 a month rolled into the loan, meaning the company had no monthly outgoings to find while both properties were being sorted. That mattered to the director, who was already stretched managing rental income across the existing portfolio.

A developer scenario: a small development company in Birmingham held a part-converted commercial building with a first charge development loan of £340,000 against a current value of £520,000 (65% LTV). Costs had overrun and the company needed a further £60,000 to complete the final phase before selling three units. We placed a second charge bridging loan of £60,000, a 12-month term, exiting on the sale of the completed units, with funds released 21 working days after application due to a slower-moving first charge lender needing internal committee sign-off for consent. This is a pattern we see often with bridging loans in Birmingham involving part-converted commercial stock.

In that case the arrangement fee was 2.25%, or £1,350, and the rate was 1.1% per month given the commercial nature of the security and the tighter combined LTV. The director had originally hoped for faster completion, but the delay in consent turned out to be the only real friction point in an otherwise straightforward case.

Both cases show the same pattern: the loan itself is quick to arrange, but the first charge lender's response time on consent is the variable that determines the real timeline.

What lenders look for

Lenders assessing a second charge bridging loan for a limited company focus on combined loan to value, the strength of the exit, and how cooperative the first charge lender is likely to be. This is one reason it pays to find a bridging loan broker who already knows how individual lenders behave on consent requests.

Most second charge bridging lenders in the UK will lend up to 65-75% combined LTV, though some specialist lenders will stretch to 80% on strong residential security with a clear exit. Commercial and semi-commercial property tends to attract more conservative LTVs, often capped around 60-65% combined, because valuations are less liquid. Directors comparing options, including those arranging bridging loans in Norwich, should check our roundup of leading bridging loan lenders before committing.

Lenders scrutinise the exit closely. Acceptable exits include a sale already under offer with a solicitor's memorandum of sale, a remortgage agreement in principle, or a development exit supported by a realistic build programme and sales comparables. Lenders want to see this in writing, not just described verbally.

Directors' personal circumstances still matter even though the borrower is a limited company. Most second charge bridging lenders will run a credit check on all directors giving personal guarantees, and will want to understand any adverse credit history, even where the underlying asset and exit are strong. A clean guarantor profile can speed underwriting considerably, while unexplained defaults or CCJs tend to trigger extra questions and sometimes a higher rate.

Timescales from enquiry to funds typically run 2-4 weeks for a second charge, longer than the 7-10 days sometimes achievable on a straightforward first charge bridging loan, because of the added consent step. The most common reason we see these applications declined or delayed is the first charge lender refusing or dragging their feet on consent, sometimes because their own terms and conditions prohibit second charges entirely. It is worth checking the first mortgage deed before you apply.

Loan typeTypical combined LTV capTypical time to funds
First charge bridging loan75-80%7-14 days
Second charge bridging loan (residential)70-80%14-28 days
Second charge bridging loan (commercial/semi-commercial)60-65%21-35 days

Common mistakes

The most frequent mistake is applying for a second charge bridging loan before checking whether the first charge lender permits it at all. Some buy-to-let mortgage products explicitly prohibit further charges without written consent, and finding this out mid-application wastes valuable time.

Another common error is underestimating the combined LTV headroom. Directors sometimes assume the second charge lender will lend against the full current value of the property, forgetting the first charge balance is deducted first. This leads to disappointment when the offered loan amount is significantly lower than expected.

We also see companies instruct solicitors who have never handled a second charge before, which slows everything down considerably. A solicitor unfamiliar with deeds of priority can add a week or more simply through unfamiliarity with the paperwork. Using a solicitor experienced in bridging transactions, ideally one already on the lender's panel, removes a lot of friction.

It is also a mistake to leave the request for consent until after the loan has already been agreed in principle. It is far better to contact the first charge lender at the very start of the process, even informally, to gauge whether they are likely to cooperate and how long they typically take. Some lenders have a dedicated team for this, others route it through general customer service, and the difference in turnaround can be weeks rather than days.

Directors also sometimes forget to factor in the cost of the first charge lender's own legal fees, which are usually charged to the borrower even though that solicitor is acting for the first charge lender's interests, not the company's. Budgeting an extra £300 to £600 for this avoids an unwelcome surprise at completion.

Finally, weak or vague exit strategies are a recurring theme. Lenders rarely say this outright, but an exit described as vague or unsupported by evidence is one of the quickest ways to see an application slow down or fail entirely.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a second charge bridging loan for a limited company?
It is a short-term loan secured against a company-owned property that already has a first charge mortgage or loan against it, with the new lender ranking behind the existing lender for repayment.

Do I need the first charge lender's permission for a second charge?
Yes. The first charge lender almost always needs to issue formal consent, known as a deed of priority, before a second charge can be registered, and this step is often the biggest cause of delay.

How much can a limited company borrow with a second charge bridging loan?
Most lenders will go up to 65-75% combined loan to value across both charges, with some specialist lenders stretching to 80% on strong residential security with a clear exit.

What rates and fees should I expect?
Rates typically sit between 0.85% and 1.25% per month, with arrangement fees usually running between 1.5% and 2.5% of the gross loan, plus valuation and legal costs.

How long does it take to complete a second charge bridging loan?
Timescales typically run 2-4 weeks, longer than a straightforward first charge bridging loan, mainly because of the time needed to obtain first charge lender consent.

What is the most common reason applications are delayed or declined?
It is rarely the borrower's credit profile. Most delays or declines come from the first charge lender being slow to respond to, or refusing, the consent request.

Can I get a second charge bridging loan quote for my limited company?
Yes. You can get a bridging loan quote by speaking with a broker who can assess your first charge position and likely lender appetite before you apply.

title: Bridging Loans for Non-Standard Construction in the UK
excerpt: Non-standard construction property is often declined by mainstream lenders, but bridging loans can fund it quickly against value and exit strategy rather than build type alone.
metaTitle: Bridging loan non standard construction uk
metaDescription: Struggling to fund a non-standard construction property? Bridging loans can secure it fast when high street lenders say no. See how rates, LTVs and exits work.
keywords: non standard construction bridging loan, bridging loan unusual property types, short-term property finance non standard build, non standard construction mortgage alternative, bridging loans for concrete construction properties, developer finance non standard construction, fast property finance unusual buildings
author: Mark Higgins
content:
A bridging loan non standard construction UK deal is short-term property finance secured against a building that mainstream mortgage lenders won't touch, such as timber frame, concrete, steel frame, or system-built properties. Bridging lenders fund these quickly because bridging loan non standard construction uk lenders assess the property's value and your exit plan rather than requiring standard construction credentials. It fills the gap left when high street banks decline the application outright. For a broader look at how this type of finance works, see our guide to what bridging finance actually involves.

We see this problem constantly. A perfectly good property, structurally sound and sometimes recently renovated, receives an automatic rejection from a mainstream lender simply because it's listed as no-fines concrete, Airey, Cornish Unit, or a steel-framed prefab from the 1960s. The building itself might be fine. The lender's tick-box criteria isn't flexible enough to look past the label.

Many borrowers are surprised by how common this actually is. Well over a million non-standard construction properties exist across the UK, many of them built during the post-war housing push when materials like steel and concrete were used to speed up construction and get families housed quickly. Decades later, those same properties face penalties from mortgage criteria that simply weren't designed with them in mind. The buildings haven't failed. The lending system hasn't caught up with them.

What this means in practice

In practice, it means the finance route for your purchase or refinance shifts away from a standard mortgage and towards a specialist short-term loan that's priced and structured differently.

Non-standard construction covers a surprisingly wide range of building types. Timber frame homes built before certain dates, concrete panel or prefabricated reinforced concrete (PRC) houses, steel frame properties, flat roof constructions, thatched roofs, and high-rise properties built with certain 1960s and 1970s system-build methods all fall into this bracket. Some of these are perfectly mortgageable through specialist high street products. Others are almost impossible to mortgage conventionally at all.

The distinction matters because it changes your options. A timber frame house built in the last twenty years to modern building regulations is a very different proposition to a 1950s Airey house with an unrepaired steel frame. Lenders know this too, which is why blanket refusals are so common. It's simply easier for a mainstream underwriter to decline anything outside standard brick and block than to assess each case individually.

Short-term property finance works here because the lender underwrites against the property's market value, its condition, and your exit strategy rather than a rigid construction checklist. Non-standard builds that would be flatly refused by a mainstream bank become financeable. The trade-off is a higher rate and a shorter term, which is why getting the exit right matters so much. If you want to see how rates on these deals compare, our breakdown of current bridging loan rates is worth a read.

Bridging isn't meant to be a long-term solution here. It's a tool to get you from an urgent purchase or refinance deadline to a point where a more permanent, cheaper form of finance can take over. Borrowers who treat it as a stopgap with a clear plan for what comes next tend to have a much smoother experience than those who go in without one. If you'd like to talk through your situation with a specialist, you can get a bridging loan quote before committing to anything.

How it works

A bridging lender secures the loan against the property, typically at a lower loan-to-value than they'd offer on standard construction, and charges monthly interest that's usually rolled up or deducted at completion rather than paid month to month.

The process starts with a valuation from a surveyor who understands the specific construction type. This matters more than people expect. A generic valuer who doesn't recognise the property's construction method or who applies standard assumptions to a non-standard build can produce a valuation that undersells the property or flags issues that don't actually exist. Using a surveyor experienced with the specific build type, whether that's a Wimpey No-Fines house or a Dorran system build, tends to produce a more accurate and often more favourable outcome.

We'd always recommend borrowers ask upfront which surveyor the lender intends to instruct and whether that surveyor has direct experience with the construction type in question. It's a simple question that can save weeks of delay. A mismatched valuer can end up recommending a full structural survey partway through the process, which pushes timescales out and sometimes derails the deal entirely if a completion deadline is looming.

Once the valuation is back, the lender confirms terms, instructs legal work, and funds typically release within two to four weeks from application. Sometimes this happens faster if the property is unencumbered and the borrower's solicitor moves quickly. Interest rates for non-standard construction bridging tend to sit slightly above standard bridging rates, reflecting the marginally higher risk profile the lender is taking on, though the gap has narrowed as more specialist lenders have entered this space.

As a rough guide, borrowers should expect monthly rates somewhere between 0.85% and 1.35% depending on the construction type, the LTV requested, and the strength of the exit. Arrangement fees typically run from 1% to 2% of the loan, with valuation and legal costs on top. These figures move around depending on the lender and the specifics of the deal, so treat them as a starting point for budgeting rather than a fixed quote.

Exit fees are less common than they used to be, but some lenders still apply them, so it's worth checking the full cost of the loan rather than just the headline rate. A good broker will lay out the total cost in cash terms, not just percentages, so there are no surprises at redemption.

Typical scenarios

Real deals make this clearer than theory. Here are two examples, one residential and one developer-led, both anonymised.

A couple in Reading found a 1960s no-fines concrete semi they wanted to buy at auction for £210,000. No mainstream lender would touch it without extensive remedial works and a specialist survey the vendor hadn't commissioned. We arranged a bridging loan of £126,000, 60% LTV, over a 9-month term. The exit was a specialist non-standard construction mortgage once the couple had commissioned an engineer's report confirming the structure was sound. Funds completed in 16 working days, well within the auction deadline. Buyers looking at properties through bridging loans in Reading run into this exact scenario often.

What made this case work was preparation. The couple had already spoken to a structural engineer familiar with no-fines construction before the auction. When the lender asked for evidence to support the exit, it was ready to go rather than being commissioned from scratch under time pressure. That single decision probably saved them two to three weeks.

A developer in Birmingham bought a steel-framed 1970s office block for conversion into eight residential units. The purchase price was £480,000 and the developer needed £312,000, 65% LTV, over a 12-month term to complete the purchase and fund early-stage works. The exit was a sale of the completed units, staged as they were finished, with the first two units sold within nine months covering most of the loan. This is a classic developer finance bridging structure, where the non-standard construction issue applies to the existing building rather than the finished product. Developers working on similar projects and needing bridging loans in Birmingham often face the same staged drawdown considerations.

This case also illustrates why staged drawdowns can be useful on non-standard construction projects. Rather than releasing the full £312,000 upfront, the lender released funds in tranches tied to the completion of specific building stages, verified by periodic site inspections. This kept the developer's interest costs down in the early months and gave the lender confidence that the works were progressing as planned before further funds were released. Similar patterns show up in bridging loans in London and bridging loans in Norwich, where non-standard construction stock is also common.

What lenders look for

Lenders look for a clear valuation from a surveyor familiar with the specific construction type, a realistic loan-to-value that reflects the property's true resaleability, and a credible, evidenced exit strategy.

Loan-to-value on non-standard construction bridging typically runs from 50% to 70%, lower than the 75% or 80% sometimes seen on standard construction bridging. Concrete system-builds and certain steel-frame types often sit at the more conservative end, while more modern timber frame or flat-roof properties in good condition can attract slightly higher LTVs. Timescales from enquiry to funds average two to four weeks, though we've completed straightforward cases in under two weeks when the valuation and legal work move without delay.

Security needs to be a first legal charge in most cases, though second charge bridging is possible on non-standard construction if there's sufficient equity. Lenders want to see evidence of the exit, whether that's an agreement in principle for a refinance mortgage, a signed sale agreement, or a schedule of works with a realistic completion timeline for developer exits. The most common reason we see these applications declined isn't the construction type itself, it's an exit strategy that's vague or unsupported by evidence.

A borrower who turns up with a specific, well-evidenced plan will almost always get a better rate and a smoother process than one who simply says they intend to sell or remortgage in due course. Bringing an agreement in principle from a specialist mortgage lender or a structural engineer's report confirming the property meets lending criteria can make the difference between an approval in principle within 48 hours and weeks of back and forth. It's also worth comparing options across specialist bridging loan lenders before committing to one provider.

It's also worth asking your broker to check whether the lender has funded that specific construction type before. Some lenders have an informal blacklist of certain system builds they simply won't touch, regardless of condition or LTV, while others have built up genuine expertise in exactly those property types. Knowing which is which before you apply saves time and avoids a declined application sitting on record unnecessarily.

Don't underestimate the value of getting the paperwork right from day one. Title deeds, planning history, any previous remedial works certificates, and building control sign-offs should all be gathered before the application goes in wherever possible. Non-standard construction cases already carry extra scrutiny, and a complete file from the outset tends to move through underwriting far more smoothly than one where documents are chased piecemeal.

Costs to budget for

Beyond the headline monthly rate, borrowers should budget for arrangement fees, valuation costs, legal fees on both sides, and potentially a broker fee. It's worth asking for a full breakdown in cash terms before committing, so there are no surprises when the loan is redeemed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I get a bridging loan on a non-standard construction property?
Yes. Bridging lenders assess the property's value, condition, and your exit strategy rather than declining automatically based on construction type, which is why non-standard builds that mainstream mortgage lenders refuse are often financeable through bridging.

What construction types count as non-standard?
Timber frame, concrete panel or PRC houses, steel frame properties, flat roof buildings, thatched roofs, and certain 1960s and 1970s system-built high-rises are all typically classed as non-standard construction.

What loan-to-value can I expect on non-standard construction bridging?
LTVs typically run from 50% to 70%, lower than the 75-80% sometimes available on standard construction bridging, with concrete system-builds and steel-frame types often at the more conservative end.

How quickly can a non-standard construction bridging loan complete?
Most cases complete within two to four weeks from application, though straightforward deals with a cooperative solicitor and an unencumbered property can complete in under two weeks.

Why do I need a specialist surveyor for a non-standard construction bridging loan?
A surveyor unfamiliar with the specific construction type can undervalue the property or flag issues that don't exist, whereas an experienced surveyor produces a more accurate valuation and helps avoid delays from unnecessary further surveys.

What exit strategies do lenders accept for non-standard construction bridging?
Common exits include refinancing onto a specialist non-standard construction mortgage, a signed sale agreement, or, for developers, a schedule of works with a realistic completion and sale timeline.

What rates and fees should I budget for?
Expect monthly rates of roughly 0.85% to 1.35% depending on construction type, LTV, and exit strength, plus arrangement fees of 1% to 2% and separate valuation and legal costs.

A bridging loan for property below market value is short-term property finance secured against the true valuation of a property rather than the discounted price you're paying for it. This allows buyers and developers to move quickly on deals where the vendor has accepted less than the property is worth. Lenders lend against valuation, not purchase price, which is why below market value deals work so well with short-term property finance when the discount is genuine and provable.

We arrange these deals every week at Boxx Finance, and the below market value angle is one of the most misunderstood parts of bridging. Buyers often assume a discount automatically means more borrowing available. The reality is more nuanced, but when structured correctly it becomes one of the smartest ways to buy property with very little of your own cash tied up. Read our guide on what bridging finance actually involves if you're new to this type of lending.

Over the years we've seen every version of this deal. From straightforward probate purchases to complicated chains involving distressed landlords and time-pressured vendors, the principle stays the same each time. A genuine discount, properly evidenced, can dramatically reduce the cash a buyer needs to put in. The word genuine carries significant weight in that sentence, because it's where most enquiries either succeed or fall apart.

What surprises many first-time bridging borrowers is how much paperwork sits behind what looks like a simple cash-in deal on the surface. Lenders in this space have seen every trick used to manufacture an artificial discount, so they build their processes around catching that before it becomes a problem. Understanding this upfront saves brokers and borrowers considerable wasted time. If you'd like to talk through your own situation, you can get a bridging loan quote from our team directly.

Below market value bridging is not a niche curiosity used by a handful of specialist investors. It forms a mainstream part of the bridging market, and most experienced lenders have a clear policy on how they treat it. The difference between a smooth completion and a stalled application usually comes down to preparation rather than the deal itself being unworkable.

What this means in practice

In practice, a below market value bridging loan means the lender bases their loan-to-value calculation on an independent RICS valuation of the property, not on the price agreed with the seller.

Say you agree to buy a property for £220,000 that an independent valuer confirms is worth £280,000. A lender offering 75% LTV on the valuation would lend up to £210,000. Because your actual purchase price is only £220,000, you'd only need to find £10,000 plus costs, rather than the £70,000 you'd need under a standard 75% LTV calculation on price.

This is the entire appeal of BMV bridging. Your discount effectively becomes your deposit. Auction buyers, probate buyers and developers picking up distressed stock chase these deals hard, which is why lenders specialising in this space have built an entire niche around it.

The catch is that lenders won't simply take your word for the discount. They need to understand why the seller accepted below value, and that story needs to stack up under scrutiny.

We often tell clients to think of it from the lender's point of view. They're being asked to lend a high percentage of the true value against a property that, on paper, someone was happy to sell for far less. Naturally they want to know what they're missing. Nine times out of ten there's a perfectly sound reason, but it still needs to be documented properly.

Costs and fees to budget for

Costs also need factoring in beyond the headline cash requirement. Arrangement fees on bridging loans typically run between 1.5% and 2% of the loan amount. Valuation fees vary depending on property type and value, but budget somewhere between £400 and £1,000 for a standard residential valuation. Legal fees, both your own and the lender's, also need to be covered, and most lenders expect these to be settled from your own funds rather than added to the loan.

Monthly interest rates on bridging loans currently sit broadly between 0.55% and 0.95%, depending on the lender, the loan-to-value, and the strength of the exit strategy. On a £210,000 loan at 0.75% per month, that's roughly £1,575 in interest each month. Many lenders allow this to be rolled up rather than paid monthly, which helps cash flow during a refurbishment or resale period. For a fuller breakdown of current pricing, see our article on current bridging loan rates.

Run the full numbers before committing to a deal rather than just focusing on the cash needed at completion. Taking the example above, a six-month bridge at 0.75% a month with fees rolled in could easily add £10,000 to £12,000 in total borrowing costs once arrangement fees, exit fees and rolled-up interest are included. That's still often cheaper than the equivalent cash needed under a standard purchase, but it needs to be part of your decision, not an afterthought once the loan is already agreed.

Exit fees are another cost that catch some borrowers off guard. Not every lender charges one, but where they do it's typically between 1% and 1.5% of the loan amount, payable when you redeem the bridge. We always ask lenders to confirm this upfront so clients aren't surprised at redemption stage.

How it works

The mechanics start with an instructed RICS valuation, because the whole loan structure hinges on an independent professional confirming the true value, not the buyer's opinion of it.

Once instructed, the valuer visits the property, assesses condition, comparable sales, and market conditions, and produces a figure. The lender then applies their LTV percentage to that figure, not the purchase price. Most bridging lenders will lend 70-75% of open market value, occasionally stretching to 80% for strong cases with clean exits.

Solicitors then need to see evidence of why the discount exists. Common legitimate reasons include probate sales where executors want a quick, certain completion, repossessions, distressed sales from landlords needing to exit quickly, or vendors selling to a connected party at a reduced price for genuine commercial reasons.

Where the discount comes from a related-party sale, such as a family member selling to another family member, lenders apply extra scrutiny and often cap the LTV lower. The heightened risk that the discount has been engineered rather than genuinely arrived at through market pressure justifies this caution.

We always advise clients to gather their evidence early rather than waiting for the solicitor to ask for it. A short written explanation from the vendor's solicitor, a copy of the probate grant where relevant, or details of the repossession timeline can all speed things up considerably. Lenders move quickly once they trust the story, and slowly when they don't.

Timescales for these deals typically run four to six weeks from application to completion, assuming the valuation comes back promptly and there are no title issues. Auction purchases often need to move faster, sometimes within the standard 28-day completion window, which is why speaking to a broker before you bid is far better than scrambling afterwards.

Regional considerations

Demand and lender appetite for below market value deals can vary by region. We regularly arrange bridging loans in London where auction and probate stock moves quickly, as well as bridging loans in Birmingham for investors targeting distressed landlord sales. We also see strong demand for bridging loans in Norwich and bridging loans in Reading, particularly from developers picking up below value stock outside the capital.

Exit strategy matters just as much as the discount itself. Lenders want to know how you'll repay the bridge, whether that's through a refinance onto a standard mortgage once any works are complete, or through a straightforward resale. A weak or vague exit plan can derail an otherwise strong application, even where the discount and valuation are solid.

Property condition also plays a role in how the deal is structured. If the property needs refurbishment before it can be refinanced or sold, some lenders will release funds in stages. An initial drawdown comes at completion with further tranches released as work progresses and is verified. This suits developers and experienced landlords who are used to managing works alongside finance drawdowns.

Credit history and background still get checked, even though the loan is asset-backed. Lenders want comfort that the borrower has a credible plan and the experience, or the right team around them, to see the deal through. First-time bridging borrowers aren't excluded, but they may find themselves working with lenders who specialise in supporting less experienced buyers, sometimes at a slightly higher rate to reflect that.

Property type has a bearing too. Standard bricks and mortar houses and flats tend to move through valuation and legal stages fastest. Ex-local authority flats, properties with cladding, or those above commercial units can slow things down. Valuers and lenders both apply extra caution to these categories regardless of the discount involved.

We also see a fair number of deals where the below market value element sits alongside a light refurbishment plan, rather than a straight resale. In these cases, the lender may want a schedule of works and a rough costed budget before agreeing terms, even at application stage. It doesn't need to be a full RICS building survey, but a clear, realistic breakdown of what's being spent and why helps enormously when the file goes to underwriting.

Insurance is another point worth flagging early. Lenders will expect buildings insurance to be in place from exchange, and where the property is unoccupied or being refurbished, standard residential policies often won't cover it. Specialist unoccupied property insurance is usually needed, and arrange this before completion rather than leaving it until the last minute.

Choosing the right lender

At Boxx Finance, our role is largely about matching the deal to the right lender from the outset. Not every lender treats below market value deals the same way, and some are considerably more comfortable with probate or repossession discounts than others. Getting this match right first time avoids wasted valuation fees and speeds up completion considerably. This matters enormously when you're working against an auction deadline or a vendor who wants a fast, clean sale. Our comparison of the best bridging loan lenders in the UK is a useful starting point if you want to understand how different lenders approach these deals.

Don't underestimate the value of a broker who's seen the specific type of discount you're dealing with before. A lender who's comfortable with probate sales might baulk at a connected-party discount, and vice versa. Knowing which door to knock on first, rather than applying broadly and hoping, is often the difference between a deal completing in four weeks and one that drags on for three months.

Frequently Asked Questions

What counts as a genuine below market value discount?
A genuine discount is one with a clear, documented reason behind it, such as a probate sale, repossession, or a distressed landlord needing a quick exit. Lenders want evidence the vendor had a real motivation to sell below value, rather than the price simply being manufactured to inflate borrowing.

How much can I borrow on a below market value bridging loan?
Most lenders will lend 70-75% of the independently valued open market value, occasionally up to 80% for strong cases with a clean exit strategy. This is calculated against valuation, not the discounted purchase price, which is what makes these deals so cash-efficient.

Do I need a RICS valuation for a BMV bridging loan?
Yes. The entire structure depends on an independent RICS valuation confirming the true value of the property. The lender's loan-to-value calculation is based on this figure rather than the agreed purchase price.

How long does a below market value bridging loan take to complete?
Typically four to six weeks from application to completion, assuming the valuation comes back promptly and there are no title issues. Auction purchases often need to move faster, sometimes within a 28-day window.

What fees should I budget for on a bridging loan?
Expect arrangement fees of around 1.5% to 2% of the loan amount, valuation fees between £400 and £1,000, legal fees for both parties, and potentially an exit fee of 1% to 1.5% payable on redemption.

Are related-party sales treated differently by lenders?
Yes. Where a discount comes from a sale between connected parties, such as family members, lenders apply extra scrutiny and often cap the loan-to-value lower. The higher risk of the discount being engineered rather than market-driven justifies this approach.

What happens if the property needs refurbishment before I can exit the bridge?
Some lenders will release funds in stages, with an initial drawdown at completion and further tranches released as work progresses and is verified. This suits developers and experienced landlords managing works alongside finance drawdowns.

If you're ready to move forward, our team can help you get a bridging loan quote. Alternatively, explore our full range of funding solutions to see how bridging fits alongside other property finance options.
