mainEntity.name: Can you get a mortgage on an unmortgageable property in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: You cannot get a standard mortgage on a genuinely unmortgageable property, which is exactly why bridging loans exist as an alternative. Mainstream lenders decline properties without a working kitchen or bathroom, with structural defects, or with short leases, whereas bridging lenders assess the asset and your exit plan instead of applying standard mortgage criteria.

mainEntity.name: What makes a property unmortgageable?

acceptedAnswer.text: A property is usually classed as unmortgageable when it lacks a functioning kitchen or bathroom, has significant structural issues, contains flammable cladding, has a lease under 70 years, or is deemed uninhabitable by a valuer. Any of these triggers an automatic decline from most high street mortgage lenders regardless of the buyer's financial strength.

mainEntity.name: How much can I borrow with a bridging loan on an unmortgageable property?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most bridging lenders will advance 60% to 75% of the property's current value, or up to around 70% of its projected post-works value where refurbishment or conversion works are planned. The exact figure depends on the property type, location, condition, and how strong your evidenced exit strategy is.

mainEntity.name: How quickly can I get short term finance for an unmortgageable property?

acceptedAnswer.text: Straightforward bridging loans on unmortgageable property can complete in 5 to 12 working days once a valuation and legal work are underway, and more complex cases involving planning or title issues typically take 3 to 4 weeks. Speed depends heavily on how quickly you provide documentation and how accessible the property is for valuation.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a good credit score to get a bridging loan on an unmortgageable property?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bad credit will generally not stop you getting a bridging loan because lenders weigh the property's value and your exit strategy far more heavily than your credit score. Some adverse credit history, including missed payments or historic defaults, is often accepted provided the security and exit are strong.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I can't sell or refinance at the end of the bridging loan term?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most bridging lenders will consider extending the term or restructuring the loan if you're close to completing your exit but need slightly longer, though this usually comes with additional fees and interest. This is why lenders and brokers stress-test the exit strategy heavily before the loan is agreed, rather than leaving it to chance.

mainEntity.name: Is a bridging loan the same as developer finance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bridging loans and developer finance overlap but are not identical, with developer finance typically referring to bridging loans structured with staged drawdowns to fund conversion or construction works. Standard bridging loans are usually drawn in one lump sum, while developer finance releases funds in stages as works progress and are inspected.

content:
Short term finance for unmortgageable property UK buyers rely on is almost always a bridging loan, because short term finance for unmortgageable property uk assesses the asset itself rather than applying a lender's standard mortgage criteria. Banks won't lend against properties with no kitchen, no working bathroom, structural issues or a short lease, but bridging lenders will, because they evaluate the property's value and your exit plan, not whether it meets a high street lending checklist.

This matters more than most people realise. Thousands of habitable-looking properties across the UK fail standard mortgage criteria every year, usually for reasons that have nothing to do with location or demand. A missing kitchen, no central heating, a collapsed roof, or a property that's structurally unsound will all get an automatic decline from a mainstream lender, no matter how strong your income or deposit is. Bridging loans exist specifically to fill that gap. If you want to understand the basics first, our guide on how bridging finance works covers the fundamentals in more detail.

We speak to buyers every week who are baffled by this. They've got a healthy deposit, a clean credit file and a good income, yet the mortgage application still gets kicked back at valuation stage. It's rarely the applicant that's the problem. It's almost always the property itself, and once you understand that distinction, the whole market makes a lot more sense.

Unmortgageable does not mean unsellable or unworkable. It simply means a specific type of lender, the high street mortgage bank, won't touch it in its current state. Bridging lenders operate to a completely different set of rules, and that's precisely why this corner of the market exists and continues to grow year on year.

What this means in practice

In practice it means you can buy, hold and renovate a property that a mortgage lender would never touch, using short-term borrowing secured against the property's current or projected value.

We see this constantly with auction purchases. A buyer wins a lot at auction, has 28 days to complete, and the property has no functioning kitchen or bathroom. No residential mortgage lender will process an application that fast, and most wouldn't lend on the property anyway. A bridging loan steps in, completes within the auction deadline, and the buyer refinances onto a standard mortgage once the work is done and the property is habitable again.

The same logic applies to landlords buying tired stock to add to a portfolio, to homeowners who've inherited a property in poor condition, and to developers picking up sites with planning potential but no current residential use. In every case, the property's unmortgageable status today isn't a barrier, it's simply the reason a bridging loan is the right tool rather than a mortgage.

We also see a fair number of clients dealing with probate properties left empty for years, where damp, an old wiring system or a condemned boiler trigger a mortgage decline. Bridging lets a beneficiary release funds against the property quickly, sort out the works, and either sell on or refinance rather than watching the estate sit in limbo while everyone argues about who pays for the roof.

Another common situation involves short lease flats, typically anything under 70 years remaining, which most mainstream lenders simply won't consider. A bridging loan can fund the purchase while a lease extension is negotiated in the background, after which the property becomes mortgageable in the normal way and the borrower refinances out at a much lower rate.

How it works

A bridging loan works by securing short-term borrowing against the property itself, released quickly and repaid through a defined exit, usually a sale or refinance once the property becomes mortgageable.

Lenders will value the property in its current condition and, where relevant, its projected value once works are complete (often called the GDV, or gross development value). Loan-to-value is calculated against whichever figure the lender is comfortable using, and terms typically run from one month up to 24 months, though most unmortgageable-property bridges we arrange sit between 6 and 12 months.

Interest is usually charged monthly and can be paid, deducted from the loan at drawdown (retained), or rolled up and repaid at the end. Most clients buying unmortgageable stock choose retained interest, because there's no rental income or cashflow yet to service monthly payments during the works period. Boxx Finance structures the majority of these deals this way for exactly that reason.

Rates on this type of short-term property finance tend to sit somewhere between 0.55% and 1.1% per month depending on the loan-to-value, the condition of the property and the strength of the exit. That translates to roughly 6.6% to 13.2% a year, though because the loan is short term, the total cost is usually far lower than that headline figure suggests once you look at the actual pounds paid over a 9 or 12 month period. For a full breakdown of how these figures compare across the market, see our guide to current bridging loan rates.

Arrangement fees typically run from 1.5% to 2% of the loan, with exit fees either built in or waived entirely depending on the lender. Valuation and legal costs sit on top, and you should budget roughly £1,500 to £3,000 for these depending on the property type and complexity of the title.

Drawdowns can be structured as a single lump sum for straightforward purchases, or released in stages against certified works for heavier refurbishment and conversion projects. Staged drawdowns protect the lender, but they also protect the borrower's cashflow, since you're only paying interest on funds actually released rather than the full facility from day one.

If you'd rather talk through the numbers for your own situation than work through the theory, you can get a bridging loan quote and we'll walk you through what's realistic for your property.

Typical scenarios

Real numbers tell the story better than theory. Here are two scenarios we've arranged that reflect exactly what happens on the ground.

Residential scenario: A first-time landlord in Reading found a two-bed terrace at auction, unmortgageable due to a collapsed rear extension and no functioning bathroom. She needed £142,000 against a purchase price of £190,000 (75% LTV on purchase, dropping to 58% LTV on the projected post-works value of £245,000), over a 9-month term. Funds released in 11 working days to meet the auction completion deadline. She exited via a buy-to-let remortgage once the works were certified complete, and the bridge was repaid in month 8. We've arranged similar deals for bridging loans in Reading and know the local auction houses and their typical timescales well.

Her total interest cost across the loan came to just under £11,400, plus a 2% arrangement fee of £2,840. Against a gross profit uplift of around £55,000 once the refurbishment was finished and the property revalued, the finance cost was a small fraction of the overall return, which is precisely why bridging made sense over waiting for a mortgage that was never going to be offered anyway.

Developer scenario: A small developer in Birmingham bought a former commercial unit with planning permission for residential conversion. The property was unmortgageable in its existing use and needed £310,000 against a £420,000 GDV (74% LTV against GDV, 62% against day-one value), over a 12-month term. This was structured as developer finance with staged drawdowns for the conversion works, and the loan exited via a sale of two of the three converted units, with the third retained and refinanced onto a term mortgage. We regularly arrange bridging loans in Birmingham for similar conversion projects across the city.

The staged drawdown structure meant the developer only paid interest on around £190,000 of the facility for the first four months, rising as further tranches were released against completed works. That kept the running cost of the loan considerably lower than if the full £310,000 had been drawn on day one, which is a point worth raising with any lender or broker before you sign terms.

Both deals completed inside two weeks of full application, which is fairly typical when the paperwork, valuation access and legal work move without delay. We see the same pace with bridging loans in London and bridging loans in Norwich, where local knowledge of valuers and solicitors keeps things moving.

What lenders look for

Lenders assessing unmortgageable property want a clear view of current value, projected value, and a credible, evidenced exit. Without all three, the application won't get past underwriting.

Loan-to-value ranges for genuinely unmortgageable property typically run from 60% to 75% of current value, or up to around 70% of GDV where works are planned. Timescales from enquiry to funds vary from 5 working days for straightforward cases to 3-4 weeks where title issues, planning conditions or complex ownership structures need untangling. Security is almost always a first legal charge, though second charge bridges are available where there's sufficient equity behind an existing mortgage.

On the exit, lenders want to see either a signed agreement of sale, a mortgage in principle from a receiving lender, or, for developer exits, a realistic sales strategy backed by comparable evidence. The most common reason we see applications declined isn't the property condition, it's a weak or unevidenced exit. Lenders are far more relaxed about a leaking roof than they are about a vague plan to sell within an unrealistic timeframe with no comparable evidence to back it up.

Most lenders in this space will want a schedule of works before they release funds for anything beyond a straightforward purchase. This doesn't need to be a full architect's specification, but it should set out what's being done, roughly what it will cost, and how long it will take. A well prepared schedule, even a simple one, speeds up underwriting considerably and often improves the rate offered.

Credit history and income still get looked at, but far more lightly than on a mortgage application. Lenders are mainly checking there's no adverse history that would raise concerns about the exit strategy, rather than running the same affordability calculations a mortgage underwriter would apply. This is one of the reasons short-term property finance suits self-employed buyers, portfolio landlords and company borrowers who often struggle with mainstream affordability checks despite having perfectly viable plans. It's also worth comparing how different lenders approach these cases, and our roundup of leading bridging loan lenders is a useful starting point.

Where we add most value as a broker is at the front end, before the application even goes to a lender. Matching the right property, the right exit strategy and the right lender appetite from day one avoids wasted valuations, wasted legal fees and the kind of last-minute declines that put auction deadlines and chain purchases at serious risk. Getting this groundwork right is usually the difference between a smooth completion and a stressful scramble in the final week.

Costs to budget for beyond the loan itself

Beyond the headline interest rate and arrangement fee, you should set aside a realistic contingency for the works themselves. Refurbishment costs on unmortgageable property have a habit of running over, particularly where structural issues only become apparent once work starts, such as hidden damp behind plaster or a roof that needs more than patching. Building in a 10-15% contingency on top of your schedule of works estimate is sensible practice, and most experienced lenders will expect to see this factored into your figures before they release funds.

You should also factor in insurance, since standard buildings cover often won't apply to an unmortgageable or unoccupied property, and you'll typically need a specialist vacant property or renovation policy for the duration of the works. Getting this in place before completion, rather than scrambling afterwards, avoids gaps in cover at exactly the point the property is most exposed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I get a mortgage on an unmortgageable property instead of a bridging loan?
No. If a property is genuinely unmortgageable, no mainstream lender will offer a standard mortgage against it in its current condition. A bridging loan lets you purchase and improve the property first, then refinance onto a mortgage once it meets standard lending criteria.

How quickly can short term finance for unmortgageable property be arranged?
Straightforward cases can complete in as little as 5 working days, though more complex title, planning or ownership situations typically take 3-4 weeks. Auction purchases with tight completion deadlines are one of the most common reasons buyers need funds released quickly.

What loan-to-value can I expect on an unmortgageable property?
Most lenders will offer between 60% and 75% of the property's current value, or up to around 70% of the projected value once works are complete (GDV). The exact figure depends on the property's condition, location and the strength of your exit strategy.

Do I need a schedule of works to apply?
For anything beyond a simple purchase, most lenders will want a schedule of works setting out what's being done, the estimated cost and the timeframe. It doesn't need to be a full architect's specification, but a clear, realistic schedule speeds up underwriting and can improve the rate offered.

What counts as a credible exit strategy?
Lenders want to see either a signed agreement of sale, a mortgage in principle from a receiving lender, or, for developer exits, a realistic sales strategy backed by comparable evidence. A weak or vague exit is the most common reason applications are declined, regardless of the property's condition.

Will my credit history affect my application?
Credit and income are considered, but far more lightly than on a mortgage application. Lenders are mainly looking for adverse history that could undermine your exit strategy, rather than running full affordability checks, which is why bridging often suits self-employed buyers and portfolio landlords.

How do I find out if my property qualifies for this type of finance?
The quickest way is to speak to a broker who can assess the property, your exit plan and lender appetite together. You can speak to a bridging finance broker to talk through your specific situation before committing to a valuation or application.

If you're weighing up your options, our funding solutions hub covers the full range of finance available for unmortgageable and hard-to-fund property, alongside bridging. Alternatively, you can start your bridging loan application and get a clear view of your options from someone who deals with these cases every week.

content:
A bridging loan whole of market search means a broker checks your deal against the full range of UK bridging lenders, rather than the two or three names they know best, so you see the true spread of rates, fees and criteria available to you. Businesses and property buyers use a bridging loan whole of market search whenever speed, flexibility or an unusual security type rules out standard high street options. This approach typically widens choice, sharpens pricing and improves the odds of approval.

In our experience, most borrowers who go direct to one lender never find out how much they overpaid. A proper market search changes that. If you'd like to see how this applies to your own deal, you can get a bridging loan quote with a broker directly.

The difference in cost between the best and worst offer on the same deal can be significant. We regularly see spreads of 0.3% to 0.5% per month between lenders quoting on identical security and loan amounts. On a £300,000 loan over six months, that gap alone can mean the difference between paying around £5,400 in interest and paying closer to £9,900. Fees vary just as widely, with arrangement fees ranging from 1% to 2.5% depending on the lender and the complexity of the deal.

What this means in practice

A whole of market search puts your deal in front of dozens of lenders instead of one, so pricing and appetite get tested properly before you commit to anything. For a broader introduction to how this type of funding works, our guide on what bridging finance actually covers is worth reading first.

There are well over 200 bridging lenders active in the UK, ranging from big institutional names to small private funders who only lend on specific property types or in certain regions. No single broker or borrower knows all of them well enough to approach each one individually. A whole of market search uses lender relationships and live criteria data to filter that list down to the handful who will genuinely say yes, quickly and at a sensible rate.

This matters because bridging lenders are not interchangeable. One lender might refuse a deal outright because the property has no kitchen, while another specialises in exactly that scenario and prices it happily. A search that only checks two or three familiar names misses this entirely, and the borrower ends up either declined or overpaying.

It also matters because lender appetite shifts constantly. A lender who was competitive on light refurbishment bridges last quarter might have pulled back from that sector entirely this month, having filled their allocation for that risk category. Brokers running genuine whole of market searches track these movements week by week, which is simply not something a borrower calling round on their own can realistically do. Current pricing trends are covered in more detail in our breakdown of current bridging loan rates across the market.

Another practical advantage concerns credit searches and valuation fees. Applying speculatively to lenders who were never going to say yes costs time and sometimes money, since some lenders charge a valuation fee upfront regardless of outcome. A proper search filters out the poor fits before any fees are paid, not after.

How it works

A whole of market search works by matching your specific deal, property, exit and timescale against live lender criteria before any application is submitted, so you only approach lenders who are actually likely to lend.

The process starts with a short fact-find: the property type, its condition, the loan amount required, the loan-to-value, your exit strategy and your timescale. A broker running a proper bridging loan search then cross-references this against an internal or software-driven database of lender appetite, which changes weekly as lenders tighten or loosen criteria depending on their loan book.

From there you typically get a shortlist of three to six lenders whose rates, fees and terms are indicated within a day or two. This is where the real value sits. Rather than a single quote, you get comparative pricing, so you can see whether a slightly higher headline rate actually comes with lower fees and a faster completion, which often makes it the cheaper option overall once you run the true cost.

A good broker will lay this out as a total cost comparison rather than just a headline rate. That means adding the arrangement fee, any exit fee, valuation cost, legal fees and the monthly interest together across the expected term, then comparing the full figure across each shortlisted lender. Two loans quoted at 0.65% and 0.79% per month can end up almost identical in total cost once fees are factored in, and sometimes the higher rate works out cheaper overall. Our comparison of leading UK bridging lenders goes into this in more depth.

Documentation requirements also vary between lenders, and this is another area where a market search saves time. Some lenders will proceed on a light-touch basis with just proof of ID, proof of the exit strategy and a valuation. Others want full accounts, bank statements and a detailed business plan, particularly on larger commercial or development-related bridges. Matching the deal to a lender whose paperwork requirements suit your timescale avoids a lot of frustration further down the line.

What this means in practice

In practice, you can bid at auction with genuine confidence that you can complete, rather than hoping a mortgage offer arrives in time. Bridging loans are assessed primarily on the property and your exit route, not on lengthy income verification, which is why they move so much faster than a standard mortgage application.

It also changes how you approach the auction itself. Serious auction buyers arrange bridging loan terms, sometimes even an agreement in principle, before they ever raise a paddle. How it works

A bridging loan for an auction purchase works by securing short-term lending against the property itself, released quickly once legal work is complete, and repaid later through a clear exit strategy such as a sale or refinance onto a mortgage.

You will typically approach a broker as soon as you have identified the lot, or ideally before the auction, with a rough purchase price in mind. The lender will want a valuation, often an automated or desktop valuation initially to speed things along, followed by a physical inspection. Your solicitor will run standard conveyancing checks in a much tighter timeframe than a normal purchase.

Interest is usually charged monthly and can be paid monthly, deducted from the loan (retained), or rolled up and repaid at the end, which suits buyers who need every penny of cash flow during a refurbishment. Most auction bridging loans run for 6 to 12 months, though some lenders will extend to 18 or 24 months if the exit plan justifies it.

Lenders scrutinise the exit most closely. This is usually a sale of the property once refurbished, a remortgage onto a standard buy-to-let or residential mortgage once the property is in a lettable or liveable condition, or in the case of a developer, refinance following planning permission or completed works. Typical scenarios

Two scenarios come up again and again in our casework, one residential and one developer-led, both showing how quickly this type of lending needs to move.

A first-time landlord in Reading spotted a two-bed terrace at auction with a guide price of £145,000, ultimately winning it for £158,000. The property had no functioning central heating, which ruled out a standard buy-to-let mortgage at the point of purchase. Funds were released in 9 working days, comfortably inside the 28-day completion deadline. The exit was a remortgage onto a standard buy-to-let product once the heating and kitchen works were finished and the property was tenanted.

A small developer in Norwich bought a disused chapel at auction for £310,000, planning to convert it into three residential units under permitted development rights already in place. We secured £217,000 against the purchase, a 70% LTV, over a 12-month term, structured as developer finance with a further drawdown facility to cover part of the conversion costs. Completion happened in 11 working days. The exit was a sale of two units and a refinance of the third onto a buy-to-let mortgage, repaying the bridging loan in full at month 10.

What lenders look for

Lenders assess auction bridging loans on loan-to-value, the strength and clarity of your exit strategy, and the condition and marketability of the security property, rather than on your income or credit history.

Typical LTVs for auction bridging loans sit between 65% and 75% of purchase price or valuation, whichever is lower, though some specialist lenders will go to 80% on strong deals with additional security. Lenders will want evidence of your exit, which usually means a mortgage broker's agreement in principle for a refinance exit, or comparable sold evidence for a sale exit. The most common reason we see applications declined or delayed is an unrealistic exit strategy, buyers assuming a remortgage will be straightforward when the property still needs significant work, or assuming a sale will happen faster than local market evidence supports.

Common mistakes

The biggest mistake auction buyers make is bidding before they have any finance arranged, then scrambling to find a lender once they are legally committed to complete. This puts you in a weak negotiating position and often means accepting a higher rate simply because time has run out.

Another common error is underestimating refurbishment costs and borrowing too tightly against the purchase price, leaving no buffer for unexpected structural or damp issues, which auction properties frequently have given they are often sold precisely because of condition problems. We also regularly see buyers assume all lenders move at the same speed. In our experience, the gap between the fastest and slowest bridging lenders on a straightforward case can be the difference between 5 working days and 20, and that gap matters enormously against a 28-day auction deadline.

Failing to instruct a solicitor experienced in auction completions is another frequent pitfall. Standard conveyancers unfamiliar with the compressed auction timetable can cause a purchase to fail, even where the finance itself was never the problem.

Alternatives or comparisons

Bridging loans are not always the right tool, and a good broker should tell you when they are not. If you already have a mortgage offer in place before the auction, and the completion date genuinely allows enough time for a standard purchase, a normal mortgage will almost always be cheaper and should be used instead.

If the property is a straightforward, mortgageable buy-to-let with no works required and you have three to four weeks before completion, a fast-track buy-to-let mortgage from a specialist lender may complete in time without the higher cost of bridging. Bridging loans should also be avoided where your exit strategy is genuinely uncertain, for example relying on a sale in a slow local market with no comparable evidence, because you risk reaching the end of the term with no way to repay.

Bridging loans are clearly the right choice when the property is unmortgageable in its current state, when the 28-day deadline simply does not allow time for standard underwriting, or when you need to move faster than other bidders to secure a lot. If you want to compare bridging loan rates against current market benchmarks before deciding, our breakdown of current UK bridging loan rates is a useful next step, and if you are weighing lenders directly our guide to the leading UK bridging lenders and their criteria covers how they differ in practice.

How to get the best outcome

The best outcome comes from arranging your finance before auction day, not after. Speaking to a broker as soon as you have shortlisted a lot means valuations and legal packs can be prepared in advance, so the moment the hammer falls, the process is already moving.

Have your exit strategy documented before you bid, not sketched out afterwards. If your exit is a mortgage refinance, get an agreement in principle in place. If it is a sale, gather comparable evidence from the local market. Lenders move faster and lend more confidently when the exit is already substantiated rather than assumed.

If you are actively bidding this quarter, it is worth taking a few minutes to get a bridging loan quote before you attend, so you know your ceiling budget and can bid with real confidence rather than guesswork. This single step avoids more failed auction purchases than any other piece of advice we give.

title: Bridging Loans for Sole Traders in the UK
excerpt: Sole traders can get bridging loans just as easily as limited companies, provided the property and exit plan stack up. Here's how lenders assess sole trader applications in practice.
metaTitle: Bridging Loans for Sole Traders in the UK
metaDescription: Bridging Loans for Sole Traders in the UK. Expert advice from Boxx Finance, a whole-of-market UK bridging finance broker.

content:
A bridging loan for sole trader UK applicants works the same way as any other bridging loan: it's short-term property finance secured against a property asset, arranged in days rather than months, and repaid through a clear exit such as a sale or refinance. Being a sole trader rather than a limited company makes almost no difference to how a bridging loan for sole trader UK application is assessed, because lenders lend against the property and the exit, not the business structure.

We arrange these deals every week for sole traders buying investment property, breaking chains, funding refurbishments, or picking up auction lots that a mainstream mortgage simply can't move fast enough to secure. The trading status barely comes into it once the numbers work. If you'd like to understand the basics first, our guide on what bridging finance actually is is a good starting point.

Sole traders coming to short-term property finance for the first time often find that lenders care far less about turnover or profit margins than they'd expected. A high street bank funding a business loan will pore over your accounts for hours. A bridging lender wants to know the property stacks up and the exit is credible. That difference alone explains why so many self-employed people find bridging loans far easier to arrange than they anticipated.

What this means in practice

In practice, being a sole trader affects paperwork slightly, not eligibility. Lenders still want to know who they're lending to and how the loan will be repaid, but they're not underwriting your business the way a bank would for a working capital loan.

Most bridging lenders treat sole traders as individuals for credit purposes. That means personal ID, proof of address, a credit check, and evidence of income or assets to show you can service interest if it's not being deducted from the loan. Your self-employed accounts, tax returns (SA302s), or business bank statements might be asked for, but usually just to confirm affordability of any monthly interest payments, not to assess the trading performance of the business itself.

The property does the heavy lifting. If you're buying or refinancing a residential investment property, a semi-commercial unit, or land with development potential, the lender's real focus is the asset value, the loan-to-value, and how convincingly you can demonstrate the exit. Sole trader status simply sits in the background of the application.

We often get asked whether a poor credit history rules a sole trader out. It rarely does on its own. Bridging lenders are used to seeing missed payments, defaults, or even historic CCJs, particularly among self-employed borrowers whose income can be irregular. What matters more is whether the security property and exit route are strong enough to offset that risk. A clean credit file helps with pricing, but it isn't usually a dealbreaker.

Age and trading history matter less too. You don't need years of accounts or a long-established business to qualify. We've placed bridging loans for sole traders who only started trading a few months earlier, because the lender was underwriting the property and the individual, not the length of time the business had existed.

How it works

A sole trader bridging loan is secured by a legal charge over property, released once valuation and legal work complete, and repaid in full at the end of a fixed term, usually 3 to 18 months.

You apply, typically through a broker who packages the deal for the right lender rather than approaching one lender cold. A valuer inspects the security property. Solicitors handle the legal charge on both sides. Once everything's satisfied, funds are released, often within 7 to 14 working days for straightforward cases, sometimes faster if the lender already has a relationship with your solicitor or has previously valued the property.

Interest is either paid monthly, deducted from the loan upfront (retained), or rolled up and repaid at the end. Most sole traders we work with prefer retained or rolled-up interest, because it keeps cash flow free while the exit is arranged. You'll need a believable exit: sale of the security property, sale of another asset, or refinance onto a term mortgage or buy-to-let product. Lenders will ask for evidence supporting whichever route you propose, not just a verbal assurance.

Rates on sole trader bridging loans in the current market typically sit between 0.55% and 1.1% per month, depending on LTV, asset type, and the strength of the exit. For a fuller breakdown of current pricing, see our guide to bridging loan rates across the UK. Arrangement fees are usually 1-2% of the gross loan, with valuation and legal costs on top. On a £150,000 loan over six months, total costs including interest and fees often land somewhere between £8,000 and £14,000, though every deal is priced individually. If you want to see how your own numbers might stack up, you can get a bridging loan quote before committing to anything.

You should also understand the difference between regulated and unregulated bridging at this stage. If the security property is or will be your main residence, the loan usually falls under FCA regulation, which brings extra consumer protections and a slightly slower process. If it's purely an investment or business property, most sole trader bridging falls outside regulation, which is part of why completions can move so quickly.

Typical scenarios

Real deals make this clearer than theory. Two examples we've handled recently show how differently this product gets used depending on the borrower's goal.

A sole trader landlord in the East Midlands needed to complete on an auction purchase within 28 days. He borrowed £145,000 against a £230,000 terraced property (63% LTV) over a 6-month term, with interest retained from the loan, exiting via refinance onto a standard buy-to-let mortgage once the property was tenanted. Funds were released in 9 working days from instruction, comfortably inside the auction deadline. We've arranged similar deals for landlords needing bridging loans in London and bridging loans in Birmingham, where auction timelines are often even tighter.

A sole trader developer in Norwich took on a small conversion project, splitting a former commercial unit into two residential flats. He borrowed £210,000 against a post-works value of £340,000 (62% LTV against GDV, released in stages) over a 12-month term, exiting through the sale of both units on completion. This is developer finance in all but name, and sole traders undertake far more of this kind of work than people assume. Lenders were comfortable because he had a track record of two previous conversions, even though both were done as a sole trader rather than through a company. We regularly place similar cases for bridging loans in Norwich.

Not every deal is investment-led either. We've also seen sole traders use bridging to break a residential chain, buying their next home before their current one sells, with the loan cleared the moment the sale completes.

Another common scenario involves sole trader tradespeople, builders, plumbers, electricians who spot a below-market property through their own network and need to move before a mainstream mortgage could ever be arranged. One Yorkshire based builder we worked with borrowed £95,000 against a £160,000 property he'd sourced through a contact, refurbished it using his own trade over four months, and refinanced onto a buy-to-let mortgage at a higher valuation once the works were done. The bridge simply bought him the time a normal mortgage application couldn't. We've seen the same pattern with tradespeople arranging bridging loans in Reading.

What lenders look for

Lenders focus on three core elements above everything else: the property, the loan-to-value, and the strength of the exit evidence. Get these right and sole trader status rarely causes friction.

Typical LTVs run 65-70% on standard residential security, dropping to 50-60% on more specialist assets like semi-commercial units, land, or properties needing significant works. Timescales from enquiry to funds released usually sit between 7 and 21 working days, though we've completed urgent auction cases in as little as 5 days when the borrower's paperwork was ready upfront.

Acceptable security includes residential investment property, semi-commercial premises, land with or without planning, and in some cases the borrower's own home, though this brings added FCA-regulated bridging rules into play if it's an investment property, the process changes. Lenders expect documented evidence of the exit: a mortgage in principle for refinance exits, an estate agent's marketing appraisal for sale exits, or a signed contract if a sale is already agreed.

The most common reason we see sole trader applications declined is a vague or unevidenced exit strategy. Lenders rarely say this outright, but an application that says "I'll sell it eventually" without a valuation, agent instruction, or refinance figures behind it is far weaker than one backed by paperwork.

Preparation makes a real difference to speed and outcome. Before approaching a lender, it helps to have your ID and proof of address ready, recent bank statements, the last two years of accounts or tax returns if available, and a clear one-page summary of the property, the loan amount needed, and the exit route. The stronger this pack is at the outset, the faster underwriting tends to move.

Working with a broker who understands sole trader bridging also helps avoid wasted time. Not every lender is comfortable with self-employed borrowers, and some price more competitively for certain asset types than others. Packaging the deal properly the first time, rather than approaching lenders one by one, is usually what separates a smooth five day completion from a frustrating month long process. It's also worth comparing how different providers approach these deals in our roundup of the best bridging loan lenders in the UK.

Costs and fees to budget for

Beyond the headline interest rate, sole traders should budget for arrangement fees, valuation fees, legal costs on both sides, and sometimes an exit fee depending on the lender. These short-term property finance costs add up quickly, so ask for a full breakdown before committing, rather than focusing on the monthly rate alone. A broker can usually get these figures confirmed upfront so there are no surprises at completion.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a sole trader get a bridging loan without full company accounts?
Yes. Lenders assess sole traders as individuals, so personal ID, bank statements, and evidence of affordability usually matter far more than formal company accounts.

Does a poor credit history stop a sole trader qualifying?
Not usually. Missed payments, defaults, or historic CCJs rarely rule out an application on their own, provided the security property and exit route are strong.

How quickly can a sole trader bridging loan complete?
Straightforward cases often complete within 7 to 14 working days, and urgent auction purchases have been completed in as little as 5 days with paperwork ready upfront.

What can be used as security for a sole trader bridging loan?
Residential investment property, semi-commercial premises, land with or without planning, and sometimes the borrower's own home, though the latter brings FCA-regulated rules into play.

What rates should a sole trader expect on a bridging loan?
Rates typically sit between 0.55% and 1.1% per month, depending on loan-to-value, asset type, and the strength of the proposed exit.

Why do exit strategies matter so much to lenders?
A vague or unevidenced exit is the most common reason applications are declined, so documented proof such as a mortgage in principle or agent appraisal carries real weight.

Should a sole trader use a broker to arrange bridging loans?
Yes, ideally. A broker who understands sole trader bridging can package the deal properly first time and avoid the delays of approaching lenders one by one.

content:
The fastest and most reliable way to finance auction property in the UK is a bridging loan, because how to finance auction property uk almost always comes down to speed rather than cost. Auction contracts demand completion within 28 days, and a standard mortgage simply cannot move that quickly. Bridging loans are built for exactly this deadline, with funds often released in under two weeks.

Every year we speak to buyers who fall in love with a lot, do their sums on the back of an envelope, and only think about funding once they're already the winning bidder. By that point the clock has started and there's no pause button. Getting the finance conversation right before auction day separates a smooth completion from a stressful scramble. If you want to talk through your own timeline, you can get a bridging loan quote before you even start bidding.

What this means in practice

Buying at auction means you exchange contracts the moment the hammer falls, and you are legally committed to completing within a fixed window, usually 28 days from the auction date. There's no negotiating that timeline. If you don't complete, you lose your deposit, typically 10% of the purchase price, and the seller can sue you for the difference if they resell at a lower price.

This is why cash buyers and short-term property finance users dominate auction rooms. A mortgage application, with its valuation queues, underwriting committees and product transfers, routinely takes six to eight weeks even when everything goes smoothly. Bridging lenders know the auction clock is ticking and have built their entire process around meeting it. For a fuller breakdown of how this type of lending works, see our guide to what bridging finance actually involves.

In our experience, buyers who turn up to auction without pre-arranged bridging loans in principle are taking a real gamble. You can still bid, but you're relying on being able to arrange everything from scratch in a month, and that's a tight ask even for an efficient lender.

The 28-day clock includes weekends and bank holidays, not just working days. If your auction falls just before Christmas or Easter, you could effectively lose a week of solicitor and lender availability before you've even started. Some auction houses will grant a short extension for a fee, usually charged daily, but you shouldn't plan around getting one.

How it works

A bridging loan for auction property is secured against the property you're buying, sometimes with additional security if the loan-to-value needs boosting. Most lenders will lend up to 70-75% of the purchase price or valuation, whichever is lower, on a first charge basis.

The process starts before the auction, not after. You get an agreement in principle from a bridging lender based on the guide price and your exit strategy. On the day you win the lot, you instruct solicitors immediately, the lender orders a valuation, and legal work runs in parallel rather than in sequence, which is the main reason bridging completions are so much faster than mortgages.

Interest is usually charged monthly, somewhere between 0.55% and 1% per month depending on the deal, and it's commonly retained from the loan rather than paid separately, so you're not finding extra cash for monthly payments during the term. You then repay the whole loan, plus any retained interest, when you sell the property or refinance onto a mortgage or refurbishment facility. For current pricing across the market, our article on bridging loan rates across the UK is a useful reference point.

On top of the interest rate, expect an arrangement fee of around 1.5% to 2% of the loan, a valuation fee that varies with property type and value, and legal costs covering both your solicitor and the lender's solicitor. Many lenders insist on their own legal representation being paid for by the borrower, which surprises first-time bridging users. Budgeting an extra 3% to 4% of the loan amount for fees on top of the interest is a sensible rule of thumb.

Boxx Finance works with a panel of bridging lenders who specifically quote against auction completion dates, which matters because not every lender moves at the same pace once you're inside that 28-day window. We've seen deals where two lenders quote almost identical rates, but one can complete in 9 days and the other needs 20, and at auction that difference can be the whole game. We regularly help buyers arrange bridging loans in London and bridging loans in Birmingham, where auction stock and competition move especially fast.

Typical scenarios

A landlord in Reading bought a repossessed two-bed flat at auction for £145,000 against a guide price of £120,000. She needed £101,500 (70% LTV) over a 6-month term, with the exit being a straightforward buy-to-let remortgage once the property had a clean title and a new tenancy in place. Funds were released in 11 working days, comfortably inside the 28-day deadline, and she refinanced onto a standard buy-to-let mortgage five months later. Buyers exploring similar deals often start by looking into bridging loans in Reading before they even attend the auction.

Her total bridging cost over the five months, including the arrangement fee and retained interest, worked out at just under £7,200. Against a purchase price of £145,000 and a flat that was valued at £158,000 once the sitting tenant issue was resolved, she still came out well ahead, and her new buy-to-let mortgage rate locked in a monthly rental yield of around 6.8%.

A developer bidding in Birmingham bought a semi-derelict end-of-terrace with planning consent for a two-storey rear extension and loft conversion. The guide price was £180,000 but it sold for £215,000. He borrowed £150,000 (70% LTV against the purchase price) over 9 months, using developer finance to cover both the acquisition and part of the works, with the exit being a sale on the open market once refurbished. Legal completion happened in 14 working days, and the project sold within the bridging term at £340,000.

After deducting his bridging costs, build costs of roughly £62,000, and selling fees, his net profit came in at just under £58,000 on a nine month project. He's since told us he wouldn't have got near that guide price margin without having finance already agreed before the hammer fell, because it meant he could bid with confidence rather than hesitating and losing the lot.

Both cases show the same pattern: speed on the way in, a clear and realistic exit, and a lender who priced the deal on the property and the plan rather than on a lengthy credit history review. Buyers further afield have had similar success with bridging loans in Norwich, where the same speed and exit principles apply.

What lenders look for

Bridging lenders assessing auction purchases focus on three things: the property, the loan-to-value, and the credibility of your exit. Most will lend between 65% and 75% LTV on residential auction property, occasionally stretching to 80% with strong additional security or a lower-risk exit.

Timescales from enquiry to funds released typically run 7 to 21 working days for straightforward cases, though we've seen genuinely simple deals complete in as little as 5 days when the buyer has everything ready, including proof of funds for any deposit shortfall, ID, and a solicitor already instructed. Security is almost always a first legal charge over the property itself, though second charges behind an existing mortgage are sometimes accepted on other assets to bridge a gap.

Lenders want firm evidence of the exit, not just a plan. For a sale exit, that means comparable sold prices and, ideally, an estate agent's marketing appraisal. For a refinance exit, they'll want to see that you meet likely mortgage criteria once works are complete, sometimes asking for a decision in principle from the onward lender before completion.

Property type also affects appetite. Standard brick-built houses and flats in decent condition are straightforward for almost every lender on our panel. Ex-local authority flats, properties above commercial premises, and anything with non-standard construction such as timber frame or concrete panel systems will narrow the field considerably, and you should expect a slightly lower maximum LTV as a result. To see how different lenders compare on cases like these, take a look at our review of the best bridging loan lenders in the UK.

The most common reason we see auction bridging applications declined is an unrealistic valuation. Buyers get caught up in the room and pay well above guide price, and the survey simply doesn't support the loan needed. Lenders rarely say this outright, but a bid that's 25%+ above guide price on a property needing heavy work is the single biggest red flag in our experience.

Credit history matters far less than most first-time bridging borrowers expect. Lenders are primarily concerned with the asset and the exit, so a few historic missed payments or a lower credit score rarely stops a deal, provided the story around them makes sense and there's nothing recent or unexplained.

Challenger bank bridging arm65-70%0.65%-0.95%10-21 working days
Private/family office lender60-70%0.85%-1.25%3-10 working days

Common mistakes

The biggest mistake is arranging finance after winning the lot rather than before. Auction houses don't care that your bridging application is still with underwriting, the 28-day clock started the moment the gavel came down, and any delay is entirely your risk to manage.

A close second is underestimating the deposit and buyer's premium due on the day. Most auction houses require the 10% deposit plus their buyer's premium, often 1% to 2.5% plus VAT, to be paid immediately, sometimes by card or bank transfer before you even leave the room. Short-term property finance covers the purchase completion, not this initial deposit, so you need that cash sitting ready separately.

Third, buyers sometimes fixate on the interest rate and ignore the total cost of the deal. A slightly cheaper rate from a lender that takes three extra weeks to complete could easily cost you the property and your deposit, which makes it the most expensive option by a wide margin, not the cheapest.

Finally, we regularly see buyers skip the legal pack entirely before bidding, then discover after exchange that there's an unusual lease, an outstanding charge, or an unresolved boundary dispute. Bridging lenders will pick these issues up during their own legal checks, and any title problem can delay or derail completion inside a deadline that offers no flexibility. Reading the legal pack and raising queries with the auctioneer's solicitor before the auction is one of the simplest ways to avoid a nasty surprise.

Frequently Asked Questions

How quickly can a bridging loan complete for an auction purchase?
Most specialist bridging lenders can release funds in 7 to 21 working days, and some straightforward cases complete in as little as 5 to 9 days when the buyer has proof of funds, ID, and a solicitor ready in advance.

What loan-to-value can I get on an auction property?
Most lenders will go up to 70-75% of the purchase price or valuation, whichever is lower, with some stretching to 80% where there's strong additional security or a low-risk exit.

Does bridging finance cover the auction deposit?
No. The 10% deposit and buyer's premium are due immediately on the day of the auction, usually by card or bank transfer, and short-term property finance only covers the purchase completion, not this upfront payment.

What happens if I don't complete within 28 days?
You lose your deposit, and the seller can pursue you for the difference if the property is resold at a lower price, so having finance arranged before you bid is essential.

Will bad credit stop me getting a bridging loan for auction property?
Not usually. Lenders focus primarily on the property and your exit strategy, so historic missed payments or a lower credit score rarely block an application provided there's nothing recent or unexplained.

What exit strategies do lenders accept?
The two most common are selling the property on the open market, supported by comparable sold prices, or refinancing onto a mortgage or refurbishment facility once you meet the onward lender's criteria.

How much does a bridging loan for auction property cost in total?
Alongside the monthly interest rate, expect an arrangement fee of 1.5% to 2%, a valuation fee, and legal costs, with a sensible rule of thumb being an extra 3% to 4% of the loan amount on top of interest.

content:
A commercial bridging loan is a short-term, secured loan used to fund a property purchase or business need quickly, typically for terms of one to 24 months, secured against commercial or residential property. Our commercial bridging loan uk explained service exists because banks move too slowly for these situations. Speed, not cost, is the whole point of the product.

Brokers like us get asked the same question most weeks: why would anyone pay more for borrowing than a standard mortgage rate? The honest answer is that most borrowers aren't comparing short-term property finance against a mortgage at all. They're comparing it against losing a deal, missing an auction deadline, or watching a development stall while a mainstream lender works through a six week underwriting queue. In that context, the cost makes sense. If you want to talk through the numbers on your own situation, you can get a bridging loan quote before committing to anything.

What this means in practice

A bridging loan buys you time and speed when a normal mortgage or business loan cannot move fast enough. It fills the gap between needing funds now and arranging longer-term finance later, or completing a sale that hasn't yet gone through. For a broader look at how this works, see our guide on how bridging finance works.

We see this most often with property chains, auction purchases, and refurbishment projects where the numbers work but the timeline doesn't suit a mainstream lender. A landlord might need to complete on a purchase in three weeks. A developer might need funds released before planning permission is fully tidied up. A business owner might need to release equity from a commercial unit before a term loan completes.

There's also a quieter category of use that doesn't get talked about as much: probate and inheritance situations. A beneficiary might need to raise funds against an inherited property to pay inheritance tax before the estate is settled, long before a sale can complete. Bridging loans fit neatly here because the exit, usually the eventual sale or refinance of the property, is clear from day one.

The loan is secured against property, usually with a first or second charge, and the interest is normally paid monthly, retained from the loan, or rolled up and paid at the end. Every bridging loan has a clearly defined exit, whether that's a sale, a refinance, or an inheritance settlement. Without a credible exit, most lenders simply won't proceed, regardless of how strong the security looks on paper.

You should understand who actually uses this product, because it isn't just property investors. We arrange short-term property finance for business owners buying commercial premises before a sale of another asset completes, for solicitors handling chain breaks on residential transactions, and for company directors needing to release cash tied up in property to cover a short-term working capital gap. The common thread is always timing, not necessarily property experience.

How it works

A bridging loan works by lending against the value of a property asset rather than primarily against income, using a fast underwriting process built around the security and the exit route. Lenders release funds in days or weeks rather than months.

The process usually starts with a decision in principle within 24 to 48 hours, followed by valuation, legal work, and a review of the exit strategy. Because there's no lengthy income assessment in the way a residential mortgage requires, the whole process moves faster, provided the solicitor and valuer aren't the bottleneck. In our experience, legal delays cause more slippage than underwriting ever does.

A typical timeline looks something like this. Day one to two covers initial enquiry and decision in principle. Day three to five involves valuation instructed and legal packs sent to both sets of solicitors. Day six to twelve sees the valuation report received and legal due diligence carried out, including title checks and searches. Day thirteen to eighteen brings the offer issued and funds released, assuming no complications with the title or the exit evidence.

Three main factors typically cause delays. The property has an unregistered title or a legal quirk that needs untangling. The solicitor instructed isn't experienced in bridging transactions and treats it like a standard purchase, missing the urgency. Or the borrower hasn't got their exit paperwork ready, such as a mortgage offer for refinance, and the lender won't release funds until that's in place.

Interest rates on commercial bridging loans typically run from around 0.55% to 1.25% per month depending on loan-to-value, security type, and how clean the exit is. For a fuller breakdown of pricing, see our guide on current bridging loan rates. Arrangement fees generally sit between 1% and 2% of the loan, plus valuation and legal costs. It's not cheap borrowing, but it's designed to solve a timing problem and then be repaid, not to be held for years.

To put figures on it, a £200,000 bridging loan at 0.75% per month over 6 months would cost around £9,000 in interest if paid monthly, plus a 1.5% arrangement fee of £3,000, plus valuation fees typically £400 to £900 depending on property type, and legal costs on both sides often totalling £1,500 to £2,500. All in, a borrower might be looking at £14,000 to £15,000 in total cost for six months' access to £200,000. A broker should walk clients through that sort of figure before they commit, not after.

Typical scenarios

Real deals make this far clearer than theory. Here are two we've arranged that show how differently this product gets used depending on who's borrowing.

A residential landlord in Norwich needed £145,000 against a £260,000 buy-to-let property (56% LTV) over an 8 month term, to complete an auction purchase before the 28 day deadline lapsed. The exit was a standard buy-to-let remortgage once the property was tenanted. Funds were released in 11 working days from initial enquiry, well within the auction deadline. We arrange similar deals for clients seeking bridging loans in Norwich throughout the year.

A developer converting a former office block into six flats needed £480,000 against a gross development value of £1.1 million (44% GDV) over 14 months, drawn in stages as works progressed. The exit was sale of the completed units, with two pre-sold off-plan. This is a classic developer finance structure, where the loan tracks the build rather than sitting as one lump sum, and it's the kind of deal we arrange weekly for clients working across the Midlands and East of England, including borrowers looking for bridging loans in London.

A third example worth mentioning is a smaller business case. A retail business owner in the East Midlands needed £90,000 raised against the mortgage-free commercial unit her shop traded from, to cover a stock purchase deadline while a term loan application worked its way through a bank's business lending team. The bridge was arranged over 4 months at 60% LTV, with the exit being repayment from the term loan once it completed. It's a smaller, less glamorous deal than the development example, but it's exactly the sort of everyday case where bridging quietly solves a cash flow problem that would otherwise cost a business a supplier discount or a seasonal stock window.

We also regularly place deals for landlords looking at bridging loans in Birmingham and investors chasing opportunities through bridging loans in Reading, where local market timing often decides whether a deal completes at all.

What lenders look for

Lenders focus on three things above everything else: the security value, the loan-to-value, and the strength of the exit. Get those three right and the rest of the application tends to move smoothly.

Most commercial bridging lenders will go up to 65-75% LTV on standard residential investment property, dropping to 50-60% for commercial or semi-commercial units, and lower still, often 45-55%, for land or heavy refurbishment projects. Security can include residential, commercial, mixed-use, and sometimes land with planning potential, though unusual assets narrow the lender pool considerably. Choosing the right lender matters too; our review of leading UK bridging lenders compared covers how they differ in appetite and pricing.

Credit history matters less than it would with a mainstream mortgage, but it isn't ignored. Most bridging lenders will still look at whether a borrower has any unsatisfied county court judgments, recent bankruptcy, or a pattern of missed payments on other secured lending. A poor credit history won't automatically rule someone out, but it usually pushes the LTV down and the rate up, and it narrows the pool of lenders willing to look at the case at all.

Timescales from enquiry to funds released typically run 7 to 21 working days for straightforward cases, and can stretch to 4-6 weeks where titles are complex or there's unregistered land involved. Lenders want documented evidence of the exit, whether that's a mortgage offer for a refinance, agreed sale terms, or a credible sales and marketing plan for a development. The most common reason we see applications declined is an exit that's vague or unrealistic given local market evidence. Lenders rarely say this outright, but a weak exit strategy kills more deals than any other single factor.

It's also worth knowing that lenders differentiate between regulated and unregulated bridging loans. A loan secured against a property the borrower or a family member lives in, or intends to live in, is regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority and comes with additional consumer protections. Commercial bridging, secured against investment or business property, generally falls outside that regulation, which is part of why it can move faster. However, this also means the onus is on the borrower and their broker to check the deal stacks up properly.

Standard residential investment65-75%7-14 days
Commercial or semi-commercial50-60%10-21 days
Land or heavy refurbishment45-55%14-28 days

Common mistakes

The single biggest mistake we see is borrowers underestimating total cost by focusing only on the headline monthly rate. Arrangement fees, valuation fees, legal costs on both sides, and exit fees all add up, and a deal that looked comfortable at the enquiry stage can feel tight by completion.

Another frequent error is assuming the exit will simply happen on schedule, without a fallback plan if it slips. Refinances get delayed, sales fall through, buyers pull out at the last minute. A good broker will always ask what happens if the exit doesn't land on time, and a good lender will usually build some flexibility into the term rather than leaving a borrower exposed to default interest the moment a deadline passes.

We'd also flag instructing a solicitor who has never handled a bridging transaction before. It might sound like a small detail, but a solicitor unfamiliar with the pace and structure of bridging loans can easily add a week or two to completion simply by treating it like a standard conveyancing matter, requesting documents in the wrong order, or not understanding what the lender's legal team actually needs to see. Choosing a solicitor with bridging experience, even if they're not the cheapest quote, usually pays for itself in time saved.

Finally, some borrowers approach one lender directly rather than going through a broker who can compare the market. Rates, fees, and appetite for a particular security type vary considerably between bridging lenders, and going direct to a single lender often means missing a better structured deal elsewhere. Given how much total cost can shift between lenders on the same deal, that comparison step is rarely worth skipping. If you'd like an independent comparison across the market, you can compare bridging loan rates with our team.

For a wider look at the options available, visit our funding solutions hub to see how bridging loans compare to other forms of business and property finance.

Frequently Asked Questions

How quickly can a commercial bridging loan complete?
Straightforward cases typically complete in 7 to 21 working days from enquiry to funds released, though this can stretch to 4-6 weeks where titles are complex or unregistered land is involved.

What is the maximum loan-to-value on a bridging loan?
Most lenders go up to 65-75% LTV on standard residential investment property, 50-60% on commercial or semi-commercial units, and 45-55% on land or heavy refurbishment projects.

Do I need a clear exit strategy to get a bridging loan?
Yes. Lenders want documented evidence of the exit, whether that's a mortgage offer for refinance, agreed sale terms, or a credible sales and marketing plan. A vague or unrealistic exit is the most common reason applications get declined.

How much does a commercial bridging loan cost?
Interest rates typically run from 0.55% to 1.25% per month depending on loan-to-value and security type, with arrangement fees of 1% to 2% of the loan, plus valuation and legal costs on both sides.

Is commercial bridging finance regulated?
Commercial bridging secured against investment or business property generally falls outside FCA regulation, unlike loans secured against a property the borrower or a family member lives in, which are regulated.

Can bad credit stop me getting a bridging loan?
Not automatically, but a poor credit history usually reduces the maximum LTV, pushes the rate up, and narrows the pool of lenders willing to consider the case.

Why would I use a broker instead of approaching a lender directly?
Rates, fees, and appetite for particular security types vary considerably between lenders, and a broker can compare the market to find a better structured deal than going direct to a single lender. If you're ready to move forward, you can arrange a bridging loan today with our team.

content:
A bridging loan 28 day completion in the UK is a short-term property loan structured and funded within roughly four weeks of application, most often used for auction purchases, chain breaks or time-pressured development deals. Boxx Finance arranges fast bridging loans for UK businesses and individual buyers who cannot wait for a mortgage timeline. Speed comes from valuation, title checks and legal work all running in parallel rather than in sequence.

28 days is the benchmark most auction houses set as their completion deadline, and it's also roughly how long a well-prepared bridging application takes from decision-in-principle to funds in a solicitor's client account. Most straightforward cases with ready paperwork hit this target, though it's not a guarantee every lender achieves.

What this means in practice

In practice, a 28 day completion means every party involved, the lender, the valuer, both sets of solicitors and often a broker, moves at the same pace with no gaps between stages. There's no room for a slow conveyancer or a valuer who can't get out to the property for two weeks.

For a residential buyer, this usually means an auction purchase where the 20% deposit has already been paid and the balance needs to land within the standard 28-day auction window, or a chain break where a sale has fallen through late and a purchase needs to complete regardless. For a developer, it's often a site purchase with planning consent close to lapsing, or a refurbishment opportunity where a vendor wants a quick, certain sale and will only accept offers with proof of funds behind them.

Both groups share the same need: certainty. The buyer isn't shopping around for the cheapest rate over five months, they're paying a premium for a lender who can genuinely deliver within the deadline. That's the trade-off borrowers need to accept before they start the process.

How it works

The mechanics of a fast bridging loan are simpler than most people expect, but the discipline required to hit 28 days is what separates a smooth deal from a stressful one.

The process typically runs like this: initial enquiry and decision-in-principle within 24-48 hours, a valuation instructed immediately (often a desktop or automated valuation model first, followed by a physical inspection), legal work running concurrently with underwriting rather than after it, and funds released once title is clean and the exit strategy is documented. Lenders offering genuinely fast completions use panel solicitors and valuers who are used to this pace, which is one reason broker relationships matter so much here.

The single biggest time saver is instructing solicitors on day one, not once the loan offer is issued. Borrowers who wait for a formal offer before engaging a solicitor routinely add a week or more to the timeline, sometimes enough to miss the deadline entirely.

Rates on 28-day bridging loans in the UK generally sit between 0.55% and 1.1% per month depending on loan-to-value, security type and how quickly the lender needs to move. Arrangement fees typically range from 1.5% to 2.5% of the loan, and most lenders also charge an exit fee or none at all depending on the product. Anyone comparing options should look at current UK bridging loan rates before assuming the headline monthly rate tells the full story.

Typical scenarios

Real deals illustrate this far more clearly than percentages alone.

A first-time landlord in Reading won a two-bedroom terrace at auction for £185,000 and needed £129,500 (70% LTV) to complete within the standard 28-day window. The valuation was booked the same day as the enquiry, legal work ran in parallel with underwriting, and funds were released in 19 working days, with the exit being a buy-to-let remortgage once the tenancy was in place.

A developer near Norwich needed £310,000 against a semi-derelict commercial-to-residential conversion valued at £520,000 post-works (60% LTV on GDV), with planning consent set to lapse in five weeks. The lender accepted the planning permission and a fixed-price build contract as evidence of the exit, and the loan completed in 22 working days, ahead of the deadline, with the exit planned as a sale of the completed units.

A business owner in Birmingham was mid-chain on a residential move when their buyer pulled out three weeks before exchange. A £95,000 bridging loan against the property being sold (48% LTV) allowed the purchase to proceed regardless, completing in 16 working days, with the exit being the eventual sale once a new buyer was found.

What lenders look for

Lenders assessing a 28-day bridging case focus on one question: can this deal actually complete without surprises. Loan-to-value typically runs from 65% to 75% on residential security and 55% to 65% on commercial or semi-commercial property, though some specialist lenders will stretch higher with additional security or a stronger exit.

Timescales from enquiry to funds genuinely achievable within 28 days require a clean title, no complex leasehold issues, no unresolved planning conditions, and a valuer who can attend within the first week. Security accepted includes residential, buy-to-let, semi-commercial and land with planning, though unmortgageable or structurally unsound property will slow or stall a case regardless of how urgent the deadline is.

Lenders require evidence of exit. They want to see either a signed mortgage offer for refinance, an agreed sale with a solicitor's letter confirming progress, or a credible development timeline with costed works and comparable evidence for GDV. The most common reasons applications decline or face delays at this stage are missing or vague exit evidence, undisclosed adverse credit that surfaces late in underwriting, and title issues such as unregistered land or absent freeholder consent.

Common mistakes

Most delays are avoidable, and they nearly always come down to preparation rather than the lender being slow.

Borrowers frequently underestimate how much documentation is needed upfront: ID, proof of income or company accounts, a clear exit plan, and evidence of the deposit or existing equity. Submitting an application with gaps means the clock effectively restarts once the lender chases missing information.

Another common mistake is choosing a solicitor who isn't experienced with bridging transactions. General conveyancers who are used to standard mortgage timelines can genuinely become the bottleneck, even when the lender itself is ready to move within days.

Borrowers also focus purely on the headline monthly rate and ignore arrangement fees, valuation costs and exit fees, only to be surprised by the total cost of borrowing once the loan completes. Developers in particular sometimes underestimate how long a physical valuation takes on a part-built or unusual property, which can quietly add a week to the timeline if it isn't flagged early.

Alternatives or comparisons

A 28-day bridging loan is the wrong choice if there's no genuine deadline forcing the pace, because the speed premium simply isn't worth paying for. If a purchase can comfortably wait 8-12 weeks, a standard mortgage or buy-to-let mortgage will almost always be cheaper.

It's also the wrong tool if the exit strategy is uncertain. Lenders will decline or heavily discount LTV where there's no clear route to repayment, and borrowers shouldn't force a bridging loan onto a deal that doesn't have one. In that situation, a longer-term development finance facility with a built-in drawdown schedule is usually the better fit, particularly for larger refurbishment or new-build projects where works span many months.

For smaller cash-flow gaps unrelated to property completion, unsecured business finance or an asset finance facility is often faster and cheaper than bridging security. Bridging loans are a property-specific tool, not a general-purpose one, and treating them that way is where borrowers get into trouble.

How to get the best outcome

The single best thing a borrower can do is start the legal and valuation process before the loan is even formally offered. Instructing a solicitor familiar with bridging transactions on day one, and having ID, bank statements and proof of exit ready before the lender asks, routinely shaves a week off the process.

Working with a broker who has direct relationships with lenders that actually deliver 28-day completions matters more than most borrowers realise. Boxx Finance deals with these timelines every week and knows which lenders genuinely hit 28 days versus which ones quote it but rarely deliver. If you want to arrange a bridging loan against a tight deadline, it's worth having that conversation before you commit to an auction lot or exchange contracts, not after.

It also pays to be realistic about LTV. Borrowers who ask for the maximum available LTV on a tight deadline often find the extra underwriting scrutiny slows the case down. Requesting a slightly lower LTV, where the numbers allow, frequently gets a faster yes.

Summary

A bridging loan 28 day completion in the UK is achievable and common, but it depends far more on preparation, a clean title and clear exit evidence than on any single lender being unusually fast. Residential buyers use it for auctions and chain breaks, developers use it for planning-sensitive purchases and refurbishment exits, and both need the same discipline around documentation and legal instruction.
