content:
The fastest bridging loan UK lenders can arrange typically completes in 3 to 7 working days for a straightforward case with a clean title and a cooperative solicitor, though most deals realistically take 10 to 14 days once valuations and legal checks are factored in. A fast bridging loan uk works by securing short-term funds against property, allowing buyers to move before a sale, auction deadline or refinance completes. Speed depends far more on preparation than on the lender's marketing claims. If you'd like tailored guidance, you can get a bridging loan quote with our team.

We arrange these deals every week at Boxx Finance, and the pattern is always the same. The applicants who genuinely get funds inside a week are the ones who had their paperwork ready before they even called us. The ones chasing a 48-hour headline rate almost always end up disappointed once their solicitor gets involved. For a broader introduction to how this type of lending works, see our guide on understanding how bridging finance works.

To put this in real terms, a typical short-term property finance loan of £200,000 against a residential property worth £350,000 might carry a rate of around 0.75% to 1% per month, plus a lender arrangement fee of 1.5% to 2%. On a straightforward case, that loan could be drawn down in a week. On a case with a leasehold flat, an unregistered title, or an overseas director involved in the borrowing entity, the same loan might take three weeks, regardless of what the lender's website promises.

What "fast" actually means once all the costs are added up needs to be clear. On that same £200,000 loan, monthly interest at 0.85% works out to around £1,700, and the 2% arrangement fee adds a further £4,000 taken from the gross loan at completion. Legal fees of perhaps £1,000 to £1,500, plus a valuation fee that might range from £400 for a standard house to £900 or more for something unusual, make the true cost of speed obvious. None of this is hidden, but borrowers who only focus on the headline turnaround time often forget to budget for it properly. For a closer look at how pricing varies between lenders, our breakdown of current bridging loan rates is a useful reference.

The lenders who genuinely move fastest tend to be smaller, specialist bridging houses rather than the big high street names. They often have decision makers who can approve a deal on a call, sometimes within hours of seeing the numbers. Valuations can be instructed the same day, and many now accept desktop or automated valuation models for lower loan-to-value deals under 50%, which shaves days off the process.

These smaller lenders also tend to underwrite manually rather than relying purely on automated credit scoring systems. That matters a great deal for self-employed applicants, company directors, or anyone with a slightly unusual income structure, because a human underwriter can look at the full picture and make a common sense decision rather than declining automatically on a technicality. In our experience, specialist lenders often beat the big banks on speed because of this human element, not just because of their smaller size. Our roundup of leading specialist bridging lenders covers several of these options in more detail.

What this means in practice

Speed comes from three sources: the applicant's paperwork, the property itself, and the solicitor acting for the borrower. If any one of these three is slow, the whole deal slows down, no matter how quick the lender claims to be.

On the paperwork side, the fastest cases are the ones where the borrower has photo ID, proof of address, three to six months of bank statements, and a clear exit strategy document ready before the application even goes in. An exit strategy is simply how the loan will be repaid, whether through the sale of the property, a remortgage onto a term loan, or funds coming in from another source. Lenders will not release funds without this being credible and evidenced.

Deals have collapsed from 5 days to 25 days purely because a borrower couldn't immediately produce proof of the source of their deposit, or because a company applicant hadn't updated their Companies House filings. These aren't unusual requests. They're standard checks that any regulated lender has to carry out, and having them ready in advance is often the single biggest factor in how fast a bridging loan actually completes.

A practical tip we give every client is to prepare a simple document pack before making contact with any lender. This should include certified ID, three months of bank statements for every director or applicant, a recent credit report, proof of the deposit source if applicable, and a one-page summary of the exit strategy with rough dates. Clients who arrive with this pack already assembled routinely see offer letters issued within 24 to 48 hours of application, compared with a week or more for those starting from scratch.

Why the property itself affects speed

The property itself also matters more than most borrowers expect. A standard freehold house in reasonable condition with no structural issues, no Japanese knotweed, and a clean title registered at the Land Registry is the quickest type of security to lend against. Add in anything unusual, such as a flat above a commercial unit, a property with a flying freehold, or land without planning permission, and the valuer's report will take longer, sometimes needing a second opinion or additional legal input.

It also helps enormously if the property has recent photographs, an up to date EPC, and any relevant planning permissions or building regulations certificates already gathered together. Valuers sometimes need to revisit a property or request further information if these documents aren't available on the first inspection, and each round trip can add three to five working days onto the overall timeline.

The role of your solicitor in completion speed

Then there's the solicitor. This is where we see more delays than anywhere else. Short-term property finance moves on legal timescales, not just lender timescales, and a solicitor who is slow to respond to enquiries, slow to raise or answer legal queries, or simply juggling too many files, can turn a 7-day bridge into a 4-week one.

Using a solicitor who has handled bridging loans before, ideally one who is used to acting quickly and understands the pressure of short-term lending timeframes, makes a genuine difference. Some lenders maintain a panel of solicitors who they know work fast, and using a panel firm can shave several days off completion compared with instructing an unfamiliar high street conveyancer.

One thing we always flag to clients is that dual representation, where the same solicitor acts for both borrower and lender, can sometimes speed things up further by removing a layer of correspondence between two separate firms. It isn't right for every case, particularly where there's a conflict of interest, but for straightforward residential bridges it's worth asking your broker whether it's an option.

Auction purchases and chain break scenarios

From a broker's perspective, the real value of a fast bridging loan often isn't the speed itself, but the certainty it brings to a chain or an auction purchase. Auction buyers in particular are under strict deadlines, usually 28 days from exchange to completion, and missing that deadline can mean losing a 10% deposit. A well-prepared bridging application, submitted with all supporting documents from day one, gives auction buyers the best chance of hitting that deadline comfortably.

For auction purchases specifically, we recommend clients speak to a broker before the auction even takes place, not after the hammer falls. Having an agreement in principle in hand before bidding means the lender has already reviewed the applicant's circumstances, so the only outstanding work after the auction is the valuation and legal completion. This alone can turn a tight 28-day deadline into a comfortable one.

We also see landlords using fast bridging loans to secure below-market-value properties that need refurbishment before they can be mortgaged conventionally. In these cases, speed matters because the seller often has other interested buyers waiting, and being able to demonstrate to the estate agent that funds can complete within two weeks can be the deciding factor in getting an offer accepted. We see this often with clients arranging bridging loans in London, where competition for below-market-value stock is especially high, as well as with those seeking bridging loans in Birmingham.

Refurbishment bridges also often come with a further tranche of funding released once works are completed, allowing the landlord to draw down an initial amount to complete the purchase and a second amount to cover renovation costs. Structuring this correctly from the outset, with a realistic schedule of works and cost estimates, tends to speed up both the initial approval and the release of the second tranche.

Chain break bridging explained

Another area where speed is genuine, and not just marketing, is chain break bridging. If a borrower's sale falls through at the last minute but they still need to complete on their new purchase, a bridge can be arranged very quickly because the security property is already known, the valuation may already exist, and the borrower's exit is simply the eventual sale of their current home. This is a scenario we regularly manage for clients arranging bridging loans in Norwich and bridging loans in Reading.

In these chain break situations, having a recent valuation report, even one commissioned for a previous mortgage application, can sometimes be reused or updated quickly rather than commissioned from scratch, saving several days. It's always worth mentioning any existing valuations to your broker at the outset, since this small detail is often overlooked under the stress of a collapsing chain.

You need to weigh up costs for speed properly. Faster bridging loans sometimes come with slightly higher arrangement fees or a marginally higher monthly rate, reflecting the additional work a lender puts in to prioritise a case. On a £150,000 loan, the difference between a standard and an expedited service might only be an extra £750 to £1,500 in total fees, which is often a small price to pay compared with losing a property purchase or an auction deposit.

Ultimately, the borrowers who get the fastest outcomes are the ones who treat bridging loans as a partnership between themselves, their broker, their solicitor and the lender, rather than simply shopping for the lowest headline speed claim. You've just had the hammer come down. Maybe you've paid a 10% deposit and signed the memorandum of sale. Now you're wondering exactly how many days you've actually got before completion, and whether that's enough time to sort your bridging loans for auction property purchases in place.

The short answer is 28 calendar days in most cases, but not always. Some online and timed auctions use 20 working days instead, which is materially shorter once you account for weekends. This matters because the wrong assumption here can cost you your deposit.

We speak to buyers most weeks who've won a property and only then started thinking seriously about how the money side works. The auction process moves fast and the excitement of winning tends to overshadow the practical countdown that starts the moment the gavel comes down. That countdown is unforgiving, and auctioneers are not sympathetic to buyers who run out of time. If you want to understand the basics first, our guide to what bridging finance actually involves is a good place to start.

The clock

Under the Common Auction Conditions, which most UK room auctions use, you have 28 calendar days from the fall of the hammer to complete. That's not 28 working days. Weekends and bank holidays count, so a 28-day window can shrink to as few as 18-19 working days depending on when the sale falls.

To put that in perspective, if you win a lot on a Wednesday in late December, you could be looking at Christmas Day, Boxing Day, New Year's Day and several weekends all eating into your 28 days without a single working day being added back. Solicitors' offices close, search departments close, and lenders often have reduced capacity over that period too. The calendar doesn't care that it's the festive season, the clock keeps ticking regardless.

Online and timed auctions work differently

Online and timed auctions are a different story. Many platforms, including some of the larger national ones, use a 20-working-day condition rather than the traditional 28 calendar days. Twenty working days is roughly four calendar weeks, but because it excludes weekends it can actually land you close to or slightly beyond 28 calendar days in practice, depending on bank holidays. You cannot assume. You must read the specific legal pack for the lot you've bought, because the completion condition is set by the auctioneer's terms, not by a single national rule.

We've seen buyers assume that because a previous purchase gave them 28 days, this one automatically will too. It's an easy mistake to make when you're juggling several lots or bidding across different auction houses in the same month. Each legal pack is its own document with its own conditions, and the completion timeframe is usually buried in the special conditions of sale rather than the headline particulars.

Some auctioneers also include a provision for late completion, typically charging daily interest on the outstanding balance if you complete after day 28. That interest rate is often set at a punitive level, sometimes 3-4% above the Bank of England base rate, specifically to discourage buyers from treating the deadline as flexible. It isn't flexible. Missing it has real financial consequences even before you get to the risk of losing the property altogether.

A day-by-day breakdown of the 28-day window

Here's a worked day-by-day table for a standard 28-calendar-day window, assuming an auction on a Wednesday with no bank holidays falling in the period:

DayWhat needs to happen
Day 0 (auction day)Hammer falls, 10% deposit paid, memorandum signed, solicitor instructed same day
Days 1-3Solicitor reviews legal pack, valuation instructed, mortgage or short-term property finance application submitted
Days 3-13Local authority, water and environmental searches (typically 5-10 working days, longer in some boroughs)
Days 5-15Valuation carried out, lender reviews report, formal offer issued if satisfactory
Days 15-22Legal work: enquiries raised and answered, mortgage or bridging offer reviewed by solicitor, report on title sent
Days 22-26Funds requested, redemption statements chased if there's an existing charge, completion statement agreed
Day 28Completion, balance of funds transferred, keys released

That leaves very little slack. If searches come back slow, or a valuation down-values the property, or a lender asks for more information mid-way through, you can burn through your buffer fast. In our experience, the applications that stall are almost always the ones where the buyer waited until day 4 or 5 to instruct a solicitor because they were still deciding whether to go with a mortgage broker or come to a specialist lender directly. If you'd like to talk through your own timeline, you can get a bridging loan quote.

Where buyers lose the most time

Local authority searches are one of the biggest variables in this whole process. Some London boroughs and busy councils elsewhere can take two to three weeks to turn around a standard search, which on its own can eat almost your entire completion window. Many experienced auction buyers get around this by paying for personal searches or insured search indemnity policies instead, which you can arrange in a day or two rather than waiting on a local authority queue.

Valuations are the other pinch point. A standard residential valuation might be booked within a few days of instruction, but if the property is unusual, non-standard construction, or has had building works without documentation, the valuer may need to refer it internally or request additional information. That can add another week if you're unlucky, which is why speaking to a broker who knows which lenders move fastest on auction purchases matters so much.

Why short-term property finance suits auction deadlines

On funding specifically, short-term property finance tends to be the more realistic option for the tight end of a 28-day timeline. A specialist bridging lender can often turn around an agreement in principle within 24 to 48 hours and complete within 10 to 14 days if the legal work moves smoothly. A mainstream mortgage lender, even one marketed as fast, usually needs the full underwriting process including a full valuation and often a manual credit assessment. That's not always compatible with a 28-day deadline once you factor in searches and legal enquiries running alongside it. You can compare bridging loans for auction purchases to see what's realistic for your timeline, and our breakdown of current bridging loan rates is worth reading before you approach a lender.

Costs matter here too. Bridging loans typically run at somewhere between 0.55% and 0.95% per month depending on the lender, the loan to value and the security offered, plus arrangement fees usually in the region of 1.5% to 2% of the loan. It isn't cheap money, but for a buyer who needs certainty of completion within 28 days, it's often the only realistic route, particularly on properties that wouldn't qualify for a standard mortgage anyway, such as those without a working kitchen or bathroom, or with short lease issues. Choosing the right lender matters too, and our guide to the best bridging loan lenders in the UK can help narrow that down.

A refurbishment bridge is also worth considering if the property needs work before you can refinance it onto a term mortgage or sell it on. These products release funds in stages, an initial drawdown to complete the purchase and further tranches released against invoices or surveyor sign-off as works progress. It's a useful structure for buyers planning to add value quickly, but it does add another layer of paperwork that needs sorting from day one, not day twenty. Specialist brokers arranging bridging loans in London, bridging loans in Birmingham, bridging loans in Norwich and bridging loans in Reading will all be familiar with these staged drawdown structures.

Getting your paperwork ready before auction day

Communication with your solicitor in the first 48 hours makes a bigger difference than almost anything else in this process. Auction solicitors who specialise in this type of work know to chase searches immediately, flag any title issues from the legal pack straight away, and liaise directly with your broker or lender rather than waiting for updates to filter through slowly. Choosing a solicitor who has never handled an auction completion before, purely because they did your last house move, is one of the most common ways buyers lose days they didn't have to lose.

It's also worth having your deposit and proof of funds for the remaining balance sorted before you even attend the auction, not after. Lenders and brokers can only move as fast as the information you give them, and a buyer who turns up to bid with an agreement in principle already in place, satisfactory identification documents ready, and a solicitor on standby will always have a smoother 28 days than one starting from scratch.

If you're planning to bid at auction in the near future, it's worth having a conversation with a broker before the day itself rather than after. Understanding what's realistically achievable with your circumstances, your deposit, and the type of property you're targeting means you go into the room, or onto the online platform, with a genuine understanding of your completion timeline rather than a hopeful assumption. Our funding solutions hub covers the full range of options if bridging isn't the right fit for your situation.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many days do you have to complete on an auction property?
In most UK room auctions, you have 28 calendar days from the fall of the hammer under the Common Auction Conditions. Online and timed auctions sometimes use 20 working days instead, so always check the legal pack for the specific lot.

What happens if I miss the 28-day completion deadline?
You'll typically be charged daily interest on the outstanding balance, often at a punitive rate of 3-4% above the Bank of England base rate. In more serious cases, you risk losing your deposit and the property altogether.

Can a mortgage be arranged in time for an auction completion?
It's possible but tight. Mainstream mortgages usually require full underwriting, valuation and manual credit assessment, which can be difficult to complete within 28 days once searches and legal enquiries are factored in.

Why do buyers use bridging loans for auction purchases?
Bridging loans can often be agreed in principle within 24 to 48 hours and completed within 10 to 14 days, making them a more realistic option than a standard mortgage when working to a tight auction deadline.

Do 20 working days give more or less time than 28 calendar days?
It depends on bank holidays, but 20 working days can sometimes stretch close to or slightly beyond 28 calendar days in practice, since weekends aren't counted.

How much does bridging finance cost for an auction purchase?
Rates typically range from 0.55% to 0.95% per month depending on the lender, loan to value and security offered, plus arrangement fees usually around 1.5% to 2% of the loan amount.

What can I do before auction day to protect my completion timeline?
Have your deposit and proof of funds ready, instruct a solicitor experienced in auction completions, and speak to a broker in advance so you can get a bridging loan quote before you start bidding.

content:
Emergency property finance in the UK almost always means a bridging loan, a short-term loan secured against property that can complete in days rather than the weeks a mortgage takes. Businesses and individuals use it when a purchase, refinance or cash need is time-critical and a conventional lender cannot move fast enough. It is expensive relative to a mortgage, but speed is the entire point.

We arrange these deals every week at Boxx Finance, and the pattern is always the same. Someone has a deadline, whether that's an auction completion date, a chain about to collapse, or a tax bill landing before a sale completes, and the high street cannot help within the timeframe. That's where bridging loans deliver real value.

What this means in practice

In practice, emergency property finance is a bridging loan secured against a property you already own, are buying, or both, structured to release funds within days to a few weeks rather than the six to twelve weeks a standard mortgage typically takes.

Lenders in this space are not banks in the traditional sense. Most are specialist bridging lenders, some backed by institutional funding lines, others privately funded. They assess the property and the exit route far more than they assess your income, which is exactly why they can move quickly.

For a residential buyer, this might mean securing a property at auction with a 28-day completion deadline, where mortgage finance simply won't be ready in time. For a developer, it might mean funding the purchase of a site with planning potential while a longer-term development facility is arranged behind it. Both scenarios sit under the same umbrella of short-term property finance, just with different exit strategies.

How it works

A bridging loan works by using the property itself, sometimes the one being bought, sometimes another asset you own, as security, with the lender releasing funds once legal charges are registered and valuation is confirmed.

The process typically runs like this. You approach a broker or lender with the scenario and the deadline. A decision in principle can often be issued within 24 to 48 hours. A valuation is instructed, sometimes a desktop or automated valuation for straightforward cases, sometimes a full physical inspection for higher value or unusual properties. Legal work runs in parallel where possible rather than sequentially, which is one of the main reasons bridging completions beat mortgage timelines.

Interest is usually charged monthly and rolled up rather than paid, meaning you don't need monthly cashflow to service the loan, you settle the accrued interest at the end alongside the capital. Rates for UK bridging loans in late 2024 and into 2025 have generally sat between 0.55% and 1.25% per month depending on loan-to-value, property type and lender appetite, and you can track how these figures move against wider lending conditions through the UK SME lending rates data we maintain. For a fuller breakdown of current pricing, our piece on current UK bridging loan rates is worth reading alongside this guide.

If your deadline is approaching fast, you can arrange a bridging loan today and get the process moving before the pressure builds further.

Typical scenarios

The scenarios we see fall into a fairly predictable set of categories, but the numbers vary hugely depending on the exit.

A landlord in Leeds needed £180,000 against a £320,000 buy-to-let property, a 56% loan-to-value, over a 9-month term, with the exit being a refinance onto a standard buy-to-let mortgage once a new tenancy was in place. Funds were released in 12 working days from first enquiry.

A developer in the Midlands needed £310,000 to complete an auction purchase of a semi-derelict property with planning consent for conversion into three flats, a 62% LTV against the as-is value, over a 12-month term, exiting via a development finance facility once works started. Completion happened in 9 working days, tight but achievable because the legal pack from the auction house was already in good order.

A residential buyer facing a broken chain in Reading needed a £95,000 bridge to complete on a new purchase while their existing home sale fell through and was re-marketed, secured against the new property at 48% LTV over a 6-month term, exiting on the eventual sale of the old home. That deal completed in 15 working days because of a slightly messier title issue that needed resolving.

We see similar patterns of demand for bridging loans in London, where high property values and auction activity create constant need for fast completions, and equally strong demand for bridging loans in Birmingham from developers working through planning-led refurbishment projects. Similar patterns show up in bridging loans in Norwich and bridging loans in Reading, where local property markets create their own version of the same time pressure.

What lenders look for

Lenders assess emergency property finance applications primarily on the property's value, the loan-to-value ratio, and the credibility of the exit strategy, rather than on income or credit history in the way a mortgage lender would.

Most UK bridging lenders will go up to 70-75% LTV on residential property, sometimes lower on commercial or semi-commercial assets, and lower still on land without planning consent, where 50-55% is more typical. Timescales from enquiry to funds genuinely can be as fast as 5 to 7 working days for a clean case with an agreed valuation and no title complications, though 10 to 15 working days is a more realistic average across the market.

Security can be the property being purchased, an existing unencumbered property, or a second charge behind an existing mortgage, provided the first charge lender consents. Lenders want firm evidence of the exit, whether that's a mortgage offer already in principle, a signed sale contract, or a development appraisal showing the numbers stack up for a refinance.

The most common reason we see applications declined or delayed is an unclear or unrealistic exit. Lenders rarely say this outright in their decline letters, but if the repayment route depends on an optimistic sale price or a refinance that assumes rates or rental yields improve, they will either decline outright or price the risk in heavily. Getting the exit narrative right before you apply saves weeks.

Loan-to-value bandTypical monthly rateProperty type
Up to 50% LTV0.55% - 0.75%Residential, low risk
50% - 65% LTV0.75% - 0.95%Residential and commercial mix
65% - 75% LTV0.95% - 1.25%Higher risk, land or heavy refurb

Common mistakes

The biggest mistake we see is underestimating how long legal work takes, even when the lender itself can move fast. A bridging loan is only as quick as the slowest party in the chain, and that's often the solicitor, not the lender.

Second, borrowers frequently assume they'll get the maximum LTV advertised by a lender's website, without accounting for the fact that pricing and rates both tighten on unusual property types, non-standard construction, or properties with short leases.

Third, many people apply to several lenders simultaneously without a broker coordinating the process, which wastes valuation fees and creates confusing paper trails when underwriters ask questions. In our experience, a single well-packaged application through a broker who knows which lender actually wants that deal gets to completion faster than three scattergun applications.

Finally, borrowers sometimes don't plan the exit early enough. If your exit is a refinance, start that conversation with a mortgage broker on day one of the bridge, not in month nine of a twelve-month term.

Alternatives or comparisons

Emergency property finance through a bridging loan is the wrong choice if you have more than a few weeks to arrange funding and your circumstances would qualify for a standard mortgage or secured loan at a fraction of the cost. If there's no genuine time pressure, a bridging loan's higher rate and arrangement fees simply aren't justified.

If you need funds for business cashflow rather than a property transaction, an unsecured business loan or invoice finance facility will usually be cheaper and simpler. If you're funding a long development project from the ground up rather than bridging a short gap, a dedicated development finance facility with staged drawdowns is a better structural fit than a bridging loan. And if your credit history and income are strong and you have four to six weeks available, a standard mortgage or secured loan will almost always beat bridging loan pricing.

Where bridging loans genuinely win is when speed or property condition rules out mainstream lending entirely, an unmortgageable property, an auction deadline, a probate sale needing to complete before administration finishes, or a chain break with no time to wait.

How to get the best outcome

Getting a good outcome starts with having your documents ready before you even approach a lender, not after. Proof of ID, proof of the property, a clear exit plan and, where relevant, a schedule of works for developer finance cases, all speed up underwriting significantly.

Use a broker who works across multiple bridging lenders rather than approaching one lender directly. Pricing and appetite vary enormously between lenders for the same deal, and a broker who places these regularly will know within an hour or two which two or three lenders are actually right for your scenario.

If you're weighing up your options and want a straightforward view on what's realistic for your timeline and property, take the time to get a bridging loan quote before committing to any single lender, since the difference between offers on the same deal can be significant.

Read up on the fundamentals too. Our guide on how bridging loans work and our review of leading UK bridging lenders both give useful background before you start the application itself.

Emergency property finance in the UK is delivered through bridging loans, and speed, not price, is the reason people use them. Get your exit strategy clear, your paperwork ready, and work with a broker who knows the lender landscape, and a genuinely fast completion is realistic. title: Using a Bridging Loan to Release Inheritance Property Value
excerpt: Inheriting a property often creates urgent cash flow and probate deadlines. Bridging loans let you release equity or buy out co-beneficiaries quickly, before probate completes or a sale finishes.
metaTitle: Using a Bridging Loan to Release Inheritance Property Value
metaDescription: Using a Bridging Loan to Release Inheritance Property Value. Expert advice from Boxx Finance, a whole-of-market UK bridging finance broker.
keywords: inheritance property bridging loan, probate bridging loan, bridging loan against inherited property, buy out siblings inherited house, short-term property finance probate, bridging loan before probate completes, developer finance inherited property
author: Tara Jameson
content:
A bridging loan inheritance property uk arrangement is a short-term secured loan taken out against a property you have inherited, or expect to inherit, used to release cash before probate finishes or before the property is sold. Executors, beneficiaries and developers use bridging loans for inheritance property to buy out co-beneficiaries, cover inheritance tax bills, or fund a refurbishment ahead of resale. Funds can often complete in two to three weeks.

Inheritance-related bridging is one of the more misunderstood corners of short-term property finance. People assume they cannot borrow against a property until probate is granted, but this is not true in most cases. Lenders have built products specifically around this gap, and we arrange them regularly for families and developers alike. If you want to understand the basics first, our guide to what bridging finance actually is is a good starting point.

What surprises clients most is how routine these deals become once you get past the initial concern. A solicitor might mention bridging loans in passing, or a beneficiary finds us through a search, and the assumption is always that this is a niche or last resort product. It is not. It is a well-established tool that solves a very specific timing problem, and specialist lenders underwrite hundreds of these cases every year.

What this means in practice

In practice, you do not have to wait for a house sale, or even for probate to be granted, before you can access the value tied up in an inherited property. This matters because HMRC often wants inheritance tax paid before probate is granted, creating a genuine problem for families.

For beneficiaries, it usually means paying an inheritance tax bill, buying out siblings or other co-owners who want their share in cash, or funding works to the property before selling it or refinancing onto a normal mortgage. For developers, it often means acquiring an inherited property from an estate at a discount, refurbishing it, and either selling or refinancing.

The key practical point is timing. Probate in England and Wales is currently taking several months longer than it did five years ago, largely due to backlogs at the Probate Registry. A bridging loan against inherited property uk lenders offer bridges exactly that gap, letting you act while the legal process continues in the background.

There is also a cashflow reality that catches people out. Inheritance tax is normally due within six months of the end of the month in which the person died, and HMRC charges interest on late payment regardless of whether probate has come through. Families who assume they can simply wait for the house sale to settle the bill often find themselves facing interest charges on top of an already stressful situation, which is precisely what short-term property finance is designed to close. If your situation is time-critical, you can get a bridging loan quote rather than waiting for probate to conclude.

How it works

The loan is secured against the inherited property itself, usually with a first charge, though second charge lending is possible where there is an existing mortgage or another loan already secured. The lender advances a percentage of the property's value, typically referred to as loan-to-value or LTV, and you repay the loan in full at the end of the agreed term, usually through a sale or refinance.

Where probate has not yet been granted, lenders will usually still proceed, provided there is a clear will, a named executor, and solicitors acting who can confirm the estate's position. Some lenders will lend pre-grant of probate on the strength of the will and a solicitor's undertaking; others insist on waiting until the Grant of Probate has been issued. This is one of the first things we check with a client, because it materially changes which lenders are available.

Interest is usually rolled up or retained rather than paid monthly, which suits beneficiaries who have no income from the property yet. Fees typically include an arrangement fee, valuation fee, and legal costs on both sides. Rates and current market conditions are covered in more depth in our piece on current UK bridging loan rates, and it's a useful reference point before you start comparing lenders.

On a practical note, most lenders in this space charge monthly rates somewhere between 0.55% and 1% depending on LTV, property type and the strength of the exit. An arrangement fee of 1.5% to 2% of the loan amount is standard, and you should budget separately for a valuation fee, which varies with property value but often sits between £400 and £1,200 for a typical residential property. Legal costs on both sides can add a further £1,500 to £3,000, so it pays to factor these into the overall sum you actually need to borrow rather than just the headline figure. For a sense of who is active in this space, our roundup of leading UK bridging loan lenders is worth a read.

Lenders will not simply take your word that the property will sell or that probate will complete smoothly. They will ask for evidence of the estate's asset position, a realistic valuation, and in many cases a solicitor's letter confirming there is nothing unusual in the will that could delay things. The stronger this evidence, the faster the underwriting moves.

Typical scenarios

A common scenario looks like this. Three siblings inherit a house in Reading worth £480,000, with no mortgage attached. Two want to sell; one wants to keep the property and buy the others out. That sibling needs £320,000 to pay off the two shares. A lender advanced £320,000 against the £480,000 property, a 67% LTV, over a 12 month term, with the exit being a straightforward remortgage onto a standard buy-to-let or residential mortgage once probate was granted. Funds released in 16 working days, largely because the will was uncontested and the solicitor provided a clean undertaking. Cases like this are typical of bridging loans in Reading, where local solicitors are familiar with the process.

A second scenario involves a developer. An investor identified an inherited property in Birmingham going through probate, agreed a purchase from the estate at £210,000 against a market value of £260,000, and needed £180,000 (69% LTV) to complete quickly before the estate accepted a rival offer. The exit was a light refurbishment followed by sale at £295,000, achieved within a 9 month term. This is the kind of developer finance deal where speed, not rate, wins the property, and it reflects the pattern we see with bridging loans in Birmingham more broadly.

We also regularly see inheritance bridging used simply to pay an IHT bill. A family in Norwich needed £95,000 against a £410,000 inherited property (23% LTV) purely to settle inheritance tax so probate could progress, with the exit being sale of the property six months later. Because the LTV was low, this was one of the more straightforward approvals we've processed this year, similar to other bridging loans in Norwich we have arranged.

A fourth scenario worth mentioning involves a more complicated estate with a property in poor condition. A family inherited a bungalow in Kent worth £340,000 in its current state, but with damp, an outdated electrical system and no working kitchen, meaning it was effectively unmortgageable on the open market. A specialist lender advanced £190,000 (56% LTV) to allow refurbishment ahead of sale, factoring the works into the valuation. The property sold for £415,000 nine months later once brought up to standard, comfortably covering the loan, interest and refurbishment costs. We see similar demand from clients seeking bridging loans in London, where older properties often need work before they can be sold or remortgaged.

What lenders look for

Lenders assessing an inheritance bridging loan focus heavily on the estate's legal position and the exit strategy, more so than on the applicant's personal income. Expect LTVs between 55% and 75% for standard inherited residential property, dropping towards 50-60% for property still going through a contested or complex probate.

Evidence required typically includes a copy of the will, confirmation of executors, a solicitor's undertaking (especially pre-grant of probate), and a clear exit route, whether that's sale, refinance, or transfer of ownership between beneficiaries. Valuations are almost always required, and lenders will want a clean legal title search on the property itself.

Timescales from enquiry to funds typically run 10 to 20 working days for straightforward cases, and can stretch to five or six weeks where probate is contested, where there are multiple beneficiaries who disagree, or where the property has unusual construction or is unmortgageable in its current state. The most common reason we see these applications declined or delayed is disagreement among beneficiaries, not property issues. If siblings cannot agree on the sale or the valuation, lenders get nervous fast, because it puts the exit strategy at risk.

Acceptable security is usually residential property in reasonable saleable condition, though some specialist lenders will consider properties needing significant work, factoring the cost of refurbishment into their risk assessment. Property in London, Reading, Birmingham and Norwich tends to attract a wider panel of lenders than more rural or unusual assets, purely because resale liquidity is stronger.

Lenders differ hugely in their appetite for pre-grant lending. Some will only lend once the Grant of Probate is in hand, treating anything earlier as too uncertain. Others have built their entire proposition around pre-grant cases, understanding the solicitor's undertaking as sufficient comfort. Knowing which lenders sit where saves an enormous amount of wasted time, and it is one of the main reasons brokers add value in this specific niche.

Pre-grant of probate, uncontested will50-65%6-12 months
Post-grant, clean title, single exit65-75%6-18 months

Common mistakes

The biggest mistake we see is families waiting for probate to be fully granted before even speaking to a broker, losing weeks unnecessarily. Many lenders can start the underwriting process, order the valuation, and prepare legal documents well before the Grant of Probate arrives, so the loan can complete within days of grant rather than starting from scratch afterwards.

Another frequent error is underestimating how much co-beneficiaries need to agree before a lender will proceed. If one sibling refuses to sign a solicitor's undertaking or disputes the valuation, the whole application stalls. We always recommend getting agreement between all parties in writing before applying, even informally, because it saves weeks later.

People also sometimes borrow more than they need, treating the loan amount as a rough figure rather than working out the actual sum required to clear the IHT bill or buy out a sibling. Every extra pound borrowed accrues interest, so it is worth having a solicitor or accountant confirm the precise figure needed before the application goes in, rather than rounding up for comfort.

A further mistake is not thinking hard enough about the exit at the point of application. Beneficiaries sometimes assume a remortgage will be straightforward once probate is granted, without checking their own mortgage affordability or the property's suitability for a standard lender. Short-term property finance is a short-term fix, and if the exit is not realistic, refinancing at the end of the term can become a genuine problem rather than a formality.

Finally, some clients focus purely on the headline interest rate and ignore the total cost of borrowing, including arrangement fees, exit fees where applicable, valuation costs and legal fees on both sides. A slightly higher rate from a lender who can move faster and lend pre-grant of probate is often far better value than a cheaper rate from a lender who insists on waiting for full probate, particularly where HMRC interest is accruing on an unpaid inheritance tax bill in the meantime.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I get a bridging loan before probate is granted?
Yes, in many cases. Some lenders will lend pre-grant of probate provided there is a clear will, a named executor, and a solicitor's undertaking confirming the estate's position. Others will only proceed once the Grant of Probate has been issued, so it depends on which lender you approach.

How quickly can an inheritance bridging loan complete?
Straightforward cases with a clean title and uncontested will typically complete in 10 to 20 working days. More complex cases involving contested probate or multiple disagreeing beneficiaries can take five to six weeks or longer.

What can an inheritance bridging loan be used for?
Common uses include paying an inheritance tax bill before probate is granted, buying out co-beneficiaries who want their share in cash, and funding refurbishment works before a sale or remortgage.

What loan-to-value can I expect on an inherited property?
Typical LTVs range between 55% and 75% for standard inherited residential property, dropping to around 50-60% where probate is contested or the estate is more complex.

What happens if my siblings do not agree on selling the property?
Disagreement among beneficiaries is one of the most common reasons applications are delayed or declined, since lenders need confidence in the exit strategy. Getting written agreement between all parties before applying helps avoid this.

How is an inheritance bridging loan repaid?
Repayment usually happens through selling the property, refinancing onto a standard mortgage once probate is granted, or transferring ownership between beneficiaries. Interest is typically rolled up or retained rather than paid monthly.

What fees should I budget for?
Alongside the monthly interest rate, expect an arrangement fee of around 1.5% to 2% of the loan, a valuation fee of roughly £400 to £1,200, and legal costs on both sides that can add £1,500 to £3,000.

If you are weighing up your options for releasing funds from an inherited property, you can explore our full range of property funding solutions or get a bridging loan quote from our team today.

title: My Buyer Pulled Out — Can I Still Buy My Next House?
excerpt: Your buyer has walked away days before your own purchase completes. Here is how a bridging loan can hold your onward purchase together while you remarket your old property.
metaTitle: My Buyer Pulled Out — Can I Still Buy My Next House?
metaDescription: Your buyer pulled out and your own purchase is now at risk. See how a bridging loan can bridge the gap, what it costs, and how the exit strategy actually works.

author: Mark Higgins
content:
Your buyer has just pulled out. Maybe it was an email, maybe a phone call from the agent. Either way, the money you were relying on to complete your own purchase has gone. You've already exchanged, or you're about to. The seller of your new home is expecting funds on a fixed date, and right now you don't have them. That gap between what you need and what you've actually got is exactly what a bridging loan is built to cover.

This situation is far more common than most people realise. Chains break down in the UK for all sorts of reasons that have nothing to do with you or your onward purchase. A buyer's own mortgage offer can fall through at the last minute, a survey elsewhere in the chain can throw up a problem, or someone simply changes their mind about moving. Whatever the reason, you're left holding a completion date that hasn't moved an inch while the funding underneath it has disappeared overnight. Buyers in fast-moving markets such as bridging loans in London and bridging loans in Birmingham face this particularly often, simply because chains tend to be longer and more exposed to delay.

The bridging market understands this problem well. Lenders see this exact scenario regularly, sometimes weekly, and the products and processes exist specifically to deal with it. The key is moving quickly, understanding your real timeline, and not wasting days hoping the buyer situation somehow resolves itself before you explore your alternatives. If you want to talk through your specific dates and numbers, you can get a bridging loan quote before committing to anything.

The clock

Count your working days from today to your completion date, not calendar days. That number is the real constraint on everything you do next.

Say you exchanged on your onward purchase three weeks ago with a completion date fixed for the 30th of the month. Today is the 9th. That gives you roughly 15 working days. A bridging lender, once fully instructed with a valuation booked and solicitors engaged on both sides, typically needs 10 to 14 working days to get funds to your solicitor. That's tight, not impossible, but it leaves almost no room for delay on your part.

If you haven't exchanged yet on the purchase, you have a little more breathing space, because you can in theory delay exchange until funding is confirmed. Once you've exchanged, though, the completion date is a contractual obligation. Missing it isn't a soft deadline you can quietly push back. In our experience, the clients who get into real difficulty are the ones who spend the first five working days hoping their buyer situation resolves itself before picking up the phone to a broker. Those are five days you can't get back. If you're unsure what a bridging loan actually involves at this stage, it's worth reading a plain-English guide to what bridging finance actually is before you go further.

Weekends and bank holidays matter more than people expect at this stage of a transaction. A completion date that looks like three clear weeks away on a calendar can shrink to ten working days once you strip out two weekends and a bank holiday. Always work from a working day count, and always build in a buffer of two or three days for the unexpected, because something usually comes up during underwriting, whether that's a query from the valuer or a title issue your solicitor needs to clear.

Be honest with yourself about how much of that count has already been used up. If your buyer pulled out five days ago and you've spent that time speaking to estate agents about remarketing or trying to persuade your buyer to reconsider, you've already lost a fifth of a three week window. The moment it becomes clear the sale isn't proceeding, start the bridging enquiry in parallel with everything else, not after.

What happens if you miss it

Missing completion on your onward purchase has real financial and legal consequences, not just inconvenience. The seller can serve a notice to complete, and if you still can't complete after that, they can rescind the contract and keep your deposit.

Under the Standard Conditions of Sale used in most residential transactions, a deposit is typically 10% of the purchase price. On a £400,000 purchase that's £40,000 at risk. Beyond the deposit, the seller may also claim damages for further losses caused by the delay, such as bridging costs of their own if they've bought onward, or lost interest.

A notice to complete typically gives you a further ten working days from the date it's served, so it's not always instant disaster the moment the original date passes. But interest usually starts accruing on the purchase price at a contractual rate from the original completion date, set out in the contract itself and typically well above a standard mortgage rate, until you actually complete. On a £400,000 purchase that can commonly add up to tens or low hundreds of pounds a day depending on the rate agreed, so every day of delay has a real cost attached even before you get anywhere near the seller pulling out entirely. Ask your solicitor to confirm the exact contractual rate at exchange, not after.

There's also the less quantifiable cost. You lose the property. You go back to searching in a market where prices and stock have likely moved on since you first found this one. If you have a family timed around a school term, a job relocation, or a tenancy notice already served on your current rental, the disruption compounds. None of this is guaranteed to happen the moment you miss a date, sellers vary in how hard they push, but the legal mechanism for them to do so is real and standard.

Solicitors on both sides will usually try to find a practical way through before anyone reaches for a notice to complete. Sellers often prefer a short, agreed delay of a few days over the cost and hassle of rescinding a contract and remarketing their own property. But don't rely on goodwill as your primary plan. Treat the legal deadline as fixed and use any flexibility from the seller as a welcome bonus rather than the basis of your strategy.

Your options

Bridging is one route through this, not the only one, and it isn't automatically the right one for every situation. Here's how the realistic options compare.

OptionSpeedTypical costMain risk
Bridging loan against existing property10-14 working days once instructed0.55%-1.25% per month, plus 2% arrangement feeExpensive if exit is delayed; property at risk if not repaid
Renegotiate completion date with sellerDays, if they agreeMinimal, possibly noneSeller may refuse, especially if they're in a chain themselves
Ask your onward mortgage lender to increase the loan2-4 weeks typicallyStandard mortgage rateRarely fast enough; affordability reassessed
Family loan or personal savings top-upImmediate if availableNone or informalNot available to most people at this scale
Walk away and lose the purchaseN/ALoss of deposit paid, legal fees already spentBack to square one, plus possible damages claim

For most people in this exact position with a chain intact until the buyer withdrew, a real property to sell, and a genuine intention to remarket it, a bridging loan is the only option on this list that reliably moves at the speed the deadline demands. Renegotiating the date is worth trying in parallel, it costs nothing to ask, but don't build your plan around a seller's goodwill.

Asking your existing mortgage lender to extend or increase your borrowing on the property you're selling is another route some people consider, but it rarely works quickly enough in practice. Mainstream lenders need to reassess affordability, may require a new valuation of their own, and typically work to timescales measured in weeks rather than days. By the time an answer comes back, your completion date has often already passed.

Family loans work well for the people who have access to them, and if a relative can lend you the shortfall quickly and informally, it's usually cheaper than bridging. The difficulty is that most people in a £150,000 to £250,000 shortfall situation simply don't have a family member who can move that kind of money at short notice, which is why bridging remains the practical fallback for the majority of buyers in this position.

Walking away is always technically an option, and occasionally it's the right one if the numbers genuinely don't work or the property you're buying has issues that make you uneasy. But it's rarely a decision to make purely on timing grounds if a bridging loan can bridge the gap. Losing a deposit and starting the search again in a moving market is usually a worse outcome than a few months of bridging interest.

How a bridging loan works for this situation

In this scenario, a bridging loan is secured against your existing property, the one your buyer has just abandoned, and the funds released are used to complete your onward purchase. Once your existing property sells, the bridging loan is repaid from the proceeds.

Because you or an immediate family member will occupy the property you're buying, or the property being used as security, this is almost always FCA-regulated bridging. That matters. Regulated status means the lender must carry out proper affordability checks, you get access to the Financial Ombudsman Service if something goes wrong, and the lender has to communicate clearly on fees, rates and risk before you commit. It also generally means a slightly more thorough underwriting process than unregulated commercial bridging, so don't expect same-day funding.

The realistic timeline: day 1-2 is application and instructing a valuer, day 3-6 is the valuation being carried out and the report landing, day 5-10 is legal work running in parallel with your solicitor handling title checks and drafting the facility documentation, and day 10-14 is completion and funds transfer. Lenders will want proof of ID, proof of the property you're buying, evidence of your existing property's value and condition, and crucially, evidence of your exit plan. This timeline holds broadly true whether you're based in Norwich or Reading, though local valuer availability can shift things by a day or two either way.

The point where these applications most often stall isn't the valuation or the legals, it's the exit evidence. If you can't yet show your unsold property is back on the market with an agent, or you're still deciding on an asking price, expect the lender to pause and ask for that before they'll proceed to offer. Get the property remarketed on day one, before you even submit the bridging application, and you'll save yourself several days.

Choosing a solicitor who's used to bridging transactions makes a genuine difference to speed. A firm that's never handled a bridging completion before can easily add three or four days simply because they're unfamiliar with the facility documentation and the additional legal charge that needs registering alongside your mortgage, if you still have one. A good broker will usually be able to recommend solicitors who work regularly with bridging lenders and can turn the legal side around quickly. If speed is your main concern, you can arrange a bridging loan today and get the process moving straight away.

Instruct the same solicitor who's already acting on your onward purchase to also handle the bridging loan, where possible, rather than bringing in a separate firm. This avoids duplicated ID checks, duplicated title searches on the property you're selling, and cuts out a layer of correspondence between two sets of solicitors who'd otherwise need to liaise on your behalf.

What it actually costs

Bridging loans are priced monthly, and the gross versus net loan distinction catches out almost every first-time borrower, so it's worth being precise here.

Say your existing property is worth £350,000 with no mortgage outstanding, and you need £180,000 to complete your onward purchase after your own savings and deposit already paid. A lender might offer up to 75% loan to value against the existing property, so £262,500 is theoretically available, well above what you need.

Here's a worked example on a £180,000 gross loan over an expected 4-month term:

Cost itemAmount
Gross loan requested£180,000
Arrangement fee (2%)£3,600, deducted from the advance
Monthly interest (0.85% per month, indicative)£1,530/month, approx 10.2% annualised equivalent
Interest retained for 4 months (rolled up)£6,120
Valuation fee£450-£750, property dependent
Legal fees (your side and lender's side)£1,200-£1,800 combined, typical range
Exit fee£0-1% of loan, lender dependent, confirm at offer
Net loan actually receivedApproximately £168,600

The gross loan is the £180,000 figure the lender quotes you. The net loan is what actually lands in your solicitor's account after the arrangement fee and, if interest is rolled up rather than serviced monthly, the retained interest are deducted upfront. If you need £180,000 to complete, you may actually need to apply for a gross facility closer to £190,000-£195,000 once fees and retained interest are accounted for. This is a common budgeting mistake. Borrowers work backwards from the net figure they need and forget the deductions, then find themselves short at the point of completion.

There's a second sizing issue specific to this scenario: because your old property hasn't sold, you'll own both it and your new home on completion day. Depending on where the property is, that can trigger an additional property purchase tax or surcharge (the rules and rates differ across England, Scotland and Wales), payable within days of completion rather than reclaimable from your old property's eventual sale proceeds. Ask your solicitor to confirm the figure early and make sure it's factored into how much you actually borrow, not treated as a separate cost to find later.

Most bridging lenders offer a choice between rolled up interest, where the total interest for the expected term is deducted from the advance upfront, and monthly serviced interest, where you pay the interest each month from your own income and the full loan amount is released at completion. Rolled up interest is far more common for this kind of onward purchase bridge, because you don't need to find monthly payments while you're also covering your existing mortgage or rent and your new home's running costs.

If you end up repaying earlier than the 4 months assumed in the example above, most lenders only charge interest for the days the loan was actually outstanding and refund the unused portion of any retained interest. This is worth confirming at the point of offer, because a small number of lenders apply a minimum term of one to three months regardless of how quickly you repay, which changes the true cost if your existing property sells faster than expected.

All figures here are indicative and will vary by lender, your credit profile, the property type and current market conditions. Confirm exact terms at enquiry rather than relying on this example as a quote. You can compare current bridging loan rates in the UK for context on where pricing typically sits before you approach a broker, and it's also worth comparing the best bridging loan lenders in the UK for this type of onward purchase bridge.

Your exit strategy

Your exit is the sale of your existing property once it's remarketed, and this is the single most scrutinised part of your application, so get it right before you apply.

Lenders don't accept vague reassurance that the property will sell eventually. They want to see it's realistically priced against comparable recent sales in the area, that it's actively listed with an agent, and ideally that there's already some level of interest or viewings booked. A property that sat on the market for eight months before your original buyer came along, at a price that was clearly too high, is a much harder exit for a lender to underwrite than one remarketed sensibly from day one.

Before you approach a bridging lender, have a frank conversation with your estate agent about why the previous sale fell through. If it was purely down to your buyer's own circumstances, chain collapse further up, a mortgage decline, a change of heart, then remarketing at the same price with the same agent is usually straightforward. If the fall through followed a survey that flagged issues, or a valuation that came in lower than the agreed price, you may need to adjust your asking price or address the issue before a lender will treat the exit as credible.

Many lenders will also want to see a second valuation opinion or at least confirmation that your agent's suggested price is in line with recent sold prices on Rightmove or Zoopla for similar properties nearby. It's sensible to pull this evidence together yourself before the lender asks for it, because it demonstrates you've thought the exit through properly and speeds up underwriting considerably.

Some borrowers also have a second exit route available, such as a remortgage of the new property once it's been renovated or once a fixed rate on another asset ends, or an expected inheritance or bonus. If you have a genuine secondary exit alongside the property sale, mention it early in your application. Lenders like to see that you're not entirely dependent on one single sale completing exactly as planned, and a credible second option can sometimes support a slightly longer term or more flexible terms.

Finally, keep your agent and your broker talking to each other, or at least keep both updated at the same time. If a viewing turns into an offer while your bridging application is still in underwriting, that's genuinely good news. It strengthens your exit evidence and can speed up your offer. But it needs to be communicated promptly so the lender's file reflects the most current position rather than working from information that's already a week or two out of date.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I get a bridging loan if my buyer has already pulled out?
Yes. This is one of the most common reasons people approach a bridging lender. As long as you have a property to use as security and a credible plan to remarket and sell it, lenders are used to arranging finance quickly in exactly this situation.

How quickly can a bridging loan complete once my buyer pulls out?
Once you're fully instructed, with a valuation booked and solicitors engaged on both sides, most bridging loans complete in 10 to 14 working days. Delays usually come from weak exit evidence rather than the valuation or legal work itself.

Will I lose my deposit if I miss my completion date?
Not immediately. The seller would typically need to serve a notice to complete, which usually gives you a further ten working days. But interest starts accruing from the original date, and if you still can't complete after the notice period, the seller can rescind the contract and keep your deposit.

How much does a bridging loan cost if my buyer pulled out?
Rates typically run from around 0.55% to 1.25% per month, plus a 2% arrangement fee, with valuation and legal costs on top. On a £180,000 loan over four months, total costs including fees and rolled up interest often come to around £11,000-£12,000.

Do I need to have remarketed my property before applying for a bridging loan?
It isn't always essential on day one, but it speeds things up considerably. Lenders want to see your exit plan is credible, so having the property back on the market with an agent, at a realistic price, before or shortly after you apply will help your application move faster.

Is this type of bridging loan regulated by the FCA?
Usually, yes. Because you or an immediate family member will occupy the property being bought or used as security, this is typically FCA-regulated short-term property finance, which means stricter affordability checks and access to the Financial Ombudsman Service if something goes wrong.

What happens if my property doesn't sell before the bridging loan term ends?
Most lenders will discuss extending the term if your sale is progressing but hasn't yet completed, though this usually comes with extra cost. It's important to raise this with your lender well before the term ends rather than waiting until the deadline arrives.

If you're facing a completion deadline after a buyer pulled out, the sooner you start the conversation the more options you'll have. You can find a bridging loan broker who can talk through your dates and numbers, or explore the full range of short-term funding solutions available before you decide on the right route forward.

Your own sale is still alive, not dead — your buyer hasn't pulled out, their chain has just slipped behind schedule, and the seller of the property you're buying has responded by setting a hard deadline. That's a genuinely different problem to a collapsed chain, and it has two possible answers: ask for more time, or bridge the gap with short-term finance while your sale catches up. Which one is right depends on how close your own sale actually is.

This is not the same problem as a dead sale

It's worth being precise about what's actually happened, because the right response depends on it. If your buyer had pulled out entirely, you'd be starting again from scratch, remarketing your property with no live buyer at all. That's not your situation. Your buyer is still there, still committed, and their purchase of your property is still moving, just more slowly than the seller of your next home is prepared to tolerate.

Sales slip for reasons that have nothing to do with whether the deal will ultimately complete. A buyer further up or down the chain is waiting on their own mortgage offer. A survey has thrown up a query that needs a follow-up valuation. Local authority searches are taking longer than the conveyancer quoted. None of these are signs the sale is failing — they're signs it's running on solicitor and lender timescales that don't care about the date your own seller has picked.

The seller of the property you're buying doesn't necessarily know or care about that distinction. From where they're sitting, a completion date has passed or is about to, and they want certainty. Your job is to give it to them, either by buying time or by removing your dependency on their patience altogether.

Ask for the extension first

Before you look at bridging loans, it's worth asking whether a straightforward extension gets you there more cheaply. If your own sale is genuinely close, exchanged and just waiting on a slightly delayed completion date, or under offer with a mortgage offer already issued to your buyer, a short extension is often the more sensible answer, and it costs you nothing beyond the seller's goodwill.

A credible extension request needs three things: a specific, realistic new date rather than a vague "soon", evidence your own sale genuinely supports that date (your solicitor confirming your buyer's mortgage offer is in place, or that exchange has already happened and you're waiting on completion), and an explanation of what's actually causing the delay so the seller understands it's not indefinite. Sellers who are themselves in a chain, buying onward, are often more sympathetic to this than a seller who has no onward purchase and simply wants their money.

An extension isn't guaranteed. Some sellers will say no regardless of how solid your evidence is, particularly if they're under their own pressure or have another interested buyer waiting in the wings. If that happens, or if your own sale — while alive — genuinely can't be pinned down to a date the seller will accept, that's the point where a bridging loan for a delayed sale becomes the more realistic option.

When bridging is the better answer

A bridging loan removes your dependency on the seller's patience entirely. Instead of asking them to wait for your sale to complete, you borrow against your existing property (or the one you're buying) to fund the purchase now, and repay the bridging loan once your sale actually completes, whenever that turns out to be.

This is usually the stronger option in three situations: the seller has refused an extension outright, your own sale's timeline is too uncertain to put a confident date on even though it's progressing, or the deal you're buying is valuable enough — a property you don't want to risk losing, or one where remarketing and starting again would cost more in time and stress than the bridging interest would cost in cash. Bridging isn't free, and it isn't the answer for every delayed sale, but where the numbers and the timeline point that way, it converts an uncertain, seller-dependent situation into one you control.

What happens if neither option lands in time

If you don't secure an extension and don't have a bridging loan in place by the seller's deadline, the consequences follow the same legal mechanism as any missed completion. The seller can serve a notice to complete, which typically gives a further ten working days. If you still can't complete once that notice period expires, the seller can rescind the contract and keep your deposit, typically 10% of the purchase price under the Standard Conditions of Sale used in most residential transactions.

None of this is inevitable the moment a deadline passes. Many sellers, particularly ones without their own onward purchase riding on it, would rather agree a short further delay than go through the cost and disruption of rescinding and remarketing. But the legal mechanism is real, so treat the deadline as fixed and any flexibility from the seller as a bonus, not your plan.

Ask your onward mortgage lender for flexibility2-4 weeks typicallyStandard mortgage rateRarely fast enough for a live deadline situation

For most people in this position, with a live sale that's simply running behind and a firm deadline from the seller, the choice really is between these first two rows. Everything else on this list either moves too slowly to matter or means giving up a purchase you've already committed money and time to.

Because you or an immediate family member will occupy the property you're buying, or the property used as security, this is almost always FCA-regulated bridging, which we arrange through our regulated bridging loan service. That means the lender must carry out proper affordability checks, you get access to the Financial Ombudsman Service if something goes wrong, and the lender has to communicate clearly on fees, rates and risk before you commit. This holds broadly true whether you're buying in Glasgow or Bristol, though local valuer availability can shift things by a day or two either way.

What matters most is proof your own sale is genuinely close: confirmation from your solicitor of where it's up to, evidence of your buyer's mortgage offer if one's been issued, and a realistic explanation of what's actually causing the hold-up.
