title: Royal Estates Face £10m EPC Bill, But Landlords Collectively Face Almost £10bn
excerpt: The Crown Estate and Duchy of Cornwall face a combined £10m bill to bring their properties up to EPC standard, but that's small change compared to the near £10bn UK landlords face collectively. Here's what it means for property finance and why acting early on a mortgage matters.
metaTitle: Royal Estates EPC Bill vs £10bn Landlord Cost | Boxx Finance
metaDescription: Royal estates face a £10m EPC upgrade bill, but UK landlords collectively face nearly £10bn. Find out what this means for property finance and mortgage planning.
keywords: EPC landlord costs, buy to let mortgage, commercial property mortgage, energy efficiency property finance, landlord mortgage UK, EPC compliance funding
author: Mark Higgins

mainEntity.name: Do all landlords need to meet the new EPC rules?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most rented residential and commercial properties in England and Wales will need to meet updated EPC standards, with some exemptions for listed buildings or where upgrades aren't cost effective. It's worth checking your specific portfolio against the latest government guidance, as rules differ for commercial and residential lets.

mainEntity.name: Can I remortgage to pay for EPC improvements?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, many landlords remortgage or use a further advance to release funds for insulation, glazing or heating upgrades. Lenders increasingly offer green mortgage products with preferential rates for energy efficient properties, so it's worth comparing options before committing to work.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I don't upgrade my property in time?

acceptedAnswer.text: Non-compliant properties could become illegal to let, meaning you'd lose rental income until the work is done. There may also be fines involved. Planning your mortgage and funding early avoids being forced into rushed, more expensive borrowing later.

mainEntity.name: Is bridging finance a good option for EPC works?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bridging finance can work well for short, defined projects where you need funds quickly and plan to refinance onto a standard mortgage once work is complete. It's more expensive than a mortgage over the long term, so it suits landlords with a clear exit plan.

mainEntity.name: Will EPC upgrades affect my property's value?

acceptedAnswer.text: In most cases, yes, and positively. Energy efficient properties are increasingly attractive to tenants and buyers, and some lenders now factor EPC ratings into valuations. A well-planned upgrade funded sensibly through a mortgage can add long-term value.

content:
The Crown Estate and Duchy of Cornwall are facing a combined bill of around £10m to bring their properties up to modern EPC standards. That sounds like a lot until you realise it's a drop in the ocean compared to the near £10bn UK landlords collectively face to do the same. If you own rental property, this is a cost you need to plan for now, not later.

What this means in practice

Energy Performance Certificate rules have been tightening for years, and further changes are on the horizon for both residential and commercial lets. Properties that don't meet minimum standards risk becoming unlettable, which is a genuinely serious problem for landlords relying on rental income to cover mortgage payments.

The royal estates making headlines with their £10m bill puts a spotlight on a much bigger issue. Multiply that figure across the thousands of private landlords and portfolio investors across the UK, and you get close to £10bn in required spending. That's insulation, glazing, heating systems and sometimes full retrofits.

For most landlords, this isn't optional spending they can put off indefinitely. It's a cost of doing business in the rental sector going forward. The question isn't whether you'll need to spend the money, it's how you fund it without damaging your cash flow or rental yields.

Sensible financial planning makes all the difference here. Rather than draining savings or scrambling for funds when deadlines loom, many landlords are looking at how a mortgage or refinance can spread the cost over a sensible timeframe while keeping their properties compliant and lettable.

How it works

Landlords typically use several practical routes to fund EPC improvements. The most common is remortgaging to release equity, particularly if the property has grown in value since it was purchased. This gives you a lump sum to pay for works without touching cash reserves.

A further advance from your existing lender is another option, and can sometimes be quicker than a full remortgage since you're not switching lenders or renegotiating the whole loan. Ask your existing lender what they can offer before assuming a full switch is necessary.

Some landlords are turning to specialist green mortgage products, which offer better rates for properties meeting certain energy efficiency thresholds, or for borrowing specifically earmarked for improvements. These aren't available from every lender, so comparing the market properly matters.

For larger portfolios or commercial landlords, bridging finance can cover short, defined projects, with a plan to refinance onto a standard mortgage once the work is finished and the property's value or rating has improved. This suits landlords who need funds quickly but have a clear repayment strategy in mind.

Lenders will want to see a clear plan for the works, realistic costings, and confidence that the property will remain viable to let once complete, regardless of which route you choose. This is where proper preparation before applying makes a real difference to the outcome.

Typical scenarios

Take a landlord we'll call Sarah, who owns four terraced properties in Leeds, all let to long-term tenants. Two of her properties currently sit at an EPC rating of D, below the standard expected under upcoming regulations. She faces a combined bill of roughly £22,000 for insulation, new boilers and double glazing across both properties.

Rather than pulling that money from savings or her rental income, Sarah looked at remortgaging one of the higher value properties in her portfolio. Because property values in her area had risen since her original purchase, she had enough equity to release the funds needed without significantly increasing her monthly payments.

A different scenario involves a small commercial landlord letting out office units near Manchester city centre. His EPC compliance bill runs to around £60,000 across three units. Given the scale, he explored a mix of a further advance and short-term bridging finance, planning to refinance the whole amount onto a longer-term commercial mortgage once the works were complete and the units revalued.

Both scenarios demonstrate the same underlying principle. Whether you're a small residential landlord or managing commercial units, the funding route needs to match the scale of the project and your long-term plans for the property. There's rarely a one-size-fits-all answer, which is exactly why speaking to someone who understands the market matters.

Common mistakes

The biggest mistake landlords make is leaving EPC planning until the deadline is close. This limits your options, often forcing you into more expensive, faster forms of borrowing because there's no time left to shop around properly.

Another common error is underestimating costs. Quotes for insulation, glazing and heating upgrades vary hugely depending on the property's age and condition, and many landlords budget based on rough estimates rather than proper surveys, only to find themselves short of funds halfway through the work.

Some landlords assume their current lender is automatically the best or only option for additional borrowing. In reality, shopping around or getting proper advice often reveals better rates or more flexible products elsewhere, particularly if your existing lender doesn't offer green mortgage incentives.

There's also a tendency to treat EPC work purely as a cost rather than an investment. Energy efficient properties tend to attract better tenants, command higher rents in some areas, and hold their value better. Viewing the spend purely negatively can lead to rushed, minimal compliance work rather than sensible long-term improvements.

Finally, some landlords simply don't factor in how EPC compliance affects saleability. If you're planning to sell within the next few years, a non-compliant property becomes far harder to shift, and buyers will often negotiate hard on price to cover the cost of works themselves.

Alternatives or comparisons

Beyond remortgaging and bridging finance, some landlords consider personal savings or unsecured personal loans for smaller works. This avoids extending mortgage terms, but interest rates on unsecured borrowing are typically much higher, making it a costly choice for larger sums.

Government grants and schemes occasionally offer support for specific improvements, such as heat pump installations, though eligibility criteria can be restrictive and funding pots limited. Check what's currently available, but most schemes don't provide enough to cover a full compliance programme alone.

Asset finance is another route worth considering for larger commercial landlords needing to fund specific equipment like heating systems or solar installations, allowing the cost to be spread against the useful life of the asset itself rather than tied to the whole property.

For those with multiple properties, a portfolio remortgage that consolidates several properties under one facility can sometimes offer better overall terms than remortgaging each individually, particularly useful when funding a rolling programme of EPC works across a whole portfolio.

How to get the best outcome

Start by getting an accurate picture of what work each property actually needs. A proper energy assessment, rather than a rough guess, avoids nasty surprises partway through a project and gives lenders confidence in your figures when you apply for funding.

Timing matters enormously. Applying for a mortgage or refinance well ahead of any deadline gives you access to a wider range of products and better rates, rather than being forced into whatever's available at short notice.

You should also compare lenders properly rather than defaulting to your existing provider. Green mortgage products, portfolio lending, and specialist commercial options all vary significantly in what they offer, and the right fit depends heavily on your specific circumstances and property type.

This is exactly the kind of situation where it pays to speak to a commercial finance specialist who can look at your whole portfolio, your timeline, and your goals, then match you with lenders genuinely suited to your needs rather than a generic product. Getting this right from the start saves both time and money.

Whether it's a straightforward remortgage or a more complex mix of facilities, having someone who understands both property and finance on your side makes the process far less stressful.

Summary

The gap between the royal estates' £10m EPC bill and the near £10bn facing UK landlords collectively shows just how significant this issue has become. Planning ahead, understanding your funding options, and acting before deadlines bite are the keys to managing this cost sensibly rather than scrambling under pressure.

title: 'Friday Afternoon Fraud': Why Homebuyers Are Losing Their Deposits to Fake Solicitor Emails
excerpt: A new warning highlights how UK homebuyers are losing tens of thousands of pounds, in one case £300,000, to scammers impersonating solicitors or estate agents at the final stage of a house purchase.
metaTitle: Conveyancing Fraud: Homebuyer Bank Scam Warning
metaDescription: UK homebuyers are losing life savings to fake solicitor emails during property purchases. Here's how the scam works and how to protect your deposit.
keywords: mortgage, landlord, remortgage, first time buyer, conveyancing
author: Mark Higgins

mainEntity.name: How can I tell if an email with bank details is genuine?

acceptedAnswer.text: Never rely solely on the email itself. Call your solicitor or conveyancer using a phone number you already have on file or can find independently, not one included in the email, and verbally confirm the account details before transferring any money.

mainEntity.name: What should I do if I think I've already sent money to a fraudulent account?

acceptedAnswer.text: Contact your bank immediately, as speed matters when trying to freeze or recover funds. You should also report the incident to Action Fraud and inform your solicitor straight away so they can alert their own bank and the wider transaction chain.

mainEntity.name: Are solicitors responsible if I fall victim to this kind of fraud?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the circumstances, including whether the solicitor's own systems were compromised or whether appropriate warnings were given. This is a developing area and outcomes vary case by case, so anyone affected should seek independent legal advice.

content:
A fresh warning about so-called conveyancing fraud has highlighted just how costly a single fake email can be for someone buying a home. According to the Guardian, victims have lost tens of thousands of pounds, and in one case as much as £300,000, after criminals intercepted communications and sent fraudulent bank details posing as a solicitor or estate agent. The buyer, believing they were following genuine instructions, transferred their deposit straight into the scammer's account.

This matters because it strikes at the single most vulnerable moment in a house purchase: the point where a large sum of money has to move quickly, based on an email, between people who may never have met in person and are often communicating under time pressure. It is a scam built entirely around trust in routine paperwork, which is exactly why it keeps working.

How the scam actually operates

The mechanics described in the report are simple but effective. A buyer is waiting for confirmation from their solicitor that everything is ready and it is time to send the deposit. Criminals, having gained access to email accounts or intercepted correspondence somewhere along the chain, send a message that looks identical to the one the buyer is expecting, complete with different bank details. The buyer transfers the money, and it is only when the real solicitor later asks where the funds are that the fraud becomes apparent. By then, the money has often already been moved on and is very difficult to recover.

The nickname 'Friday afternoon fraud' reflects the timing that criminals often exploit, when transactions are being rushed through before a weekend and there is less time to double check anything by phone before banks close.

What this means for buyers, sellers and landlords

For anyone currently going through a purchase, sale or remortgage, the lesson is not that conveyancing itself is unsafe, but that email is not a secure enough channel to trust blindly when large sums are involved. Landlords buying additional properties, first time buyers moving their entire savings in one go, and people selling to fund a chain are all exposed in the same way, because the fraud targets the process rather than any particular type of buyer.

Solicitors' firms generally warn clients about this risk at the outset of a transaction, but the report suggests that warning alone is not stopping people falling victim. Anyone due to send a deposit or completion funds should treat a change in bank details, or even a first-time set of bank details arriving by email, as something to verify independently. That means phoning the solicitor's office on a number sourced separately, not one taken from the email itself, and confirming the details verbally before sending anything.

It is also worth building in time rather than transferring money at the last possible moment. Rushed transactions, particularly late in the week, are precisely the conditions criminals rely on.

Frequently Asked Questions

How can I tell if an email with bank details is genuine?

Never rely solely on the email itself. Call your solicitor or conveyancer using a phone number you already have on file or can find independently, not one included in the email, and verbally confirm the account details before transferring any money.

What should I do if I think I've already sent money to a fraudulent account?

Contact your bank immediately, as speed matters when trying to freeze or recover funds. You should also report the incident to Action Fraud and inform your solicitor straight away so they can alert their own bank and the wider transaction chain.

Are solicitors responsible if I fall victim to this kind of fraud?

It depends on the circumstances, including whether the solicitor's own systems were compromised or whether appropriate warnings were given. This is a developing area and outcomes vary case by case, so anyone affected should seek independent legal advice.

If a delay in a property transaction leaves you needing funds quickly while a dispute or fraud investigation is resolved, it can help to explore short-term property finance options designed to bridge exactly these kinds of gaps.

content:
HMRC is preparing to send valuation inspectors into homes across the UK as part of the new mansion tax, with agents given powers to demand entry to properties to assess whether they are worth more than £2m and therefore liable under the High Value Council Tax surcharge. As reported by City AM, this marks the first time in years that homeowners could face a physical inspection to determine a tax bill based on the current value of their property, rather than a historic council tax band.

For most people this will never come up. But for anyone who owns, or is thinking of buying, a property that could plausibly sit near or above the £2m mark, this is a real practical shift. It moves valuation away from paperwork and desk-based estimates towards inspectors who can turn up and look at the property itself.

Why this matters even if your home isn't worth £2m

The obvious group affected is owners of higher-value homes, particularly in London and the South East where £2m properties are far more common than the headline figure suggests. But there's a wider ripple effect. Buyers looking at property in that bracket now need to factor in the possibility of a formal valuation visit as part of ownership, not just at the point of purchase. That could influence how attractive certain homes are, how quickly they sell, and how sellers price them if they're trying to stay just under the threshold.

Landlords with high-value portfolio properties should also pay attention. If a rental property is valued above £2m, the annual cost of holding it changes, and that has knock-on effects for rental pricing and investment returns. Anyone weighing up whether to buy, extend, or improve a property that sits near the boundary will now need to think harder about whether renovations could tip it over the line and trigger a valuation and a bigger bill.

What an HMRC visit could mean in practice

The source summary confirms that valuation agents will be able to demand entry to assess a property's worth, but doesn't detail the exact process, timeline, or how appeals will work. Homeowners in the affected bracket should expect more clarity from HMRC in the coming months on how inspections will be scheduled, what evidence agents will use, and what rights owners have to challenge a valuation they disagree with. Until then, it's sensible for owners of higher-value homes to keep good records of their property's condition, any structural issues, and comparable sales nearby, since these are the kinds of details that typically matter in a valuation dispute.

What this means for buyers and sellers near the threshold

Anyone buying or selling a property close to £2m should factor the mansion tax into their planning now rather than after a sale completes. A property priced just under the threshold could become more desirable, while one just over it may need a seller to be realistic about how the new tax affects buyer appetite. For those needing to move quickly, whether to complete a purchase, fund a renovation before a valuation review, or bridge a cash flow gap while a property sale or tax matter is resolved, it can be worth taking time to explore short-term property finance options rather than being forced into a rushed decision.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is affected by the mansion tax valuation inspections?

Based on current reporting, it applies to owners of properties HMRC believes could be worth over £2m, which fall under the new High Value Council Tax surcharge. Most UK homeowners with lower-value properties will not be affected.

Can I refuse entry to an HMRC valuation inspector?

The source reporting states that agents will be able to demand entry to assess a property's value, though full detail on the legal process and homeowner rights has not yet been published. Homeowners with concerns should wait for further official guidance from HMRC before assuming what their options are.

Will this affect council tax as well as the new mansion tax?

title: HMRC softens 20-hour rule guidance for landlords incorporating their property business
excerpt: HMRC has updated its guidance to confirm landlords working under 20 hours a week can still count as running a business for Incorporation Relief purposes, following pressure from Property118.
metaTitle: HMRC changes 20-hour rule guidance for landlords
metaDescription: HMRC has amended its guidance on the 20-hour test for landlord Incorporation Relief after a Property118 open letter. Here's what it means for landlords.
keywords: mortgage, stamp duty, landlord, capital gains tax
author: Mark Higgins

mainEntity.name: Does this guidance change mean I automatically qualify for Incorporation Relief?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. HMRC has confirmed that spending fewer than 20 hours a week on your properties does not automatically disqualify you, but you still need to show that your activity amounts to a genuine business under the wider test, taking into account factors such as scale and how actively the portfolio is managed.

mainEntity.name: What is Incorporation Relief and why does it matter to landlords?

acceptedAnswer.text: Incorporation Relief allows certain business owners, including some landlords, to defer capital gains tax when they transfer assets such as rental properties into a limited company, provided the activity qualifies as a business rather than simple property investment.

mainEntity.name: Should I incorporate my rental properties now that HMRC has changed its guidance?

content:
HMRC has changed its published guidance on the so called 20-hour test that determines whether a landlord can claim Incorporation Relief when moving a property portfolio into a limited company. The revised wording now expressly confirms that someone who spends fewer than 20 hours a week on their property activities may still be treated as running a business for the purposes of section 162 of the Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992. The change follows an open letter from the landlord campaign group Property118, as reported by Property118.

This matters because Incorporation Relief is one of the main routes landlords use to defer capital gains tax when they transfer personally held rental properties into a company structure. Whether HMRC accepts that a landlord is genuinely running a business, rather than simply holding investments, has long been the key test for qualifying. The 20-hour figure had become something of an unofficial benchmark, even though it was never a statutory requirement, and many landlords and their advisers were worried that HMRC was using it as a hard cut-off when deciding claims.

Why the 20-hour figure caused so much confusion

The number of hours a landlord spends managing their properties has never been written into tax law as a fixed threshold for Incorporation Relief. Instead, the legal test is whether the activity amounts to a business, which has always depended on a range of factors including the scale of the portfolio, the level of active management involved, and the degree of organisation behind it. The concern raised by Property118 was that HMRC's own internal guidance appeared to treat 20 hours a week as something close to a pass or fail mark, which risked catching out landlords with smaller portfolios who nonetheless actively manage their properties, just not for 20 hours every week.

By updating the guidance to confirm that fewer than 20 hours does not automatically rule someone out, HMRC has removed a source of real uncertainty for landlords planning incorporation. It does not mean the hours test disappears entirely, but it does mean landlords should no longer assume they fail the business test purely because they cannot demonstrate 20 hours of weekly involvement.

What this means if you are considering incorporating

For landlords weighing up whether to move properties into a limited company, this guidance change is a positive development, but it is not a green light to assume Incorporation Relief will automatically apply. HMRC will still look at the wider picture, including how the portfolio is managed, whether there is a genuine ongoing business rather than passive letting, and how the transfer is structured. Landlords considering incorporation should still take proper tax advice before making any transfer, since getting this wrong can mean an unexpected capital gains tax bill rather than the deferral they were hoping for.

It is also worth remembering that incorporation brings its own costs and complications beyond the tax position, including potential stamp duty land tax charges in England and Northern Ireland, or the equivalent Land and Buildings Transaction Tax in Scotland and Land Transaction Tax in Wales, along with mortgage refinancing and lender criteria that differ for limited company borrowing.

The bigger picture for landlords

This episode also shows that landlord groups and advisers can influence how HMRC applies its own guidance, particularly where that guidance risks going further than the underlying law actually requires. For landlords who had paused incorporation plans because of concerns about the 20-hour rule, it may be worth revisiting those plans with an adviser now that the guidance has been clarified. Anyone restructuring a portfolio, whether through incorporation or otherwise, will often need short-term funding to bridge the transition, and it can be useful to explore short-term property finance options as part of that planning process.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does this guidance change mean I automatically qualify for Incorporation Relief?

No. HMRC has confirmed that spending fewer than 20 hours a week on your properties does not automatically disqualify you, but you still need to show that your activity amounts to a genuine business under the wider test, taking into account factors such as scale and how actively the portfolio is managed.

What is Incorporation Relief and why does it matter to landlords?

Incorporation Relief allows certain business owners, including some landlords, to defer capital gains tax when they transfer assets such as rental properties into a limited company, provided the activity qualifies as a business rather than simple property investment.

Should I incorporate my rental properties now that HMRC has changed its guidance?

This depends on your individual circumstances, including your portfolio size, how you manage it, and your wider financial plans. The guidance change reduces one area of uncertainty, but landlords should still get professional tax advice before transferring properties into a company structure.

title: Mortgage Declined A Week Before Exchange — Your Realistic Options
excerpt: If your mortgage offer has just been withdrawn days before exchange, a same-week remortgage is unlikely but a bridging loan can still hit the date while you sort out the underlying problem.
metaTitle: Mortgage Declined A Week Before Exchange — Your Realistic Options
metaDescription: Mortgage declined days before exchange? Here's what's actually achievable in the time left, what it costs, and how a bridging loan can still meet your date.
keywords: mortgage declined before exchange, mortgage offer withdrawn last minute, bridging loan after mortgage decline, late mortgage decline reasons, down valuation mortgage refused, emergency bridging loan for house purchase, refinance after bridging loan
author: Mark Higgins
content:
You got the call, or worse, the email. Your mortgage has been declined or the offer pulled, and exchange is days away. You've told the solicitor, the vendor, maybe the removals firm. Right now you don't know if this is fixable or if the whole purchase collapses this week. A bridging loan for a declined mortgage is often the fastest way to keep the purchase alive.

It's a horrible position and you're not the first person it's happened to. We speak to buyers in exactly this situation more often than you'd think, usually because a lender changed its mind late, a valuation came back lower than expected, or something in the applicant's circumstances shifted between application and completion. Now let's deal with the numbers, because the numbers decide what happens next, not the panic.

Before anything else, take a breath and get the facts straight. Ring your broker or the lender directly and ask for the decline reason in writing, not just a summary over the phone. That single document shapes everything you do in the next 24 hours, so don't skip it or assume you already know why.

Lenders decline mortgages for dozens of reasons that have nothing to do with you personally. Sometimes an internal policy change happened while your application was sitting in the underwriting queue. Sometimes a surveyor was cautious on a property type the lender has had problems with before. Knowing which category you're in changes the whole conversation. If you want the full background on how this type of lending works, our guide on what short-term property finance actually involves is worth a read alongside this.

The clock

Most late mortgage declines land between 5 and 10 working days before exchange, sometimes even after exchange but before completion, which is worse because you're now contractually committed. A standard high street lender needs 10 to 20 working days to fully underwrite a fresh application, sometimes longer if a valuation has to be booked and returned.

If exchange is in 6 working days, you do not have time for a normal remortgage application with a different mainstream lender to complete before that date. That's not pessimism, it's how mortgage underwriting timelines actually run in the UK. A same-lender appeal or underwriter review can sometimes complete in 2 to 5 days if the issue is a paperwork error rather than a policy or valuation problem. A broker resubmission to a different lender, done properly with a decision in principle first, typically needs 7 to 15 working days minimum before you're near completion, not exchange.

That gap between what you need and what a mainstream lender can deliver is exactly why bridging loans exist for this trigger. A bridging loan can often complete in 5 to 10 working days from a clean application, sometimes faster if the valuation and legal work move quickly, which is why it becomes the realistic fallback rather than the first choice.

The 5 to 10 day process works in parallel rather than in sequence. You'll get an agreement in principle within a day or two if the case is straightforward, a valuation instructed almost immediately after, and legal work running alongside it. That parallel running is the entire reason bridging can hit dates that a standard mortgage simply cannot.

Not every decline is equal. A decline because of a hard credit policy issue, such as a missed payment that's just shown up on a credit file, behaves very differently to a decline because the valuation came back at £310,000 against a purchase price of £335,000. The first is often fixable with the same lender. The second usually isn't, because no amount of paperwork changes a surveyor's opinion of value.

There's a middle category too called affordability recalculation. If a lender's income multiple changed, or if a bonus or overtime element got stripped out of the assessment, the numbers simply might not stack up anymore at the original loan amount. In that case you're not fixing a mistake, you're looking at a genuinely different borrowing capacity, and that changes the maths on the whole purchase.

Timing also depends heavily on whether you're buying with a chain above and below you or as a simple onward purchase. Every additional link in a chain adds another set of solicitors, another set of deadlines and another party who can also pull out if things drag. A five day fix for you might still not save the transaction if someone three links down the chain gets nervous and walks.

Days of the week matter more than people think as well. A decline that lands on a Thursday afternoon effectively costs you the whole of that week and the following Monday morning before anyone can meaningfully act on it. Bank holidays make this worse again, so always count working days properly rather than calendar days when you're being told a timeframe. If you're weighing up whether the numbers work for your situation, it's worth checking current bridging loan rates and costs before you commit.

What happens if you miss it

If you've exchanged and can't complete, the consequences are contractual and financial, not just disappointing. Under a standard Law Society contract you risk losing your deposit, which is usually 10% of the purchase price, and the seller can potentially sue for damages or resell the property and pursue you for any shortfall.

On a £400,000 purchase that's £40,000 gone, not as a penalty exactly, but because that's how the deposit is structured under the contract. If the seller then has to sell to someone else for less, say £385,000, they can in theory pursue you for that £15,000 difference plus their additional legal and marketing costs. It rarely gets that far in practice, but the legal exposure is real and solicitors will tell you so plainly.

If you haven't exchanged yet, the immediate risk is smaller in legal terms but still serious. You risk losing the property to another buyer, forfeiting any survey, valuation and legal fees already paid, and potentially collapsing a chain that other people are relying on further down the line. Estate agents and vendors move on quickly when a buyer's finance falls through, especially in a competitive local market.

Think about the numbers here too. A survey might have cost £500 to £1,200 depending on the level of detail, legal fees to this point could easily be £800 to £1,500, and a mortgage valuation or arrangement fee already paid to the original lender might not be refundable. None of that is life changing money on its own, but combined with the stress and the lost time, it adds up to a genuinely bad week.

A collapsed purchase at this stage can leave a mark on your onward plans if you've given notice on a rental, sold your own property with a completion date fixed, or committed funds elsewhere. This is simply what actually happens when a chain breaks a week out.

We've seen cases where the buyer had already given a landlord notice on a rented flat, meaning a failed purchase left them with nowhere to live and no deposit back from the failed sale. That combination, homeless in a fortnight and out of pocket, is precisely the scenario that pushes people towards a fast bridging solution rather than starting the mortgage search again from scratch. If you're in this position right now, you can get a bridging loan quote to see where you stand before making any other decisions.

Buyers who've been through a last minute collapse often describe the following weeks as more stressful than the original house hunt, simply because trust in the process has gone. That emotional cost is a real factor when you're deciding whether to push through with bridging or start again, even if it never appears in a spreadsheet.

If you're selling your own property at the same time, a collapsed onward purchase can put your own sale at risk too. Your buyer may have a chain of their own waiting, and a delay on your side can cause the whole thing to unravel in both directions. This is often the detail that tips people towards bridging, because it protects not just their purchase but the sale underneath it.

It's also worth checking your buildings insurance and any exchange-related deposits that might be sitting with agents or solicitors. Money held in a client account isn't automatically at risk the same way a completed transfer would be, but it's worth confirming exactly what's been paid where before you assume the worst about what you'll get back.

Your options

Bridging is one route, not the only one, and a decent broker will walk you through all of them before recommending anything.

OptionSpeedRealistic for 5-7 days?Main trade-off
Same-lender underwriter appeal2-5 working daysSometimes, if it's a documentation issueOnly works if the decline wasn't a hard policy or valuation refusal
Broker resubmission to new mainstream lender7-15+ working daysRarely in time for exchangeThorough but too slow for this specific deadline
Ask vendor/solicitor for a short extensionImmediate if agreedPossible, not guaranteedVendor has no obligation to agree, may lose the property anyway
Bridging loan to complete, remortgage later5-10 working days typicalUsually yesHigher interest cost, needs a credible exit
Withdraw from the purchaseImmediateYesLoses the property and any fees paid so far

The extension request costs nothing and should happen in parallel with everything else, but don't rely on it. Vendors under their own financial pressure often won't or can't wait. For most people in this exact position, a bridging loan for UK property purchases when a mortgage falls through becomes the only route that reliably meets the actual date, which is why it comes up so often in this scenario specifically.

The same-lender appeal route is always worth trying first, because it costs you nothing but a phone call and a day or two of waiting. Ask specifically what triggered the decline, whether it was underwriting policy, credit scoring, affordability calculation or valuation, because the answer tells you instantly whether an appeal has any realistic chance.

If the answer is affordability, for example a change in employment status or a drop in bonus income, appealing rarely works because the lender's calculation genuinely no longer supports the loan. If the answer is a documentation gap, missing bank statements, an unexplained deposit, a query on payslips, that's often fixable within days if you can produce what's missing quickly.

Running two or three of these options at once is often the smartest approach, provided you're honest with each party about what you're doing. There's no rule against asking your solicitor for a short extension while simultaneously getting a bridging application moving, as long as everyone involved understands the situation and you're not misrepresenting anything to any single party.

What you shouldn't do is spend three or four days hoping the same-lender appeal will work before starting to explore bridging. Given how tight the timeline already is, that delay alone can be the difference between a completed purchase and a collapsed one. Start the bridging conversation on day one even if you're hopeful the appeal succeeds, because you can always arrange a bridging loan today and stand it down later if it isn't needed.

How a bridging loan works for this situation

A bridging loan is a short-term loan secured against the property, arranged specifically to complete now while a longer-term mortgage is sorted out afterwards. If the property is your own home or one you or an immediate family member will live in, this is usually regulated bridging under the FCA, which brings additional borrower protections. If it's a buy-to-let or investment purchase, it's generally unregulated, and the rules and paperwork differ.

Timeline-wise, from a clean application a specialist lender can often value, underwrite and complete within 5 to 10 working days. What speeds it up: an already-instructed solicitor, a straightforward valuation with no unusual construction or planning issues, and having your exit strategy documented before you apply rather than explained verbally on the phone.

On cost, it's worth being upfront rather than vague. Rates for short-term property finance typically run from around 0.55% to 1.25% per month depending on loan size, loan to value and lender, plus arrangement fees usually in the region of 1.5% to 2% of the loan, and exit fees on some products. On a £300,000 loan over four months at 0.85% a month, that's roughly £10,200 in interest before fees, which sounds steep until you compare it against losing a £30,000 deposit. It's worth comparing this against typical bridging lender fees and criteria so you know whether the deal you're offered is competitive.

Loan to value matters enormously here. Most bridging lenders will go to 70% to 75% of the property's value on a straightforward residential case, sometimes higher with additional security or a lower risk profile. If your original mortgage was at 90% loan to value, short-term property finance alone won't cover the same gap, and you'd need to bring more cash to the table or blend it with other funds already earmarked for the purchase.

What the lender needs from you: proof of the property's value, often a desktop or AVM valuation initially or sometimes a full physical valuation, proof of the deposit or equity you're bringing, ID and proof of address, and crucially, evidence of how you'll repay the loan. What you need from the lender: an agreement in principle within 24 to 48 hours if the case is clean, followed by formal offer once valuation and legals are back.

Solicitors matter more than people expect in this process. If your existing conveyancer is already up to speed on the purchase, ask them directly whether they can act on the bridging loan too, or at least liaise quickly with the lender's solicitor. A solicitor who already has the file, the searches and the title information can save two or three days compared with instructing someone new from a standing start.

Getting your exit strategy right

Where these applications typically stall is the exit strategy. Applications get declined or delayed most often not because the property is wrong but because the borrower hasn't yet secured, or can't yet evidence, the mortgage they'll refinance onto. Lenders want to see this in writing, not just hear it described as a plan, ideally as a decision in principle from a mainstream lender or a clear, dated timeline showing when a fuller mortgage application will go in.

A realistic exit might look like this. You take a bridging loan for 6 months, use that time to fix the underlying issue that caused the original decline, whether that's waiting for a new payslip to season, clearing a small default, or simply switching lenders with fuller documentation, and then remortgage onto a standard product once the picture is clean again. Lenders offering short-term property finance want to see that this isn't wishful thinking but a plan with dates attached.

Other acceptable exits include selling another property you own within a set timeframe, an inheritance or other lump sum due within months, or an existing mortgage offer elsewhere that simply hasn't completed in time. Whatever it is, write it down, put dates against it, and be ready to evidence it rather than just describe it on a call.

Broker fees for arranging bridging loans are usually separate from lender arrangement fees, commonly in the range of £500 to £1,500 or a percentage of the loan, though a good broker will be transparent about this from the first conversation rather than burying it in the offer letter. Given the time pressure you're under, paying a broker fee to get the right lender first time is almost always cheaper than the cost of the deal collapsing entirely. Brokers working with clients in Billingham, Caerphilly, Andover and Kendal see this exact scenario regularly, so local experience with lenders can help too.

Most bridging loans use rolled up or retained interest, meaning you don't pay monthly instalments at all, and the interest is added to the loan and settled in full when you repay or remortgage. This matters if cashflow is tight, because it means the pressure sits at the end of the loan rather than every month in between.

Second charge bridging is another variation worth knowing about, particularly if you already own a property with equity in it and the issue is a top-up rather than the whole purchase price. Rather than replacing your existing mortgage, a second charge bridge sits behind it, secured against the same property, and can sometimes be arranged even faster because there's no need to disturb the existing first charge lender.

Valuation type can also make a real difference to speed. A full physical valuation, where a surveyor visits the property in person, typically adds two to four days compared with a desktop or automated valuation model, which can sometimes be turned around within hours. Ask your broker early on which type the lender is likely to use, because it directly affects whether you'll hit a tight exchange date.

Get all your documents ready before you even speak to a lender. Bank statements for the last three months, proof of ID, proof of address, evidence of the deposit source and a clear written explanation of the original decline will all be asked for eventually, so having them ready from the first call can genuinely save a full working day.

None of this is a decision to make alone at midnight scrolling forums. Speak to a broker who arranges bridging regularly, be completely honest about why the original mortgage was declined, and get the exit strategy in writing before you sign anything. That combination, honesty about the problem and clarity about the way out, is what actually gets these cases through in the days you have left.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I get a bridging loan if my mortgage was declined a week before exchange?
Yes, in most cases. Bridging lenders can often value, underwrite and complete within 5 to 10 working days, which is why it's the main fallback option when a mainstream mortgage falls through this close to exchange.

How fast can a bridging loan actually complete?
From a clean application with an instructed solicitor and a straightforward valuation, many specialist lenders can complete within 5 to 10 working days, sometimes faster if the valuation and legal work run in parallel.

What does it cost compared to losing my deposit?
Rates typically run from around 0.55% to 1.25% per month plus arrangement fees of 1.5% to 2%. On a £300,000 loan over four months that's roughly £10,200 in interest, which is usually far less than losing a 10% deposit on exchange.

Will I need to prove how I'll repay the bridging loan?
Yes. Lenders want a clear, dated exit strategy, ideally a decision in principle from a mainstream lender or evidence of another repayment source, rather than a plan simply described over the phone.

What if the decline was due to affordability rather than paperwork?
If it's an affordability recalculation, such as a change in income or bonus, appealing with the same lender rarely works because the underlying numbers no longer support the loan, so bridging becomes the more realistic route.

Should I still try to appeal the original decline?
Yes, it costs nothing but a phone call and a day or two, so it's worth running alongside a bridging application rather than instead of one, especially if the decline was a documentation issue.

How much can I borrow against the property?
Most bridging lenders will lend up to 70% to 75% of the property's value on a straightforward residential case, so if your original mortgage was at 90% loan to value you may need to bring additional funds.

content:
The government has revealed just how much work is going into the digital infrastructure that will sit behind the Renters Rights Act, with digitisation described as being at the centre of preparations for the new law. For landlords and letting agents, this is a signal that the reformed private rented sector will not just have new rules on paper, but new systems designed to check compliance and enforce them in practice.

As reported by Letting Agent Today, officials have been detailing the scale of the legal and technical preparation involved in getting the Act ready for operation, with a strong emphasis on the digital tools that will underpin enforcement and compliance across the sector.

Why digitisation matters more than the headline reforms

Much of the public conversation around the Renters Rights Act has focused on the big-ticket changes: the end of Section 21 evictions, new grounds for possession, and stronger rights for tenants challenging rent increases. But laws like this only bite if there is a working system to enforce them. Building digital infrastructure to support registration, record-keeping and case management suggests the government wants the new rights to be checkable and traceable, not just theoretical.

For landlords, that means the days of loosely kept paperwork and informal tenancy management are likely to feel increasingly out of step with how the sector is regulated. Where enforcement was previously patchy because it relied on tenants complaining or local authorities stumbling across problems, a more digitised approach points toward more consistent oversight of who is letting property, how, and whether they are meeting their obligations.

What this means for landlords and letting agents right now

Nothing here changes the substance of the Renters Rights Act itself, but it does change the practical reality of compliance. Landlords who have been treating the reforms as a distant deadline should take this as a reminder that the machinery to check compliance is being actively built, not just discussed. Letting agents in particular are likely to be drawn into any new digital reporting or registration requirements, since they often act as the point of contact between landlords and official processes.

The sensible response is to get ahead of the administrative side now: making sure tenancy records, deposit protection, gas and electrical safety certificates, and any licensing paperwork are in good order and easy to produce. A more digitised enforcement environment tends to reward landlords who are already organised and penalise those relying on gaps in the system to avoid scrutiny.

Portfolio landlords and cash flow considerations

For landlords with multiple properties, adapting to new digital compliance systems can mean added administrative time and, in some cases, costs tied to bringing properties or paperwork up to standard ahead of enforcement going live. Where landlords need to fund improvement works, licensing costs, or portfolio restructuring to stay compliant, short-term finance options are sometimes used to bridge the gap while longer-term plans are put in place. Landlords weighing up their options as the Renters Rights Act beds in may find it useful to look at Boxx Finance's funding solutions as one avenue worth exploring.

No. This news is about the scale of the legal and digital preparation behind the Act, not a change to the substance of the reforms themselves. The core changes, such as the end of Section 21, remain as previously set out.

title: Why a call for public records on social housing delivery matters for the wider property market
excerpt: A letter in The Guardian argues for public records tracking what developers and councils promise on social housing against what actually gets built, exposing a transparency gap that shapes housing supply nationwide.
metaTitle: Social Housing Records Call Highlights UK Supply Gap
metaDescription: A Guardian letter calls for public records on social housing delivery. Here's what the transparency debate means for buyers, renters and landlords.
keywords: property market, landlord, renter, homeowner, housing market, planning permission
author: Mark Higgins

mainEntity.name: What is a Section 106 agreement and how does it relate to social housing?

acceptedAnswer.text: A Section 106 agreement is a legal commitment made by a developer to a local authority, often as a condition of planning permission, which can include obligations to provide a set number of affordable or social housing units within a scheme. The letter's argument is that there is currently no consistent public record showing whether these commitments are actually fulfilled once a development is complete.

mainEntity.name: Why does a shortfall in social housing affect people who are not looking for social housing themselves?

acceptedAnswer.text: When planned social and affordable housing does not materialise as intended, the resulting demand does not disappear, it shifts into the private rented and owner-occupied markets, adding further pressure to prices and rents that affects buyers and tenants across the board.

mainEntity.name: Could greater transparency on social housing delivery slow down new developments?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is possible that increased scrutiny could add administrative steps or encourage local authorities to hold firmer on affordable housing requirements during negotiations, though the source letter frames this as a matter of accountability rather than suggesting it would necessarily delay schemes overall.

content:
A letter published in The Guardian has called for public records tracking what developers and local authorities promise when it comes to social housing, what actually gets delivered, and what it costs residents to live in it. The letter, from Marco Scalvini, responds to a Guardian editorial on London's social housing and argues that without proper transparency, it is impossible to know whether commitments made during planning are being honoured once schemes are built. This might sound like a niche planning issue, but it touches something every homeowner, renter and landlord already feels day to day: the chronic shortage of affordable and social homes that keeps pressure on prices and rents across the wider market.

As reported by The Guardian, the letter picks up on a broader argument that social housing should be treated as an economic asset rather than a cost, and pushes that idea further by asking a simple but awkward question: how do we actually know what is being delivered against what was promised? Developers frequently agree to include a proportion of affordable or social units as a condition of planning permission, often through Section 106 agreements. But without consistent, publicly accessible records, it is difficult for anyone outside the local authority to verify whether those obligations are met in full, watered down through later negotiation, or delayed indefinitely.

Why this matters beyond social housing itself

The private and social housing markets are more connected than they might appear. When planned social housing quotas are not delivered as promised, the shortfall does not simply disappear. It adds to pressure on the private rented sector, keeps competition for existing homes higher than it should be, and can slow the pace at which new sites move from planning to completion if disputes over obligations drag on. For anyone trying to buy their first home, or a landlord assessing demand in a given area, the health of the local social housing pipeline is a genuine, if often invisible, factor in the numbers.

For developers and housebuilders themselves, greater public scrutiny of delivery records could change how schemes are planned and phased from the outset. If commitments made at the planning stage are going to be tracked and published, that adds a layer of accountability that has not consistently existed before. It could also affect how quickly schemes get the green light, since local authorities may face more pressure to hold firm on affordable housing requirements rather than allowing them to be renegotiated downward later in the process.

What it means for buyers, renters and landlords right now

Nothing changes overnight as a result of one letter, but the debate it reflects is part of a wider conversation about housing supply that has been running for years and shows no sign of resolving quickly. For buyers and renters, the practical takeaway is that the supply shortfall behind high prices and rents is not just about how many homes get planning permission, it is also about how many of the promised affordable and social units actually get built, and how long that takes. For landlords and property investors, understanding the social housing picture in a given local authority area can offer useful context when assessing long-term demand, especially in areas where large regeneration or mixed-tenure schemes are underway.

Anyone actively developing or converting property, including landlords adding units or investors taking on schemes with an affordable housing component, will already know that navigating planning obligations and delivery timelines can affect cash flow and project sequencing. Where that creates a short-term funding gap between phases of a project, it is worth knowing what options exist, and Boxx Finance's funding solutions hub sets out some of the ways bridging and development finance can support projects moving through these stages.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a Section 106 agreement and how does it relate to social housing?

A Section 106 agreement is a legal commitment made by a developer to a local authority, often as a condition of planning permission, which can include obligations to provide a set number of affordable or social housing units within a scheme. The letter's argument is that there is currently no consistent public record showing whether these commitments are actually fulfilled once a development is complete.

Why does a shortfall in social housing affect people who are not looking for social housing themselves?

When planned social and affordable housing does not materialise as intended, the resulting demand does not disappear, it shifts into the private rented and owner-occupied markets, adding further pressure to prices and rents that affects buyers and tenants across the board.

Could greater transparency on social housing delivery slow down new developments?

It is possible that increased scrutiny could add administrative steps or encourage local authorities to hold firmer on affordable housing requirements during negotiations, though the source letter frames this as a matter of accountability rather than suggesting it would necessarily delay schemes overall.

title: Bridging Loans: Paying Inheritance Tax Before Your House Sells
excerpt: HMRC wants inheritance tax within six months of death, but you can't sell the property until probate comes through. Here's how executors bridge that gap with real numbers and real options.
metaTitle: How To Pay An Inheritance Tax Bill Before The House Has Sold
metaDescription: Executors facing an inheritance tax bill before probate completes have real options. Compare HMRC schemes and bridging loans with worked figures and timelines.
keywords: inheritance tax bridging loan, pay IHT before probate, HMRC direct payment scheme, inheritance tax instalment option, bridging loan against inherited property, probate bridging loan, IHT six month deadline
author: Tara Jameson
content:
You've just lost someone and now HMRC wants money for a house you're not allowed to sell yet. The grant of probate hasn't come through. The clock on inheritance tax is already running whether you've registered it or not. You are not the first executor to sit with this exact problem, and bridging loans for inheritance tax before probate can solve it.

This is one of the more common reasons families end up looking at a bridging loan for inheritance tax before probate completes, and you should understand exactly how the timeline and the money work before you decide anything. Executors we speak with in Wokingham, Cardiff, Eastbourne and Maidenhead face the same six-month deadline pressure, regardless of where the property sits.

Most people dealing with this have never touched probate law before and never expected to. You're grieving, you're suddenly responsible for someone else's financial affairs, and a government department is sending letters about deadlines while you're still sorting out a funeral. It's a lot to carry at once, and the paperwork rarely waits for you to feel ready. If you want to understand how this type of borrowing works before going further, this guide to how bridging finance works is a useful starting point.

The clock

HMRC generally expects inheritance tax to be paid by the end of the sixth month after the month the person died. If someone died on 14 March, the tax is due by 30 September. Interest starts accruing from that date on any unpaid balance, currently charged at a rate set by HMRC that moves with the Bank of England base rate, so it changes during a long probate.

The problem is that probate itself rarely moves that fast. A grant of representation commonly takes 3 to 6 months from application in straightforward cases, longer if the estate is contested, if there's no will, or if the Probate Registry has a backlog, which it frequently does. You can easily reach month 5 or 6 with no grant, no ability to sell, and a tax bill already due. Every estate is different, and these are general timeframes rather than a fixed rule, so check the specific position with the estate's solicitor early rather than assuming a standard pattern will apply.

Register the estate for inheritance tax purposes as soon as reasonably possible after death, rather than waiting until you feel the paperwork is in order. The IHT400 form and its various schedules take time to complete properly, especially where the estate includes multiple properties, business assets, or lifetime gifts that need to be accounted for. Executors who leave this until month four or five of the six-month window often find they've lost valuable time they didn't need to lose.

Solicitors handling probate will usually tell you the same thing early on: get the valuation of the property done properly and get it done quickly. A formal RICS valuation, rather than an estate agent's guess, carries more weight with HMRC and reduces the chance of a dispute over the taxable value later. Delays here ripple through everything else, since you can't finalise the IHT400 without a settled figure for the property.

What happens if you miss it

Missing the six-month deadline does not usually stop probate proceeding, but it does start interest accruing on the unpaid tax, and that interest compounds the longer the estate takes to sell the property. HMRC will not usually delay probate for this reason, and in practice you often need to show HMRC the tax has been dealt with, or arranged for, before the Probate Registry will issue the grant in the first place.

There's a knock-on effect too. Without a grant, executors can't legally sell the property, can't access most of the deceased's non-jointly-held bank accounts, and can't complete the estate administration. If the family is also trying to move on with practical matters, like clearing or maintaining the house, unpaid tax and mounting interest just adds pressure to an already slow process. It rarely causes catastrophic loss, but it steadily erodes what beneficiaries eventually receive.

There's also a personal liability angle that catches some executors off guard. HMRC can, in certain circumstances, pursue executors personally for unpaid inheritance tax if they've distributed estate assets before settling the bill. This is exactly why many executors feel they can't simply wait things out and hope HMRC will be patient. The pressure to find the money quickly is often as much about protecting themselves as it is about protecting the estate.

Left unresolved for long enough, mounting interest can genuinely eat into what beneficiaries eventually receive by several thousand pounds, particularly on larger estates where the tax bill runs into six figures. It's rarely dramatic in any single month, but three, four, five months of accruing interest at HMRC's rate adds up in a way that's easy to underestimate when you're focused on getting through probate itself. If your situation is already at this stage, it may be worth taking a moment to compare bridging loan rates so you know what your options look like before interest builds further.

Your options

There is more than one way to bridge this gap, and a solicitor or accountant dealing with probate regularly will usually walk you through all of them before recommending borrowing against the property.

OptionHow it worksMain drawback
HMRC Direct Payment SchemeBanks and building societies release funds directly to HMRC from the deceased's own accounts, including ISAs, without needing the grant firstOnly works if the deceased held enough cash; many estates are property-heavy with little liquid cash
IHT instalment optionTax on the property itself can be spread over 10 annual instalmentsInterest applies to the unpaid balance, and the first instalment is still due by the six-month deadline, so it doesn't remove the initial cashflow problem
Loan from beneficiaries or familyA beneficiary advances funds personally, often repaid once the estate settlesNot everyone has spare capital, and informal loans need proper documentation to avoid disputes later
Bridging loan against the propertyShort-term loan secured on the inherited property, repaid when it sellsInterest and fees reduce the eventual estate value; lending pre-grant is a smaller, more specialist part of the market

The Direct Payment Scheme is worth checking first because it costs nothing beyond the transfer itself, but it depends entirely on the deceased having held enough in accessible accounts. Many estates simply don't have that much sitting in cash, particularly where the property is the bulk of the value.

The instalment option helps spread the pain but it is often misunderstood. It does not mean nothing is due for ten years. The first instalment is still expected by the original six-month deadline, and HMRC charges interest on the outstanding balance throughout, so you're still facing an immediate payment even if it's smaller than the full bill.

Loans from beneficiaries can work well where there's a willing family member with cash sitting in savings, but they need to be set up properly. A simple written agreement setting out the amount, the repayment trigger, and whether interest applies protects everyone involved, including the person lending the money. Skipping this step because "it's family, we don't need paperwork" is one of the more common regrets executors mention afterwards, particularly if the sale takes longer than expected or other beneficiaries start asking questions.

It's also worth mentioning that some estates combine two or three of these options rather than relying on just one. You might use whatever cash the Direct Payment Scheme can release, top up with a family loan for part of the shortfall, and bridge the remaining gap. There's no rule that says it has to be one clean solution, and mixing approaches can sometimes reduce the total borrowing needed and therefore the total interest paid.

How a bridging loan works for this situation

A bridging loan secured against the inherited property is the option most executors reach for when the estate has no spare cash and the beneficiaries can't or won't fund a loan personally. It works by using the property itself as security, with the loan repaid from the sale proceeds once probate completes and the house is marketed.

Most lenders in this space want to see the grant of probate already issued before they'll lend, because that's the point at which the executor has clear legal authority to deal with the property and, crucially, to grant the lender a legal charge over it. This is the more common route and tends to move faster through underwriting, typically 2 to 4 weeks from application to funds, sometimes quicker with a cooperative solicitor and a clean title.

A smaller, more specialist part of the market will lend pre-grant, against the reasonable expectation that probate will be granted, usually where the will is uncontested and the executor's identity is clear. This is genuinely a niche corner of the industry, fewer lenders offer it, pricing tends to be higher, and it needs careful legal structuring since the charge can't be formally registered until the grant exists. If you're in a genuine pre-grant cash crisis this is worth exploring, but expect a smaller pool of willing lenders and more conditions attached. If you're weighing this route, it can help to arrange a bridging loan today rather than waiting until the deadline is imminent.

Where the property was the deceased's main residence and will pass to someone who intends to live in it, this is likely to fall under FCA-regulated bridging lending, which brings additional borrower protections. Where the property is being inherited purely as an investment, or will be sold on rather than occupied, it is more likely unregulated. This genuinely varies estate by estate and needs to be checked with the lender and the estate's solicitor rather than assumed either way.

Applications on inheritance-related bridging loans most often stall on two things: probate delays pushing past the loan's expected timeline, and disagreements between multiple executors or beneficiaries about whether borrowing is the right approach at all. Getting everyone with authority to sign aligned before you start the application saves weeks.

In practice, the lender will want a fairly standard set of documents to get moving: certified copy of the grant of probate (or evidence probate has been applied for, in the pre-grant cases), the will itself, ID and address verification for all executors, a recent valuation of the property, and confirmation of the outstanding IHT liability directly from HMRC or the solicitor's correspondence. Having these ready before you approach a broker genuinely speeds things up, sometimes by a week or more compared with chasing documents after the application has already started.

Brokers who work in this space regularly will also flag whether the property has any complications that could slow underwriting, things like unusual construction, leasehold with a short remaining term, or multiple beneficiaries with competing interests. Flagging these upfront rather than letting a lender discover them mid-application avoids the frustrating experience of getting close to an offer only to have it pulled back for further checks. Choosing carefully from among the best bridging loan lenders in the UK can also make a meaningful difference to how smoothly this stage goes.

What it actually costs

Here's a worked example using a typical estate scenario. Say the inherited property is valued at £450,000, the inheritance tax bill is £70,000, and you need six months to get through probate, market the property and complete a sale.

ItemAmount
Loan required (gross)£70,000
Arrangement fee (indicative 2%)£1,400
Net loan advanced to HMRC£68,600
Monthly interest (indicative 0.85% pcm)£595 per month (approx. 10.2% annualised)
6 months' interest (retained or serviced)£3,570
Exit fee (indicative 1%, lender dependent)£700
Valuation and legal costs (indicative)£1,200 - £1,800
Total cost of borrowing over 6 monthsApprox. £6,870 - £7,470

The gross loan is the £70,000 you actually need for the tax bill. The net loan, £68,600 in this example, is what actually lands after the arrangement fee is deducted, which matters because if you need the full £70,000 in HMRC's account, you may need to borrow slightly more than the bill itself to cover the fee. This gross-versus-net gap catches out a lot of first-time borrowers who assume the amount they ask for is the amount they'll receive.

On a £450,000 property, £70,000 borrowed against it represents a loan to value of around 15.5%, which is comfortably within what most bridging lenders will accept, even before factoring in that the loan will be repaid in full once the property sells. Lower loan to value ratios like this generally attract more competitive pricing than borrowers see on higher-risk bridging, simply because the lender's security cushion is so large relative to the debt.

Compare that with a smaller estate, say a £280,000 property with a £45,000 tax bill. The loan to value there sits closer to 16%, similar in proportion, but the fixed costs, valuation, legal fees, arrangement fee, represent a bigger percentage of the total loan simply because they don't scale down as much as the loan itself does. This is why brokers sometimes suggest that very small IHT bridging loans can feel disproportionately expensive in percentage terms, even though the lender's approach barely changes.

These figures are indicative only, will vary by lender, loan size and how the estate is structured, and you should confirm them at enquiry rather than rely on them as a quote. Rates move with market conditions, and current UK short-term property finance rates are worth checking directly with a broker before you commit to a figure. You can also look at current UK bridging loan rates for a general sense of where pricing typically sits before approaching lenders.

Many executors choose to have interest retained within the loan rather than paid monthly, meaning the interest is added to the balance and settled in full when the property sells, rather than needing to find monthly payments from an estate with limited cash flow. This is worth discussing directly when you compare bridging loan rates and terms, since not every lender structures it the same way.

It's also worth asking a broker about early repayment terms before you commit. Some lenders charge a minimum interest period, meaning even if the property sells in month two, you might still be charged three months' interest. Others calculate daily, so you only pay for the days the loan was actually outstanding. On a fast-moving sale this difference can be worth several hundred pounds, and it's a fair question to raise before signing anything.

Your exit strategy

The exit here is almost always the sale of the property once probate is granted and it goes to market. Lenders will want to see realistic evidence that the property is saleable at a value that comfortably covers the loan, which usually means a recent valuation and, ideally, some indication of local market demand.

A second, less common exit is refinancing the inherited property onto a standard mortgage if a beneficiary intends to keep it rather than sell, using a mortgage to repay the short-term property finance. This only works if that beneficiary can qualify for a mortgage in their own right and the numbers stack up, so it needs confirming early rather than assumed as a fallback.

Lenders will not accept a vague intention to sell as a plan on its own. They generally want to see the property already instructed to an estate agent, or close to it, alongside realistic market comparables, before they'll release funds with confidence. A well-prepared exit strategy, backed by paperwork rather than assumptions, tends to move an application through underwriting noticeably faster than one built on good intentions alone.

It's worth thinking about timing realistically rather than optimistically. If probate typically takes 4 months in a straightforward case and the property might take a further 3 to 4 months to sell in a normal market, a 6-month bridging term can feel tight. Many brokers will suggest arranging the loan over 9 or 12 months even if you expect to repay sooner, simply to build in a buffer against the sort of delays that are common with probate sales, chain issues, or a slower than expected market. Repaying early on most bridging products doesn't carry a heavy penalty, so the extra breathing room rarely costs much if you don't end up needing it.

Where multiple beneficiaries are involved, it's also worth agreeing early on who has authority to instruct the estate agent, negotiate offers, and sign off on the eventual sale price. Delays caused by beneficiaries disagreeing over asking price or acceptable offers are one of the more common reasons a bridging loan runs longer than planned, and that extra time comes with extra interest attached. Sorting out decision-making authority before the loan even starts is a small step that can save real money later.

Finally, keep the solicitor handling probate and the broker arranging the short-term property finance talking to each other directly rather than relaying information through you. Probate solicitors and bridging brokers who are used to working on these cases together tend to move things along faster, simply because they understand what the other side needs and when, rather than waiting for an executor already stretched thin to pass messages back and forth. For a full overview of the wider options available beyond bridging, our funding solutions hub covers the range of routes executors and beneficiaries can consider.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I get a bridging loan to pay inheritance tax before probate is granted?
Yes, though it's a smaller, more specialist part of the market. Most lenders prefer to see the grant of probate already issued, but some will lend pre-grant against the reasonable expectation that probate will be granted, usually where the will is uncontested and the executor's identity is clear.

How quickly can a bridging loan for inheritance tax be arranged?
Where the grant of probate is already in place, funding typically takes 2 to 4 weeks from application, sometimes quicker with a cooperative solicitor and a clean title. Pre-grant lending usually takes longer due to the additional legal structuring involved.

What happens if I miss the six-month inheritance tax deadline?
Probate can usually still proceed, but interest starts accruing on the unpaid tax from that date. HMRC will generally want to see the tax dealt with, or arranged for, before the Probate Registry issues the grant, and executors can in some cases be pursued personally for unpaid tax if assets are distributed too early.

How much does a bridging loan for inheritance tax typically cost?
Costs vary by lender and loan size, but alongside the arrangement fee (often around 2%) and monthly interest, you should budget for an exit fee and valuation and legal costs. On a typical £70,000 loan over six months, total borrowing costs often fall somewhere between roughly £6,870 and £7,470.

Do I need a formal valuation of the property before applying?
Yes, lenders and HMRC both generally expect a formal RICS valuation rather than an estate agent's estimate. This carries more weight with HMRC and reduces the chance of a dispute over the taxable value, and lenders will also want it to assess loan to value.

What documents do lenders need for an inheritance tax bridging loan?
