Typically a certified copy of the grant of probate (or evidence probate has been applied for in pre-grant cases), the will, ID and address verification for all executors, a recent property valuation, and confirmation of the outstanding IHT liability from HMRC or the solicitor.

How is a bridging loan for inheritance tax usually repaid?
The most common exit is sale of the property once probate is granted and it goes to market. A less common alternative is refinancing onto a standard mortgage if a beneficiary intends to keep the property, provided they can qualify for a mortgage in their own right.

If you're facing this situation now, it's worth speaking to a broker directly rather than waiting for the deadline to close in. You can get a bridging loan quote or find a bridging loan broker to talk through the specifics of your estate before interest has a chance to build further.

title: A Quarter of Flats for Sale Are Landlord Sell-Offs, But Buyers Are Wary
excerpt: One in four flats on the market are being sold by landlords exiting buy-to-let, as falling profits and tighter regulation push many out. But demand for flats remains soft.
metaTitle: Why Landlords Are Selling Flats, And Who's Buying
metaDescription: One in four flats for sale are landlord exits, driven by falling profits and new rules. Here's what it means for buyers and remaining landlords.
keywords: property market, mortgage, landlord, first-time buyer, buy-to-let
author: Mark Higgins

mainEntity.name: Does more landlord selling mean flat prices will fall?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily straight away, but a larger pool of sellers competing for a smaller pool of interested buyers tends to put downward pressure on asking prices over time, particularly for flats that need work or sit in leasehold blocks with higher service charges.

mainEntity.name: Is now a good time to buy a flat from a landlord?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can be, since landlords selling for financial or regulatory reasons are often more open to negotiation than owner-occupiers. But buyers should still do their usual checks on service charges, lease length and building safety before assuming a bargain.

mainEntity.name: Why are buy-to-let profits falling for landlords?

acceptedAnswer.text: The source points to a mix of stricter regulation and squeezed margins, on top of costs landlords already face such as mortgage interest, maintenance and compliance, which together are making letting less profitable than it used to be for many.

content:
Landlords are selling up in large numbers, with one in four flats currently on the market having been put up for sale by a landlord rather than an owner-occupier, according to This Is Money. The exodus is being driven by falling rental profits and stricter regulation on buy-to-let, but the report raises an awkward question: with so many flats flooding the market, is anyone actually queuing up to buy them?

This matters because it points to two things happening at once. Landlords are finding flats less worthwhile to hold onto, and buyers are not necessarily rushing in to fill the gap. For anyone trying to make sense of the property market right now, whether they are hoping to buy their first home, sell an investment property, or work out whether to keep letting, this shift is worth paying attention to.

Why landlords are selling now

Buy-to-let has become less attractive for a combination of reasons that have been building for a while: tighter mortgage rules, additional tax changes affecting landlords, and rising costs of compliance with safety and energy regulations have all squeezed profit margins. On top of that, tenant demand and rental yields have not always kept pace with the costs of running a flat, particularly in blocks with service charges or leasehold complications. Put simply, for a growing number of landlords the sums no longer add up the way they once did, and selling looks like the sensible option.

What it means if you are trying to buy

A glut of landlord-sold flats hitting the market in theory means more choice and potentially softer prices for buyers, since sellers who are exiting an investment are often more motivated to agree a deal than someone selling their family home. But the source is clear that demand for flats is not guaranteed. Many buyers, especially first-time buyers, have become more cautious about flats generally, put off by service charges, leasehold uncertainty, and stories about buildings with unresolved safety issues. That means the extra supply does not automatically translate into a buyer's bargain. It may take patience, and a willingness to negotiate hard, to turn this into a genuine opportunity.

What it means if you are a landlord

If you are a landlord weighing up whether to sell, you are far from alone, and that is precisely the problem. A market where a quarter of flats for sale are landlord exits is a crowded one, and crowded markets tend to mean slower sales and more haggling over price. Landlords thinking about selling may need to be realistic about timelines and pricing, particularly if their flat sits in a block or area where several other units are also being marketed by landlords at the same time. For those weighing up whether to sell now or wait, the practical question is less about long-term rental yield and more about how quickly a sale needs to happen and what condition the flat is in to attract a cautious pool of buyers.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does more landlord selling mean flat prices will fall?

Not necessarily straight away, but a larger pool of sellers competing for a smaller pool of interested buyers tends to put downward pressure on asking prices over time, particularly for flats that need work or sit in leasehold blocks with higher service charges.

Is now a good time to buy a flat from a landlord?

It can be, since landlords selling for financial or regulatory reasons are often more open to negotiation than owner-occupiers. But buyers should still do their usual checks on service charges, lease length and building safety before assuming a bargain.

Why are buy-to-let profits falling for landlords?

The source points to a mix of stricter regulation and squeezed margins, on top of costs landlords already face such as mortgage interest, maintenance and compliance, which together are making letting less profitable than it used to be for many.

For landlords who decide selling isn't the right move and instead need to refinance, raise capital against a property, or bridge a gap while a sale is negotiated, it's worth exploring what options exist through Boxx Finance's funding solutions.

title: HMRC's landlord tax guidance is still shifting, and a new tribunal case shows why incorporation is riskier than it looks
excerpt: A fresh tribunal ruling has landed just days after HMRC amended its 20-hour rule guidance for landlord Incorporation Relief, raising fresh questions for landlords weighing up incorporating their portfolios.
metaTitle: New Tribunal Case Adds to Landlord Tax Uncertainty
metaDescription: HMRC's 20-hour guidance for landlord Incorporation Relief has already changed once. A new tribunal case suggests more grey areas are still to come.
keywords: mortgage, landlord, capital gains tax
author: Mark Higgins

mainEntity.name: What is the 20-hour rule for landlords?

acceptedAnswer.text: It refers to guidance HMRC uses, alongside other factors, to help decide whether a landlord's property activities amount to a genuine business rather than a passive investment, which affects eligibility for reliefs such as Incorporation Relief. HMRC has recently amended its guidance on this point after it caused confusion among landlords and advisers.

mainEntity.name: Does this new tribunal case change the rules on Incorporation Relief?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not directly. The case is not a Section 162 Incorporation Relief case, but according to Property118 it touches on similar questions about how business activity is assessed for tax purposes, which is why it is being watched closely by landlords and tax advisers.

mainEntity.name: Should I delay incorporating my property portfolio because of this?

acceptedAnswer.text: That depends entirely on individual circumstances, and this is a decision that needs proper professional tax advice rather than general guidance. What this story shows is that the rules in this area are still evolving, so getting advice before acting is more important than ever.

content:
HMRC has already been forced to amend its guidance once on the so called 20-hour rule, the test used to decide whether a landlord is running a genuine property business eligible for Incorporation Relief when they move a portfolio into a limited company. Now, just a week before that change was made, the First-tier Tribunal handed down a separate property tax judgment that, according to specialist landlord publication Property118, exposes another area of uncertainty that has so far gone largely unnoticed. For landlords weighing up whether to incorporate, it is another reminder that the rules around this decision are far from settled.

Why the 20-hour rule matters so much

Incorporation Relief allows landlords to transfer their rental properties into a limited company without triggering an immediate capital gains tax bill, but only if HMRC accepts that what is being transferred is a genuine business rather than simply a passive investment. The number of hours a landlord spends actively managing their properties each week has become a key part of how HMRC assesses that. When HMRC's own guidance on this point proved unclear or inconsistent, it created real uncertainty for landlords trying to plan ahead, which is presumably why HMRC felt compelled to amend it.

The tribunal case highlighted by Property118 is not directly about the 20-hour rule or Incorporation Relief under Section 162 of the relevant tax legislation, but the publication argues that part of the judgment touches on similar territory, namely how tax authorities and tribunals assess what counts as a business activity for tax purposes. That is precisely the kind of grey area that landlords considering incorporation need to understand before they commit.

What this means if you are thinking about incorporating

For landlords with a handful of properties run alongside a full-time job, or those who use letting agents to handle the day-to-day management, this is a live and practical concern rather than an abstract legal point. If HMRC or a tribunal takes the view that too little personal time and effort has gone into managing a portfolio, the case for treating it as a business, and therefore the case for Incorporation Relief, can weaken considerably.

The wider lesson from both the amended guidance and this newer case is that the rules in this area are still being tested and clarified, sometimes in ways that only become clear after a tribunal has ruled. Landlords who assumed their situation was straightforward under the old guidance may now need to revisit that assumption, and anyone part way through an incorporation should take proper advice on where they stand before going further.

The financial planning angle

Incorporating a property portfolio is rarely just a tax decision. It often involves restructuring finance, refinancing mortgages into a company name, and sometimes needing to move quickly once a tax or legal position becomes clear, particularly if a transaction needs to complete before a deadline or before circumstances change again. Landlords going through this process sometimes need short term finance to bridge the gap between one structure and the next, which is where specialist lenders can play a part. Boxx Finance's funding solutions page is worth a look for landlords who find themselves needing flexible finance while they sort out the tax and legal side of an incorporation.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the 20-hour rule for landlords?

It refers to guidance HMRC uses, alongside other factors, to help decide whether a landlord's property activities amount to a genuine business rather than a passive investment, which affects eligibility for reliefs such as Incorporation Relief. HMRC has recently amended its guidance on this point after it caused confusion among landlords and advisers.

Does this new tribunal case change the rules on Incorporation Relief?

Not directly. The case is not a Section 162 Incorporation Relief case, but according to Property118 it touches on similar questions about how business activity is assessed for tax purposes, which is why it is being watched closely by landlords and tax advisers.

Should I delay incorporating my property portfolio because of this?

That depends entirely on individual circumstances, and this is a decision that needs proper professional tax advice rather than general guidance. What this story shows is that the rules in this area are still evolving, so getting advice before acting is more important than ever.

title: Holiday Let Mortgage Demand Is Rising Even as Tax Rules Get Tougher
excerpt: Nearly nine in ten mortgage brokers report growing demand for holiday and short-let finance, new data shows, as investors chase higher yields despite a harder tax and regulatory backdrop.
metaTitle: Holiday Let Demand Rises Despite Tax Changes
metaDescription: Brokers report a surge in holiday and short-let mortgage demand as investors chase higher yields, despite tougher tax rules. Here's what it means for landlords.
keywords: property market, mortgage rate, mortgage, landlord, buy-to-let, homeowner
author: Mark Higgins

mainEntity.name: Is a holiday let mortgage the same as a buy-to-let mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Holiday let mortgages are a specialist product, priced and underwritten differently from standard buy-to-let mortgages because lenders treat the income as more seasonal and variable, and because the properties are usually let on a short-term basis rather than to a single long-term tenant.

mainEntity.name: Why are holiday let yields often higher than standard buy-to-let?

acceptedAnswer.text: Short-let and holiday properties can typically be let at a higher rate per night or week than the equivalent monthly rent achieved on a standard tenancy, particularly in tourist areas, though this needs to be weighed against higher management costs and periods when the property sits empty.

mainEntity.name: Has the tax treatment of holiday lets changed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, the tax rules around furnished holiday lettings have become less favourable than they previously were, which is one of the reasons this is described as a less favourable regulatory environment for investors, even though demand for finance in this area is still rising.

content:
Almost nine in ten mortgage brokers say they are seeing more demand for holiday and short-let finance, according to new data from The Cumberland Building Society's inaugural Holiday Let Index, even though investors in this corner of the property market are dealing with a less generous tax and regulatory environment than before. The finding suggests that, for a certain type of landlord, the appeal of higher rental yields is still outweighing the extra costs and red tape that now come with running a short-let property.

As reported by BuyAssociation, the higher yields available from holiday lets compared with conventional buy-to-let are one of the main reasons brokers are being asked about this type of finance more often. That is a notable signal at a time when many landlords have been retreating from the private rental sector altogether, put off by rising costs, stricter energy efficiency expectations, and changes to how furnished holiday lettings are taxed.

Why yields are pulling investors toward short lets

Traditional buy-to-let has become a harder sum to make work for many landlords. Mortgage rates remain elevated compared with a few years ago, and tax relief on mortgage interest has been restricted for standard rental properties. Holiday and short-let properties, by contrast, can often command significantly higher weekly or nightly rates than a long-term tenancy would generate over the same period, particularly in popular tourist areas. For investors doing the maths, that yield gap can be enough to justify the extra work involved in managing a short-let, such as more frequent turnover, cleaning, and marketing.

This does not mean the sums are easy. Short-let income can be seasonal and less predictable than a fixed monthly rent, and running costs are typically higher. But the broker data suggests enough investors are satisfied with the trade-off that demand for this type of mortgage finance is climbing.

The tax and regulatory backdrop has got tougher

It is worth being clear-eyed about the environment this demand is happening in. The favourable tax treatment that furnished holiday lettings used to enjoy has been curtailed, and local authorities in various tourist hotspots have been tightening planning rules and licensing requirements around short-term lets in response to concerns about housing availability for local residents. None of that has disappeared. What the Cumberland's index points to is that, despite these headwinds, appetite has not collapsed. Investors appear to be recalculating rather than retreating, weighing the higher gross yields against the higher compliance burden and deciding the numbers still work for them.

What this means if you are considering a holiday let

For homeowners or landlords thinking about moving into this market, the message from brokers is that lenders are actively active in this space and that specialist holiday let mortgage products exist and are being used. But anyone weighing this up should go in with eyes open about the regulatory patchwork, which varies by local authority and by nation, and should not assume that headline yield figures translate directly into net profit once management costs, void periods and tax are factored in. Getting advice on both the mortgage product and the tax treatment before committing is sensible, given how much both areas have shifted recently.

For investors who need to move quickly, whether that is to secure a property before a licensing deadline, to fund refurbishment works to bring a property up to holiday-let standard, or to bridge the gap between purchase and arranging a specialist mortgage, short-term finance can play a useful role. Anyone in that position may want to look at the funding solutions available through Boxx Finance to understand the options.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a holiday let mortgage the same as a buy-to-let mortgage?

No. Holiday let mortgages are a specialist product, priced and underwritten differently from standard buy-to-let mortgages because lenders treat the income as more seasonal and variable, and because the properties are usually let on a short-term basis rather than to a single long-term tenant.

Why are holiday let yields often higher than standard buy-to-let?

Short-let and holiday properties can typically be let at a higher rate per night or week than the equivalent monthly rent achieved on a standard tenancy, particularly in tourist areas, though this needs to be weighed against higher management costs and periods when the property sits empty.

Has the tax treatment of holiday lets changed?

Yes, the tax rules around furnished holiday lettings have become less favourable than they previously were, which is one of the reasons this is described as a less favourable regulatory environment for investors, even though demand for finance in this area is still rising.

title: Can I Borrow Against A Property I've Inherited But Not Yet Sold?
excerpt: If probate is granted or nearly there, a bridging loan can often release cash from an inherited property before it sells, but multiple beneficiaries and title timing decide whether a lender will move.
metaTitle: Can I Borrow Against A Property I've Inherited But Not Yet Sold?
metaDescription: Wondering if you can borrow against an inherited property before selling it? Here's how bridging loans work post-probate, what lenders need, and the costs involved.
keywords: bridging loan against inherited property, borrowing against inheritance before sale, probate bridging loan, releasing equity from inherited property, bridging loan multiple beneficiaries, short-term property finance probate, bridging loans for inherited property
author: Mark Higgins
content:
You've just inherited a property, or a share of one, and you need money out of it now. Maybe it's to pay a tax bill. Maybe a sibling wants their share and you don't have it sitting in cash. Maybe you simply don't want to wait six months for an estate agent to find a buyer. You're grieving, you're dealing with solicitors and forms you never wanted to read, and now there's a financial clock running too. If you're asking whether you can borrow against a property you've inherited but not yet sold, the short answer is often yes, provided a few key conditions are met.

The good news, in practical terms, is that once probate is granted, or close to it, a property you've inherited can often be used as security for a bridging loan for inherited property before it sells. The less good news is that timing, title, and other beneficiaries all matter more than most people expect, and they're the three things that trip this process up. Let's go through it properly. For a broader introduction to how this type of lending works, our guide on what bridging finance actually involves is a useful starting point.

This is one of those situations where the emotional side and the financial side pull in different directions. You want to move quickly and quietly. Solicitors, lenders and HMRC all work to their own timetables, and none of them are especially interested in how urgent it feels from where you're sitting. Understanding the mechanics early on gives you a real chance of getting money out of the property without waiting for a full sale to complete.

Short-term property finance against inherited property has become far more common over the last few years. Executors and beneficiaries are increasingly aware that they don't have to sit on an illiquid asset while bills, tax demands and family pressures build up around them. Lenders in this space have adapted their processes to deal with probate cases specifically, which wasn't always the case a decade ago. If you'd like to talk through your own circumstances, you can get a bridging loan quote at any stage of the process.

Part of the reason this type of lending has grown is simply demographic. More estates now include property that's genuinely valuable, particularly in parts of the South East and London where a modest three bedroom house can easily be worth £500,000 or more. That creates a real gap between the value tied up in the estate and the cash actually available to deal with tax bills, repairs, or family payouts. Bridging exists precisely to fill that gap for a short period.

It's also worth saying that this isn't a niche or unusual product. Most established bridging lenders have dealt with dozens if not hundreds of probate cases, and many have specific underwriting teams or processes built around them. Executors in Coventry, Rochdale, Truro and Fulham have all used this route successfully. You're not asking a lender to do something strange or risky from their point of view. You're asking them to do something they already have a template for, provided the basics of title and consent are in order.

The clock

The relevant deadline here isn't fixed by law in the way an auction deposit or a mortgage offer expiry is. It's set by your own circumstances, but it still behaves like a deadline once probate is granted.

If there's inheritance tax to pay, HMRC generally expects payment within six months of the end of the month in which death occurred, with interest accruing after that point even where a payment plan on the property portion has been agreed. If that six-month window is already tight, and probate itself often takes 12 to 20 weeks from application in current conditions, you may have very little runway left by the time the grant actually lands on the doormat.

In practice, this means the tax bill can become due before you've even got legal authority to deal with the property. That's a genuinely stressful position to be in, and it's one of the most common reasons executors approach a broker in the first place. HMRC will charge interest on late payment, currently running at a rate that makes delay an expensive option, so waiting it out rarely helps.

To put some rough figures on it, an estate with a house worth £600,000 and no other significant assets could easily generate an inheritance tax bill of £100,000 or more once the nil rate bands are applied and used up. Finding that sum from savings simply isn't realistic for most families, which is exactly the scenario bridging loans are designed to solve. Borrowing against the property itself to pay HMRC, then repaying the loan once the house sells, is one of the most common single uses of probate bridging seen by brokers.

Some families try to cover the inheritance tax bill from other assets in the estate, such as savings accounts or investments held by the deceased, using the government's Direct Payment Scheme. That works well when there's enough liquid money sitting there. It works far less well when the estate is mostly one house and not much else, which is an extremely common situation in the UK, particularly where someone has lived in the same property for decades and their wealth is tied up in bricks and mortar rather than cash.

There's a further wrinkle worth knowing about. HMRC does allow inheritance tax on property to be paid in ten annual instalments, with interest charged on the outstanding balance. Some executors assume this removes the pressure entirely, but in practice most solicitors will only recommend this route if there's a genuine reason the property won't be sold quickly, since interest still accrues throughout and a single upfront payment funded by bridging is often cheaper overall once you run the numbers.

If the pressure is a sibling or co-beneficiary who wants their inheritance released now rather than waiting for a sale, the clock is more personal, but no less real. Family relationships strain fast when one person is sitting on an asset worth £300,000 and another needs £75,000 for a deposit on their own place. Three months of stalling over probate paperwork can do more damage to a family than most people expect, and it's not unusual for a straightforward inheritance to turn into a genuine falling out purely because nobody had a way to release cash quickly.

This kind of pressure tends to build quietly at first and then boil over. One beneficiary might have exchanged on a house purchase and be relying on their share of the inheritance for completion funds. Another might simply be frustrated that a property sitting empty for months feels like wasted value. Bridging can defuse this by allowing one beneficiary to be paid out early against the security of the property, without forcing a rushed sale that undervalues the asset for everyone else.

There's also a third type of clock that people sometimes overlook, which is the property itself deteriorating or becoming a liability while it sits empty. Empty properties attract higher insurance premiums, they're a target for squatters and vandalism, and standing water or a burst pipe over winter can do tens of thousands of pounds of damage before anyone notices. Executors sometimes need funds simply to maintain the property, arrange security, or carry out essential repairs so it doesn't lose value before it's sold.

It's not unusual for an inherited property to need a genuinely significant amount of work before it can even go on the market. A house that hasn't been updated in thirty or forty years might need a new kitchen, rewiring, or damp treatment before an estate agent will value it fairly. Bridging loans can sometimes stretch to cover this kind of work as well as the initial cash release, provided the numbers still stack up against the eventual sale value.

What lenders actually want to see

Bridging lenders who deal with probate cases regularly aren't nervous about the concept of lending against an inherited property. What they are careful about is confirming who actually has the legal power to grant them security over it, and that's where a lot of the process time gets spent.

In most cases, a lender will want to see either the grant of probate itself, or at minimum clear evidence that probate has been applied for and is progressing, often alongside a solicitor's undertaking confirming the expected timescale. Some specialist lenders will lend before probate is granted at all, sometimes called pre-probate or grant-only bridging, but the terms tend to be tighter, the rate slightly higher, and the pool of lenders willing to do it is smaller.

Pre-probate lending in particular relies heavily on the solicitor's undertaking rather than the grant itself. This is essentially a formal promise from the solicitor acting for the estate that they'll register the lender's charge as soon as probate comes through and that no other party will be granted priority in the meantime. Not every solicitor is comfortable giving this kind of undertaking, and it's worth checking with the firm handling the estate early on whether they're willing to do so, since this can determine which lenders are even an option.

Expect a lender to ask for the death certificate, the will if one exists, details of all named executors and beneficiaries, and confirmation of how many people have a legal interest in the property. If there are four siblings named as equal beneficiaries, all four generally need to be aware of and consent to a loan being secured against the property, even if only one of them is the one who actually needs the money released quickly.

This consent point catches a lot of people out. It's not enough for one sibling to say the others are fine with it. Lenders will typically want some form of written confirmation, and solicitors acting for the estate will usually insist on this too, partly to protect themselves and partly because disputes between beneficiaries are one of the most common reasons probate cases end up in difficulty later on.

Where a beneficiary is a minor, or lacks mental capacity, the position becomes more complicated still, and a lender will usually want to see how that interest is being managed, often through a trust arrangement or a court appointed deputy. These cases aren't impossible to fund, but they typically take longer and involve more legal input than a straightforward case with adult beneficiaries who are all in agreement.

Title is the other area lenders scrutinise closely. If the property was owned solely by the deceased, the title needs to pass through probate before it can be registered in the name of the executor or beneficiaries, and a lender's legal charge can only sit behind that registration. If the property was jointly owned, for example between the deceased and a surviving spouse, the position is often simpler because the surviving owner may already hold legal title outright, depending on how the joint ownership was structured.

It's worth checking early whether the property was held as joint tenants or tenants in common, since this materially changes how the title passes and how quickly a lender can move. Joint tenancy usually means the surviving owner automatically inherits the whole property outright, which can simplify a bridging application considerably. Tenancy in common means the deceased's share passes according to the will or intestacy rules, which brings the full probate process back into play.

Valuation is also treated slightly differently on probate cases. Lenders will usually want an independent RICS valuation rather than relying purely on the figure used for probate purposes, because probate valuations are sometimes conservative and don't always reflect what the property would genuinely achieve on the open market. A £280,000 probate valuation might come back at £310,000 or more once a surveyor actually walks the property, which affects how much can be borrowed.

Surveyors instructed for bridging purposes will also flag anything that might affect saleability, such as a leasehold with a short remaining term, structural issues, or an unusual construction type. These points don't necessarily stop a loan going ahead, but they can affect the loan to value ratio a lender is willing to offer, or the rate charged to reflect the slightly higher risk.

How much you can actually borrow

Bridging lenders typically work on loan to value ratios of up to 70 or 75 per cent of the property's open market value, sometimes slightly higher for very strong cases with clean title and straightforward probate. On a property worth £400,000, that could mean access to somewhere between £280,000 and £300,000, although the actual figure released to you will depend on the specific lender, the condition of the property, and how clean the paperwork is. Our guide to current bridging loan rates in the UK breaks this down in more detail.

It's worth being realistic about what gets deducted before any money reaches your account. Arrangement fees on bridging loans are commonly around 1.5 to 2 per cent of the loan amount, and there will be valuation fees, legal fees on both sides, and sometimes a broker fee depending on how the deal is structured. On a £200,000 bridging loan, it wouldn't be unusual for total costs before interest to run into several thousand pounds.

As a rough working example, a £200,000 loan at 1.75 per cent arrangement fee would mean £3,500 taken as a fee, plus a valuation fee that might run to £500 or £600 depending on the property and surveyor, plus legal costs on both sides that could add a further £1,500 to £2,500. Before any interest is even considered, it's realistic to expect £6,000 to £7,000 in costs on a loan of that size, which is why it's important to borrow with a clear plan rather than simply the largest amount available.

Interest rates on probate bridging tend to sit in a similar range to standard bridging loans, often somewhere between 0.55 per cent and 1.1 per cent per month depending on the lender, the loan to value ratio, and how straightforward the case is. That translates to an annual cost that can look steep compared to a mortgage, but bridging isn't designed to be held for years. It's designed to solve a short, specific problem and then be repaid, usually once the property sells or once the estate is settled and refinanced through another route.

To give a sense of scale, a £200,000 loan at 0.75 per cent per month held for six months would generate roughly £9,000 in interest, assuming it's rolled up rather than paid monthly. That's a meaningful sum, but set against a £100,000 inheritance tax bill paid late with HMRC interest running, or a family dispute that risks a forced undervalue sale, it's often the cheaper and calmer option overall.

Most lenders in this space will let interest be retained or rolled up rather than paid monthly, which matters a great deal for executors who don't have spare income to service loan payments while they're also dealing with the estate. Retained interest means the total cost is deducted from the loan amount at the outset, while rolled up interest is added to the balance and repaid in full at the end. Either way, you're not usually expected to find monthly cash from somewhere else while the loan is outstanding.

Terms are usually set at somewhere between six and twelve months, occasionally longer if there's a specific reason the sale or refinance is expected to take longer, such as a property needing planning permission or renovation work before it can be marketed effectively. Most probate bridging cases are repaid well within the agreed term though, particularly once the property goes on the market and a buyer is found in a reasonably normal timeframe.

It's also worth asking a lender about early repayment charges before signing anything. Many bridging lenders charge interest only for the actual period the loan is outstanding, with no penalty for repaying early, which suits probate cases well since a sale can sometimes complete faster than expected once the property is properly marketed. Others charge a minimum term of interest regardless of when you repay, so it pays to check this detail rather than assume. Comparing lenders is also worth doing before committing, and our roundup of the best bridging loan lenders in the UK is a good place to start.

Getting the paperwork moving early

The single biggest thing that speeds up a probate bridging case is getting the legal and administrative groundwork moving before you approach a lender, rather than after. Lenders can move quickly on their side, often within two to three weeks from application to funds, but only if the underlying legal position is already clear.

That means instructing a probate solicitor as early as possible, even if you're not certain yet whether you'll need to borrow against the property. Having the application for probate already submitted, with a solicitor able to confirm timescales and progress, puts you in a far stronger position than approaching a lender with nothing more than a death certificate and an intention.

It's also worth gathering the property's details early, including any existing mortgage or charge that might still be registered against it, the council tax band, an estimate of condition and any obvious repair needs, and photographs if you have them. Lenders will want this information regardless, and having it ready from the start avoids a week or two of back and forth that often happens when applications are submitted with gaps.

A useful habit is to keep a simple folder, physical or digital, with copies of the death certificate, the will, any correspondence with HMRC, the probate application reference once submitted, and details of every named beneficiary including current contact information. Lenders and solicitors will ask for versions of the same documents repeatedly through the process, and having them ready to send saves real time at each stage.

If there are multiple beneficiaries, it's worth having an honest conversation with them as early as possible about the plan to borrow against the property. Getting everyone's agreement in writing at the outset, even informally by email, tends to smooth the underwriting process considerably later on. Solicitors dealing with the estate can usually help formalise this consent once the broad shape of the plan is agreed.

It also helps to be upfront with beneficiaries about the actual cost of borrowing, rather than leaving it as a vague concept. Showing them a rough breakdown of fees and interest, and explaining how much will be repaid from the eventual sale proceeds, tends to reduce suspicion and speeds up agreement. Most disputes in this area come from a lack of information rather than genuine disagreement about the plan itself.

Where this tends to go wrong

The most common reason a probate bridging case stalls isn't the lender being difficult, it's disagreement or delay among beneficiaries. If one sibling out of three isn't responding to calls or emails, or is quietly opposed to the idea of borrowing against a property they'd rather just see sold outright, the whole process can grind to a halt regardless of how willing the lender is to proceed.

Another common issue is underestimating how long probate itself will take. Current processing times through the Probate Registry have been running longer than in previous years, and any complexity in the estate, disputed wills, unclear asset ownership, or missing paperwork from the deceased's own records, can add weeks or months onto what should be a straightforward application. It's sensible to plan on the assumption that probate will take longer than the official guidance suggests, rather than shorter.

A less obvious but surprisingly common problem is missing or outdated identification for beneficiaries living abroad. Estates increasingly involve beneficiaries who emigrated years ago and no longer hold current UK identification documents that satisfy anti money laundering checks. Sorting this out through certified copies and international verification can add several weeks to a case that would otherwise move quickly, so it's worth flagging early if any beneficiary is based overseas.

Valuation disputes can also slow things down, particularly where the property needs work and there's disagreement between beneficiaries about what it's genuinely worth. A RICS surveyor's figure is usually treated as the reliable benchmark, but if beneficiaries have wildly different expectations going in, that conversation is best had before a lender is involved rather than during underwriting.

Finally, some executors approach bridging loans without a clear exit plan, simply assuming the property will sell within the loan term without having actually spoken to an estate agent or tested the market. Lenders will always want to understand the exit, whether that's a straightforward sale, a beneficiary buying out the others using their own mortgage, or a refinance onto a standard buy to let mortgage if the plan is to keep and let the property. Having that exit mapped out, even loosely, makes underwriting considerably smoother and gives everyone more confidence the loan will be repaid on schedule.

It's also worth having a fallback exit in mind, not just the preferred one. If the plan is to sell on the open market but the property doesn't attract offers within the expected timeframe, knowing whether an extension is possible, or whether a beneficiary could refinance the loan personally, gives everyone more confidence going in. Lenders tend to respond well to executors who've clearly thought a step or two beyond the obvious plan.

Why speaking to a broker early helps

Probate bridging sits in a slightly specialist corner of the lending market, and not every bridging lender is comfortable with it. Some will only lend once probate is fully granted, others will consider pre-probate cases but only with a solicitor's undertaking in place, and a smaller number specialise almost entirely in estate and inheritance related lending.

A broker who works regularly in this space will know which lenders are actively looking at probate cases at any given time, what each one will and won't accept in terms of beneficiary consent, and roughly how quickly each can move once an application goes in. That knowledge alone can save weeks compared to approaching lenders directly without that context. If you'd rather have someone find the right option for you, you can find a bridging loan broker to guide you through the process.

There's also a real benefit in having someone who can compare offers properly rather than accepting the first one presented. Two lenders quoting on the same case can differ meaningfully on arrangement fees, whether interest is retained or rolled up, and how flexible they'll be if the sale takes slightly longer than planned. A broker who knows the probate lending market can usually narrow this down to two or three genuinely competitive options rather than leaving you to compare quotes without that context.

It also helps to have someone acting as a single point of contact between the solicitor handling the estate and the lender's underwriting team, particularly when there are multiple beneficiaries involved and communication needs to be clear and consistent. Executors are often dealing with enough already without also chasing valuation reports and legal undertakings between two different professional teams.

If you're an executor or beneficiary weighing up whether borrowing against an inherited property makes sense for your situation, it's worth having that conversation before probate is granted rather than after. Even a rough idea of timescales and likely loan amounts can help you plan around a tax deadline or a family situation with far more confidence than guessing. For a wider view of the options available to you, our funding solutions hub covers alternatives worth considering alongside bridging, and you can always arrange a bridging loan today to get things moving.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I borrow against a property I've inherited but not yet sold?
Yes, in most cases. Once probate is granted, or in some cases while it's still in progress with the right undertakings in place, an inherited property can be used as security for a bridging loan.

Do all beneficiaries need to agree before a loan can be secured against the property?
Generally yes. Lenders will usually want written confirmation that every named beneficiary is aware of and consents to the loan, even if only one person needs the funds released.

Can I borrow against the property before probate is granted?
Some specialist lenders offer pre-probate or grant-only bridging, relying on a solicitor's undertaking to register the charge once probate comes through. Terms are usually tighter and rates slightly higher than post-probate lending.

How much can I borrow against an inherited property?
Most lenders work on loan to value ratios of up to 70 to 75 per cent of the property's open market value, with the exact figure depending on the lender, the property's condition, and how straightforward the paperwork is.

How long does it take to get a probate bridging loan in place?
Once the legal groundwork is clear, lenders can often move within two to three weeks. Delays usually come from probate itself, beneficiary consent, or missing documentation rather than the lender's own process.

What happens if the property doesn't sell within the loan term?
Many lenders allow extensions, and some charge no penalty for early or late repayment beyond the interest accrued. It's worth checking a lender's approach to this before taking out the loan.

Is it cheaper to borrow against the property or pay inheritance tax in instalments?
It depends on the case, but a single upfront payment funded by a bridging loan is often cheaper overall than HMRC's ten-year instalment option once ongoing interest is taken into account.

title: Flats destroyed by fire, mortgages still due: what the Spectrum Building case reveals about freeholder risk
excerpt: Leaseholders at a Dagenham block gutted by fire in 2024 are still paying mortgages on destroyed flats after their freeholder went bankrupt, exposing a gap in protection that buyers and landlords need to understand.
metaTitle: Freeholder Collapse Leaves Leaseholders Paying for Burnt Flats
metaDescription: A fire-hit block in east London shows what happens when a freeholder goes bust. Here's what it means for leaseholders, buyers and landlords in the UK.
keywords: mortgage, landlord, buy-to-let, conveyancing
author: Mark Higgins

mainEntity.name: Can a leaseholder stop paying their mortgage if the freeholder goes bust?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, the mortgage obligation is separate from the freeholder's solvency. Even where a property is destroyed and an insurance payout is delayed by an insolvent freeholder, the lender still expects repayments to continue, since the loan is secured against the leasehold interest.

mainEntity.name: How can a buyer check a freeholder's financial stability before purchasing?

acceptedAnswer.text: A solicitor can look into the freeholder's corporate structure and filing history, and it's reasonable to ask the managing agent or freeholder directly how buildings insurance is held and administered. There's no foolproof check, but asking these questions before exchange is far better than finding out after a disaster.

mainEntity.name: What happens to insurance payouts when a freeholder becomes insolvent?

acceptedAnswer.text: Claims can become caught up in administration or bankruptcy proceedings, which can significantly delay any payout to leaseholders and create uncertainty over who is actually responsible for progressing repairs or compensation.

content:
Two years after fire tore through the Spectrum Building in Dagenham, east London, some leaseholders are still paying mortgages on flats that no longer exist. Their freeholder, Arinium, went bankrupt shortly after the 2024 blaze, and residents are now stuck waiting for insurance payouts with no clear timeline and ongoing loan repayments on homes they cannot live in, as reported by The Guardian.

One leaseholder, Sarah Williams, queued overnight in a car park back in 2016 to secure a flat in the newly built block, describing it at the time as the only home she could afford in London. That flat is now gone, but the mortgage on it isn't.

Why a freeholder going bust matters so much

Most leaseholders assume that if something catastrophic happens to their building, the buildings insurance policy and the freeholder's obligations will sort things out fairly quickly. The Spectrum Building case shows that assumption can be wrong. When a freeholder becomes insolvent, insurance claims, repair obligations and payout processes can all get tangled up in administration, leaving leaseholders in limbo for years rather than months.

For an ordinary buyer, this is a risk that sits almost entirely out of view during a normal purchase. Conveyancing tends to focus on the lease terms, ground rent and service charge history, not on how financially stable the freeholder or its parent company actually is. Yet it's the freeholder's solvency that determines how smoothly an insurance claim gets handled if the worst happens.

What this means for buyers and current leaseholders

Anyone buying a flat, particularly in a newer block, should be asking harder questions about who owns the freehold and how that company is structured and funded. A freeholder with a fragile or opaque financial position is a red flag, even if the building itself looks fine and the service charges seem reasonable. This is worth raising directly with a solicitor during conveyancing, and it is a legitimate question to put to the managing agent or freeholder before exchange.

For those who already own a leasehold flat, it is worth checking who insures the building, whether that policy is held directly by a solvent freeholder or through a chain of companies, and what would actually happen to a claim if the freeholder collapsed. Being told an answer is easier than discovering there isn't one after a fire.

The buy-to-let and landlord angle

Landlords with leasehold flats carry the same exposure, but with an added complication: a destroyed or uninhabitable property also means lost rental income on top of a mortgage that keeps running. Lenders generally still expect payments regardless of the building's condition, since the mortgage is secured against the leasehold interest and the debt itself, not contingent on the flat being habitable. That combination of no rent, no home, and no clear payout date is precisely the trap the Spectrum Building leaseholders are living through.

It reinforces the case for landlords to treat freeholder due diligence as seriously as tenant referencing, and to understand the practical difference between a well capitalised freehold structure and one that could unravel under pressure.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a leaseholder stop paying their mortgage if the freeholder goes bust?

No, the mortgage obligation is separate from the freeholder's solvency. Even where a property is destroyed and an insurance payout is delayed by an insolvent freeholder, the lender still expects repayments to continue, since the loan is secured against the leasehold interest.

How can a buyer check a freeholder's financial stability before purchasing?

A solicitor can look into the freeholder's corporate structure and filing history, and it's reasonable to ask the managing agent or freeholder directly how buildings insurance is held and administered. There's no foolproof check, but asking these questions before exchange is far better than finding out after a disaster.

What happens to insurance payouts when a freeholder becomes insolvent?

Claims can become caught up in administration or bankruptcy proceedings, which can significantly delay any payout to leaseholders and create uncertainty over who is actually responsible for progressing repairs or compensation.

For landlords or leaseholders who find themselves needing to move quickly, whether to cover a shortfall, refinance, or bridge a gap while an insurance claim drags on, it's worth looking at what short-term funding options exist through Boxx Finance's funding solutions.

content:
Landlords and property investors who restructure how a property is beneficially owned, often for tax planning or to prepare for inheritance, are sometimes told by brokers or lenders that this could be a problem for their mortgage. A new analysis published by Property118 pushes back on that assumption, arguing that where the legal title to a property and the lender's registered charge remain unchanged, a shift in beneficial ownership should not, in itself, be the source of alarm that some in the mortgage market treat it as.

This matters because beneficial ownership changes are a common tool used by landlords, particularly those running portfolios through trusts or family arrangements, to manage tax exposure or plan for how property will pass down through a family. The concern has always been that lenders might see any change to who benefits from a property as a trigger for a breach of mortgage terms, even when nothing about the legal ownership or the charge securing the loan has actually moved.

What the legal position actually says

According to the Property118 piece, mortgage brokers report that many lenders still become uneasy at the mere mention of trusts or beneficial interests, regardless of whether legal title and the registered charge are untouched. The article's central point is that the legal position is considerably clearer and less complicated than the market's reaction to it suggests. If a lender's charge over the property remains fully intact and enforceable, and legal ownership has not changed, the underlying security for the loan has not been weakened.

The harder question raised is why some lenders still treat what is essentially a routine commercial or family restructuring as though it were a red flag requiring extensive scrutiny or even consent processes more suited to a change of legal owner. That gap between the legal reality and the lender's operational caution is where landlords can end up losing time and money, even when they are doing nothing that undermines the mortgage itself.

What this means for landlords considering restructuring

For a landlord thinking about moving property into a trust, or altering how beneficial interests are held between family members or a limited company structure, the practical takeaway is not that lenders will never object. It is that an objection, if one comes, is not automatically justified by the legal position. Landlords should expect that some lenders will still ask questions, request additional paperwork, or take longer to process a case simply because trusts and beneficial ownership are unfamiliar territory to underwriting teams, not because the loan security has genuinely changed.

This is where working with a broker who understands the distinction between legal title and beneficial interest becomes valuable. Being able to explain clearly, and early, that the registered charge is untouched can help avoid delays or unnecessary friction with a lender, particularly at remortgage or when a lender carries out a periodic review.

Why this matters beyond the legal technicality

Landlords who assume any beneficial ownership change will automatically breach mortgage conditions may hold off on legitimate tax or succession planning out of unnecessary caution. Equally, those who proceed without understanding how lenders might react risk running into administrative delays at an inconvenient moment, such as during a sale, remortgage, or when raising further finance against a portfolio. Understanding that the legal charge is the key protection lenders actually rely on helps landlords have a more informed conversation with brokers and lenders alike.

Where restructuring does coincide with a genuine need for finance, whether to bridge a gap during a property transaction or to fund wider portfolio changes, it is worth exploring the options in advance. Boxx Finance's funding solutions page sets out some of the routes available to landlords and investors navigating these kinds of situations.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does changing beneficial ownership affect my mortgage if the legal charge stays the same?

According to the Property118 analysis, if the legal title and the lender's registered charge remain unchanged, a shift in beneficial ownership should not, on its own, undermine the mortgage or breach its terms, though individual lenders may still have their own policies or require notification.

Why do some lenders still object to trust or beneficial ownership arrangements?

The source suggests this is often down to caution and unfamiliarity within lending institutions rather than a genuine legal problem, meaning some lenders treat routine restructuring with more suspicion than the underlying legal position actually warrants.

Should I tell my lender before restructuring beneficial ownership?

It is generally sensible to check your mortgage terms and speak to your lender or broker before making changes, since even where the legal position is sound, some lenders may have their own consent requirements or want reassurance that the charge remains fully intact.

title: Development Finance Is Expiring And The Units Haven't Sold — What Are Your Options?
excerpt: Your development facility matures soon but the units are still on the market. Development exit bridging loans can buy time to sell properly instead of forcing a discount sale.
metaTitle: Development Finance Is Expiring And The Units Haven't Sold — What Are Your Options?
metaDescription: Facility maturing with unsold units? See how development exit bridging loans work, real costs, lender requirements and when refinancing isn't the right call.
keywords: development exit finance, development finance refinance, bridging loan for unsold units, developer finance, commercial bridging loans, exit strategy bridging loan, development loan maturity
author: Tara Jameson

mainEntity.name: placeholder

acceptedAnswer.text: placeholder

content:
Your development finance facility has a maturity date. You know it well because you've been watching it get closer for months. The build is finished, the units are on the market, and the sales aren't coming through quickly enough. The clock on your original facility doesn't care about market conditions. It just runs out. If you're facing this now, it's worth speaking to a development exit bridging loans specialist before the deadline forces your hand.

This is one of the most common calls a bridging loan broker gets, and it's rarely a surprise to the developer when it happens. You've built well, the scheme looks good, but sales velocity in the current market has slowed and your facility end date was set when conditions looked different. The good news is that development exit bridging loans built for exactly this situation exist as a distinct product from the loan that funded your build, and they're usually cheaper and easier to obtain than people expect, because the hardest part of the risk — construction — is already behind you.

We see this pattern often enough that it follows a fairly predictable shape. A developer secures a facility 18 to 24 months ago based on a sales forecast that made sense at the time. Interest rates rise, buyer affordability tightens, mortgage offers take longer to come through, and the pace of completions slows even though viewing numbers might still be reasonable. None of that is a reflection on the scheme itself. It's simply the market moving underneath a facility that was priced and timed for a different set of conditions. For a broader look at how this type of lending works, our guide to what bridging finance actually involves is a useful starting point.

The frustrating part for most developers is that the units are genuinely good. They've built to spec, the finish is right, the location works, and the feedback from viewings is positive. The problem isn't the product, it's the timing mismatch between a fixed-term loan and a sales process that runs on its own schedule. That mismatch is exactly what development exit finance is designed to solve, and understanding how it works can turn a genuinely stressful few weeks into a manageable, well-priced bridge to full repayment. We've supported developers in Salford, Southport, Morecambe and East Kilbride through exactly this situation.

The clock

Most development facilities give you a fixed term of 18 to 24 months from drawdown, and lenders typically build in little to no grace period once that date passes. If your facility matures in 30 to 90 days and you're reading this, you're in the window where action now genuinely changes the outcome.

Say your facility matured on the 1st of the month and you have 60 days left. A development exit refinance typically takes 3 to 5 weeks from application to completion if the paperwork is in order, sometimes longer if there's a fresh valuation queue at the lender's panel surveyor. That leaves you a working margin, but not a generous one. If you're inside 30 days, you need to be on the phone to a broker today, not next week, because valuation instructions and legal work don't compress well under pressure. If that's you, it's worth taking a moment now to arrange a bridging loan today rather than waiting for the position to worsen.

It's worth being honest with yourself about where you actually sit on that timeline, rather than working from a vague sense that there's still time. Pull out the original facility letter, find the maturity date in black and white, and count the days. Developers often carry a rough mental estimate that turns out to be a few weeks more optimistic than the actual contractual date, and those weeks matter enormously once you're inside the final month.

The other number that matters is your default interest rate. Most development facilities step up to a penalty rate the day after maturity, often adding 1% to 2% per month on top of your existing rate. On a £1.5 million facility that's an extra £15,000 to £30,000 a month simply for running over, money that adds nothing to your scheme and comes straight off your profit.

It's also worth checking whether your facility letter includes any automatic extension provision, sometimes called a tolerance period or standstill clause. Some development facilities allow for a short automatic extension of 30 to 60 days, often at an increased margin, without requiring a formal renegotiation. This isn't universal and shouldn't be assumed, but it's a five-minute check of your documents that could buy you valuable extra time, or at least tell you definitively that no such cushion exists and you need to move now.

Beyond the headline default rate, look carefully at how interest is calculated once you're in default. Some facilities apply the penalty rate to the whole outstanding balance from the date of breach, others apply it only going forward from the maturity date. The difference between those two approaches on a £2 million facility over a three month delay can easily be £15,000 to £20,000, so it's worth asking your existing lender or your solicitor to clarify exactly how the calculation works if you do end up running past the date. For a sense of how current pricing compares, see our overview of bridging loan rates across the UK market.

What happens if you miss it

Missing the maturity date doesn't usually mean immediate repossession, but it starts a clock of its own, and the costs escalate quickly and mechanically.

The first thing that happens is the default interest rate kicks in, usually automatically and without much warning beyond what's already in your facility letter. Second, many development lenders will start charging monitoring or extension fees for the privilege of not calling the loan in immediately. Third, and this is the one developers underestimate, your relationship with that lender changes. You go from being a borrower they want to keep, to a borrower they're managing down. Requests for updated sales information become more frequent, sometimes weekly, and the tone of communication shifts.

Monitoring fees vary by lender but typically run from £500 to £2,000 a month once you're past maturity, on top of the default interest. Some lenders will also instruct their own asset manager or monitoring surveyor to visit the site or the completed units, and that cost, often £750 to £1,500 per visit, usually gets added to the loan balance rather than invoiced separately. It's a small figure individually but it adds up over several months of delay.

If matters drag on for months with no credible plan, some development lenders will appoint a receiver or move toward enforcement, particularly if the facility is with a lender whose fund has its own liquidity pressures. This is genuinely rare when a developer is communicating proactively and has a workable plan, but it's not a theoretical risk either. Lenders rarely say this outright, but the single biggest factor in whether they extend patience is whether you approached them first with a plan, rather than waiting for them to chase you.

There's a practical reason lenders behave this way, beyond simple caution. Development lenders, particularly the specialist funds rather than the high street names, often have their own investors or warehouse funding lines that expect capital to be recycled on a predictable timetable. A facility that overruns without explanation disrupts that cycle, and it's this pressure, more than anything specific to your scheme, that drives the shift in tone. Understanding that helps explain why a calm, evidenced conversation early tends to land so much better than radio silence followed by a panicked call in week eleven of a stalled sale.

It's also worth knowing that most facility letters give the lender fairly wide discretion once you're in default, including the right to demand full repayment on relatively short notice, instruct their own sales agents on the units, or take control of the sales process entirely. In practice this is a last resort rather than a first response, but it's the backstop that makes proactive engagement so important. A lender who trusts that you're managing the situation competently is far less likely to reach for those powers.

Your options

Refinancing onto development exit finance is one route, but it isn't automatically the right one for every scheme, and a responsible broker will walk you through the alternatives honestly before recommending it.

OptionTypical costSpeedBest suited to
Development exit bridging loan0.55%-0.95% per month, 1.5%-2% arrangement fee3-5 weeksCompleted units, credible sale price, need breathing room
Extension with existing lenderOften default rate or negotiated uplift, plus extension fee1-2 weeks if agreedGood relationship, lender has appetite, short delay only
Discount sale of units nowLost margin, potentially 10%-20% off askingFastest cash routeGenuinely unsellable scheme, no time or funds for exit finance
Auction sale of remaining unitsBelow open-market value, auction fees4-8 weeks to completionSmall number of stubborn units, need certainty over price
Bring in equity or joint venture partnerDilution of profit share, negotiation timeVariable, often slowStrong scheme but developer needs balance sheet support

Extending with your existing lender sounds simplest, but many development lenders don't want to extend, either because their fund has its own redemption pressures or because policy doesn't allow it beyond a short grace period. It's worth asking, but don't build your plan around an assumption that they'll say yes.

When you do ask, come prepared rather than simply requesting more time. Lenders respond far better to a specific proposal, for example a three month extension at an agreed uplifted margin, supported by evidence of two units under offer and a revised marketing plan for the remainder, than to an open-ended request. Treat that conversation the same way you'd treat a fresh loan application, because in effect that's what it is. Discounting units to force a quick sale protects you from default interest but usually costs far more in lost margin than the interest saved. On a £3 million gross development value, a 15% discount to force a sale is £450,000 gone. Compare that to three or four months of exit finance interest, which on a typical facility size runs to a fraction of that figure, and the arithmetic usually favours buying time rather than panic selling.

Auction can work well for a specific type of problem, namely one or two stubborn units in an otherwise successful scheme, rather than a whole development that isn't moving. Modern method of sale auctions, run through many of the online platforms now used by UK estate agents, typically achieve completion within 56 days of an accepted offer, which is often faster and more certain than a prolonged open-market chase for a unit that's been sitting for months. The trade-off is price, since auction buyers expect a discount for that certainty, but for the right unit it can be the cleanest way to draw a line under a lingering problem.

Bringing in an equity or joint venture partner is usually the slowest option on this list and the one that requires the most groundwork, but it can be the right answer where the scheme is fundamentally sound and the issue is balance sheet capacity rather than saleability. This route works best when you start the conversation early, ideally before you're within weeks of a maturity date, because negotiating a fair profit share under time pressure rarely produces a deal either side is happy with.

How a bridging loan works for this situation

Development exit finance refinances your existing facility with a new loan secured against the completed units, priced on the basis that construction risk has gone and all that remains is a sales and marketing exercise. This is meaningfully different from the loan that built the scheme, and lenders treat it as a lower-risk proposition, which shows up directly in the rate.

The process typically runs like this. You instruct a broker, who approaches lenders with a track record in development exit specifically, since not every bridging lender does this well. A valuer is instructed to produce an up-to-date market valuation reflecting current achievable sale prices, not the original appraisal figures from when you first raised development finance. Legal work runs in parallel, redeeming the existing facility and registering the new charge. Most straightforward development exit cases complete in 3 to 5 weeks, though anything with title complications, multiple units under one charge, or slow original lender redemption statements can run longer. To see how different lenders approach this, our review of the best bridging loan lenders in the UK may help.

It's worth understanding why lenders price this so much more keenly than the original development facility. Construction risk, the biggest single driver of build finance pricing, covers things like contractor failure, cost overruns, planning issues and build delays. Once practical completion is achieved and building control sign-off is in place, that entire category of risk disappears. What's left is essentially an asset-backed loan against a tangible, inspectable, finished property, which is a much more straightforward underwriting proposition and one that a wider pool of lenders is comfortable pricing keenly.

What the lender needs from you: up-to-date practical completion certificates, an EPC and building control sign-off for each unit, a current sales and marketing report showing enquiry levels and viewings, any reservations or exchanged contracts already in place, and a redemption statement from your existing lender. What frequently stalls these applications isn't the lending decision itself, it's slow production of the redemption figure from the outgoing lender, particularly if that lender is itself trying to extract better terms before releasing the charge. Chase that document on day one.

Beyond the paperwork above, most lenders will also want a short narrative from you, sometimes just a page, explaining why sales have been slower than forecast and what's changed to give confidence in the revised timeline. This isn't a formality. Underwriters read this closely, and a clear, honest explanation, for example a shift in local buyer demand or a competing scheme nearby affecting pricing, lands far better than a vague assurance that things will pick up. If you've already dropped asking prices, changed selling agent, or introduced incentives such as contribution to stamp duty or legal fees, mention it, since it demonstrates you're actively managing the sales process rather than waiting passively. It's also sensible to have your selling agent produce a written update alongside your own figures. A one-page summary from the agent covering current asking prices, recent comparable sales in the immediate area, footfall or enquiry numbers over the last 8 to 12 weeks, and their own view on likely timescale to sell out, adds real credibility to your application and often speeds up the underwriting decision because it answers questions the underwriter would otherwise have to chase separately. This type of lending is unregulated, because the security is a completed commercial or investment development rather than a property you or an immediate family member intend to live in. That means the FCA consumer protection rules that apply to regulated residential bridging don't apply here, and the commercial terms of the facility letter are what govern the relationship, so read them carefully or have your solicitor do so.

A short-term property finance facility of this type is common enough that most active bridging lenders have a specific product line for it, separate from their standard development or regulated bridging books. That specialisation tends to mean sharper pricing and faster underwriting than trying to force a general bridging product to fit.

One point worth flagging is loan-to-value. Development exit lenders typically lend up to 65% to 75% of the current open-market value of the completed units, sometimes higher for very strong schemes with clear sales evidence, but rarely to the very top of that range without some form of pre-sale activity to support it. If your existing facility balance sits close to or above that threshold on the updated valuation, it's worth having that conversation with your broker early, since it may affect how much of the balance can be refinanced and whether you need to bring in additional funds or sell a unit or two before completion of the new facility. If you're unsure where you stand, you can get a bridging loan quote to clarify your position quickly.

What it actually costs

Numbers matter more here than almost anywhere else in this decision, so here's a realistic worked example for a small developer with a facility that's about to mature.

Say your original development facility outstanding balance is £1.8 million, secured against eight completed units with a combined current market value of £2.9 million based on an updated valuation. You have three units under offer, likely to complete within 8 to 10 weeks, and five still being marketed.

ItemFigure
Gross loan requested£1,800,000
Arrangement fee (1.75% of gross)£31,500 (deducted from advance)
Valuation fee£2,800 (paid upfront)
Legal fees (lender's and your own, estimate)£8,500
Monthly interest rate (indicative)0.75% per month (approx 9.4% annualised)
Net loan advanced after fees£1,765,700 (before legal deductions)
Interest over 6-month term (retained, non-compounding example)£81,000
Exit feeNil to 1% depending on lender (confirm at enquiry)

The distinction between gross and net loan matters enormously here and it's the single thing that catches developers out most often. The gross loan is £1.8 million, the figure that redeems your existing facility. But the arrangement fee is typically deducted from the advance, not paid separately, so the actual cash that lands in your account, or in this case goes toward redemption, is lower than the headline figure. If your existing facility redemption figure is genuinely £1.8 million on the day of completion, you need to ask the new lender to gross up the facility so the fee doesn't leave you short at redemption. This is a completely normal request and any broker who's done this before will structure it correctly first time.

On interest, most development exit lenders let you retain interest for the term, meaning it's deducted upfront from the advance rather than paid monthly, which helps cashflow while you're mid-sale with no rental or trading income coming in. A monthly rate of 0.75% sounds modest until you annualise it, and 9.4% a year is meaningfully more than the development facility rate you may have started with, though usually less than the default rate you'd be paying if you did nothing. All figures here are indicative and must be confirmed at enquiry, since pricing moves with lender appetite, loan size and loan-to-value.

Worth running the comparison the other way too, so the arithmetic is completely clear. If that same £1.8 million facility ran three months past maturity at a default rate of, say, 1.5% a month on top of an original rate of 0.9%, you'd be paying roughly 2.4% a month, which works out at around £43,000 a month, or £129,000 over the three months. Against that, six months of exit finance at 0.75% a month costs £81,000 including the buffer, and crucially buys you twice as long to complete the sales, with a lender who isn't escalating monitoring fees or asking for weekly updates. Set out side by side like that, most developers find the decision straightforward. If you want to check whether these figures still apply to your scheme, you can always compare bridging loan rates against your current facility.

It's also worth factoring in the cost of your own time and stress into this decision, even though it doesn't appear on any lender's fee sheet. Chasing a difficult existing lender, fielding weekly requests for sales updates, and negotiating from a position of pressure all take time away from actually selling units and running your business. Refinancing onto a facility with a lender who isn't actively hostile to your situation has a value that's real even if it's harder to put a precise figure on.

For current market context on where short-term borrowing costs sit more broadly, the UK SME lending rates data is a useful reference point when you're trying to judge whether a quote you've been given is reasonable for the current environment.

Your exit strategy

A lender funding your development exit will want to see a credible, evidenced route to repaying the new facility, and this is where preparation makes the difference between a smooth application and a stalled one.

Start by setting out unit by unit exactly where each sale stands. For units under offer, include the buyer's mortgage offer if you have sight of it, the solicitor's name and the expected exchange or completion date.
