For units still being marketed, include current asking price, any recent price adjustments, number of viewings over the last month, and any feedback themes from those viewings. Underwriters respond well to specificity, and a granular unit-by-unit table tends to move an application forward far faster than a general statement that sales are progressing well. It's also worth thinking beyond a single exit route. Most lenders like to see that you have a primary strategy, typically continued open-market sale, alongside a fallback, such as switching a stubborn unit to a build-to-rent or single-let strategy if it hasn't sold within an agreed timeframe. Having that second option articulated, even if you never need to use it, demonstrates the kind of planning that gives a lender confidence in the overall facility term you're asking for. Six months is a common term for development exit finance, but it isn't the only option. Depending on how many units remain and current sales momentum, some developers take a shorter three month facility priced slightly more keenly, on the basis that most units are already under offer and only completion timing is the issue. Others take nine to twelve months where the scheme is larger or the local sales market is genuinely slower, giving proper breathing room without needing to refinance again at the end of a tight six month term. Talk this through with your broker rather than defaulting to whatever term feels standard, since getting it right the first time avoids a second scramble further down the line. Finally, keep your selling agent, solicitor and broker talking to each other rather than relying on you to relay information between all three. The fastest development exit completions tend to be the ones where the professional team is coordinated from day one, with the valuer able to speak directly to the agent about comparable evidence, and the solicitor chasing the outgoing lender's redemption statement in parallel with the new facility documentation rather than waiting for it to be sent to you first. If your facility is approaching maturity and the units haven't sold as quickly as you'd hoped, the single most useful thing you can do today is pick up the phone to a broker who arranges development exit finance regularly, set out where you are honestly, and let them tell you what's realistic given your timescale. The earlier that conversation happens, the more options remain on the table, and the less any of this costs you in the end. For a wider view of the options available, our funding solutions hub covers the full range of short-term finance products, or you can find a bridging loan broker today to talk through your specific situation.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is development exit finance?
Development exit finance is a short-term loan used to refinance an existing development facility once construction is complete, secured against the finished units rather than the build itself. It's typically cheaper than the original development loan because construction risk has been removed.

How quickly can a development exit loan complete?
Most straightforward cases complete in 3 to 5 weeks from application, provided the paperwork, valuation and redemption statement from the existing lender are in order. Cases with title complications or multiple units under one charge can take longer.

What happens if my development facility matures before I've sold the units?
Most lenders move to a default interest rate the day after maturity, often adding 1% to 2% per month, and may start charging monitoring fees. In rare cases where there's no credible repayment plan, lenders can move toward enforcement, so it's important to speak to your lender or a broker before the maturity date arrives.

How much can I borrow against completed but unsold units?
Development exit lenders typically lend up to 65% to 75% of the current open-market value of the completed units, sometimes higher for strong schemes with clear sales evidence, though rarely to the top of that range without pre-sale activity.

Is development exit finance regulated?
No, this type of lending is unregulated because the security is a completed commercial or investment development rather than a home the borrower or an immediate family member intends to live in. The relationship is governed by the commercial terms of the facility letter.

What documents does a lender need for a development exit application?
Lenders typically ask for practical completion certificates, an EPC and building control sign-off for each unit, a current sales and marketing report, details of any reservations or exchanged contracts, and a redemption statement from the existing lender.

Can I extend my current development facility instead of refinancing?
It's worth asking, but many development lenders won't extend beyond a short grace period, particularly if their fund has its own redemption pressures. Any request should be supported by evidence of sales progress and a specific proposal rather than an open-ended ask for more time.

title: Selling to Your Own Tenant: The Direct Sale Route More Landlords Are Considering
excerpt: With thousands of landlords exiting the rental market, selling directly to a sitting tenant is emerging as a way to avoid void periods and agent fees while giving tenants a genuine route to ownership.
metaTitle: Could Your Tenant Become Your Buyer? Direct Sales Explained
metaDescription: Landlords leaving the rental market are exploring direct sales to sitting tenants. Here's what it means for landlords and tenants weighing up the option.
keywords: mortgage, rental market, landlord, buy-to-let, homeowner
author: Mark Higgins

mainEntity.name: Does a tenant automatically get first refusal when a landlord decides to sell?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, there is no automatic legal right of first refusal for most residential tenancies in this context. It comes down to whether the landlord chooses to offer the tenant the opportunity before going to market, which is exactly the awareness gap this approach aims to close.

mainEntity.name: Is a direct sale to a tenant cheaper than selling on the open market?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can be, mainly through avoiding estate agent fees and reducing the risk of void periods while the property sits empty and unmarketed. However, both parties should still budget for independent valuation and legal costs to make sure the transaction is fair and properly documented.

mainEntity.name: What happens if the tenant cannot get a mortgage approved in time?

acceptedAnswer.text: This is one of the main risks of the approach, and it is why timelines and finance readiness need to be discussed openly early on. If a tenant's mortgage falls through, the landlord may need to consider the open market after all, so having a realistic backup plan matters.

content:
A growing number of landlords looking to exit the rental market are considering an option that sidesteps the usual estate agent process altogether: selling the property directly to the tenant already living in it. As reported by Property118, this route, sometimes referred to as tenant2owner, is less about tenants specifically wanting to buy where they rent and more about making sure tenants know this is even an option worth exploring when their landlord decides to sell.

The context matters here. Savills reported that 254,000 previously let homes have left the rental sector, a figure that underlines just how many landlords are currently weighing up their exit strategy. For many of them, the standard route of instructing an agent, arranging viewings around a sitting tenant, and hoping a chain-free buyer turns up is neither quick nor cheap. A direct sale to the existing tenant offers a way to shortcut a lot of that friction, provided both sides are willing and able to make it work.

Why this appeals to landlords selling up

Landlords exiting buy-to-let are often trying to avoid three things: void periods, agent fees, and the complications of a property chain. Selling to a tenant who is already in situ can, at least in theory, address all three. There is no need to market the property or coordinate viewings around someone else's tenancy, no estate agent commission to factor into the sale price, and no chain to collapse at the last minute because a buyer three links down pulled out.

It is also worth landlords remembering that a sitting tenant already knows the property intimately, its quirks, its maintenance history, its running costs. That familiarity can smooth negotiations in a way that a stranger touring the house for twenty minutes simply cannot replicate. For landlords who have built a reasonable relationship with their tenant over the years, this route can feel like the least disruptive way to draw a line under a tenancy and a portfolio position at the same time.

For landlords still weighing up whether to sell outright or restructure their portfolio first, understanding the wider financing options available for buy-to-let property, including how bridging finance can support buy-to-let transactions, is worth doing before committing to any single exit route.

What it means for tenants hoping to buy

For tenants, the appeal is obvious: a realistic, and potentially less stressful, path to homeownership without having to compete on the open market against other buyers for a property they may not even know is coming up for sale. But a direct sale is not automatically simpler for the tenant. They will still need to secure a mortgage or other finance, still need a valuation and legal work done properly, and still need to negotiate a fair price rather than simply accepting whatever the landlord first suggests.

The key point Property118 makes is that tenant2owner is fundamentally about awareness. Many tenants never consider that buying the home they already live in is even possible, simply because landlords rarely raise it before instructing an agent. Once that conversation happens, both sides can work out whether a deal makes sense on price, timing and mortgage readiness.

Where the practical complications sit

None of this removes the need for proper process. A landlord and tenant negotiating directly still need an independent valuation to agree a fair market price, separate legal representation for each side, and clarity on timescales, particularly around when the tenancy formally ends and completion happens. Landlords should also be mindful of their existing mortgage terms and any early repayment charges that might apply if they are selling ahead of a fixed deal ending.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does a tenant automatically get first refusal when a landlord decides to sell?

No, there is no automatic legal right of first refusal for most residential tenancies in this context. It comes down to whether the landlord chooses to offer the tenant the opportunity before going to market, which is exactly the awareness gap this approach aims to close.

Is a direct sale to a tenant cheaper than selling on the open market?

It can be, mainly through avoiding estate agent fees and reducing the risk of void periods while the property sits empty and unmarketed. However, both parties should still budget for independent valuation and legal costs to make sure the transaction is fair and properly documented.

What happens if the tenant cannot get a mortgage approved in time?

This is one of the main risks of the approach, and it is why timelines and finance readiness need to be discussed openly early on. If a tenant's mortgage falls through, the landlord may need to consider the open market after all, so having a realistic backup plan matters.

Landlords considering their next move, whether that is a direct sale, a portfolio restructure, or bridging support while a sale completes, can find an overview of options at Boxx Finance's funding solutions hub.

title: "Cash Buyers Only" — What It Means, And How To Buy Anyway
excerpt: Seeing 'cash buyers only' on a listing feels like a locked door, but it usually just means the seller wants speed and certainty, and a bridging loan can offer exactly that.
metaTitle: "Cash Buyers Only" — What It Means, And How To Buy Anyway
metaDescription: Confused by a 'cash buyers only' listing? Find out what it actually signals to agents and how a bridging loan can get you treated as a cash buyer.
keywords: cash buyers only meaning, buying a cash buyers only property, bridging loan cash buyer, what does cash buyers only mean, non-standard construction mortgage, short lease cash buyers only, bridging loans for auction property
author: Mark Higgins
content:
You've found the property. Then you read the listing again and see it: 'cash buyers only'. Your stomach drops because you assumed that ruled you out. It doesn't, and the reason it doesn't is the whole point of this article, and understanding how a bridging loan for cash buyers only properties works is the key to it.

The clock

Sellers who write 'cash buyers only' almost always want a fast, certain completion, and that usually means a real deadline, not a vague one. A typical version of this looks like: the seller wants to complete within 2 to 3 weeks, sometimes 4, because they're clearing a repossession, closing an estate, or have already committed to buy their own next property.

Count it properly. If the agent says they need completion in 15 working days, a solicitor typically needs 5 to 10 of those for searches, enquiries and exchange, leaving very little room for a mortgage lender's underwriting, valuation and offer process, which commonly runs 4 to 6 weeks on a standard residential mortgage. That gap is precisely why the listing says 'cash buyers only' in the first place. It isn't a snobbish filter against ordinary buyers. It's the seller's way of pre-screening for anyone whose funding can move as fast as a cash transaction, because a slow, conditional mortgage buyer is a real risk to their timetable.

Think about what the seller has actually experienced before writing that phrase into the listing. Very often it follows a previous sale falling through, sometimes weeks into a mortgage application, after a lender's valuer flagged something the seller had no idea would be a problem. Once bitten, agents and sellers become understandably cautious, and 'cash buyers only' becomes shorthand for 'we can't afford another six weeks of waiting to find out the deal is dead'.

It's also worth understanding the mechanics of why standard mortgage timelines run so long, because it explains why the seller's caution is rational rather than arbitrary. A typical high-street mortgage application involves an agreement in principle, a full application with income verification, a property valuation instructed by the lender (not chosen by you), underwriting review, and then a formal mortgage offer, each stage adding days or weeks, and each stage carrying a small chance of the whole thing collapsing. Multiply that risk across a chain of buyers and sellers and it's easy to see why a seller with a hard deadline wants none of it. For a broader look at how this type of funding works, see what bridging finance actually involves.

A bridging loan is built to close that exact gap. Completion in 7 to 14 days is realistic once a valuation is done and legal work moves promptly, sometimes faster on a straightforward case with an experienced solicitor. That is why, functionally, a bridging loan buyer looks and behaves like a cash buyer to the agent and seller, even though the money is borrowed.

It's worth being realistic about the lower end of that range too. A genuinely fast bridging completion, inside 7 days, usually only happens when the valuation can be done quickly (sometimes a desktop or drive-by valuation rather than a full physical inspection), the legal title is clean with no unusual restrictions, and both solicitors are responsive and experienced with bridging transactions. If any one of those slips, a realistic expectation shifts to 10 to 14 days, which is still comfortably faster than almost any mortgage-backed purchase.

What 'cash buyers only' actually means

In practice, 'cash buyers only' almost never means the seller is checking your bank balance. It means they need the deal to complete quickly and without the property having to pass a mainstream mortgage lender's valuation criteria.

There are two broad reasons agents use the phrase, and it matters which one applies to your target property.

The first is about the seller's situation, not the property. Repossession sales, deceased estates going through probate, and sellers who've already exchanged on their own onward purchase all want speed and certainty above everything else. They don't want a chain of three other transactions behind a mortgage offer that might get pulled at the last minute. A cash-equivalent buyer removes that risk entirely. This kind of pressure comes up often for buyers working with brokers in Newark and Weymouth, where auction and probate stock moves quickly.

Repossession sales in particular tend to have hard external deadlines set by the lender who repossessed the property, often driven by internal targets to recover the debt within a set period. Estate sales through probate can carry similar pressure if there are outstanding debts, inheritance tax due, or multiple beneficiaries keen to see the asset converted to cash and distributed. In both cases, the seller (or the party instructing the sale) has very little flexibility on timing, which is why the listing wording tends to be blunt rather than negotiable.

The second reason is about the property itself, and this is the one that needs proper scrutiny. Many mainstream mortgage lenders won't lend against certain property types at all, or only at reduced loan-to-value, because their valuation surveyors are instructed conservatively. Common triggers include non-standard construction (concrete, steel-frame, timber-frame pre-1960s builds), a lease under roughly 70 years remaining, missing kitchen or bathroom facilities, visible structural movement, or a known infestation of Japanese knotweed within a certain distance of the building. None of these necessarily make the property unmortgageable forever, but they make it unmortgageable to most high-street lenders right now, at this valuation, which is exactly why the seller wants a buyer who doesn't need a high-street mortgage.

Other triggers worth knowing about because they come up regularly: flats above commercial premises such as shops or takeaways, properties with flying freeholds, ex-local authority flats in blocks over a certain number of storeys without an EWS1 fire safety certificate, agricultural ties or restrictive covenants limiting occupation, and properties with an unusually small floor area, often below 30 square metres, which many mainstream lenders decline outright regardless of condition. If you're viewing a property and something about it feels slightly unusual, it's worth asking the agent directly why the listing says 'cash buyers only', because the answer often points straight to one of these issues.

This is the reframe worth holding onto: an agent's mental model of 'cash buyer' is really 'a buyer whose funding isn't dependent on a slow, conditional mortgage application that could collapse'. A bridging loan buyer fits that description. The funds aren't conditional on a High Street lender's rigid criteria, the process moves in days rather than weeks, and completion isn't contingent on a chain. Agents who've dealt with bridging loan buyers before will usually accept an offer backed by one exactly as they would a cash offer, sometimes asking for proof of funds or an agreement in principle from the lender before agreeing terms.

It's worth preparing that proof of funds document before you even make an offer, rather than scrambling for it afterwards. A decision in principle or agreement in principle letter from a bridging lender, obtained through a broker within a day or two, carries real weight with agents because it shows you've already done the groundwork. Turning up with that letter in hand puts you on genuinely equal footing with a buyer holding cash in the bank, and agents notice the difference. If you want to move on this quickly, it's worth taking the time to get a bridging loan quote before you view further properties.

What happens if you miss the deadline

If your funding can't complete inside the seller's window, the realistic outcomes are limited and none of them are good. The seller accepts a different, genuinely cash-backed offer instead, sometimes at a lower price because certainty is worth money to them. You lose the property outright.

If you've already paid a reservation fee, at auction or through an estate agent's reservation agreement, that fee is commonly non-refundable if you fail to complete within the agreed period, typically 28 days for auction purchases. On top of the lost fee, some auction contracts allow the seller to claim additional costs or damages if you pull out after exchange, and you could forfeit any deposit paid, often 10% of the purchase price.

Run the numbers on that for a moment, because they're often bigger than buyers expect. On a £200,000 auction purchase, a 10% deposit is £20,000, and a typical buyer's premium or reservation fee might add a further £1,000 to £2,000 on top. If completion fails within the 28-day window because funding wasn't ready, that £20,000 deposit is at real risk of forfeiture, and the seller can, in many cases, still sue for any shortfall if they're forced to resell at a lower price. That's not a hypothetical risk, it's a standard clause in most auction contract packs, and it's precisely why timing has to be sorted before you bid, not after.

There's also a quieter cost that's easy to underestimate: reputational, in the narrow sense of your relationship with that agent. Agents remember buyers whose funding fell through, and it can make them less willing to put your future offers forward on other properties they handle. In a market where a handful of local agents control most of the stock you want, that's a real, practical cost even though it's not a number on an invoice.

This reputational cost compounds if you're an active investor or developer looking at multiple properties from the same agents over time. Word travels between local agents faster than most buyers assume, particularly in smaller towns or specialist niches like auction property and probate sales, including areas such as Ely and Bedford. A buyer known for completing reliably, even when using short-term property finance, tends to get first look at off-market stock and better cooperation on price. A buyer known for funding collapses tends to get quietly deprioritised, regardless of how attractive their offers look on paper.

Your options

Bridging is not the only route into a 'cash buyers only' property, and a responsible broker should show you the alternatives honestly before assuming bridging is the answer.

OptionTypical speed to completionBest suited toMain drawback
Genuine cash from savings/sale proceedsAs fast as legal work allows, often under 2 weeksBuyers with funds already liquidTies up capital, not everyone has it
Bridging loan7 to 14 days typical, sometimes longer if valuation or legal work is complexBuyers with a clear, credible exit and equity elsewhereHigher cost than a mortgage, short-term debt secured on property
Specialist mortgage (non-standard construction/short lease)4 to 8 weeks typicalBuyers not under a hard deadline, properties that will actually qualifyUsually too slow for a genuinely urgent 'cash buyers only' seller
Borrowing against another property you own2 to 6 weeks depending on productBuyers with substantial equity in an existing propertyPuts a second property at risk, still needs underwriting time
Walk away and wait for a mortgageable propertyN/ABuyers not attached to this specific propertyYou lose the opportunity, possibly a genuinely good one

Read that table carefully before deciding anything. If the property has a structural defect so serious that even a specialist mortgage lender with a lenient surveyor would refuse it, that's a property no sensible lender wants as security, at any loan-to-value, bridging included. That scenario exists and it's better to establish it early with a proper valuation than to commit and find out later.

It's worth digging a little deeper into the specialist mortgage row of that table, because it's the option most first-time buyers overlook entirely. A handful of lenders in the UK specialise in non-standard construction, short leases, or ex-local authority flats, and their rates and criteria have improved noticeably over the past few years as this corner of the market has matured. If your timeline genuinely has some flexibility, perhaps because the seller's deadline is softer than the listing suggests, it's worth asking whether a specialist mortgage could work instead of bridging, simply because the ongoing cost is usually lower.

For most 'cash buyers only' situations though, where the issue is speed, chain risk, or a fixable property quirk like a short lease that can be extended, a bridging loan sits in a sensible middle ground: fast enough to satisfy the seller, flexible enough on property type to actually get past a valuer, provided your exit strategy stacks up.

How a bridging loan works for this situation

A bridging loan for a 'cash buyers only' purchase works by lending against the property you're buying (and sometimes an additional property you already own) for a short term, typically 3 to 18 months, with the expectation you'll repay it via sale, refinance, or another clear source of funds.

The realistic timeline looks like this. Day 1 to 2: you instruct a broker and submit an application with proof of ID, proof of income or assets, and details of your exit strategy. Day 2 to 5: the lender instructs a valuation, and this is the single most important step for a 'cash buyers only' property, because it tells you definitively whether the property issue that triggered the listing wording is something the lender is comfortable with. Day 5 to 10: legal work proceeds in parallel, with your solicitor and the lender's solicitor handling searches and the loan agreement. Day 10 to 14: funds are released and completion happens.

It helps to understand what's actually happening behind the scenes during that valuation stage, because it's where most 'cash buyers only' deals either get confirmed as workable or run into trouble. The lender's valuer isn't just confirming a sale price, they're specifically assessing whether the issue that made the property unmortgageable on the high street (the short lease, the construction type, the missing bathroom) affects the property's value as security for a short-term loan. A bridging valuer's tolerance for these issues is generally far higher than a mainstream mortgage valuer's, but it isn't infinite, and a good broker will flag likely problem areas to the lender before the valuation happens, not after.

What the lender needs from you: a credible, provable exit route (sale of the property, sale of another asset, or refinance onto a term mortgage once any issue like a short lease has been resolved), evidence of how you'll cover monthly interest if it isn't rolled up, and a realistic view of the property's value from an independent valuer, not the guide price or asking price.

Documentation moves faster if you prepare it before you apply rather than scrambling once the clock starts. Typically that means: photo ID and proof of address for all borrowers, three to six months of bank statements, evidence of the deposit or equity you're contributing, and a clear one-page summary of your exit strategy with dates. Buyers who arrive with this ready, rather than assembling it piecemeal after the application starts, routinely shave several days off the process, which matters enormously when you're working to a 14-day seller deadline.

This is where applications for 'cash buyers only' properties most commonly stall, and it's worth being blunt about it: the exit strategy has to survive contact with the actual property defect. If your plan is 'buy now with bridging, refinance onto a mortgage in six months once the lease is extended', the lender wants to see that the lease extension is realistically achievable in that window, not just hoped for. Vague exits get declined or get offered at a lower loan-to-value than the buyer expected, and that mismatch causes more failed bridging applications on quirky properties than almost anything else.

A worked scenario helps here. Take a residential buyer who finds a 1930s ex-council flat with 68 years left on the lease, listed 'cash buyers only' because most mortgage lenders want a minimum of 70 to 80 years unexpired. The buyer takes a bridging loan to complete in 12 days, then uses the following months to formally extend the lease under statutory rights, after which she refinances onto a standard mortgage. The bridging loan bridges a genuinely temporary, fixable problem, which is exactly the kind of case that tends to work well.

Worth noting on that example: a statutory lease extension under the Leasehold Reform Act typically requires the leaseholder to have owned the property for two years before applying, though this rule has been subject to reform discussion and can change, so it's always worth checking current requirements with a solicitor. Some buyers in this exact situation instead negotiate an informal lease extension directly with the freeholder immediately after completion, which can be faster but usually costs more in premium than the statutory route. Either way, the bridging loan buys the time needed to pursue whichever route makes sense.

A developer scenario looks different but rests on the same logic. A small developer buys a semi-derelict property at auction, 'cash buyers only' because it has no working kitchen or bathroom and visible roof damage, both of which make it unmortgageable to a standard residential lender. He uses a bridging loan, sometimes structured with an element of developer finance for refurbishment costs, to complete within the 28-day auction deadline, carries out the works, then either sells the finished property or refinances onto a standard buy-to-let mortgage once it's habitable and mortgageable again.

On a scenario like that, it's common for the bridging facility to be structured with an initial advance to cover the purchase, plus a further tranche released in stages against completed works, verified by the lender's surveyor at each stage. This staged approach protects both parties, the lender isn't releasing all the refurbishment funds upfront against unfinished work, and the borrower isn't paying interest on money that's sitting unused. Buyers new to bridging are often surprised by this structure, expecting a single lump sum, so it's worth asking your broker early how a particular lender structures refurbishment drawdowns.

If the property you're buying is one you or an immediate family member will live in, the loan will generally fall under FCA-regulated bridging lending, which brings additional consumer protections. If it's for investment, buy-to-let, or commercial purposes, it's typically unregulated. Always confirm which applies to your specific purchase with your broker or solicitor before signing anything, because the protections and the paperwork differ.

Speaking to a lender who understands non-standard properties early, before you commit to a purchase, changes the outcome more than almost any other single decision in this process. If you're weighing this up, it's worth taking the time to arrange a bridging loan chat with a broker before you make an offer, not after.

What it actually costs

A bridging loan for a 'cash buyers only' property is not cheap, and treating it as a like-for-like substitute for a mortgage without doing the sums is the fastest way to end up disappointed. Here's a realistic worked example.

Say the property is valued at £220,000 by the lender's own surveyor (not the asking price), and you need £160,000 to complete after your own deposit. That's a loan-to-value of roughly 73%, well within typical bridging ranges, which commonly run up to 70-75% on standard residential security, though this varies by lender and should always be confirmed at enquiry as indicative only.

Cost itemIndicative figureNote
Gross loan requested£160,000The amount you ask to borrow
Arrangement fee (approx. 2%)£3,200Often deducted from the advance rather than paid upfront
Valuation fee£400 to £900Depends on property type and value, non-standard construction often costs more
Legal fees (your solicitor + lender's solicitor)£1,200 to £2,000Higher if the property has a title or lease issue to resolve
Monthly interest (indicative 0.85% per month)£1,360/monthAnnualised equivalent is approximately 10.2% per year, confirm actual rate at enquiry
Exit fee (if applicable)1% of loan, £1,600Not all lenders charge this, check terms
Net loan actually receivedApprox. £156,400Gross loan minus arrangement fee deducted at completion

The gross versus net distinction matters more than most first-time bridging borrowers expect. You might apply for and be approved for a gross loan of £160,000, but if the arrangement fee is deducted at completion rather than added to the loan, the actual cash reaching your solicitor could be closer to £156,400. If you've budgeted the full £160,000 to cover the purchase price and costs, that shortfall catches people out at exactly the wrong moment, days before completion.

Over a 6-month term with rolled-up interest rather than monthly payments, total interest could run to roughly £8,160, plus the £3,200 arrangement fee, £1,600 exit fee and legal and valuation costs, meaning the true cost of borrowing £160,000 for six months could sit somewhere around £14,000 to £15,000 all in. That's a meaningful sum, and it only makes sense if the alternative, losing the property or the deposit, costs you more, or if the property genuinely has upside once the underlying issue (short lease, missing kitchen, whatever triggered the 'cash buyers only' label) is resolved.

It's worth comparing that £14,000 to £15,000 all-in cost against what you'd stand to lose without bridging. On the earlier auction example, a forfeited £20,000 deposit plus a non-refundable reservation fee could easily exceed the total cost of the bridging loan itself. Framed that way, bridging often isn't the expensive option, it's the option that avoids the genuinely expensive outcome of losing the deposit entirely.

Rolled-up interest versus serviced interest is another decision worth thinking through properly rather than defaulting to whichever the lender suggests first. Rolling up interest, so it's added to the loan and repaid at the end, keeps your monthly outgoings at zero during the bridging term, which suits buyers who need every spare pound for refurbishment costs or who don't have spare income to service payments. Serviced interest, paid monthly like a normal loan, keeps the eventual redemption figure lower, which suits buyers who have the cashflow to manage it and want to minimise total cost. Ask your broker to run both scenarios with real numbers before choosing.

If you'd like to see how these figures compare across lenders before committing, reviewing current UK bridging loan rates gives a useful benchmark, checking UK SME lending rates gives a wider sense of where borrowing costs sit in the current market, and comparing the best bridging loan lenders in the UK is worth doing before you commit to any one provider.

Your exit strategy

Your exit is the single thing a bridging lender cares about most, more than the property's quirks, more than your income, more than the interest rate you'd prefer. Without a credible exit, the application doesn't get approved, full stop.

For a 'cash buyers only' purchase, lenders will generally accept three types of exit. The first is sale of the security property itself, common with auction buyers who plan to renovate and flip, or with buyers who bridge to secure a chain-free purchase and intend to sell their previous home shortly after. The second is refinance onto a standard mortgage once the underlying issue is resolved, such as a lease extension completing, a structural repair being certified, or a kitchen and bathroom being installed to make the property mortgageable. The third is sale of another asset entirely, such as a second property, an investment portfolio, or an inheritance already confirmed through probate.

Lenders will typically want to see evidence supporting whichever exit you propose, not just a written statement of intent. For a sale exit, that might mean a recent estate agent valuation or, ideally, an actual sale already agreed on your existing property. For a refinance exit, it means either a mortgage agreement in principle from a specialist lender or, at minimum, clear criteria confirmation that the property will qualify once the defect is resolved. For an inheritance exit, it means a grant of probate already issued, not merely an expectation that one will be granted eventually.

Lenders rarely say this outright, but the exits that get quietly declined most often are the ones that depend on something outside the borrower's control happening on a specific timetable, like a leasehold enfranchisement claim that could be contested, or a mortgage offer from a specialist lender that hasn't actually been obtained yet, only assumed to be available. If your refinance exit depends on a specialist mortgage lender accepting the property once the defect is fixed, get an agreement in principle from that lender, or at least a clear indication from a broker that it's realistic, before you commit to the bridging loan. That single step separates exits that survive underwriting scrutiny from ones that look sensible on paper but fall apart under questioning.

It's also sensible to build in a contingency exit, a fallback plan if your primary exit slips beyond the loan term. Bridging lenders will often extend a term for a fee if there's clear evidence the exit is progressing but simply needs more time, but this isn't guaranteed, and relying on an extension as your actual plan rather than a genuine backup is a risky way to structure a purchase. A realistic contingency might be a second, slightly less favourable buyer lined up for a quick sale, or a second specialist lender identified as a fallback refinance option.

Who this is wrong for

Bridging is the wrong tool if you don't have a clear, provable way to repay it within the term, full stop, no matter how good the property deal looks. If your only plan is a vague hope that something will work out, a broker worth using will tell you that directly rather than pushing the application through anyway.

It's also the wrong tool if the interest and fees would eat up so much of your expected profit or equity gain that the deal only makes sense on paper if everything goes perfectly. Build in a buffer for delays, because legal work slipping by two or three weeks is common rather than exceptional, and every extra week on a bridging loan costs real money. If your numbers only work assuming a flawless, on-time exit with no room for error, that's a warning sign worth taking seriously rather than dismissing as pessimism.

Finally, it's the wrong tool if you haven't had the property properly valued or surveyed and you're relying on the seller's description of the issue that triggered 'cash buyers only'. Structural problems in particular can be far more extensive, and far more expensive, than they first appear, and a bridging loan secured against a property that turns out to be worth significantly less than expected is a genuinely difficult position to be in. A proper survey, even a basic one, before you commit to any funding route is money well spent regardless of how the purchase is financed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does 'cash buyers only' mean I can't use a bridging loan?
No. A bridging loan buyer can complete as quickly as a genuine cash buyer, which is what most sellers using this phrase actually require, so you're rarely ruled out by it.

Why do sellers write 'cash buyers only' in the listing?
It usually reflects either a hard deadline on the seller's side, such as a repossession or probate sale, or a property issue like a short lease or non-standard construction that mainstream mortgage lenders won't accept.

How quickly can a bridging loan complete on a 'cash buyers only' property?
Completion in 7 to 14 days is realistic once a valuation is done and legal work moves promptly, sometimes faster on a straightforward case with an experienced solicitor.

What proof do I need to show an agent that my bridging loan funding is as good as cash?
A decision in principle or agreement in principle letter from a bridging lender, usually obtained through a broker within a day or two, gives agents the same confidence as proof of cash funds.

What happens if I miss the seller's completion deadline?
The seller may accept a different cash-backed offer, and you risk losing any reservation fee or deposit already paid, which is commonly non-refundable if completion fails within the agreed period.

What exit strategies do bridging lenders accept for these purchases?
Lenders generally accept sale of the security property, refinance onto a standard mortgage once the property issue is resolved, or sale of another asset such as a second property or confirmed inheritance.

How much does a bridging loan cost compared to losing a deposit?
A typical bridging loan might cost £14,000 to £15,000 all in over six months, which is often less than the deposit and fees you'd forfeit by failing to complete on an auction or reservation contract.

If you're ready to move forward, it's worth taking the time to compare bridging loan rates or explore the full range of business funding solutions available before you commit to an offer.

title: Quick Bridging Loans for Property: Fast UK Solutions
excerpt: Need funds released fast against property? Here's how a quick bridging loan actually works in the UK, what lenders check, realistic timescales, and how to avoid the delays that catch buyers out.
metaTitle: Quick bridging loan for property uk
metaDescription: How to get a quick bridging loan for property in the UK, including timescales, rates, lender criteria and common mistakes that slow deals down or get them declined.
keywords: fast bridging loan UK, short-term property finance, bridging loan rates UK, developer finance, auction property finance, bridging loan for property investors, how bridging loans work
author: Mark Higgins
content:
A quick bridging loan for property UK buyers use is a short-term secured loan, typically arranged in days rather than weeks, that lets you complete a purchase or release funds against property before longer-term finance or a sale comes through. Lenders in this market lend against the value of the security rather than your income, which is why a quick bridging loan for property UK can often complete faster than a standard mortgage. Terms usually run from one month to eighteen months, with exit through sale, refinance, or development completion.

The speed is the entire point of the product. Nobody takes out a bridging loan because it's cheap. They take it out because a mortgage won't complete in time, a chain has broken, an auction deadline is looming, or a property needs work before a normal lender will touch it. Understanding that trade-off properly, rather than just chasing the fastest headline rate, is what separates a smooth completion from a stressful one. If you want a deeper grounding in how this product works, our guide on what bridging finance actually involves covers the basics in more depth.

In the years we've been arranging short-term property finance for clients across the UK, the pattern is always the same. Someone finds a good property, the numbers work, but the timing doesn't. Either their existing sale is dragging on, their mortgage offer has fallen through at the last minute, or they've spotted an auction lot that ticks every box but comes with a hard 28 day completion deadline. Bridging exists precisely for that gap. We've helped clients in Newbury, Newtownabbey, Weston-super-Mare and Windsor secure funding quickly for exactly this kind of situation.

What surprises most first-time bridging borrowers is just how quickly things can move once a lender is genuinely committed to the case. It isn't unusual to see valuation instructed within 24 hours of an enquiry, legal work running in parallel, and funds released inside a fortnight. Compare that to a standard purchase mortgage, which even in a straightforward case can take six to eight weeks from application to completion, and you can see why speed carries a premium.

We've also noticed that demand for this type of finance has grown steadily over the past few years, partly because mortgage lending criteria has tightened and partly because more buyers are competing for the same limited stock of property. When a seller has two offers on the table and one buyer can prove they've got bridging loans lined up while the other is still waiting on a mortgage offer, it's often the bridging-backed buyer who gets the nod. Sellers and estate agents increasingly understand this, which is why speed of finance has become almost as important as the offer price itself in some transactions.

It's also worth saying that bridging isn't just for people in a corner. Plenty of experienced landlords and developers use it as a deliberate strategy, buying quickly with a bridge, adding value, then refinancing or selling once the work is done. Used this way it's simply a tool for moving faster than the rest of the market, rather than a last resort when everything else has gone wrong.

What this means in practice

In practice, a quick bridging loan means you're borrowing against an asset you already own or are buying, secured by a legal charge, with the lender's main concern being how you'll repay it and whether the property covers their exposure if things go wrong.

For a residential buyer, this usually looks like buying a new home before the old one sells. You bridge the gap, complete on the new purchase, then repay the loan once your existing property sells. For a landlord or investor, it might mean buying a property at auction where you've got 28 days to complete and a mainstream mortgage simply can't move that fast.

For developers, quick bridging loans and developer finance often blend together. A developer might bridge to acquire a site with planning potential, then either refinance onto a development facility once planning is granted, or exit via sale once units are built and sold. The lender's underwriting changes depending on which of these scenarios you're in, because the risk profile is different each time.

What ties all of this together is that the lender is pricing the deal on the property and the exit, not on your payslips. That's why someone with an unusual income pattern, a limited company structure, or a slightly patchy credit file can still get funded quickly, provided the numbers on the property stack up and the repayment route is credible.

It's also worth being clear that speed doesn't mean a lender skips due diligence. What it means is that the process is streamlined and everyone involved, from the lender's underwriter to the solicitors on both sides, understands that time is the priority. A good broker will have already flagged the key risk points before the case even lands on an underwriter's desk, which is exactly what shaves days off the process rather than weeks. If you're weighing up whether now is the right time to proceed, you can get a bridging loan quote and get a clear picture of your options.

Another point worth making is that lenders in this space tend to be more flexible with the type of security they'll accept. Houses, flats, semi-commercial units, land, even properties with an unusual construction type or a short lease can all potentially be used as security, provided the numbers work and the lender has experience with that asset class. This flexibility is one of the main reasons short-term property finance fills so many gaps that mainstream lending simply can't reach.

We regularly see cases where a client has been turned down by their high street bank purely because the property doesn't fit a standard lending box, only to find that a specialist bridging lender is entirely comfortable with the same asset. It's rarely about the borrower being unsuitable, it's usually about the property or the timescale sitting outside what a mainstream lender's systems are built to process.

How pricing actually works

Bridging loans are priced monthly rather than as an annual percentage, because the whole point is that they're short-term. You'll typically see rates quoted somewhere between 0.55% and 1.25% per month, depending on the loan-to-value, the type of security, and how clean the exit strategy looks to the lender. For a closer look at how rates compare across the market, see our breakdown of current bridging loan rates UK.

On a straightforward residential bridge at 65% loan-to-value with a solid exit through sale, you might be looking at the lower end of that range, perhaps 0.55% to 0.70% a month. Push the loan-to-value up towards 75%, add in a light refurbishment element, or rely on refinance as the exit rather than a confirmed sale, and the rate can climb towards 0.9% to 1.1% a month or higher.

On top of the monthly rate, you'll usually see an arrangement fee of around 1.5% to 2% of the loan amount, a valuation fee that depends on the property and can range from a few hundred pounds to well over a thousand for something unusual or high value, and legal costs covering both your solicitor and the lender's solicitor. Some lenders also charge an exit fee, though this is becoming less common as competition in the market has pushed lenders to simplify their fee structures.

It's worth running the actual numbers rather than just eyeballing the headline rate. On a £300,000 bridging loan over six months at 0.75% a month, the interest alone comes to £13,500, plus an arrangement fee of perhaps £4,500 to £6,000, plus legal and valuation costs. That's a meaningful sum, and it only makes sense if the alternative, whether that's a lost purchase, a broken chain, or a missed auction deadline, costs you more.

Many lenders allow interest to be retained or rolled up rather than paid monthly, which means you don't need to service the debt during the term. This is particularly useful for buyers who need every penny of their cash for the purchase itself and can't stretch to monthly payments on top. The rolled-up interest simply gets added to the balance and repaid in full at the end.

To put these figures into further context, consider a smaller case, say a £120,000 bridge over four months at 0.65% a month on a straightforward residential property. That works out at £3,120 in interest, an arrangement fee of around £1,800 to £2,400, plus perhaps £500 to £800 for valuation and a similar amount for legal costs on each side. All told, the borrower might be looking at total costs somewhere between £6,000 and £7,000 for a loan that solves a chain-break problem worth far more than that in avoided losses.

At the other end of the scale, a £1.5 million bridge on a semi-commercial property at 70% loan-to-value over nine months, priced at 0.95% a month, would generate interest of around £128,000 across the term, plus an arrangement fee that could easily reach £25,000 to £30,000. These aren't small numbers, and this is exactly why the exit strategy has to be watertight before a loan of that size gets approved. Lenders will scrutinise larger cases far more closely, and rightly so, because the consequences of a failed exit are proportionately larger too.

Broken down further, borrowers sometimes ask whether it's cheaper to pay interest monthly rather than rolling it up. In cash flow terms, rolling up interest is usually more convenient, but it does mean you're paying interest on interest if the loan runs its full term, since the rolled-up amount compounds slightly compared to servicing it monthly. For shorter loans of three to six months the difference is marginal, but on longer bridges of twelve months or more it's worth asking your broker to run both scenarios so you can see the actual pound-for-pound difference before deciding.

Speed in practice: what actually happens week by week

It helps to walk through a realistic timeline, because a lot of the anxiety around short-term property finance comes from not knowing what to expect at each stage.

In the first day or two, a broker will take your details, understand the property, the loan amount required, and crucially the exit strategy, then approach lenders who are a good fit for that specific case. This isn't a case of sending the same application to twenty lenders and hoping one bites. A decent broker will know which lenders are strong on auction purchases, which are comfortable with unusual security types, and which move fastest on straightforward residential bridges.

Within 24 to 48 hours, you'd expect an indicative offer, sometimes called a decision in principle, setting out the likely rate, fees, and loan-to-value the lender is comfortable with. This isn't a guarantee, but it gives you enough to know the deal is viable and to instruct solicitors with confidence.

From there, the valuation gets instructed. Some lenders now accept desktop or automated valuations for lower-risk cases, which can save several days compared to a full physical inspection. For most bridging cases though, a surveyor will still need to visit the property, and this typically happens within three to five working days of instruction.

Legal work runs alongside the valuation rather than after it. Your solicitor and the lender's solicitor will be exchanging enquiries, checking title, and dealing with any specific requirements the lender has attached to the offer. This is often where delays creep in, not because the lender is slow, but because searches, ID checks, or missing documents on the borrower's side hold things up.

Provided everything runs smoothly, funds can be released anywhere from seven to fourteen days from initial enquiry, though we've seen genuinely urgent cases complete in as little as three or four days when every party is pulling in the same direction and the security is straightforward.

It's worth flagging where things typically slow down, because forewarned is genuinely forearmed here. The single biggest cause of delay is missing or incomplete identification documents, particularly for borrowers using a limited company or a trust structure, where the lender's solicitor will need to see the full chain of beneficial ownership. Getting this together before you even make the enquiry can save several days later on.

The second most common hold-up is undisclosed issues at the property that only surface at valuation stage, such as unrecorded planning breaches, missing building regulations sign-off for previous works, or a lease with an unusually short unexpired term. None of these necessarily kill a deal, but they do require the lender's underwriter to reassess, which naturally adds time. Flagging anything unusual about the property upfront, even if you think it's minor, gives your broker the chance to find a lender who's comfortable with it from the outset rather than discovering the problem halfway through.

The role of loan-to-value and how much you can actually borrow

Most bridging lenders will go up to 75% loan-to-value on standard residential property, though some will stretch to 80% in certain circumstances, particularly where there's strong additional security or a very clear exit route. For commercial or semi-commercial property, loan-to-value tends to sit lower, often capped around 65% to 70%, reflecting the harder to predict resale market for that type of asset.

Land without planning permission is at the more cautious end of the scale, with many lenders capping loan-to-value at 50% or less, simply because the value of undeveloped land can swing significantly depending on planning outcomes. Land with planning already in place moves the risk profile considerably, and loan-to-values often improve as a result.

It's also common for bridging loans to be structured against multiple properties rather than a single asset. If you own an unencumbered buy-to-let alongside the property you're purchasing, a lender might take security across both, allowing a higher overall loan amount than either property could support individually. This is often how experienced landlords and investors use bridging to move quickly on new opportunities without needing to sell existing stock first. Choosing between lenders at this stage is easier with our comparison of the best bridging loan lenders UK has to offer.

Second charge bridging is another route worth understanding. If you already have a mortgage on a property but have built up equity, a lender can take a second charge behind your existing mortgage, releasing some of that equity without disturbing your current deal. This works well for people who don't want to remortgage their main lender, perhaps because they're on an attractive fixed rate they don't want to break.

To make the loan-to-value figures more concrete, imagine a property valued at £400,000 with an existing mortgage of £150,000. A lender offering a second charge bridge at 70% total loan-to-value would allow total borrowing of £280,000 across both charges, meaning up to £130,000 could potentially be released as a second charge bridging loan, subject to the usual affordability and exit checks. This kind of structure is popular with homeowners looking to fund a renovation or bridge a short-term cash need without disturbing a competitive first mortgage rate.

Cross-charging across multiple properties works in a similar way. A landlord with three unencumbered buy-to-lets worth £200,000 each could potentially secure a bridging loan against all three at 65% loan-to-value, generating up to £390,000 in total borrowing, even if no single property alone would have supported that amount. This kind of structure is particularly useful for portfolio landlords looking to move quickly on a new acquisition without disturbing existing tenancies or waiting on individual property sales.

Exit strategies and why lenders care so much about them

If there's one thing that determines whether a bridging application sails through or gets bogged down in questions, it's the exit strategy. Lenders aren't just lending against today's value, they're effectively underwriting your plan for repaying them, and a vague answer here will slow everything down.

Sale of the security property is the most straightforward exit and the one lenders find easiest to assess. If you're bridging to buy a new home while your current one is under offer, having a solid buyer, a completed chain, and ideally a memorandum of sale in place makes the whole application move faster.

Refinance onto a term mortgage is another common exit, particularly for properties bought at auction in poor condition that need work before a mainstream lender will consider them. Here, the lender will want to see evidence that you're likely to qualify for that future mortgage, whether that's based on rental income for a buy-to-let remortgage or your personal income for a residential one.

Development exit, where the loan is repaid from the proceeds of selling completed units, requires a realistic sales strategy and often a track record from the borrower. Lenders will look closely at build costs, timescales, and comparable sales in the area to sanity check whether the numbers actually work.

Whatever the exit route, having a fallback plan matters. Experienced brokers will always ask what happens if plan A doesn't materialise on schedule, because lenders ask exactly the same question, and having a credible answer ready speeds up underwriting considerably.

A useful habit is to think about your exit in terms of a primary route and a genuine secondary route, not just a vague hope that things will work out. For example, if your primary exit is selling your current home, a sensible secondary exit might be refinancing onto a buy-to-let mortgage if the sale takes longer than expected and you decide to let the property out instead. Presenting both options to a lender upfront, with rough figures attached to each, demonstrates exactly the kind of forward planning that experienced underwriters want to see.

It's also worth understanding what happens if an exit genuinely stalls close to the end of the term. Most reputable lenders would rather discuss an extension than force a problem, provided you communicate early and the fundamentals of the deal haven't changed. Waiting until the last week of the term to raise a concern is far riskier than flagging a potential delay a month or two in advance, since it gives everyone time to explore options such as a short extension or a switch to an alternative exit route.

Common scenarios where a quick bridging loan makes sense

Auction purchases remain one of the most common uses of bridging loans in the UK. Once the hammer falls, you're contractually committed to completing within a set period, usually 28 days, and losing your deposit if you fail to do so. A mainstream mortgage application, with its underwriting timescales and potential for delays, simply isn't built for that pressure.

Broken chains are another frequent trigger. You've exchanged on your onward purchase, then the buyer of your existing property pulls out at the last minute. Rather than losing your new home, a bridging loan lets you complete anyway while you find a new buyer for your original property.

Uninhabitable or unmortgageable properties come up constantly too. A property without a working kitchen or bathroom, one with structural issues, or one that's simply been left empty too long can all fall outside standard mortgage lending criteria. Short-term property finance lets you buy now, carry out the necessary work, then refinance onto a normal mortgage once the property meets lending standards again.

Business owners sometimes use bridging against property to release working capital quickly, perhaps to cover a tax bill, take advantage of a supplier discount, or bridge a gap in cash flow while awaiting payment from a large contract. Because the loan is secured against property rather than assessed on business trading history, it can move faster than a traditional business loan.

Divorce and inheritance situations also come up more often than people expect. Where a property needs to be bought out from a former partner or a share of an inherited estate needs settling quickly, bridging loans can allow one party to raise the necessary funds without forcing an immediate sale of the property involved. This is often less disruptive for everyone concerned than trying to arrange a sale under time pressure and emotional strain.

Another scenario worth mentioning is downsizing chains where an older property needs light modernisation before it can be marketed at its best price. Rather than selling as is and accepting a lower offer, some clients use a short bridging loan to fund cosmetic works, redecoration, or a new kitchen, then market the property at a higher price point once the improvements are complete. Provided the uplift in sale price comfortably exceeds the cost of the works and the finance, this can be a sensible way to maximise proceeds.

What lenders actually look for behind the scenes

Beyond the headline loan-to-value and exit strategy, lenders are assessing a handful of practical points that don't always make it into the marketing material.

They'll want to understand the condition of the security property, since this affects both its current value and how easily it could be sold if the loan needed to be recovered. A property in reasonable order with no obvious structural concerns will always move through underwriting faster than one flagged for potential issues at valuation stage.

They'll also look at your track record, particularly for larger loans or more complex scenarios like development exits. This doesn't mean you need decades of property experience, but having some relevant background, whether that's previous refurbishment projects, landlord experience, or a professional background in construction or property, all helps build lender confidence.

Source of deposit or equity contribution matters too. Lenders will typically want to see where your portion of the funding is coming from, whether that's savings, proceeds from a previous sale, or a gift from family, and will need supporting evidence rather than just a statement of intent.

Finally, they'll assess whether the numbers leave enough headroom. A deal that only just balances, with no margin for the property to sell for slightly less than hoped or for the project to run slightly over budget, will raise more questions than one with realistic contingency built in.

Location also plays a bigger part in underwriting than many borrowers expect. A property in a strong, liquid market with good transport links and consistent demand will typically be viewed more favourably than one in a remote area with a thin pool of potential buyers, simply because the lender's fallback position, repossessing and selling if things go badly wrong, is far easier to execute in the former than the latter. This doesn't rule out lending on rural or unusual locations, but it can affect the loan-to-value on offer and occasionally the rate too.

Lenders will also sense-check the overall story of the deal rather than just the individual numbers in isolation. If a borrower's stated exit relies on a sale price that looks optimistic compared with recent comparable sales in the area, an experienced underwriter will pick up on that quickly, and it's far better for a broker to address this upfront with realistic figures than to have a lender query it midway through the process.

Why using a broker speeds things up rather than slowing them down

Some borrowers assume going direct to a lender is faster than going through a broker, but in practice the opposite is usually true for bridging loans. The bridging market has dozens of active lenders, each with different appetites, criteria, and processing speeds, and knowing which one fits your specific case saves time that would otherwise be lost to rejected or delayed applications.

A broker who works in this space regularly will also know how to package a case properly from the outset, anticipating the questions an underwriter will ask and providing the answers upfront rather than in a slow back and forth. This alone can shave several days off a typical timeline.

There's also the fee negotiation side. Because brokers work across multiple lenders and see live pricing regularly, they're often able to negotiate terms that an individual approaching a single lender directly wouldn't have access to, simply because they understand where there's flexibility and where there isn't.

Finally, a broker acts as a single point of contact throughout, chasing valuers, liaising with solicitors, and keeping momentum going when things naturally stall, which they inevitably do at some point in almost every transaction. That coordination role matters more in bridging than in most other types of lending, precisely because the timescales are so tight.

There's also a less obvious benefit to using a broker, which is knowing when not to proceed with a particular deal at all. An experienced broker will occasionally tell a client that the numbers don't stack up, that the exit strategy is too optimistic, or that the cost of bridging outweighs the benefit compared with waiting a few weeks for a slower but cheaper option. This kind of honest steer, even when it isn't what the client wants to hear, is often just as valuable as helping a good deal move quickly.

Practical steps before you apply

Before approaching a lender or broker, it's worth having a handful of things ready, since this alone can take days off the process. Proof of identity and address for all parties involved, recent bank statements, and details of the security property including any existing mortgage balance should all be gathered in advance.

Having a clear one paragraph explanation of your exit strategy ready to share is also invaluable. It doesn't need to be lengthy, but it should answer the obvious question of how and when the lender will get their money back, with enough specificity to sound credible rather than aspirational.

If the property needs work, getting a rough schedule of costs together, even an informal one from a builder, helps enormously. Lenders don't expect a fully costed project plan at enquiry stage, but a sensible estimate shows you've thought it through properly.

Finally, instructing a solicitor who has genuine experience with bridging loans, rather than one who occasionally handles it alongside standard conveyancing, can make a real difference to how quickly legal work progresses. Bridging solicitors understand the urgency and the specific requirements lenders attach to these loans, which avoids unnecessary back and forth later in the process.

It's also worth having a candid conversation with your broker about worst-case timescales before you commit to anything, particularly if you're working against a hard deadline such as an auction completion date. Ask what could realistically go wrong, how much buffer time is built into the plan, and what the fallback position looks like if the valuation comes back lower than expected. Going in with your eyes open on these points means far fewer surprises later, and it's the difference between a bridging loan that solves your problem smoothly and one that simply creates a new set of problems further down the line.

Frequently Asked Questions

How quickly can a quick bridging loan for property UK actually complete?
In straightforward cases with a cooperative solicitor and a clean title, funds can be released in as little as three to four days, though seven to fourteen days is a more typical timeframe from initial enquiry to completion.

What can I use a bridging loan for?
Common uses include auction purchases, breaking a broken property chain, buying an uninhabitable or unmortgageable property, releasing working capital for a business, and settling divorce or inheritance situations quickly.

How much does a quick bridging loan for property UK cost?
Rates typically range from 0.55% to 1.25% per month depending on loan-to-value and exit strategy, plus an arrangement fee of around 1.5% to 2%, along with valuation and legal costs.

What loan-to-value can I get on a bridging loan?
Most lenders go up to 75% on standard residential property, with some stretching to 80% in strong cases. Commercial and semi-commercial property tends to be capped around 65% to 70%.

Do I need to make monthly payments on a bridging loan?
Not necessarily. Many lenders allow interest to be rolled up or retained, meaning it's added to the balance and repaid in full at the end rather than serviced monthly.

What happens if my exit strategy falls through?
Most reputable lenders would rather discuss an extension than force a problem, provided you raise concerns early. Having a credible secondary exit route in place from the outset makes this conversation far easier.

Is it better to use a broker than go direct to a lender?
Yes, in most cases. A broker who knows the market can match your case to the right lender, package the application properly, and keep momentum going, which usually results in a faster and smoother completion than going direct.

If you're ready to move forward, you can get a bridging loan quote or explore our full range of funding solutions to find the right fit for your situation.

title: Why some landlords are choosing to sell with tenants still in place
excerpt: Selling a rental property with tenants still living in it can keep income flowing during the sale and may even open the door to a tenant buyer, according to Property118.
metaTitle: Selling With Tenants: A Smarter Exit for Landlords?
metaDescription: Property118 explains why selling a buy-to-let with sitting tenants can protect rental income and widen the buyer pool, including tenant purchasers.
keywords: mortgage, landlord, first-time buyer, buy-to-let
author: Mark Higgins

mainEntity.name: Does selling a property with a tenant in it lower the sale price?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can affect the pool of buyers, since some purchasers want vacant possession, but it doesn't automatically mean a lower price. Investor buyers and sitting tenants themselves may pay a fair price for a property that already comes with an income stream or a home they know well.

mainEntity.name: Can I sell my rental property to my existing tenant?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, and Property118's piece specifically highlights this as an option worth exploring, since a long-standing tenant who wants to stay may be a motivated buyer, avoiding the cost and delay of finding someone new.

mainEntity.name: What happens to the tenancy agreement if the property is sold?

acceptedAnswer.text: A sale doesn't automatically end a tenancy. Existing tenancy terms generally transfer to the new owner, which is part of why a tenanted sale suits landlord buyers who want the income to continue uninterrupted.

content:
Landlords looking to sell a rental property are often told to get the tenant out first, tidy the place up, and market it empty. But a new piece from Property118 argues that approach can actually weaken a landlord's position, not strengthen it. Selling with tenants still in place keeps rent coming in while a buyer is found, and it removes the pressure that comes with an empty property sitting on the market with no income to offset the mortgage or running costs.

The logic is straightforward. An empty rental property is a cost, not an asset, while it waits for a sale. Every week without a tenant is a week of mortgage payments, insurance and maintenance with nothing coming back in. That pressure can push a landlord towards accepting a lower offer just to bring the process to an end. A tenanted property, by contrast, continues to generate income throughout the sales process, which takes away some of the urgency to settle for the first offer that lands.

Who actually buys a tenanted property

There's a common assumption that a sitting tenant automatically shrinks the pool of buyers, since owner-occupiers generally want to move in themselves rather than inherit someone else's tenancy. That's true to an extent, but it misses two groups who are often more motivated than owner-occupiers: other landlords looking for a ready-made income stream, and, as the Property118 piece points out, the existing tenant themselves. A tenant who has lived in a property for years, knows its quirks and would rather buy than move, can be a genuinely strong buyer, and selling to them avoids the disruption, cost and voids that come with marketing to a stranger.

What this means for landlords weighing up an exit

For landlords thinking about selling in the current market, the decision isn't just about price, it's about timing and cash flow during the sale itself. Keeping a tenant in place protects income while you wait for the right offer rather than the fastest one. It also avoids the void period that typically follows an eviction or a tenant leaving voluntarily, which can stretch on for weeks or months depending on how quickly the property can be readied and remarketed.

That said, selling with tenants in situ isn't automatically the right call for every landlord or every property. Some buyers will only consider vacant possession, particularly first-time buyers relying on a mortgage that requires them to move in, so a tenanted sale can narrow that particular slice of demand even as it opens up others. Landlords also need to be realistic about condition and access, since viewings and valuations have to work around someone else's home. For those juggling a sale alongside refinancing, or needing to move capital between properties while a tenanted sale plays out, understanding options like bridging finance for buy-to-let can be useful, since it explains how short-term funding can bridge the gap between one property decision and the next without forcing a rushed sale.

The bigger picture for buy-to-let landlords

This isn't a new phenomenon so much as a shift in how landlords are being encouraged to think about exiting the sector. With many landlords reassessing their portfolios amid rising costs and regulatory change, the ability to sell without losing rental income in the meantime matters more than it used to. A tenanted sale that keeps cash flowing, and that potentially converts a tenant into a buyer, can be a more controlled and less stressful way to leave the sector than a rushed, vacant sale driven by mounting costs.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does selling a property with a tenant in it lower the sale price?

It can affect the pool of buyers, since some purchasers want vacant possession, but it doesn't automatically mean a lower price. Investor buyers and sitting tenants themselves may pay a fair price for a property that already comes with an income stream or a home they know well.

Can I sell my rental property to my existing tenant?

Yes, and Property118's piece specifically highlights this as an option worth exploring, since a long-standing tenant who wants to stay may be a motivated buyer, avoiding the cost and delay of finding someone new.

What happens to the tenancy agreement if the property is sold?

A sale doesn't automatically end a tenancy. Existing tenancy terms generally transfer to the new owner, which is part of why a tenanted sale suits landlord buyers who want the income to continue uninterrupted.

Landlords weighing up a sale, a refinance, or how to manage cash flow during a transition between properties can find more on the options available via Boxx Finance's funding solutions.

title: How Fast Can You Get a Bridging Loan in the UK?
excerpt: Bridging loans can complete in as little as three to seven days in genuine emergencies, though two to four weeks is the realistic timeframe for most straightforward cases. Here's what actually drives the speed.
metaTitle: How quickly can i get a bridging loan uk
metaDescription: Bridging loans typically complete in 2-4 weeks, sometimes faster. Find out what really determines speed, what slows applications down, and how to move faster.
keywords: fast bridging loan UK, bridging loan completion times, emergency bridging loan, bridging loan process explained, short-term property finance speed, developer finance timescales, bridging loan valuation timescale
author: Mark Higgins
content:
A bridging loan in the UK can complete in as little as three to seven working days when everything lines up, but a realistic average for most straightforward cases is two to four weeks from first enquiry to funds in your account. The get a bridging loan quote process for property investors depends far more on how quickly you and your solicitor move than on the lender itself. Speed is largely earned, not given.

That's the honest answer, and it's one worth sitting with before you commit to a completion date you've promised to a vendor, an auction house, or a chain of buyers behind you. Bridging loans are marketed as fast finance, and they can be, but the marketing rarely explains what actually needs to happen behind the scenes to make that speed possible.
