title: Bridging Loans: Your Path to a New Home Before Selling
excerpt: A bridge to mortgage arrangement lets you buy or refinance a property now with a bridging loan, then move onto an agreed mortgage once conditions are met, all without reapplying from scratch.
metaTitle: Bridge to mortgage uk
metaDescription: How bridging loans in the UK convert into a mortgage, typical rates, lender criteria and when this route makes sense for buyers and developers.
keywords: bridge to mortgage, bridging loan to mortgage conversion, short-term property finance UK, developer finance exit, bridging loan exit strategy, fast property finance, specialist property finance UK, bridging loans for property investors
author: Tara Jameson

mainEntity.name: What is a bridge to mortgage product in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: A bridge to mortgage product is a bridging loan arranged with a follow-on mortgage pre-agreed, so once conditions like completed works or an established tenancy are met, the bridging loan is redeemed by the new mortgage without a separate application process starting from scratch.

mainEntity.name: How long does a bridge to mortgage deal take to complete?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most bridge to mortgage arrangements take 2 to 4 weeks from enquiry to funds released for the initial bridging loan, with the mortgage conversion itself typically completing within 9 to 14 working days once the agreed exit conditions have been satisfied and evidenced to the lender.

mainEntity.name: What loan to value can I get on a bridge to mortgage deal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Loan to value on the bridging portion of these deals typically runs between 65% and 75%, depending on property condition, title complexity and the strength of the exit, with lower LTVs applied where significant works or a lease extension are needed before the mortgage can complete.

mainEntity.name: Is the mortgage guaranteed once I take out the bridging loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: The mortgage is not automatically guaranteed, because most bridge to mortgage offers are conditional on specific requirements being met, such as works reaching a certain standard, a minimum tenancy period, or a lease extension being registered, and failing to meet these can delay or block the conversion.

mainEntity.name: Can developers use a bridge to mortgage structure?

acceptedAnswer.text: Developers regularly use bridge to mortgage structures at the end of a build, particularly on units they intend to retain and let rather than sell, moving from development finance into a bridging loan and then into a buy-to-let mortgage once a qualifying tenancy is in place.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I cannot meet the mortgage conditions in time?

acceptedAnswer.text: If the mortgage conditions are not met by the end of the bridging term, you will typically need to extend the bridging loan, arrange a mortgage or bridging loan elsewhere, or sell the property, and any of these routes usually costs more than completing the original conversion on schedule.

mainEntity.name: Are bridge to mortgage rates higher than standard bridging loans?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bridge to mortgage rates are broadly in line with standard bridging loan rates, typically 0.55% to 0.95% per month, though the combined cost of both the bridge and the follow-on mortgage arrangement fees should be compared against a standalone bridge or mortgage before deciding.

content:
A bridge to mortgage UK arrangement is a form of bridging loans for UK property buyers where the short-term loan is pre-agreed to roll into a standard mortgage once certain conditions are met, usually within the same lending group. It removes the risk of being left without an exit at the end of the bridging term, because the mortgage offer sits behind the bridge from day one. Property investors, developers and homeowners use it when a property is not immediately mortgageable but will become so once works, lease extensions or tenancy arrangements are complete.

The idea sounds simple and, in practice, it mostly is. But the detail of how these deals are underwritten, priced and structured matters a great deal, and getting it wrong costs borrowers real money. This guide walks through what a bridge to mortgage product actually does, how the mechanics work, what lenders want to see, and where this route is the wrong answer entirely. For a broader introduction to the product itself, our guide to what bridging finance actually covers is a useful starting point.

Brokers who arrange this type of finance regularly will tell you the same thing. The product itself is not complicated, but the timing assumptions baked into it are where deals succeed or fail. Get the timeline right and a bridge to mortgage structure can save you weeks of stress and a second round of underwriting. Get it wrong and you can end up paying for a bridging loan far longer than planned, at a rate that stings.

This is also a corner of the market where lender appetite shifts more often than borrowers expect. A specialist lender happy to pre-agree a mortgage conversion against a lease extension in one quarter might tighten that appetite the next, particularly if they have had a run of extensions taking longer than solicitors first estimated. That is one reason working with a broker who places these deals regularly, rather than approaching a single lender cold, tends to produce better outcomes.

What this means in practice

In practice, a bridge to mortgage deal means you take out a bridging loan to complete a purchase or refinance now, with a term mortgage already agreed in principle to follow on once the property or your circumstances meet the mortgage lender's criteria.

This matters because standard bridging loans leave the exit as your problem to sort later. With a bridge to mortgage product, the same lender, or a linked mortgage lender within the same group, has effectively pre-underwritten the eventual mortgage. You still need to satisfy final conditions, but you are not starting the mortgage application from a cold start once the bridge matures.

Typical situations where this applies include buying an uninhabitable property that will not qualify for a standard residential mortgage in its current state, purchasing a property with a short lease that needs extending before a mortgage lender will touch it, or acquiring a buy-to-let where the lender wants to see an established tenancy before offering a term product. Developers use a similar structure at the end of a build, moving from development finance into a bridge and then into a long-term mortgage or buy-to-let product once units are complete and let.

The honest view is that bridge to mortgage products suit a narrower set of borrowers than pure bridging loans. They work best when the eventual mortgage criteria are genuinely predictable and largely within your control, such as completing refurbishment works or letting a property. They work less well when the exit depends on external factors like a sale falling through or a planning decision, because no lender will pre-commit a mortgage against an outcome nobody can guarantee. If you would like to get a bridging loan quote, it is worth doing so early so the timeline can be checked against your circumstances.

It is also worth being clear about who these products actually suit day to day. Landlords buying tired stock at auction, developers holding back a final unit to let rather than sell, and homeowners caught in a chain break are the three groups who come up again and again in this market. Each has a different risk profile in the eyes of a lender, and pricing reflects that even within the same broad product category.

For a landlord, the main variable is how quickly works can be completed to a standard that satisfies both building control and the follow-on mortgage lender's surveyor. For a developer, it is usually about balancing sales income against retained rental stock, and making sure the retained unit does not sit empty burning bridging interest while a tenant is found. For a homeowner in a chain break, the variable is almost entirely outside their control, the sale of their existing property, which is why lenders price this scenario slightly more cautiously than a straightforward refurbishment case.

There is also a category of borrower who overlooks bridge to mortgage products simply because they assume, wrongly, that pre-agreeing a mortgage this early in the process is either impossible or prohibitively expensive. Neither is usually true. Where the exit is genuinely predictable, most specialist lenders are keen to write this business because it reduces their own risk of a bridging loan running past term with no clear way out.

How it works

The mechanics start with the bridging loan itself, secured against the property by way of a first legal charge, sometimes second charge if there is an existing mortgage that will be redeemed later. Loan to value on the bridging element typically runs between 65% and 75% of the property's current or as-is value, sometimes higher against strong security with a clear improvement plan.

Alongside the bridge, the lender or a partner mortgage lender assesses your eligibility for the follow-on mortgage using largely the same criteria a standard mortgage application would need, income, affordability, credit history and the anticipated end value of the property. Where this differs from separately arranging a bridge and then a mortgage later is that both pieces are agreed together, often with a single valuation instruction covering both stages and a legal process that anticipates the switch from day one.

Rates on the bridging portion generally sit between 0.55% and 0.95% per month depending on loan size, LTV and the strength of the exit, with the follow-on mortgage priced at whatever rate is standard for that product type at the point of conversion. Arrangement fees on the bridge are typically 1.5% to 2% of the loan, and there will usually be a separate arrangement fee on the mortgage side too, so it pays to have both costed out before committing. For a closer look at how pricing varies across the market, our overview of current bridging loan rates sets out the typical ranges in more detail.

On a £150,000 bridging loan at 0.75% per month over a 9-month term, the interest cost alone runs to roughly £10,125, before arrangement fees, valuation fees and legal costs on both sides are added. Add a 2% arrangement fee and you are looking at another £3,000, plus valuation costs of perhaps £500 to £800 depending on property type, and legal fees that typically run £1,200 to £1,800 for the bridging side alone. None of that is unusual for this market, but it needs to be weighed honestly against the alternative of simply waiting.

The conversion itself is not always automatic. Most bridge to mortgage products require you to satisfy specific conditions, works completed to a certain standard, a tenancy in place for a minimum period, or a lease extension registered, before the mortgage lender releases funds to redeem the bridge. If those conditions are not met by the end of the bridging term, you are back to needing a standard exit, whether that is a mortgage elsewhere, a sale, or a further bridging term. This is worth understanding properly before you sign anything, and a conversation with a broker who arranges bridging loans day to day will flag the specific triggers that apply to your deal.

Most lenders active in this space will issue a formal offer letter on the bridge alongside a separate agreement in principle, sometimes a full mortgage offer, on the follow-on product. It is worth reading both documents carefully, because the conditions attached to the mortgage offer are usually more specific than borrowers expect. A condition might state, for example, that the EPC rating must reach C rather than simply D, or that the tenancy must be evidenced by a minimum of three months of rent received into a UK bank account rather than simply a signed AST.

Valuations are another area where the mechanics matter. Many bridge to mortgage products use a single surveyor instructed at the outset to provide both the current, as-is valuation for the bridging loan and an estimated end value for the mortgage. This saves a second valuation fee and speeds up the process, but it also means the end valuation is essentially an estimate made before works are complete. If the market moves against you, or the works do not add the value anticipated, a revaluation at conversion stage can come in lower than expected, which affects how much the mortgage lender is willing to release.

Legal costs also tend to run higher on a bridge to mortgage deal than on a standalone bridging loan, simply because solicitors are drafting for two transactions rather than one. Most borrowers should budget for legal fees in the region of £1,800 to £2,800 across both stages, depending on complexity, with lease extension cases sitting at the higher end because of the additional conveyancing work involved in registering a new long lease.

Typical scenarios

A landlord in Bournemouth bought a two-bedroom flat at auction for £210,000 needing a full rewire and new kitchen before any mortgage lender would consider it. She took a bridging loan of £147,000, 70% LTV, over a 9-month term, with a mortgage pre-agreed to complete once the works passed building control sign-off and an EPC of D or above was achieved. Works finished in month five, the mortgage lender re-valued the property at £245,000, and the switch to a 5-year fixed buy-to-let mortgage completed 14 working days after the works certificate was submitted.

The numbers on that deal are worth breaking down a little further. Her bridging interest over the five months actually used came to just over £5,500 at 0.75% per month, well below the full 9-month cost she had budgeted for, because she completed the works two months ahead of schedule. Her arrangement fee on the bridge was £2,940, and legal and valuation costs across both stages added a further £2,100. Against a property that increased in value by £35,000 once works were complete, the overall cost of the bridge to mortgage route looked sensible in hindsight, though she admits she budgeted conservatively for a longer works period in case of delays.

A small developer near Oxford was converting a former commercial unit into three residential flats. Development finance covered the build, but the final unit needed a bridge to mortgage structure because two flats sold quickly while the third was retained for rental. The bridging loan on the retained unit was £128,000 against a £190,000 valuation, 67% LTV, over a 6-month term, converting to a buy-to-let mortgage once a tenant had been in place for three months. The switch completed in 11 working days once the tenancy evidence was submitted.

This case is a good example of how lenders think about tenancy evidence in practice. The mortgage lender wanted to see not just a signed AST but three months of rent actually landing in the developer's business account, matched against the tenancy agreement, before releasing funds. Finding a suitable tenant took six weeks longer than the developer had originally hoped, which ate into the contingency built into the bridging term, though the deal still completed comfortably within the 6-month window.

A homeowner in Doncaster needed to complete a chain-break purchase while her existing home was still on the market. She used a bridging loan of £180,000 against a £260,000 property, 69% LTV, over a 12-month term, with a residential mortgage pre-arranged to convert once her existing property sold and her income was reassessed on a standalone basis. Her house sold in month four and the mortgage completed within three weeks of the sale.

Chain-break cases like this one tend to carry a slightly wider margin of safety in the bridging term precisely because the exit depends on a sale, not on works or paperwork the borrower controls directly. In this instance the 12-month term gave plenty of breathing room, and the borrower ended up paying bridging interest for only four months before her house sold and the switch to the residential mortgage went through.

A landlord based near Blackburn used a bridge to mortgage structure to buy a property with a 42-year lease that needed extending before any buy-to-let lender would lend against it. The bridging loan of £95,000 against a £140,000 valuation, 68% LTV, ran over a 9-month term while the lease extension was processed through solicitors, with the mortgage releasing funds to redeem the bridge nine working days after the new 999-year lease was registered.

Lease extension cases like this one are among the more predictable exits in this market, provided the freeholder is cooperative and the statutory process runs without a valuation dispute. In this instance the extension took just over seven months from formal notice to registration, comfortably within the 9-month bridging term, though the landlord notes that had the freeholder contested the premium payable, the process could easily have run past the 9-month mark and required an extension to the bridge.

What lenders look for

Lenders assessing a bridge to mortgage application look first at whether the eventual exit is genuinely achievable within the bridging term, not just plausible. Loan to value on the bridging portion usually caps at 70-75% for straightforward cases, dropping to 60-65% for properties needing substantial works or with title complications such as short leases.

Timescales from enquiry to funds released typically run 2 to 4 weeks for a bridge to mortgage deal, slightly longer than a vanilla bridging loan because the lender is underwriting two products at once. Security accepted is generally residential or mixed-use property with a clear, saleable title, though some specialist lenders will consider commercial units destined for residential conversion.

Evidence of exit is scrutinised closely. For refurbishment cases, lenders want a realistic schedule of works with a contingency built in, ideally with a schedule of costs from a builder or quantity surveyor. For lease extension cases, lenders want confirmation from a solicitor that the extension is achievable and roughly how long it will take, because delays here are common and expensive. For tenancy-dependent exits, lenders typically want to see rental demand evidence for the area and, once let, an AST of at least 6 months.

The most common reason bridge to mortgage applications are declined is a mismatch between the bridging term and the realistic time needed to satisfy the mortgage conditions. Borrowers regularly underestimate how long lease extensions take, or how long it takes to find a suitable tenant in a slower rental market, and lenders who have seen this play out repeatedly will often decline rather than lend against an exit timeline they do not believe.

Beyond the exit itself, lenders also look closely at the borrower's track record. First-time landlords attempting a heavy refurbishment project with a bridge to mortgage structure will generally face more scrutiny than an experienced investor who has completed several similar projects before. This is not because the product is unavailable to newer landlords, but because the lender's confidence in the timeline being achievable is partly built on evidence of past delivery.

Credit history matters too, though slightly less than on a standard residential mortgage, since many bridge to mortgage lenders are more focused on the asset and the exit than on a spotless credit file. That said, a poor credit history can affect the pricing and terms of the follow-on mortgage even where the bridging lender is relatively relaxed, so it is worth checking this early rather than assuming the bridge and mortgage will be judged on identical criteria. Comparing how different providers approach this, as set out in our review of the best bridging loan lenders in the UK, can help narrow down which lenders suit your situation.

Income evidence for the mortgage stage is generally requested upfront, even though the mortgage itself might not complete for six to twelve months. This is partly to give an early indication of affordability and partly because lenders know that income situations can and do change over the course of a bridging term, particularly for self-employed borrowers or those with variable income.

Property SituationTypical Bridging LTVTypical Term
Auction purchase needing works65-70%6-9 months
Short lease requiring extension65-70%6-12 months
New-build unit awaiting tenancy70-75%3-6 months
Chain-break purchase65-75%9-12 months

If you are weighing up whether a bridge to mortgage structure fits your situation, it is worth taking the time to get a bridging loan quote across a few specialist lenders before committing, since pricing and conversion conditions vary more than borrowers expect.

It is also worth asking any lender you are considering how they handle a near-miss, where the exit condition is almost but not quite satisfied by the end of the bridging term. Some lenders will grant a short, formal extension at the original rate if the delay is minor and well evidenced. Others will move you onto a default rate immediately, which can be considerably more expensive. This single point of difference between lenders is often overlooked by borrowers focused mainly on the headline rate.

Common mistakes

The single biggest mistake is assuming the mortgage conversion is guaranteed simply because it has been discussed with the lender. Most bridge to mortgage offers are conditional, and conditions not fully met at the point of conversion can mean the mortgage does not proceed as planned, leaving you needing an extension or a separate exit at short notice.

Another frequent error is underestimating professional and administrative timescales. Lease extensions, in particular, routinely take longer than solicitors initially estimate, especially where a freeholder is unresponsive or a valuation dispute arises under the formal statutory process. Borrowers who build no slack into the bridging term often find themselves paying default interest rates while waiting for paperwork that is entirely outside their control.

Borrowers also sometimes fail to check whether the follow-on mortgage lender's criteria might change between agreement in principle and actual conversion, particularly around affordability stress testing or rental cover ratios on buy-to-let products. Rates and criteria can move during a 6 to 12 month bridging term, and a mortgage that looked comfortably affordable at the outset can tighten by the time conversion is due. Reviewing current market movement through something like the UK SME lending rates index gives a useful sense of the direction rates are heading, even though that resource focuses on business lending rather than residential.

Finally, a mistake that costs more than people expect is not comparing the combined cost of bridge plus mortgage against simply waiting and buying with a standard mortgage later, if that option genuinely exists. Bridging loans are not cheap money, and paying two sets of fees and a bridging rate for six months only makes sense if the alternative, waiting, genuinely costs you more in lost opportunity or a lost purchase.

A less obvious mistake is failing to check whether the follow-on mortgage is genuinely with a separate, regulated mortgage lender or whether it sits within the same group as the bridging lender under slightly different terms than first understood. Some borrowers assume the mortgage side is fully independent and shop around unnecessarily late in the process, only to find the pre-agreed terms were actually the most competitive option available once conversion conditions are factored in.

It is also worth flagging that borrowers sometimes treat the bridging term as the full available time to satisfy conditions, without allowing time at the end for the actual legal conversion process itself. Redeeming a bridge and completing a mortgage is not instant, it typically takes 1 to 3 weeks once conditions are met, and that window needs to sit inside the bridging term, not tacked on afterwards.

Alternatives or comparisons

A bridge to mortgage structure is the wrong choice if your exit depends on something genuinely uncertain, such as a sale completing on a property you do not yet have a buyer for, or a planning application with a real risk of refusal. In those cases, a standard bridging loan with a broader, more flexible exit strategy, or simply waiting until the uncertainty resolves, is the sounder route.

If you already qualify for a mortgage today and the property is mortgageable in its current state, there is no reason to add a bridging loan into the mix at all, go straight to a mortgage broker and skip the additional fees entirely. Bridge to mortgage products exist specifically to solve the gap between where a property or borrower stands today and where a mortgage lender needs them to be, and they add cost that is only justified when that gap genuinely exists.

Some borrowers are better served by a straightforward bridging loan paired with a separate mortgage application arranged independently once the exit condition is met, rather than a pre-packaged bridge to mortgage product. This tends to suit borrowers who want the flexibility to shop the whole mortgage market at conversion, rather than being tied, even loosely, to terms agreed at the outset. The trade-off is a small amount of uncertainty at the exit stage in return for potentially better mortgage terms later, and which side of that trade-off suits you depends largely on how competitive the pre-agreed mortgage terms actually are compared with the wider market.

For developers with several units to deal with at the end of a build, a mix of approaches often works best, selling some units outright, using a bridge to mortgage structure on units being retained for rental, and refinancing others separately once lettings are established. Treating every unit the same rarely produces the best overall outcome, and this is an area where speaking to a broker who can look across the whole project, rather than one unit in isolation, tends to add real value.

Ultimately, the right structure comes down to how predictable your exit genuinely is, how much that predictability is worth to you in fees and rate, and how much flexibility you are willing to trade away in exchange for the certainty of a pre-agreed mortgage sitting behind your bridging loan. Frequently Asked Questions

What is a bridge to mortgage UK product?
It is a short-term bridging loan that is pre-agreed to convert into a standard mortgage once specific conditions, such as completed works, a lease extension or an established tenancy, are met, usually through the same lender or a linked mortgage lender.

How long does a bridge to mortgage deal usually take to arrange?
Most applications take 2 to 4 weeks from enquiry to funds released, slightly longer than a standard bridging loan because the lender is underwriting both the bridge and the follow-on mortgage at the same time.

What loan to value can I expect on the bridging element?
Typical LTVs run between 65% and 75% for straightforward cases, dropping to 60-65% where the property needs substantial works or has title complications such as a short lease.

What happens if I do not meet the mortgage conditions in time?
If conditions are not satisfied by the end of the bridging term, you will need an alternative exit, such as a mortgage elsewhere, a sale, or a further bridging term, which can mean additional cost and delay.

Is a bridge to mortgage product more expensive than a standard bridging loan?
Costs are broadly similar on the bridging side, though legal fees tend to run higher because solicitors are working across two transactions, and there is usually a separate arrangement fee on the mortgage element too.

Who is a bridge to mortgage structure best suited to?
It suits borrowers whose exit is largely within their control, such as completing refurbishment works, extending a lease or letting a property, rather than those relying on external factors like a sale falling through.

Can I still shop around for a mortgage once the bridge is in place?
It depends on the product. Some borrowers prefer a standalone bridging loan followed by an independently arranged mortgage for more flexibility, while a pre-packaged bridge to mortgage deal offers more certainty but less room to shop the wider market at conversion.
